Lawyer accused of fraud says bad cheque didn't hurt the bank
Nicholas Cartel is self-representing on charge he wrote bad cheque to cover his firm's financial collapse
The fraud trial for a suspended Ontario lawyer ping-ponged back and forth Tuesday on whether TD Bank had suffered any harm or risk of loss as a result of a bad cheque the lawyer wrote.
Nicholas Cartel, a class-action and litigation specialist, is on trial on a single count of fraud over $5,000 relating to a $300,000 personal cheque he wrote in 2023, which prosecutors allege was done to help cover up the financial collapse of his and his wife’s law firm. That cheque bounced five days after being deposited into a TD bank account belonging to the law firm.
In the second day of testimony in provincial court in Toronto, a witness representing TD was grilled by both the defence and prosecution about what harm, if any, the bank incurred as a result. Proving fraud under the Criminal Code requires proving that someone either suffered a loss or was exposed to a risk of economic deprivation.
“There was no negative balance at the end of the day?” Cartel asked TD employee Tonya Cole in cross-examination.
“That’s correct, yes,” Cole replied.
Prosecutors Megan Rauser, left, and Dihim Emami converse outside court at the end of the first day of Cartel's criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)
Cartel has not denied he wrote the bad cheque for $300,000 on a personal account at RBC — which he maintains was a joint account with his wife, Singa Bui. But he says his wife, not he, deposited the cheque to the TD trust account of their firm, Cartel & Bui LLP. And then she was the one, he says, who immediately after obtained a $2.2-million certified cheque from TD to send to a client of the firm.
Prosecutors allege the certified cheque couldn’t have been issued without the top-up from the $300,000 deposit, because the law firm’s trust account was already in shortfall. Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.
When Cartel’s personal cheque from RBC bounced five days later, TD had to go into his firm’s trust account and take out the $300,000.
Prosecutor Dihim Emami focused on that in his re-examination of Cole.
“It's fortuitous that this account had funds subsequent for TD to recover their $300,000, correct?” he asked. “If this account was depleted … or for a whole host of reasons other influxes of money didn't come in, TD might never have recovered that amount, correct?”
“That's possible, yes,” Cole said.
Home buyers and sellers left in lurch
The collapse of Cartel & Bui LLP in December 2023 left more than 25 home buyers and sellers in southern Ontario in the lurch for amounts ranging from $66,000 up to $2.16 million, in the case of one couple — money they had either transferred to the firm's trust account to buy a home or were expecting in payouts after selling their home.
Bui has admitted in lawsuits against her and Cartel that she started pilfering money from the firm’s trust account as far back as 2014 to fund the couple’s "luxury lifestyle," in a Ponzi-like scheme where incoming funds from new clients would cover for amounts she had stolen. She and Cartel bought two Toronto homes for $6 million total, sent their children to private school, took "luxurious vacations" and, she said, “decorated our home and office with elegant furnishings and expensive art.”
Cartel has long maintained he didn’t know about the embezzlement until December 2023, but a Superior Court judge overseeing more than 15 lawsuits against the couple and their former law firm has questioned those claims, saying at one point in June 2024: “Did she pay for nice gifts for you? Did you buy a car that she paid for? Did she pay mortgage payments? How can you not know, when you're living with her and you've got a home together and you've got children together, where $6 million went?"
The judge later sent both Cartel and Bui to jail, for 30 days and 20 days respectively, for contempt, ruling that they "have taken active steps to hide their finances and to frustrate the court."
Now-disbarred real estate lawyer Singa Bui leaves a Toronto courthouse in October 2024 after being sentenced to 30 days in provincial prison for civil contempt of court. The sentence was later reduced to 20 days. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)
A Law Society of Ontario ruling in April 2024 suspending Cartel from practising law commented that “while it is conceivable that Ms. Bui acted alone and that Mr. Cartel had no knowledge or involvement, there are good reasons to believe otherwise,” including that various of Cartel’s explanations were “difficult to accept.”
Bui has since been disbarred while the Law Society’s disciplinary case against Cartel has yet to come to a final hearing.
Bogus signatures
In his criminal trial, Cartel is representing himself after a falling-out with his former defence lawyer Richard Posner.
Court records from a separate case, where Cartel challenged Posner’s invoices, show Posner criticizing Cartel for being “arrogant and patronizing” toward staff at Posner’s firm. Posner also told Cartel he was “completely uncomfortable” with Cartel’s wish to interact mainly over email “given the tenor of your writing.” Cartel had made claims in emails to Posner's firm that, among other things, the prosecution in his case had drafted a fraudulent document to pressure Cartel into agreeing to certain facts ahead of trial.
Cartel, in turn, accused Posner of “deliberate willful blindness” to documents that would supposedly help exonerate him. He also said Posner’s assistant “forced condescending, unsolicited opinions of culpability onto” him.
In another email, Posner states that if Cartel is going to testify in his own defence, it will take “a few days” to coach him because “without extensive preparation, Mr. Cartel will not present well as a witness.”
- CBC Investigates Lawyer couple accused of stealing millions from homebuyers while law society stalled
- CBC Investigates Lawyers at centre of $7M real estate embezzlement case charged with fraud
The dispute between them also reveals that Cartel put together documents that contained bogus signatures of another lawyer, George Tsimiklis. The signatures appear on the witness line of two affidavits Cartel swore in his dispute with Posner.
“Although the document bears my signature … I did not sign it either in person or electronically, and I did not authorize Mr. Cartel or any other person to affix or reproduce my signature on it,” Tsimiklis says in his own sworn statement filed in the case.
Cartel says the documents were only in draft form and he never intended them to be submitted to court.
Tsimiklis was a colleague of Cartel and has previously witnessed affidavits for him and represented Cartel’s wife, Bui.
Cartel told CBC during a break in his trial on Monday that he emailed the documents to a court clerk but only as drafts and he wasn’t formally filing them. He blamed the clerk for misunderstanding instructions and placing the affidavits with the bogus signatures into the court file.
Asked how the signatures got onto his affidavits in the first place, Cartel claimed it happened because different pages from different documents got compiled together by the court clerk, including some pages that had Tsimiklis’s genuine signature from past filings.
That explanation, however, doesn’t square with the fact that Tsimiklis’s bogus signatures don’t appear on their own page but rather at the bottom of the newly created affidavits.
Cartel is currently suing CBC, Toronto Life magazine and the Toronto Sun newspaper for their coverage of his and his wife’s ordeals.
His trial is scheduled to resume in November.

Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?
Trump approves execution by firing squad for 2009 Fort Hood shooter
President Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
It would be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades — and the first by firing squad since World War II.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the news on X Monday night, writing, "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in an order released Tuesday that Hasan's execution will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.
But Hasan could delay those proceedings if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts, said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center.
"The fact that the president has approved Mr. Hasan's death sentence is another step closer to his execution," Maher said. "But that does not mean that his execution will be imminent."
For example, Ronald Gray, who committed multiple rapes and murders near Fort Bragg in the 1980s, is still on military death row despite having had his sentence approved by President George W. Bush in 2008.
It's not clear why the Pentagon is moving forward now, or why it specifically chose a firing squad as the execution method. But some death penalty experts that NPR interviewed suspect it could be connected to Tennessee's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, which has dominated headlines and reignited debate over the past week.
"For years now, states have been pushing this rock of Sisyphus uphill … They're spending millions of dollars, and yet they're having botched executions," said Corinna Lain, whose book, Secrets of the Killing State, was published last year. "So this moment in time is one where states are really thinking about: what are we doing and what best serves the death penalty? Whether the answer to that is firing squad is another question entirely."
The White House referred NPR's questions to the Pentagon, which declined to elaborate beyond Parnell's post.
In his announcement, Parnell said Trump had acted on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said last September that he was "100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."
"This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth told several media outlets, including The Hill, at the time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
Hasan was working as an Army psychiatrist in Nov. 2009, when he opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — "God is great" — before killing 13 people and injuring another 32. The attack ended when he was shot by civilian security officers at the scene, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan acted as his own lawyer during his 2013 trial, at which he admitted that "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." The American-born Muslim said he had "switched sides" and turned against the U.S. because of its military actions in the Middle East.
The military jury found Hasan guilty on all counts. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death, which triggered an automatic appeals process that ended only when the Supreme Court denied his final petition in the spring of 2025.
Hasan is one of just four people currently on military death row — all of whom were convicted of murder — according to the Death Penalty Information Center. They are all incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
The military's last firing squad execution was in 1945
The first recorded execution by shooting on what would become U.S. soil happened in Jamestown, Va., in 1608, when one of the colony's early council members, Capt. George Kendall, was put to death for mutiny. Firing squads have been used relatively sparingly since, including during the Civil War.
"On the one hand, it is one of our earliest forms of execution," said Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno, who has been studying execution methods for 36 years. "On the other hand, it's always been controversial because people associate it with extreme barbarity and … the Wild West."
The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945: Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, the only U.S. soldier to be executed for that reason since the Civil War.
"They didn't even tell his wife that he had been executed; they just said that he had died in Europe," journalist Charles Glass, who wrote a book about World War II deserters, told NPR in 2013. He said Slovik's case only became public knowledge about a decade later, when an investigative reporter published a book about it in the mid-'50s.
Most of the known U.S. military executions during World War II were done by hanging, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last time the U.S. military carried out an execution of any sort was in 1961, when Private John Bennett was hanged for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.
"We basically have gone out of the business — until now — of executing people through the military justice system," said Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.
The military officially suspended the death penalty after a 1983 court ruling, but reinstated it the following year and specifically designated lethal injection as the standard method. Fidell says that changed with new Army regulations in 2023.
"The regulation was changed to make the choice or the method of execution a matter for the president's discretion," he said. "And obviously, the president has, in this case, approved the use of a firing squad."
Under the current rules, once the president approves an execution, the secretary of the Army decides the time, location and method, to take place within 60 to 150 days.
Fidell said he was not surprised by Trump's approval, given his administration's embrace of the death penalty overall and the severity of Hasan's offenses. But he suggested some might find the social media announcement inappropriate.
"The military has lived without executions since 1961, and yet we have here a really serious case," Fidell said. "I think it would have been a lot better had a more formal, dignified means been chosen to disseminate this information."
The Pentagon hasn't held a formal press briefing since May.
The death penalty is already under scrutiny
Denno, who studies the death penalty, doesn't think the timing of the Pentagon's announcement is a coincidence.
Denno says Pike's case "is probably the worst that's ever happened." But it's far from the only botched legal injection in recent years, she says, pointing to what she calls a pattern of convicts being "tortured unnecessarily" that has prompted some jurisdictions to seek out alternatives.
The Justice Department made firing squads available for federal executions earlier this year, following a directive from Trump. Seven states now have firing squads on the books as an execution method, which Denno says is the highest number ever recorded.
Denno says firing squads are "the least inhumane method of execution that we have," since, when done properly, death can occur in seconds.
But she acknowledges that those have been plagued by issues, too, including last year in South Carolina, when an autopsy revealed that the shooters may have prolonged a prisoner's death by missing his heart.
"There is a humane way to take a life. It's called life without parole," said Lain, the author.
Lain says lethal injections, because of their relative lack of gore, have kept the death penalty "out of sight, out of mind" for many people over the last five decades.
But she sees signs of change. Data analysis by the Death Penalty Information Center shows that death sentences have declined by 90% over the past three decades. Fewer than 50 new ones have been imposed each year since 2015. A 2025 Gallup poll put public support for the death penalty at a five-decade low, with opposition highest among younger generations.
"The death penalty in this country is dying its own slow death," she said. She thinks the federal government's embrace of the firing squad, including in Hasan's case, could hasten it even more.

Quick Answer
macOS 27 Golden Gate has far more useful features than the ones you will notice immediately after updating. I tested more than 27 of them and picked the 27 worth trying, including Siri AI, custom Safari extensions, smarter Shortcuts, new Photos tools, and several smaller additions. Go through this list, and you will likely find a few features that can make the way you use your Mac easier.
Apple has finally released macOS 27 Golden Gate, and unlike the last few macOS updates, this one feels like a much bigger update. Apple has changed how macOS looks, added the new Siri AI, brought several Apple Intelligence features to its built-in apps, and made noticeable changes to Safari, Photos, Notes, Calendar, and many other places that you will notice once you start using your Mac.
I have been using macOS 27 and trying these features on my Mac, and some of them are genuinely useful. Some of my favorites is the new Siri that does many more things than previous, also Safari that lets you create your own extension simply by describing what you want it to do.
There are plenty of smaller additions like this throughout macOS 27. Some solve problems I have had with macOS for a long time, while others add things that previously required a third-party app or a much longer workaround. In this article, I will show you the best macOS 27 Golden Gate features I have found so far, what has changed, and how you can try them on your Mac.
Table of Contents
27 Best macOS 27 Golden Gate Features
macOS 27 Golden Gate comes with countless new features and small changes, and covering every single one of them in one article isn’t possible. After digging deeper into the update and trying many of these features myself, I have picked the best 27 that I found the most useful and that I think most Mac users should know about. Some are easy to notice, while others are hidden inside the apps and settings you already use every day.
Talk With Siri AI and Continue Your Previous Conversations
Siri has received one of its biggest changes on the Mac with macOS 27. Instead of only appearing as the small Siri interface we have been using for years, Siri AI now has its own app where you can start a conversation, ask follow-up questions, and return to your previous conversations later.
This is particularly useful when I have already given Siri all the context about something, and whenever needed, I can reopen that conversation instead of explaining everything again.
To use the Siri AI app on your Mac, first make sure Siri is enabled.
Once it is enabled, open the Siri app, where you will find all your previous conversations in the left sidebar and the chat window on the right. You can select any previous conversation to continue chatting or start a new conversation with Siri. If you right-click on any conversation in the sidebar, you will also see additional options to pin or delete the conversation.
Search Your Mac and Ask Siri Directly From Spotlight
Spotlight is one of the features I use almost every day on my Mac. With macOS 27, it also becomes a quick way to access Siri AI, so I don’t have to open the dedicated Siri app whenever I have a small question.
You just have to press Command + Space to open Spotlight and continue typing normally when you want to find an app, file, document, or setting. When you want to ask Siri AI something instead, just type your query normally and hit return to get an answer. You can also access whatever you have searched in Spotlight in the dedicated Siri app as a separate conversation.
I prefer using this for quick questions and keeping the Siri app for longer conversations where I know I will need follow-up questions.
Create Your Own Safari Extension Just by Describing It
Safari already supports extensions, but I still have to find an extension that does exactly what I need. With macOS 27, I can simply describe the functionality I want, and Safari can create an extension for me using Apple Intelligence.
I tried this with Instagram. I sometimes watch Reels on Instagram’s website, but it doesn’t give me a playback bar to quickly move forward or backward in a Reel. Instead of searching for an extension, I asked Safari to create one using this prompt:
Prompt: Create an extension for Instagram that adds playback controls to Reels and lets me move forward or backwards in the video while watching a Reel.
Surprisingly, it worked. After enabling the generated extension, I could seek forward and backwards while watching Instagram Reels. If there is a small website-specific feature you have always wanted, this gives you a way to try building it yourself.
To create one:
- Open Safari on your Mac and visit the website for which you want to create an extension.
- Click on the Page menu inside Safari’s address bar and select Describe Extension.
- Describe exactly what you want the extension to do. “I recommend keeping the request focused on one particular problem instead of asking it to change several unrelated things on the website.”
- Safari will first check whether an existing extension from the App Store can do what you described. If you don’t want one of the suggested extensions, click Create to generate your own.
- Once Safari creates the extension, click Try and test it on the website. Don’t save it immediately; use the website normally for a few minutes and make sure the extension actually behaves the way you expected.
- If something isn’t working correctly, click Edit and describe what you want Safari to change. Once you are happy with the result, click Save to keep the extension.
If you are new to browser extensions, you can check our list of the best Safari extensions for Mac to see what else extensions can add to Safari.
Create Shortcuts by Simply Explaining What You Want
Shortcuts can automate plenty of repetitive tasks on a Mac, but creating a complicated shortcut manually isn’t always easy. macOS 27 lets you describe what you want in normal language, and Apple Intelligence can put together the required Shortcut actions for you.
For example, I created a simple shortcut for work. Whenever I start working, I need to open TechPP, Gmail, Google Docs, and WordPress. Instead of opening each website manually, I created a shortcut that opens all four websites in Chrome whenever I run it.
Prompt: Create a shortcut that opens techpp.com, Gmail, Google Docs, and WordPress in Chrome.
Here’s how you can create it:
- Open the Shortcuts app on your Mac and click the plus (+) button.
- Enter the prompt in the Describe a shortcut field and let Apple Intelligence create the shortcut for you.
- Once it is created, click Run or the Play icon to test it.
Use Visual Intelligence to Understand What’s on Your Screen
Visual Intelligence on the Mac works differently from the camera-based experience on the iPhone. In macOS 27, I can select something already visible on my screen and ask Siri AI about it, which is useful when the thing I am looking at is easier to show than describe.
Suppose I see a chair in an image and want to know what kind of chair it is or find similar designs. Instead of describing its shape, material, and appearance, I can press Command + Shift + 6, select the chair on the screen, and choose Ask Siri to ask about it. There is also an Image Search option when I want to find visually similar results online.
Adjust How Much Liquid Glass You Want on Your Mac
Apple introduced Liquid Glass across its operating systems last year, but macOS 27 now gives you more control over how transparent the interface actually looks. Instead of having to accept one fixed appearance, there is now a slider that lets you choose how clear or tinted you want Liquid Glass to be.
To adjust it:
- Open the System Settings on your Mac and click Appearance in the sidebar.
- Find the Liquid Glass adjustment inside the Appearance settings.
- Move the slider toward the left if you want the interface to look clearer and more transparent. Move it toward the right if you want more tint and less of the background showing through.
Hide Extra Menu Bar Icons and Access Them When You Need Them
My Mac’s menu bar gets crowded quickly because several utilities I use throughout the day add their own icons. macOS 27 handles this better with a new overflow control that hides icons when there isn’t enough space and gives you a double-arrow button to reveal them whenever you need them. This means I don’t have to remove a useful menu bar utility just because I don’t need its icon visible every minute. This is especially useful on MacBooks with a notch, where menu bar space is already limited.
Let Safari Automatically Organise Your Tabs Into Topics
I am terrible at keeping my browser tabs under control, particularly when I am researching something and have several unrelated pages open at the same time. Safari already has Tab Groups on Mac, which are useful when you manually organize related tabs. macOS 27 takes this a step further by using Apple Intelligence to automatically identify related tabs and organize them into topics. Each topic gets a label and a tab count, and you can collapse a topic when you aren’t working on it without actually closing those tabs.
For example, while researching for this article, I might have 10–15 tabs open about different macOS features, along with a few Amazon shopping tabs and some work-related pages. Instead of showing all of them together in one long row, Safari can automatically identify which tabs are related and organise them into separate topics such as macOS 27, Shopping, and Work. I can keep the macOS 27 topic expanded while I am researching and collapse Shopping and Work to hide those tabs temporarily. Whenever I need them again, I can simply expand that topic without having to search through all my open tabs.
To enable it:
- Open Safari on your Mac and click Safari in the menu bar at the top left of the screen.
- Choose Settings, and then switch to Tabs section.
- Then click the drop-down menu right to Organise tabs and select Automatically Create Topics.
- Continue browsing normally and open a few pages related to the same subject. Safari will identify related tabs and place them under a topic when it recognises the connection.
Change the Perspective of a Photo With Reframe
Cropping can remove unnecessary space from a photo, but it can’t change the angle from which the photo appears to have been taken. The new Reframe feature goes further by using Apple Intelligence to change the perspective and angle of an existing image.
I find this useful when I like a photo but wish I had taken it from a slightly different angle or positioned the subject differently. To use it:
- Open the Photos app on your Mac and double-click the photo.
- Click the Edit button in the top-right corner to open the photo editing tools.
- Click Tools and select Reframe from the available options.
- Drag the photo or use the available perspective controls to change how you want the final image to be framed. I recommend making smaller adjustments first instead of immediately trying to create a completely different camera angle.
- Once you have the angle you want, click Reframe and wait for Apple Intelligence to generate the additional parts required for the new perspective.
- Pay particular attention to faces, hands, and other objects whose shape is easy to recognize. If everything looks right, Finally click Save Changes.
Expand a Photo Beyond Its Original Frame With Extend
There have been times when I had a good portrait photo but couldn’t use it as a wallpaper or inside a presentation because converting it to a wider aspect ratio would crop an important part of the image, and where the new Extend feature comes in. It generate additional content outside the original frame with Apple Intelligence.
To try it, open the image in Photos, click Edit, and open Tools. Select Extend, drag the edges beyond the original photo or choose the aspect ratio you need, and click Extend to generate the missing area.
Check the newly generated areas carefully before saving the result. If you don’t like what it created, adjust the frame and try again instead of keeping an obviously generated section.
Remove Unwanted Objects From Photos With Clean Up
Apple introduced the Clean Up tool with Apple Intelligence, and macOS 27 improves how it handles larger unwanted objects. If I take a photo at a tourist spot and someone is standing in the background I can select that person and let Photos remove them.
Here’s how you can remove an unwanted object from a photo:
- Open the Photos app on your Mac and double-click the photo you want to edit.
- Click Edit in the upper-right corner and open Tools.
- Select Clean Up, and your Mac will analyse the image. In some cases, Photos may automatically highlight objects it thinks you might want to remove.
- Click on a highlighted object to remove it, or use the Erase brush to paint over the object yourself. You can also circle the object if that makes it easier to select.
- And, finally, click Clean Up.
Resize the iPhone Mirroring Window
iPhone Mirroring is useful when I want to access something on my iPhone without picking it up, but using everything inside a phone-sized window on a large Mac display isn’t always ideal. macOS 27 fixes this by letting you resize the iPhone Mirroring window just by dragging its corner. You can also use keyboard shortcuts to quickly resize the iPhone Mirroring window. Press Command + Plus (+) to increase the window size and Command + Minus (-) to decrease it. If you want to return the window to its default size, press Command + 0.
But macOS 27 takes resizing a step further with supported apps. When you open a resizable app and make the iPhone Mirroring window wider, the app can actually adjust its layout and show more content instead of simply making the same iPhone interface bigger.
For example, if I open a supported app and drag the iPhone Mirroring window into a wider layout, I can get more usable screen space and information inside the app. Not every app supports this yet, so in unsupported apps, resizing may simply make the existing interface larger or smaller. You can press Command + 9 whenever you want to return the window to the standard iPhone size.
Let Your Mac Suggest Better Names for Files and Folders
My Downloads folder has taught me how quickly bad filenames can become a problem. A name such as “Untitled” or “Document 2” becomes useless once I forget what is inside them.
With macOS 27, Apple Intelligence can suggest names for files and folders based on what they contain. Instead of having to open a document again just to remember what it was about, macOS can look at the content and suggest a name that actually describes it.
First, you have to make sure this feature is enabled on your Mac. To do so, open Finder and click the Finder button in the menu bar. Next, choose Settings and make sure you are in the General tab. Now, check the box next to Suggest Filenames.
Now, to use this feature, right-click any document, photo, screenshot, or folder in Finder and select Rename. Wait for around five seconds, and Finder will show you a few suggested names based on the file’s contents. You can select the name you like and use it instead of typing one manually.
Create and Edit Calendar Events by Describing Them
macOS 27 makes creating Calendar events faster by describing the event naturally instead of filling in every field separately. I can type something like “Pankaj’s birthday next Monday,” and Calendar can use those details to create the event.
To try it, open Calendar, click the plus (+) button, and enter your description in Describe Event. You can also describe changes to an existing event instead of manually changing individual details.
Draw Directly Inside Apple Notes on Your Mac
Not everything you want to save in a note needs to be written as text. For example, if you’re planning the layout of a room, sketching a quick idea, making a simple diagram, or noting down something that is easier to remember visually, a quick drawing can be more useful than typing it out. With macOS 27, you can now create these drawings directly inside a note on your Mac and keep them saved along with the rest of your notes.
Previously, you could create drawings in a note from an iPhone or iPad, but macOS didn’t let you draw directly inside Notes on the Mac. Now, you can use your mouse or trackpad to create a quick sketch without leaving the Notes app.
Here’s how you can draw inside a note:
- Open the Notes app.
- Click the Markup button in the Notes toolbar to open the drawing tools.
- Choose the drawing tool you want to use, and adjust its thickness and colour depending on what you are trying to draw.
- Start drawing directly inside the note using your mouse or trackpad.
- Once you are finished, click the Markup button again to exit the drawing tools and continue working on the rest of your note.
Generate Images in More Styles With Image Playground
I tested Image Playground on Mac when Apple first introduced it, and one of my biggest complaints was how limited the available styles felt. Now, Apple has made Image Playground much more flexible in macOS 27. You now get more styles, including create photorealistic images, and the Any Style option lets you describe the kind of visual appearance you want instead of choosing only from a small set of presets. You can also choose square, portrait, or landscape output depending on where you plan to use the image.
Another change I find more useful is targeted editing. If most of the generated image looks good but there is one part I want to change, I can select that area and describe the change instead of generating the entire image again and hoping everything else remains the same.
If you are using Image Playground for the first time, I recommend reading our complete Image Playground guide for Mac, where we have covered the interface, creating images, using your own photos, and managing generated images in more detail.
Record Your Mac Screen With System Audio
This is one of my favorite smaller additions in macOS 27, especially because I regularly work on tutorials. macOS has had a built-in screen recorder for a long time, but recording the sound coming directly from the Mac hasn’t been nearly as straightforward as recording the screen itself.
The difference between system audio and microphone audio is important here. If I am recording a tutorial and an app plays a sound, system audio captures that sound directly. I don’t have to turn up my MacBook speakers and let the microphone record them along with keyboard sounds, fan noise, and everything else happening in the room.
Here’s how you can record your Mac screen with system audio:
- Press Shift + Command + 5 on your keyboard to open the built-in screenshot and screen-recording toolbar.
- Choose whether you want to Record Entire Screen, Record Selected Portion, or Selected Window depending on what you want to capture.
- Click Options in the toolbar and enable Include System Audio so that sounds playing on your Mac are included in the recording.
Add Extra-Large Widgets to Your Mac Desktop
I have been using widgets on my Mac desktop since Apple introduced them with macOS Sonoma. but the existing widget sizes don’t always work when an app has more information to show.
macOS 27 adds new Extra Large widget sizes, including a portrait layout for supported widgets. The additional space lets apps show considerably more information on the desktop.
To add an extra large widget on your desktop:
- Right-click anywhere on your Mac desktop and select Edit Widgets.
- Find the app whose widget you want to add and look through the available widget sizes. If the app supports the new sizes, you should see Extra Large or Extra Large Portrait among the options.
- Select the size you want and add the widget to your desktop.
If you haven’t used desktop widgets before, we have a complete guide explaining how to add widgets to your Mac desktop, including how to customise the widgets already on your Mac.
Share Photos and Videos in Full Resolution With Shared Albums
Shared Albums are convenient when I want to collect photos from a trip, event, or family function in one place, but there has always been a compromise: the photos and videos shared through them weren’t necessarily kept in their original quality.
Apple changes that with the new Shared Albums experience in macOS 27. Newly created permanent Shared Albums can store photos and videos at full resolution
Let Android and Windows Users Add Photos to Your Shared Albums
The Shared Albums update gets even more useful if your friends or family don’t all use Apple devices. Previously, you needed several WhatsApp chats, Google Drive folders, and people sending pictures individually
With macOS 27, people on Android and Windows can access the updated Shared Albums through a web browser, and they don’t necessarily need an Apple Account to participate. More importantly, you can allow them to contribute photos instead of limiting them to viewing the album.
Save Any Frame From a Video Directly as a Photo
Sometimes the best photo from a moment is actually hidden inside a video. Before macOS 27, if we spotted an interesting moment in a video, the easiest way to save it as a photo was to take a screenshot. But a screenshot doesn’t preserve the video frame as cleanly as a dedicated photo, and you may end up with lower quality or unwanted elements from the screen. With macOS 27, you can now save any video frame directly as a separate photo in your Photos library.
Open the video in Photos, pause it at the moment you want, and check the nearby frames until you find the best one. Then right-click the frame and select Save Video Frame as Photo. The saved frame appears in your Photos library, where you can edit and share it just like any other photo.
Start a Slideshow Directly From a Photo Album
I usually organise photos from a trip or event into an album, but when I want to show those pictures to someone, opening them one by one isn’t the nicest way to do it. macOS 27 makes this easier by letting me start a slideshow directly from an album in Photos, so I can show the entire collection without having to open every photo individually.
Slideshows themselves aren’t new on the Mac, but I like that I can now start one directly from an album I have already organised. Once the slideshow starts, I can quickly customise how it plays by changing the transition and duration, adding music, and deciding whether it should loop.
Here’s how you can start a slideshow from an album:
- Open the Photos app on your Mac and find the album you want to show.
- Control-click the album and select Start Slideshow from the menu.
- Once the slideshow starts, click Customise if you want to change how it plays.
- Adjust the Transition & Duration settings to control how quickly the photos move from one to another, and choose music if you want something playing in the background.
Change How Fast and Expressive Siri Sounds
I don’t always want Siri to speak at the same pace. If I am following instructions, a slightly slower response can be easier to understand. And if the current voice feels too slow, you can make it speak faster. macOS 27 also lets you change more than just how fast Siri speaks. On supported Macs and voices, you can also adjust how expressive the voice sounds. Increasing this setting gives Siri’s speech more variation and emphasis, which can make the spoken responses feel more natural and animated.
Get Better Resolution Support for External Displays
macOS 27 improves external display support, including 5K at 120Hz on certain compatible ultrawide monitors. Apple has also improved how macOS restores window positions and display arrangements after disconnecting and reconnecting a monitor, which I find more useful when regularly docking and undocking a MacBook.
After connecting your monitor, open System Settings, select Displays, and choose the external monitor to see the available resolutions and refresh rates.
Make Buttons and Other Controls Easier to See With Show Borders
macOS 27 adds a new Show Borders accessibility option that makes the boundaries around buttons and other interface controls easier to distinguish. This can be useful if you don’t want some controls to blend into the background with the Liquid Glass design.
To enable it, open System Settings and click Accessibility in the left sidebar. Select Display from the right-side panel, find Show Borders, and turn on the toggle next to it. You can also try Reduce Transparency from the same section if transparency itself is making parts of the interface difficult to see.
Explore Cities With More Detailed 3D Views in Apple Maps
Apple has improved the 3D city experience in Maps with more detailed buildings and surroundings in supported locations. I don’t use 3D Maps every time I need directions, but it can be useful when I want to understand the layout of an unfamiliar area before visiting it.
To try it, open Maps and search for the city or location you want to explore. Click View in the menu bar, select Show 3D Map, and enable Satellite if you want to explore the area using the detailed imagery.
Try the New Golden Gate Wallpapers and Screen Savers
Finally, macOS 27 comes with new Sunset and Night views of the Golden Gate Bridge, along with a new abstract wallpaper. The Golden Gate scenes can also be used as screen savers.
To try them, open System Settings and select Wallpaper from the left sidebar. Browse through the new macOS 27 backgrounds and select the one you want to use.
macOS 27 Feels More Useful Once You Start Finding the Smaller Changes
After trying more than 27 new macOS 27 features, creating custom Safari extensions is still the one I enjoyed the most, while several smaller additions have also made my everyday Mac experience better. If you enjoyed this guide, also check out our 27 best iOS 27 features you should try on your iPhone.
FAQs about macOS 27
1. Do All macOS 27 Features Work on Every Mac That Supports macOS 27?
No. Your Mac may support macOS 27 but still miss some features because individual features can have additional hardware, language, or region requirements.
2. Can Safari Extensions I Create Be Shared With Other People?
Not directly. Safari’s Describe Extension feature creates custom extensions for your own use. You can sync compatible extensions across your own Apple devices, but Apple currently doesn’t provide an option to send a generated extension directly to another person.
3. Can I Downgrade to macOS 26 After Installing macOS 27?
Yes, as long as macOS 26 supports your Mac. However, downgrading isn’t available like a normal software update and may require erasing your Mac and reinstalling the older macOS version. So, make sure you have a complete backup before proceeding.

3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz, The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.
Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.
But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.
"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.
Middle East
Israelis grapple with reports that Netanyahu was warned of Oct. 7 attacks years ago
A message from Hamas' leader in Gaza
One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.
Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.
On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."
He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.
"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.
A telephone call from the Emirati leader
Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.
The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.
The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times.
The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.
Egypt's top intelligence chief warned Israel, an official says
A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.
The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.
The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.
A former Israeli adviser says Egypt repeatedly warned Israel
Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."
Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.
"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."
Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.
The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.
NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.

MUMBAI: Putting its July 2026 rules on penalties for academic misconduct on hold and reverting to the (milder) April 2015 policy for two pending mid-semester examinations on Oct 10 and 11, IIT-Bombay’s senate, at its emergency meeting on Wednesday, agreed on an interim procedure under which faculty members may record suspected dishonesty by a student in a prescribed form, with students allowed to submit their own written accounts in a different sheet.
The revision comes in the wake of the death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode, who was allegedly found copying by an invigilator. The institute subsequently postponed exams scheduled for Sept 26 and 27 after faculty sought a clear SOP for handling suspected malpractice.
According to the interim arrangement now finalised, there will be two different forms in the event of a suspected case of cheating, and it is optional for the student concerned to submit their version. The matter will then be placed before the departmental disciplinary action committee (DDAC), which will decide how the case proceeds. Faculty members and students will be required to appear before the committee and provide additional information as needed. The committee will meet only a week after the entire exam season ends.
A source said the forms were only a means of collecting information and did not amount to pressing charges. 
Decisions would rest with the disciplinary committee.
Wednesday’s meeting was opened to all faculty, beyond the senate’s membership, to seek suggestions.
The report on the interim rules, a copy of which is with TOI, states faculty who suspect cheating or notice signs of stress must “alert a quick response team (QRT) of counsellors.” The aim is to provide immediate support “while minimising disturbance to the student concerned and others writing the examination.”
Invigilators, the report states, must “collect unauthorised material, including chits, phones, devices and answer papers, with minimal conversation and disruption. They may photograph material that must be returned, such as a phone. If a student’s identity is in doubt, they may photograph the student at the desk.”
The original answer book will be collected and the student allowed to continue writing in a fresh one for the remaining exam time. After the exam, the invigilator may complete the form and offer the student an opportunity to record their account at a designated venue in the presence of additional staff, said the report.
The signed faculty form, collected material, original answer book and student’s form, if submitted, will be handed to the head of the department conducting the course. “Digital material may be emailed. Phones must be returned after the examination, with students acknowledging receipt by signing the form.” The QRT helpline must be alerted for counselling whenever the student leaves the hall.
Under the 2015 guidelines, using a mobile phone during an exam attracted an FR (fail-repeat) grade. The July 2026 policy added a semester’s suspension, which sources said would not apply to a first offence under the interim arrangement. Repeat offences would attract suspension. Using phones, chits, books or other unauthorised material during toilet or bio-breaks would continue to attract FR and a semester’s suspension.
Security guards will no longer frisk students before exams. Faculty questioned searches resembling those at airports, saying they suggested everyone was a “suspect”.
“We want to convey we trust our students, though we will verify by doing thorough invigilation,” said a faculty member. Another source said an invigilator who suspected something could call a counsellor and ask the student to empty pockets.
The report states disciplinary proceedings must ensure students have a fair opportunity to present their viewpoints to the departmental committee and provide an appeal before an institute committee. Disciplinary action will follow if unauthorised practices are established.
Sources said the arrangement would “ease the burden on faculty handling suspected cheating, with professional counsellors providing support.” The disciplinary committee, however, will determine the outcome.
The drafting committee comprised Profs Suvarn Kulkarni, Pratibha Sharma, Varsha Apte and Amitava De and four student representatives. Sources said they spent about 30 hours preparing the interim procedure. Clear instructions would be shared with invigilators before the weekend exams, a source added.
Students may now bring bags into the exam building, reversing the earlier restriction, but must leave them outside the hall. The report states the institute’s goal is to “create an environment conducive to quality teaching and learning while maintaining assessment integrity. Its default assumption is that students are committed to learning and following examination rules.”
As per the academic calendar approved by the Senate, end semester examinations are scheduled for 13 days from November 10 to 21 and will be held on Saturdays and Sundays as well.

Electric shock gloves deemed too painful by US Army are being rolled out by ICE
An October 2024 US Army trial found that role-playing soldiers stopped resisting within seconds of being shocked, with test subjects reporting lingering fear and soreness
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is moving forward with plans to equip its officers with electric-shock gloves despite an internal military study showing the devices caused intense pain and fear during testing on Army personnel.
ICE signed a $16.7 million contract in August to purchase 6,000 pairs of the devices, known as the G.L.O.V.E., short for “Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter,” according to government records obtained by American Oversight and reported by the Associated Press.
The Department of Homeland Security previously indicated in a public notice that it planned to spend up to $20 million on the technology to acquire thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” by March. The contract reportedly describes the equipment as “a low-impact tool” intended for situations where a person actively resists arrest or poses a clear threat, according to American Oversight, a nonpartisan government watchdog group.
Manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC, based in Lexington, Kentucky, the equipment functions as standard patrol gear until an officer activates a switch. The device delivers an electrical charge upon direct contact with skin, targeting peripheral nerve endings to cause immediate pain rather than the full-body neuromuscular incapacitation typical of a Taser.
According to an October 2024 U.S. Army study conducted at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, test participants playing the role of combative inmates stopped resisting seconds after receiving shocks. The report noted that test subjects were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again.”
The 38-page report — conducted by the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Demonstration and Assessment Team — noted that the trial did not produce statistically relevant data to make predictions on efficacy, nor did it evaluate the device’s broader health or safety effects on humans.
The study concluded that “after experiencing the effects of the GLOVE … participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply.”
Researchers observed that although the device did not significantly alter transport times during inmate escorts, it “increased the efficiency” of forced cell extractions and disturbance responses, and it reduced physical exertion for guards.
“GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the Army study reported, adding that “inmate compliance was immediate.”
However, tests also showed that wet or oily skin intensified the shock, with one participant reporting discomfort lasting 30 minutes.
ICE leaders had access to the study before finalizing the purchase contract. The agency has defended the acquisition, framing the gloves as de-escalation tools that offer a safer alternative to lethal force when handling civil disturbances or subduing subjects during arrests and deportations.
But civil rights groups and lawmakers have raised concerns over potential misuse as the devices are integrated into federal immigration enforcement.
The procurement comes amid a broader expansion of authority for ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations division. Internal government documents obtained by legal advocacy group Democracy Forward and shared with The Independent reveal that HSI has also been tasked with probing voter registration groups and targeting noncitizen voter allegations ahead of the midterms, using data supplied by right-wing activists and federal voter roll databases.
Advocates warn that giving expanding enforcement powers to the agency increases the potential for harm. Records obtained earlier this year by American Oversight revealed a nearly 400 percent spike in ICE use-of-force incidents during the first months of the second Trump administration, alongside record-high deaths in custody. According to American Oversight, ICE officers have shot and killed at least five people since last year, including two U.S. citizens.
“The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight, said. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.”
Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said in August that the discreet nature of the device increased the risk of abuse.
“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” Borchetta said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”
Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada noted that ICE has failed to respond to an August 27 inquiry sent by 16 Democratic senators demanding details on deployment policies and safety protocols.
“Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric-shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” Cortez Masto said.
Proponents of the technology maintain that the devices reduce injuries during physical confrontations. John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, said that the stimulus was designed to create a quick distraction.
“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you,” Peters said. “I call it like a bee sting. For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage.”
Compliant Technologies guidelines state the gloves require biannual recertification and prohibit use against high-risk populations, including pregnant women, children, the elderly or individuals displaying only verbal defiance.
The manufacturer has also faced legal challenges over the device’s use. A pending lawsuit in Kentucky alleges a 43-year-old man died in a county jail after officers shocked him 40 times using a combination of a Taser and the shock gloves.
White House border czar Tom Homan indicated that operational deployment may take time as ICE finishes training modules and administrative policies.
In a statement to the Associated Press, ICE stated that “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics,” though the agency did not directly address the findings of the military study.
The Independent has contacted ICE for further comment.

OpenAI will begin automatically watermarking text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union, the company has announced. It will also offer the watermarking feature in other regions, but it will be off by default outside of the EU.
The move in Europe is driven by a need to comply with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. It requires marking content produced by AI models in a way that another tool can detect. Unfortunately, there is still no completely effective and reliable way to do that. A few standards already exist, like SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy to circumvent for anyone with basic know-how.
The same is likely true for OpenAI’s watermark. Its method is proprietary; the company calls it textGrain, and has published a technical paper explaining how it works. But in general, it works like other LLM watermarking tools we’ve seen in the past: It puts patterns in the word choices that are not clear to a human reader, and that don’t meaningfully change the general quality of the output, but that someone with a key can use a specialized detector to find. OpenAI says it will be giving access to the detector to a limited number of researchers and organizations, and providing a request-for-approval process for others to be added over time.

India's 'cockroach' protesters are back - this time asking poll chief to resign
- Published
India's influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" protesters are set to get back on the streets - this time seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voter rolls.
A pressure group which began as an online satirical movement, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) recorded its first major victory in July when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms.
The CJP leaders have now called upon their supporters to gather at the sprawling Shivaji Park grounds in Mumbai city at 4pm local time (10:30 GMT) on Friday "to save democracy" and seek CEC Kumar's resignation.
CEC Kumar or the Election Commission have not responded to the calls for his resignation from the CJP or opposition parties. They have also not responded to allegations of vote theft or elections being rigged. The BBC has asked them for comment.
In recent days, the CJP has shared a number of messages, reels and posters with their 25 million followers on Instagram and more than 400,000 followers on X, asking them to turn up in large numbers to "strengthen the voice of democracy".
The Mumbai protest, it said in a press statement on Thursday, is the first in a series of demonstrations it plans to hold across the country in October, culminating in a rally in the capital, Delhi.
CJP say Mumbai police have denied them permission, but security is being tightened in the city as large crowds are expected to gather, with some of the state's main opposition parties also pledging support, external.
The CJP called the protest after last week's report in The Indian Express, external that CEC Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.
The differences were reported to be mostly over a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
Last week's Indian Express report said the two commissioners had also been raising questions over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself.
The EC defended its way of working and said in a statement, external that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously.
But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation.
Leader of the opposition and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi has repeatedly accused the commission of "stealing votes from the opposition" and said those officers who were indulging in "vote theft" were "traitors".
Another senior opposition leader, Mamata Banerjee, has demanded the CEC's arrest.
On Wednesday, the INDIA alliance - an opposition grouping that includes nearly two dozen parties and has both Gandhi and Banerjee as members - said they would also organise protest rallies across the country in the coming days. On 6 October, all opposition MPs plan to march to the Election Commission office in Delhi, they added.
Many of the opposition parties have also pledged support to the protest in Mumbai.
Despite Mumbai police denying them permission to hold the protest, Dipke has insisted that they will assemble and if the police arrest them, they will launch a "Jail Bharo Andolan (fill the prison movement)".
In a short animation video posted on its social media accounts on Wednesday, the CJP said it was a citizen's right to be able to vote and to not allow an eligible voter to cast their vote was an "issue of serious concern in a democracy".
"We demand transparency and accountability from the commission and want the CEC to resign. This is not a fight for one party, it's for free and fair elections and every citizen's right to vote," it added.

Former Australian Catholic bishop sentenced for abusing Indigenous men
A former Australian Catholic bishop has been sentenced to more than six years in prison for sexually abusing two young Indigenous men
PERTH, Australia -- A former Australian Catholic bishop was sentenced Wednesday to six years and six months in prison for sexually abusing two young Indigenous men.
A District Court of Western Australia state jury convicted Christopher Saunders, 76, in August of 13 out of 19 charges of sexual abuse that occurred between 2008 and 2019 in his sprawling Broome Diocese on the country’s tropical northwest coast.
Saunders will become eligible for parole in February 2031.
Saunders was acquitted of six charges involving a third accuser. He was accused of indecent dealing with a child over the age of 16. The age of consent in Western Australia is 16, but the law raises it to 18 if the older person is in a position of trust, power or responsibility.
Four charges involving a child younger than 13 were dropped on the first day of Saunders’ three-week trial.
Saunders is one of the most senior Australian Catholics to be convicted in a global clergy abuse scandal that has faced the Vatican for years.
Cardinal George Pell was convicted of abusing choirboys, and Archbishop Philip Wilson was convicted of covering up child sex abuse by a priest. But both clerics successfully appealed their convictions.
Prosecutors alleged Saunders lured young Indigenous men to his church-owned house with alcohol and cigarettes paid for with church funds.
Saunders led the remote Broome Diocese from 1996 until he resigned in 2021. The Outback diocese covers an area larger than France with only 50,000 people. Most of the region’s Catholics are Indigenous.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, said the sentence recognized the gravity and serious nature of Saunders’ offenses.
The sentence also recognized the profound impact on the victims and survivors of Saunders’ crimes, Costelloe said.
“To each victim and survivor who courageously revealed what they had endured, we want to say this: We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church,” Costelloe said in a statement.
The Vatican began investigating Saunders in 2022, then handed the Western Australia Police Force a report on its findings the following year. Police charged Saunders in 2024.
While the report was never officially made public, the findings were leaked to Australia’s Seven Network television news, which reported Saunders likely sexually assaulted four Indigenous youths and potentially groomed another 67 Indigenous youths and men.

India’s supreme court has demanded accountability from the government and the senior election body over a controversial exercise that has led to the deletion of tens of millions of voters from the electoral roll and prompted mass protests.
Demonstrations have erupted across the country in recent days as opposition parties, student groups and the youth-led Cockroach movement have demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
They have accused Kumar of overseeing a direct attack on India’s democracy through an exercise to verify and “purify” the electoral roll in states across the country, which so far has led to 130 million names being removed. In Delhi, hundreds of people were detained as they tried to protest over the weekend.
On Monday, the supreme court issued notices to Narendra Modi’s government, the ECI and Kumar to demand answers over concerns raised about the voter list revision, saying they expected all “to respond in a clear, transparent manner”.
The ECI has claimed the exercise is simply cleaning electoral rolls of duplicate, dead and ineligible names, as well as removing “illegal infiltrators”. However, large numbers of people in Delhi and states such as Bihar and West Bengal say they have been wrongly stripped of their vote and have struggled to get it back.
There are accusations that revision of the electoral rolls particularly targets minorities such as Muslims, who are traditionally not voters of Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The opposition alliance, led by the Congress party, have accused the ECI of being hand in glove with the government over alleged vote “chori” or cheating. Kumar was chosen to head the ECI by a panel headed by Modi.
While the exercise, known as the special intensive revision (SIR), began last year, widespread outrage only recently erupted after a report in the Indian Express newspaper revealed multiple irregularities in the process, which were flagged in more than a dozen internal objections.
The two petitions taken up by the supreme court on Monday alleged that the credibility of the ECI was now in question and called for an independent inquiry into the decisions taken by Kumar in how the SIR process was conducted.
“Deletions of voters have been made in the largest democracy,” said Menaka Guruswamy, a lawyer acting for one of the petitioners. “We have grown up with free and fair elections, that is not the case now.”
Another advocate told the supreme court judges that if action was not taken to ensure that India’s electoral rolls remained fair, “this country will burn”. Another hearing in the cases will be held next week.
The controversies over the ECI have once again driven India’s young people on to the streets in protest, amid rising frustration at the Modi government.
The Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which led massive unrest over the summer that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, have once again mobilised and called for the resignation of Kumar. Thousands of CJP supporters took to the streets of Mumbai last Friday in protest and another demonstration was held on Saturday in Delhi.
In Delhi, police have been criticised for their heavy-handed approach to stopping any student groups protesting in the heart of the capital. Officers have been accused of sexually assaulting three journalists at the protests over the weekend and hundreds of young people were forced on to police buses. Delhi police said it was investigating the assault claims.

When my term life insurance policy expired in 2013 and I had to get a new one, I thought my widow-maker heart attack in 2005 might be a sticking point. Instead, eight insurers turned me down because they said I had “untreated cancer.”
They were referring to the tiny amount of prostate cancer found three years earlier.
My urologist/urological oncologist at the University of Chicago saw no need for surgery or radiation. Instead, he recommended active surveillance, close monitoring with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood tests, biopsies, and later MRIs of my cancer, which he swore I would die with and not from. The plan has worked well for me.
But I quickly learned that insurance underwriters with cash on the table saw my situation differently than my doctor did.
I previously had paid $184 a month for $600,000 in term coverage. After the rejections and continued negotiations, the only policy I could land was $100,000 in universal life — a conversion of my original plan with no new medical exam required, same $184 premium. Losing most of my coverage made the financial consequences of a cancer diagnosis painfully clear.
I wasn’t looking for a preferred rate reserved for people with spotless medical histories. Mine isn’t spotless.
What bothered me most was the phrase “untreated cancer.” I hadn’t ignored medical advice — I had followed it. My second-opinion urologist had told me in 2010 to hold off on treatment. He called my Gleason 6 or Grade Group 1 cancer “lame.” I wasn’t insulted.
Pathologist Donald Gleason developed his scoring system in the 1960s at the Minneapolis Veterans Administration to grade prostate cancer by how cells are arranged under a microscope. Today, pathologists assign two pattern scores, each ranging from 3 to 5, and add them together for a Gleason score of 6 to 10. Gleason 6 (3+3), also called Grade Group 1, sits at the bottom of the scale. Doctors recommend active surveillance for men like me with this low-risk cancer. Former President Joe Biden’s cancer falls near the other end: His office announced in May 2025 that he had Gleason 9, or Grade Group 5 — the highest grade group — and that the cancer had spread to his bones.
Recently, I decided to explore whether a man in my situation, unchanged for nearly 16 years, would fare any better today. I asked two insurance brokers — both Gleason 6 patients themselves — to walk through a hypothetical case: a 64‑year‑old man with a new Gleason 6 diagnosis and a past heart attack. In effect, I sent a younger version of myself out shopping for a term policy. Let’s call him Young Howard.
Their assessments weren’t formal underwriting decisions, but they revealed the same obstacles I faced years ago. One broker found some insurers might postpone a decision about Young Howard for three to five years. They’d want to see stable PSA results and no upgrading. Young Howard could follow his urologist’s advice to the letter and still wait years to find out whether he’s insurable. And, of course, he’d be three to five years older by then and have higher rates.
The heart attack added its own penalty under the insurance industry’s “table rating” reflecting a mortality risk when an applicant’s health or lifestyle doesn’t qualify for “standard rates” but the insurer still wants to offer coverage. Each table adds 25% to the standard premium.
One broker estimated the heart attack could land Young Howard in Table 6, roughly 150% above standard rates. A $1,000 annual premium could jump to $2,500.
In this scenario, the heart attack now drives the pricing, while the prostate cancer delays the application.
The brokers’ ballpark estimates for Young Howard ran into thousands of dollars a year.
One broker echoed my frustration: “Insurance companies haven’t caught up to what [the experts] know: Prostate cancer rarely escapes the prostate if the patient has stable PSA and a Gleason 6.”
Insurers, of course, assess the chance an applicant might die during the policy term — from any cause. My heart attack in 2005 fits squarely into that calculation. And a Gleason 6 biopsy can’t guarantee that more aggressive disease won’t appear later. Follow‑up matters.
But I reject the idea that a man who keeps every surveillance appointment has “untreated cancer.” Clarifying how insurers interpret “untreated” versus monitored cases could help us better understand their decisions. The medical record should tell insurers far more than those two words.
Underwriters should be more open about their decisions and respond to the information the doctors share.
Brokers can’t forecast that every man on active surveillance will be denied or charged more. But they strongly suggest that the challenges I faced haven’t disappeared since 2013.
For patients, the insurance issue adds to their worries, making them feel understood and less alone in facing these challenges.
Would surgery or radiation improve Young Howard’s chances of getting affordable coverage? I don’t have the answer. But it’s worth asking insurers — especially if a patient is considering treatment partly to resolve an insurance concern.
I still have unanswered questions. Among them: How do insurers weigh years of stable findings? Do they follow specific policies or guidelines for men on active surveillance? When a man has both prostate cancer and heart disease, how much does each condition influence the decision?
Clear explanations from insurers would foster trust and hope, helping patients and doctors feel more confident in their decisions.
In 2013, I needed life insurance and ended up with far less than I wanted. I followed my doctors’ advice. I’m still waiting for a clear explanation of why that made me so hard to insure.
Howard Wolinsky is a Chicago-based medical journalist and editor of The Active Surveillor, a Substack newsletter that covers active surveillance news. He brought the insurance problem to the attention of the American Urological Association’s Insurance Roudtable earlier this year.
