Meta has started testing a new video-first feed for Facebook in India, where users will now encounter a full-screen, Reels-centric user experience upon opening the application. Under the new interface, selected Indian users open directly into an immersive video player. The traditional chronological feed has been moved to a secondary tab, while participants retain the ability to opt out of the default video layout. In India, the FB app has now started testing a new, reels-first experience that will put full-screen video front and centre when some people open the app. “Designed for those who we think want more video, the experience offers a more visual, video-first way to discover content, creators and conversations on Facebook,” the company said. Meta first hinted at bringing the feature to India in a blog post in July, when Facebook head Tom Alison said the company was considering how to enhance the experience of users who wanted to connect with creators and focus on entertainment. “People are showing us they want more immersive, visual, video-forward experiences, and video is where conversations are happening, communities are forming, and even commerce is starting to take place,” he wrote. He added that the feature would first launch in countries where video content has seen strong traction before eventually coming to the US. Meta’s ecosystem, including Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and WhatsApp, spans almost half of the world’s population, counting 3.58 Bn daily active users and nearly 4 Bn monthly users. India alone contributes over 1 Bn users across these platforms, making it one of the most critical platforms for Meta globally. However, the tech giant has faced hurdles in dealing with the government of late. A BBC investigation earlier this year alleged that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale. As a result, MeitY summoned Meta’s executives while the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) initiated an investigation. Meta claimed it had taken action to take down the policy-violating content and block associated accounts, and ultimately agreed to report child safety matters directly to the authorities.

While thousands of Indian students head overseas annually for medical degrees, comprising a heavily monitored segment under the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), parliamentary disclosures indicate that centralised tracking of specific discipline-wise student outflows remains complex.
But for many, the journey culminates in a grueling, high-stakes afternoon inside an Indian examination hall. When the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) released the results for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) June 2026, the pass rate had plummeted sharply to just 12.4%, triggering nationwide discussions, student protests, and scrutiny over what is locking foreign medical graduates out of medical practice.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
The panic after the paper
Dr. Chaynika Soni, a medical intern in a Government Hospital in Rajasthan who cleared the exam in her second attempt after graduating from Belarus in 2024, recalls, “Every single year after the exam, you’ll see the same thing. Students come out saying, ‘The paper was impossible.’ ‘It was too hard.’ ‘Nobody could solve it.’ Coaching centers will upload videos saying, ‘The paper was unexpected.’ Telegram groups will be filled with panic.”
This panic was visible during the June session, where candidates faced sudden structural shifts. Describing his experience with the exam pattern, Dr. Kshitij Anand said, “The questions were relatively long and time-consuming. I felt the questions were completely unrelated to what I studied. There were some questions I could get direct answers for, but it wasn’t much. They give you questions and options in a way that you take time to figure out answers but not enough time to think.”
He adds that the introduction of unfamiliar video modules caught aspirants off guard: “The Board gave us video questions which I agreed were manageable, but it was a new pattern. The FMGE conducted last January was way more image-based, and the options were comparatively easier to tap than this one. Also, the diagrams I have never seen before.”
Acknowledging these pressures, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, points out that “More video-based questions (this time), clinical-based questions will be tough for FMG’s [as they are] not exposed to Indian setting and less time make the exam tough.”
Inside the recall analysis
As the National Board of Examinations does not release official FMGE question papers, student-reconstructed “recall” papers serve as the baseline for preparation. A look at the high-weightage sections — Community Medicine (PSM), Internal Medicine, and Obstetrics and Gynaecology — reveals distinct hurdles.
Community Medicine heavily tests India-specific public health administration, including domestic health committees like the Bhore or Kartar Singh committees, local staffing norms at Primary Health Centres, and administrative schemes that foreign universities naturally omit. For a student trained overseas, this often translates to unfamiliar civic administration rather than core medicine.
Conversely, Internal Medicine acts as a control case focused on universal clinical reasoning, ranging from ABG analysis to emergency cardiac protocols. Meanwhile, Obstetrics and Gynaecology balances international diagnostic criteria with clinical application, though candidate performance frequently hinges on interpreting embedded clinical images, manoeuvres, or diagnostic scans.
Weighing these system dynamics, Dr. Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge for the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA), explains, “In departments such as Medicine, Surgery, and Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Indian hospitals generally see a very large number of patients. This gives doctors and students exposure to a wide variety of clinical presentations and allows them to learn how to manage patients even when resources are limited. I would particularly highlight Community Medicine... If an FMG studies Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Community Medicine properly, focuses on clinical concepts, and practices clinical and image-based questions, they should find these areas much more manageable in the FMGE.”
Conceptual depth and the gap in coaching materials
Beyond traditional curriculum differences, candidates found that the depth of questioning defied standard coaching modules. Dr. Ruhi Kumari, who appeared in the June session, explains, “We weren’t trained that way. For example, there was a question on cholera; the answer was an increase in cAMP. I knew it was an increase in cAMP (cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate), but the options were given in biochemistry language. Like, you have to know what cAMP is in biochemistry; only then can you answer that. No coaching institute is teaching anyone like this. Only USMLE tutors do. Because USMLE has always asked in-depth questions. Many clinical questions expect you to have clinical experience. But that’s just unfair, because I will only get that experience after I visit the clinic.”
Dr. Kumari further notes the obsolescence of traditional prep material: “Marrow [an online platform) questions were considered the standard before this exam, but I can tell you they are not anymore. There were a lot of questions that weren’t even asked in many previous years' papers, that flustered everyone... Honestly, I am not sure which resource would give me the most apt training, because no institute is teaching you like that at present. Doing INICET papers is not going to help you, or even NEET-PG papers.”
Logistics, exam conditions, and the transparency debate
The academic difficulty was further compounded by severe logistical hurdles on test day. Dr. Samar Kumar outlines the physical toll: “The first issue was related to examination centres. Multiple centres had inadequate facilities. Some did not have coolers or fans, and in some cases, even drinking water was not adequately available. As you know, the FMG examination is five hours, and overall it takes eight hours. Maintaining concentration in such tough conditions, especially during extreme summer, is something beyond the capacity of many students and FMG doctors particularly when they are not provided with adequate facilities.”
He added regarding the sudden format changes, “The second and most important issue was the sudden introduction of video-based questions in the FMG June 2026 examination. FMGs opposed this later as well and conducted protests regarding this issue in Delhi, Gautam Nagar. The demand of the students was to provide compensation for the sudden introduction of video-based questions, but NBEMS denied the demand.”
Adding to student frustration is a perceived lack of institutional accountability. Dr. Kumar said, “Moreover, the FMG examination does not have any kind of transparency. The questions and answers have never been shown to FMGs. Thus, no one knows how they failed by just one mark, five marks, or ten marks... Then why does NBEMS say that they cannot show the questions and answers together? Why can’t the examination questions and their corresponding answers be disclosed?”
FMGE versus NEET-PG and the time crunch
Comparing the screening test to domestic evaluations, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, notes that “NEET PG exam standard is being given in FMGE exam as the board-making exam is the same NBE.”
While Indian MBBS graduates prepping for NEET-PG sit within a mature ecosystem of shared question banks and peer networks, foreign-trained graduates often experience thinner access to these informal pipelines.
Dr. Samar Kumar contrasts the two exams, “Recently, FMGE has also included video-based and lengthy clinically oriented questions, which adds another dimension to the examination... FMGE continues to have 300 questions, whereas NEET-PG has moved from the earlier 200-question format to 180 questions. Therefore, FMGE tests not only clinical knowledge and application but also a candidate’s ability to maintain concentration and consistency throughout a long examination. NEET-PG, on the other hand, has its own competitive dynamics, including negative marking and a highly competitive selection process. But if you remove these factors from NEET-PG, then it becomes easier than FMGE.”
This time crunch is intensified by structural scheduling. Dr. Anjali Ayappan from Kochi points out, “Two months is simply not enough preparation time for FMG students, especially considering the amount of syllabus and the situation most FMGs are already in. And bringing the next exam forward to October is especially bad for the June pass-outs. They barely get any time to prepare after the result, and then suddenly they’re expected to appear again in October.”
The long road to registration
Clearing the exam is only the first milestone; graduates face a complex administrative labyrinth before they can practice. Dr. Parvathy Sabu, who cleared the exam and works in a Government Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, said, “Internship posts for FMGs are fewer across almost every State, and protests to increase seats are seen often... By the time you get PR [permanent registration], best-case scenario, approximately 8 years have gone by (including course duration) and a lot of money. Abroad MBBS is a very long-term investment that many don’t realise initially. I think the integration into Indian healthcare and internship issues are the biggest challenges faced by FMGs.”
Reflecting on these cumulative pressures, Dr. Madhavi Gurung, an FMG aspirant who studied in the U.K., concludes, “Many of my friends skipped FMGE and are now doing residency in the U.S., some are working non-training jobs in the U.K., and some are on track to settle in Australia. The struggle doesn’t end after NEET-UG. And with rising competition and reservation quotas, the system is tough. Every year wasted in endless NEET attempts can drain your mental health and confidence. I’m now planning to take AMC Part 1 by the end of this year and hopefully move abroad permanently.”

Dehradun-based medtech startup Sunfox Technologies has raised $7 Mn (around ₹67 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Ashish Kacholia, Lashit Sanghvi, Alchemy Capital, and 3one4 Capital. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its portable cardiac diagnostics platform Spandan across India, grow its team, and invest in R&D, clinical evidence, engineering, and new cardiac technologies. It will also build regulatory, distribution, and commercial capabilities across the US, Europe, and Africa, the startup said in a statement. Sunfox said it has regulatory approvals in India, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, and South Africa, and is pursuing clearances in the US and the European Union. The fundraise follows a ₹15 Cr (around $1.8 Mn) round led by Venture Catalysts in 2024. Founded in 2016 by Rajat Jain, Arpit Jain, Sabit Rawat, Nitin Chandola, and Saurabh Badola, Sunfox develops portable and AI-enabled cardiac diagnostic solutions for hospitals, clinics, telemedicine networks, public health programmes, and home-based monitoring. Its Spandan devices allow users and healthcare workers to record ECGs using a smartphone and share them with doctors for remote interpretation. According to the startup, the platform can flag cardiac patterns requiring urgent attention, helping healthcare teams identify patients who need further assessment or treatment. Its digital service platform, Spandan One, supports remote ECG reviews, case coordination, and tele-ECG network management. In public health settings, nurses or health workers can record ECGs at primary and community health centres and send them to doctors or cardiologists at district hubs for review. Sunfox claims around 60,000 Spandan devices have been deployed across India, reaching more than 20,000 villages. Its Spandan One platform is used to screen around 5 Mn patients annually, it added. The startup, which secured investment from all five participating investors on the first season of Shark Tank India, also claims a presence in more than 15 countries. Sunfox competes in the portable ECG segment with the likes of Agatsa, which offers SanketLife devices, and Cardiotrack, which provides handheld ECG devices and remote interpretation solutions.

The vanishing world of India's street magicians
- Published
Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.
Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.
The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.
He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.
Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.
"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
- Published
Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.
In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.
Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".
"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.
It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.
Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.
It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.
Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".
"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

On Tuesday (October 6, 2026), Kenya confirmed its first Ebola case after a Kenyan national who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died in Nairobi. According to media reports that quoted Kenya’s Health Minister Aden Duale, he had lived in the DRC for years and had travelled back home by road before taking a flight to Nairobi.
After the DRC declared an Ebola outbreak in May, Uganda also reported cases and deaths from Ebola. However, after Uganda was declared free of the disease by the World Health Organisation (WHO), the cases have occurred only in the DRC. This is the first case in which an Ebola death has occurred in another country, raising significant concern regarding transmissibility for public health authorities.
What are the details of the case
According to Mr. Duale, the Kenyan national had been living in the DRC for several years and had fallen ill about a month ago. He had been treated in several hospitals in the DRC and died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had travelled by road from DRC to Uganda and then boarded a flight to Nairobi, undergoing public screening with other passengers at the airport, but missed being picked up. He went home and was taken to hospital by a relative when he became sicker. He tested positive for the dangerous Bundibugyo strain, which has neither specialised treatment nor a vaccine until now. (Human trials for a vaccine were started in July, and three other candidates are in the pipeline.)
Eight of the patient’s family members and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined. Screening at all airports. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the flight he took from Uganda are also being traced. The traced individuals will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be allowed to leave if they do not show any symptoms.
Why is this fresh cause for concern?
The virus is highly infectious and spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids. This is the 17th outbreak in the DRC and is said to be its deadliest, having claimed over 4,000 lives since May this year. Over 8,300 cases have been confirmed across the country.
Meanwhile, the WHO has warned that the epidemic will surpass the regional 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed over 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Despite an outbreak in the region, the global health body has not been in favour of imposing travel and trade restrictions on the affected regions. However, not all international travellers are required to fill out a self-declaration form specifying whether they have been in any of the Ebola-affected countries or if they have suffered any symptoms lately.
In Kenya, health authorities explained that the patient who died had managed to pass through the screening without raising any red flags because the medicines he was on probably masked the symptoms as he walked past.
The course ahead
Now that the virus has entered Kenya, the key task for health authorities in the country is firstly to stop the chain of transmission, beginning with the primary contacts already isolated. As per the outbreak protocol, this includes rapid contact tracing, immediate isolation of anyone who develops symptoms, and testing. Strict infection-control measures must be put in place in Kenya, and targeted information on prevention and control disseminated among communities.
Screening and surveillance have been intensified at airports in Kenya. However, at a time when it is impossible to stop global movement, it’s crucial to make sure that all nations maintain vigilance at their entry ports and pick up patients with detectable symptoms. Port authorities should also stress on the seriousness of honestly declaring travel history and symptoms.

A mysterious death of a woman in Russia following a lab accident has stoked fears about plague spreading. But the odds of that actually happening remain very low, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention saying on X Tuesday afternoon that the circumstances of the case remain unconfirmed and that there is “no indication of a broader threat to the United States” at this time.
“We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the agency said. “CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely.”
Last week, a young researcher died from severe pneumonia of “unknown” origin after reportedly breaking a test tube at her workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. The hospital that treated her before her death was placed under quarantine, and her coworkers at the lab were isolated, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
Christian Lindmeier, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday that the group has been in touch with Russian authorities. Based on currently available information, WHO says the public health risk to the general population is very low.
“I think that’s the correct assessment,” says Gigi Gronvall, an immunologist and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We don’t know anything about anything right now.”
Russian authorities have said contact tracing hasn’t yielded any signs of dangerous pathogens spreading, according to the Associated Press. Infamous for causing millions of deaths in Europe during the Middle Ages, plague is rare today. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is found in wild rodents and their fleas in many parts of the world. It’s spread to humans through the bite of an infected flea and occasionally through direct contact with an infected animal. Antibiotics can cure plague, but they must be started as soon as an infection is suspected.
Pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales infectious droplets that contain the bacteria. In July 2025, an Arizona man died from pneumonic plague after exposure to infected cats. It can also spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. But human-to-human transmission is rare, with the last reported occurrence happening in 1924 in Los Angeles. The possibility, though, is why the CDC says it’s important to rapidly identify cases and treat them.
“Once you know that somebody has been exposed to it, and even if you have a doubt that somebody has been exposed to it, you can immediately start antibiotics to prevent the person getting afflicted with the disease and to avoid the continuous spread of the disease,” says Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
Dalal says if the Russian lab worker did die from plague, he is confident that the disease could easily be contained. “With Covid, that was a virus we had not dealt with in the past,” he says. That required novel interventions, while “here, we do have antibiotics to deal with this.”
The incident also occurred in a remote part of Russia, which could naturally limit its spread. “Siberia is not exactly Paris,” Gronvall says. “There’s not a lot of travel going back and forth.”
Whether plague is the culprit or not remains an open question. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal public health and consumer protection agency, said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.” But the US has urged the country to share as much information as possible, while other nations that share borders or are near Russia, including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan, have set up quarantine protocols.

In its first live event in two years, Microsoft today announced its newest Surface laptop, outlined a host of changes coming to Windows 11, and shared a vision of how local-AI and agentic workflows could reshape personal computing for those in the dev community as well as home enthusiasts.
Surface Laptop Ultra
Originally teased in May 2026, the new Surface Laptop Ultra will be Microsoft’s first offering to take advantage of the new Nvidia RTX Spark SoC (system on a chip). The device has a starting price of $2,599, and comes in various SoC and memory configurations, with either a 5120-core or 6144-core Blackwell GPU and up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified memory. It will begin shipping on October 16 and is available for pre-order now.
While the new Ultra is clearly focused on the developer crowd, graphical performance was highlighted during the presentation to show off just how capable the laptop can be. By leaning on unified memory allocation rather than the physical VRAM limits of a traditional GPU, the laptop can assign its resources to handle modern gaming tasks as well as local AI development and deployment. The new Gears of War: E-Day was shown running on the system, meaning that even without a traditional gaming GPU, AAA titles are on the table.
RTX Spark Dev Box
Joined on stage by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, President of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri also unveiled the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box. This is a $5,999 anodized aluminum black box “designed to meet the needs of frontier developers.” The Spark Dev Box ships with a custom “developer-optimized” build of Windows 11 pre-configured for AI development and local AI use. With 128GB of unified memory and the onboard Nvidia RTX GPU, the box claims one petaflop (that’s 1,000 teraflops) of AI compute performance.

Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record
- Published
Harry Kane has reached another significant England milestone by equalling Peter Shilton's 36-year-old record as the most-capped Three Lions player.
The Bayern Munich striker made his 125th appearance for the national team against the Czech Republic in the Nations League on Tuesday.
Kane is already his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in a full international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut.
He may be 33 but remains a key player for club and country. BBC Sport has a look at the origins story of the England captain.
- England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender 
  - Published21 minutes ago
From safe hands to hot-shot striker
When a six-year-old Harry Kane arrived for trials with Ridgeway Rovers in 1999, the youth side - who a generation earlier had produced David Beckham - thought they had found themselves a new goalkeeper.
Dave Bricknell, former Ridgeway Rovers coach: "We're doing a little shooting session, and I ask for a lad who can go in goal.
"This little boy puts his hand up and says: 'I'll go in goal.' We give him some gloves, and he performs heroics - makes some fantastic saves. He's tipping it round the post, tipping a couple over the bar.
"I'm thinking this is great, we've got a goalkeeper. And then this woman came up to me and said he's better on the pitch.
"We put him on pitch and he smacked goals in left, right and centre. So he ends up being our centre forward."
Kane's prolific form for Ridgeway Rovers and his Waltham Forest district side caught the attention of professional scouts. Arsenal initially snapped up the youngster but decided not to keep him, while Watford also passed up the opportunity to sign Kane.
Trevor Bailey, Kane's manager at Waltham Forest: "Harry could have done nothing all game, but if that chance came up it was in the onion bag.
"He was always on the move up front. When he got a chance, guaranteed four out of five he was going to score or set someone up."
Alex Welsh, former academy coach at Arsenal: "I first met Harry in the academy and he was a very competent goalkeeper, but his real desire was to score goals.
"I am absolutely convinced that is the reason why he is such a clinical striker - he intuitively knows what the goalkeeper doesn't like. He shoots early when the goalkeeper's not set."
Bricknell: "I believe he was second top-scorer at Arsenal behind Benik Afobe, and then for some reason they decided at 11 years of age that they didn't want him anymore."
The 'model student' with a Beckham Mohican
Kane attended Larkswood Primary Academy before moving to Chingford Foundation School, where he was inevitably the star of the football team. But, as a dedicated student, Kane impressed his teachers across the board.
Mark Leadon, Kane's PE teacher: "Aged 11, Harry was technically very gifted, with a great first touch, and a very clever player. He always knew where to go, right from an early stage.
"He was also a very good cricketer - he opened the bowling from year seven to 10 and batted at four or five. But he loved football. He was never a prima donna, and he would always put a shift in.
"What came through more than anything else was his determination to succeed. That work ethic was clear."
Luke Robinson, Kane's childhood friend and team-mate: "The only thing on his mind was football.
"We used to have a laugh, a couple of games of Fifa, but he was always driven. He'd always keep himself to himself.
"He loved David Beckham, he came in with the Mohican, everyone was laughing but he loved it. He loved football, 24/7, he lived and breathed football."
'Gold medallist? He wasn't even on the podium'
It was Tottenham Hotspur who offered Kane hope after his earlier disappointments, but the future England captain was by no means the pick of the bunch for his age group.
Kane's desire to learn and improve endeared him to the Tottenham academy staff and he signed scholarship terms with the club on his 16th birthday in July 2009.
Alex Inglethorpe, former Tottenham youth-team coach: "When I joined Spurs as under-18 coach, Harry was 13.
"I'd like to say he was the gold medallist in the group and we'd all spotted he was going to be the fantastic player, but I'd be lying. He probably wasn't even on the podium.
"If there was something that endeared him to you it was that he was very, very low maintenance. It became fairly evident when Harry became a scholar he was someone who could finish.
"He was wonderfully demanding to coach because he always wanted to stay out and do extra. That obsession to improve is undoubtedly his greatest strength.
"It was probably around 16 he started having an impact on the youth team. We trusted him to come off the bench and have an impact - anywhere from right wing, number 10, centre-forward, sometimes in midfield."
Living the loan life
Kane went to League One Leyton Orient - making his professional debut in January 2011 at Rochdale, coming on for veteran striker Scott McGleish. Kane would score five times in nine starts.
McGleish: "Harry was not like other Premier League players, where you feel they're going to come in 'Billy Big Time'. He wanted the experience of learning what I call men's football.
"From the word go he was ready to fight for his place. In training, he was willing to just knuckle down and work hard.
"You could see in training and subsequently the matches he had ability and a desire to go further, but you're still looking like a young 17-year-old: very slight, still needing to physically develop, not the quickest but technically excellent."
After a few first-team games for Spurs, he went on loan to Millwall in January 2012 to Championship strugglers Millwall. Kane's nine goals helped save Kenny Jackett's side from relegation.
Former Millwall defender Alan Dunne: "I've seen a lot of players come to the Den and freeze, because within five minutes they're being called names they've never heard before and they can't cope with that pressure.
"But it didn't faze him - he was a focused lad, he was confident in his ability."
Former Tottenham manager Tim Sherwood: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall, and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there.'
"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him."
After making his Premier League debut for Tottenham in August 2012, Kane was sent on loan again. The 19-year-old only made three appearances in the top flight for Norwich because of injury, and then had a loan spell at Leicester where he and future England team-mate Jamie Vardy struggled for regular starts.
Off the mark for Tottenham
After four loan spells in three seasons, Kane spent the entire 2013-14 campaign with Tottenham. But it was not until April, after Andre Villas-Boas had been sacked and replaced by Sherwood, that a 20-year-old Kane was handed his first Premier League start for Spurs, scoring his first top-flight goal in the process against Sunderland and also netting in the following two games against West Brom and Fulham.
Sherwood: "It didn't feel a gamble at all to give Harry that start. It was almost overdue to be honest.
"Roberto Soldado was in front of him in the team, and nobody wanted Roberto to do well more than me - but every single day in training Harry was outperforming him. He didn't let me down.
"Harry wanted to get to the top, and nothing was going to stop him achieving that because of the ability, desire and mentality he possesses.
"I was the biggest believer Harry Kane ever had, because I used to think he was a mix between Teddy Sheringham and Alan Shearer."
Kane becomes a Spurs legend
Kane never looked back after scoring 21 top-flight goals the following season - and earning his first England call-up in March 2015.
He ended up as the club's all-time top scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances - and three Premier League Golden Boots, but no trophies
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola, who tried to sign him, said in 2023: "What an exceptional player – the numbers and, more than the goals, the quality. Harry Kane remains one of the best strikers I have ever seen in my life."
Former Spurs team-mate Son Heung-min: "Leader, brother, legend.
"Since day one it has been a joy to play by your side. So many memories, amazing games and incredible goals together."
Then Tottenham boss Ange Postecoglou: "Harry was brilliant throughout. You want to work with the best players and he is a hell of a striker and I thought he could help me.
"He has left an indelible mark at this football club, will go down as one of the greats."
Kane keeps banging in goals at Bayern
The only thing missing from Kane's career CV was trophies - and in 2023 he joined German side Bayern Munich, where he has continued to impress.
He has scored 152 goals in 154 games for the club, won the Bundesliga Golden Boot three times and won two German titles and a German Cup.
Former Bayern defender Lothaur Matthaus: "Kane has reinvented the centre-forward game, as Manuel Neuer did with goalkeepers.
"I don't see a better striker in the world right now. Not just because of his goals, but because of his versatility and the positions he plays.
"Kane also demonstrates qualities as a passer, dribbler, and tackler. He is simultaneously a goalscorer, playmaker, box-to-box player, and tackler."
Ex-England striker Shearer, speaking this summer: "To me he looks fitter and stronger than before.
"He's come into this World Cup off the back of a brilliant campaign for Bayern Munich and looks very sharp and very confident - as you would do after scoring 61 goals in one season. Those numbers are just ridiculous."
BBC pundit Chris Sutton: "He has to be in that bracket when you talk about the world's best. Harry Kane has instincts that are simply uncoachable."
Some of these interviews were first published in 2016

Growing human activity across the Himalayas and surrounding high-altitude forests is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, according to a BBC report based on two studies by Indian researchers.
The Himalayan monal (Lophophorus impejanus), known for the striking green, blue and copper feathers of the male bird, is the state bird of Uttarakhand and the national bird of Nepal. Two separate studies conducted by researchers from Uttarakhand over five years have identified the growing pressure that infrastructure development, tourism and changing weather patterns are placing on the species.
The research suggests that monals are being pushed towards higher elevations as their natural habitats become increasingly crowded. The birds have also been found to alter their calls in response to rising levels of human-generated noise in busy mountain valleys.
Scientists say these changes are significant because the monal occupies a sensitive ecological zone between lower forested slopes and high-altitude alpine meadows. Such behavioural and habitat shifts could serve as an early warning of broader environmental stress across the northwestern Himalayas.
"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" Vishal Singh, an expert on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas, said, as quoted by the BBC.
One of the studies examined how Himalayan monals respond to different sound environments. Researchers from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, led by Dr Rajeev Lochan along with Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, studied the birds' calls inside the Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand.
Over the course of the study, the team collected and examined more than 700 vocalisations from two contrasting locations — Chopta Valley and Madmaheshwar Valley.
The analysis found a clear difference between birds living in quieter areas and those exposed to greater human activity. Monals in noisier surroundings produced calls with a higher peak pitch, apparently helping their voices stand out against low-frequency sounds from vehicles and conversations among visitors.
However, the researchers said this adaptation could have wider consequences. Changes in vocal patterns may influence the birds' ability to establish and defend territories or communicate with potential mates.
"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.
The second study focused on how changes in climate and habitat could affect Himalayan monal populations over the coming decades. Researchers used climate and habitat modelling to assess the species' likely distribution through the end of the century across Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh.
The findings indicate that rising temperatures, along with growing human activity in alpine meadows, are forcing monals towards higher elevations. As the birds move further uphill towards isolated mountain peaks, the amount of suitable habitat available to them is expected to shrink.
"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.
The researchers' findings highlight how human development and climate change are affecting not just where Himalayan species can survive, but also how they behave and communicate.

Mumbai’s away Ranji Trophy match against Himachal Pradesh, scheduled from October 18 to 21, has been shifted from Dharamshala to the Luhnu Cricket Ground in Bilaspur following heavy rain in the hill town.
The Dharamshala ground could not be prepared in time because of the inclement weather, prompting the Himachal Pradesh Cricket Association (HPCA) to inform the BCCI about the change of venue.
“We have been getting heavy rain in Dharamshala, because of which we couldn’t get the ground ready. That’s why we informed the BCCI about the change,” HPCA secretary Manuj Sharma told Sportstar.
Sharma, however, was hopeful that the iconic Himachal Pradesh Cricket Association Stadium would be ready to host the team’s next home fixture.
Dharamshala has endured persistent rain in recent weeks. Earlier, India Women A’s matches against Australia A were also moved out of the venue because of the weather.
Bilaspur, in the southwestern part of Himachal Pradesh, is a hill town best known for the Bhakra Dam and the Gobind Sagar Lake.
Mumbai will begin its Ranji Trophy campaign at home against Chandigarh before travelling to Bilaspur.

A Florida mailman has been arrested for allegedly driving under the influence while on the job, according to police.
Eliezer Valcourt, 32, is accused of being nearly three times over the legal limit when he was stopped in his U.S. Postal Service truck by Fort Lauderdale Police on Tuesday night, local outlet WSVN reported, citing an arrest report.
Fort Lauderdale Police told The Independent that they received a traffic complaint at around 8 p.m. “The caller reported a marked United States Postal Service vehicle stopped in the roadway with the driver inside,” police said.
Calls were coming in that the truck’s driver had been screaming while driving down the road, the arrest report said.
Police told The Independent that when they showed up, Valcourt “appeared to be intoxicated,” and a DUI officer was called to conduct an investigation. Before the cops stopped Valcourt’s truck, he nearly hit an officer, according to the arrest report.
Valcourt allegedly appeared unsteady on his feet with glassy, watery eyes and drooping eyelids, the report said. He was also allegedly slurring his speech, and the DUI officer reported a strong smell of alcohol on his breath.
Before starting a sobriety test, Valcourt stopped to pull a toothbrush out of his pocket and brush his teeth, according to the report. The DUI officer reported seeing seven of eight possible clues while Valcourt was completing a walk-and-turn exercise and said that he nearly fell at the end.
Valcourt told police he had been working since 9 a.m. and was almost done with his route. He reportedly denied drinking.
The mailman was arrested and booked into a local jail on two DUI-related charges. He later posted his bond and is expected to be released Wednesday night, WSVN reported.
The Independent has reached out to USPS for comment.

Trump said these words during an unscripted, tangential portion of a speech he gave at a Nebraska political rally. Many people, including high-level Democratic politicians and pundits, appeared to interpret him as saying the destruction of two large California cities would be a small price to pay for ending the war. White House spokesperson Steven Cheung replied on X that, on the contrary, Trump "was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped."
On Oct. 5, a rumor circulated online that, while speaking at a rally, U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran could "take out" Los Angeles or San Diego and that it would be a "very small price to pay" amid the war on Iran.
The joint U.S.-Israel military operation has killed thousands of Iranians, beginning with the assassination of Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader of Iran, on Feb. 28, 2026. According to an October poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, only 28% of Americans approve of how Trump is handling Iran, as the cost of gas and groceries continued to soar.
"Trump on Iran: Let 'em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it's a small price to pay," one X post showing a video of Trump speaking was captioned (archived). It had more than 15 million views.
The video was authentic, and the quote was correctly attributed to Trump. While speaking about economic sacrifices during the war at a Nebraska rally on Oct. 5, Trump said (at 1:47:01):
I want to see a tremendous victory. You want to see a tremendous victory 'cause it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the war it's just artificial. It's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay and it's going to be over with very soon. It's essentially almost over with and they might keep going a little long. You know, they always say they have a big threshold for pain — they need it, let me tell you, they need it. But it's gonna end very soon and it'll end one way or the other and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things.
California leaders, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the mayors of Los Angeles and San Diego, denounced Trump's comments.
"After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California," Newsom posted on X, "Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous."
We sought comment from the White House, which directed us to a statement on X (archived) by spokesperson Steven Cheung. Cheung wrote that Trump was "clearly" stating that "U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped."
It was unclear what Trump was referring to when he made the comment about "a small price to pay" and the White House's response didn't provide further context.

Delhi’s new draft electoral roll has 97,53,577 names. In February 2025, 94,94,607 people voted in the Delhi assembly elections. Eighteen months later, the roll of eligible voters has just 2,58,970, or 2.7%, more names than the number of people who turned out to vote last year.
Now, in 24 of Delhi’s 70 assembly constituencies, the gap has disappeared altogether: The draft roll contains fewer names than the number of people who actually voted in those seats in 2025.
The numbers raise a fundamental question about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR): Has the exercise removed large numbers of people who were genuine, eligible voters and actually cast their ballots in 2025? Or did the electoral rolls used for that election contain a large number of names that should never have been there — including people who had died, shifted or were duplicated? The Election Commission of India (ECI) needs to account for the discrepancy.
An Alt News analysis of constituency-wise data procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from ECI’s own records shows that the draft roll published on August 31, 2026, under the SIR has fewer names than the number of people who voted in the 2025 election in 24 constituencies.
Delhi SIR in Numbers
The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, has resulted in more than 13 crore names being excluded from draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories, according to The Indian Express. In Delhi, the draft roll has shrunk by 58,73,159 names, or 37.6%, compared with the 2025 electoral roll.
The SIR began with a base list of 1.45 crore names — 11.16 lakh fewer than the electoral roll used for the 2025 election. Every elector on the base list was to receive an enumeration form from a booth level officer (BLO) and return the completed form. Forms that were not returned were marked “uncollectable” and assigned one of the ASDDO categories: absent, shifted, dead, duplicate or other. These electors were then excluded from the draft roll. Across Delhi, 47,56,722 forms, which is nearly a third of the base list, were marked uncollectable.
The exclusions were unevenly distributed. In South East Delhi, an average of 43.5% of the base-list names in each constituency were marked uncollectable, compared with 24.3% in Outer North Delhi.
The 24 Constituencies Which Throw up a Puzzle
In February 2025, Sangam Vihar had 2,05,647 names on its electoral roll, and 1,25,723 people voted. BJP’s Chandan Kumar Choudhary won the seat by 344 votes — the narrowest margin in the city. The SIR draft roll now lists 1,14,412 electors in Sangam Vihar: 91,235 fewer than the 2025 roll and 11,311 fewer than the number of people who actually voted.
The disparity extends across 24 constituencies. A total of 28,89,268 people voted in these seats in 2025, while the SIR draft roll now has just 27,66,145 names. This means that, even under the impossible assumption that every person on the current draft roll voted in 2025, at least 1,23,123 people who actually voted last year are no longer on the draft rolls of these constituencies.
That is a floor, not an estimate of the actual number. The real number of 2025 voters missing from the draft rolls can only be higher.
These 24 constituencies had 49,14,127 electors in 2025, of whom 58.8% voted. The SIR draft roll now contains 27,66,145 names — just 56.3% of the 2025 electorate, below the 58.8% turnout. In Tughlakabad, 56.1% of electors voted in 2025, while the draft roll contains just 49% of the 2025 electorate. In New Delhi, 56.7% voted; the draft roll contains 48.1%.
Across these constituencies, the electoral roll has fallen by 21,47,982 names, or 43.7%, since 2025. Of these, 4,10,759 names were already absent from the SIR base list, while 17,37,223 forms were marked uncollectable during the revision. Tughlakabad has the highest uncollectable rate in Delhi, at 47.8% of its base list.
All seven constituencies in South East Delhi — Jangpura, Kasturba Nagar, Sangam Vihar, Kalkaji, Tughlakabad, Badarpur and Okhla — are among the 24 constituencies where the draft roll is smaller than the number of people who voted in 2025.
In four seats the gap between the draft roll and 2025 turnout is larger than the margin that decided the seat. These are: Sangam Vihar, New Delhi, Delhi Cantt and Rajinder Nagar. In New Delhi, Arvind Kejriwal lost by 4,089 votes. The seat had 1,08,788 electors in 2025; the draft roll has 52,368, which is 9,318 short of the number of people who voted.
The Cuts are not Over
It is also worth remembering that the draft roll is not the final roll; it is likely to shrink further.
After the uncollectable forms were set aside, a second round of exclusions began. Electors whose names appeared on the draft roll are now being served notices requiring them to produce documents. Those unable to establish their eligibility risk being excluded from the final roll. In these 24 constituencies, 9,78,541 electors — about 35% of those on the draft roll — have been served notices. Across Delhi, the figure is 33.13 lakh.
The impact could extend well beyond these 24 constituencies. If just one in 10 of the electors served notices is ultimately excluded, 39 of Delhi’s 70 constituencies would have fewer names on the final roll than the number of people who voted there in 2025.
The Question the EC has to Answer
In other words, in February 2025, the ECI’s roll for these 24 constituencies had 49.14 lakh names, and 28.89 lakh people voted. Its own revision now leaves just 27.66 lakh names on the draft roll — fewer than the number of people who actually voted in those constituencies 18 months ago. And the roll is still shrinking.
The numbers demand an explanation. Either the SIR has excluded large numbers of genuine, living residents who voted in the 2025 election, or the rolls on which the ECI conducted that election contained lakhs of names that should not have been there. Either way, the discrepancy is one the Commission needs to account for.
It is also, in substance, the same Election Commission. The Delhi election was conducted under chief election commissioner (CEC) Rajiv Kumar, with Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as election commissioners. Gyanesh Kumar took over as CEC on February 19, 2025, just days after the results. He has since overseen the SIR exercise.
Questions from Inside the Commission
These numbers come at a time when the SIR is itself facing scrutiny within the Election Commission.
An investigation by The Indian Express, published on September 23, reported that two of the three members of the Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, objected on record at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders issued during the nationwide rollout of the SIR. In several instances, they recorded that decisions had been taken without their knowledge. The report does not examine Delhi, but one of the concerns it raises is directly relevant to the revision here.
Who decided? The ECI has repeatedly responded to allegations of electoral-roll manipulation by pointing out that rolls in each constituency are prepared and maintained under the authority of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), a statutory official. But according to The Indian Express, both Commissioners raised concerns that this safeguard was being weakened. Joshi flagged the increasing centralisation of the electoral-roll database, while Sandhu recorded that state election officials had said they did not have full access to ERONet, the software used to maintain the rolls.
That raises a question for Delhi: when 17.37 lakh names were marked uncollectable across 24 constituencies, and all seven constituencies in South East Delhi were among those with the highest rates, who made those determinations? Were they made by the constituency-level EROs, as the statutory framework envisages, or were decisions being taken or directed elsewhere? The ECI has not publicly explained this.
Alt News has sent questions to the Election Commission of India seeking an explanation. This report will be updated if and when a response is received.
The constituency-level data used in this report was procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from records published by the Election Commission of India and the chief electoral officer (CEO), Delhi. Alt News independently verified the figures against the original ECI and CEO Delhi documents. The constituency-wise figures for electors issued notices are as compiled by Mandate Analytics.
SIR-related data for Delhi and other states is available at macinsights.in.

Can Man City juggle WSL title defence and Champions League?
- Published
When Manchester City began the defence of their Women's Super League title there was one question on everyone's minds.
Can they compete on multiple fronts?
In previous years, City have struggled to go far in the Women's Champions League at the same time as challenging for the WSL title.
They made just three signings in the summer and retained most of their squad from last season when they won a first WSL title in a decade.
Manager Andree Jeglertz would have to rotate his squad and live up to expectations - and so far he has done a good job.
Jeglertz's substitutions pay off
It has been an impressive start to the season for City, who have won every game in the WSL and are yet to lose in Europe.
Their squad depth has been important, as Jeglertz is yet to name the same starting XI, but it has not impacted their rhythm.
And his substitutions have had an impact with Beth Mead assisting against Birmingham City and Kerstin Casparij scoring with her first touch against Arsenal.
City also came from 2-0 down at Bayern Munich to draw their opening Champions League game and also came from behind to level 1-1 with Real Madrid.
They have also gained six points from losing positions in the WSL, the most by any team.
It remains early days but is Jeglertz showing he can juggle competing demands well?
"If you look at all the games we have played this season so far, I think the substitutions and changes we have made in the last half an hour has quite often turned the game around," said Jeglertz following their 4-2 win over Arsenal.
"We really have finished off on a high. We have never dropped that. I think that is something for us to [take forward].
"You can only start with 11 players but you can make five substitutions. The ones that have come in, no matter who it is, have always affected it in a good way."
Despite finishing runners-up to Chelsea in the WSL in both 2019 and 2020, City did not go beyond the last-16 stage in Europe during those seasons.
They came second in the WSL again in 2021 and reached at least the quarter-finals in both domestic cup competitions and the Champions League.
But that took its toll on them the following two years as they fell in the qualifying stages of the Champions League and dropped to third, then fourth in the WSL.
They do not want to repeat it again.
England international Lauren Hemp, who has been in electric form, said their draws in Europe were "not our standard" despite facing tough opposition.
Manager Jeglertz was pleased with their second half display against Real Madrid but like Hemp, still craves more as he knows the challenge will only get harder.
"We have played two teams that are definitely at a very high level. If you want to go far in the tournament, you also need to win these games," said Jeglertz.
"We have two points and haven't lost and we had two good halves. But we're still looking for a 90 minutes where we feel we can do a great game.
"It's an OK start. It's not ideal but it's a good start. We know what is needed from us for the rest of the tournament."
City show squad depth is strong
City know there is a long way to go. It is only five games into the WSL season and they have another four matches to play in the league phase in Europe.
Several players including Vivianne Miedema, Sydney Lohmann, Rebecca Knaak and Risa Shimizu are recovering from injury, while Sam Coffey picked up a knock in their crucial victory over Arsenal on Sunday.
But they have already showed their squad depth is good enough and they have resilience which will be needed later down the line.
Of their 16 goals scored in the WSL this season, 10 have come in the second half, including three in stoppage time.
Key players such as Kerstin Casparij, Khadija Shaw and Yui Hasegawa have all played fewer minutes at this stage than they did last season in the WSL.
USA international Coffey, one of their most crucial midfielders, has featured in every game but has only played 90 minutes once as Jeglertz has rotated effectively.
This was shown on Sunday as vice-captain Casparij came on against Arsenal to give her side the lead in the 63rd minute.
"At half-time I knew I was going to come on so I had a good chunk of time to prepare and get ready to play my game," said Casparij.
"That's what Andree does. He's really clear with us and it allows me to play my game, trust my instinct, trust my gut and play with a lot of freedom.
"We've got incredible resilience and mentality within this team. We've got incredible players coming off the bench, changing the game.
"That is so important because it's the whole team that you need, especially in a long season like this. Nothing is won yet but we have to keep up this mentality."

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
They insist "there are no epidemic risks for the population".
The US, however, has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice. He accused the media of reporting "false information".
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Rospotrebnadzor had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
- infected flea bites
- contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
- the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.
