More fire, more ash, more crime, more death. And a globally important ecosystem driven ever more rapidly towards a point of no return. That is the prospect for the Amazon rainforest for at least the next four years if Flávio Bolsonaro holds on to the lead he established this week in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.
This appears to be of far more concern to the outside world than to voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.
The far-right son of the former president and jailed coup-monger Jair Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote, putting him in pole position before the 25 October runoff with the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was backed by 44.2%.
The result is an unnerving jolt to climate and nature campaigners. Taken out of context, this appears to be a vote against the forest. The current administration of Lula (as the veteran Brazilian president is best known) has reduced deforestation in the Amazon by almost 50%. But that success secured little noticeable electoral traction for either Lula or pro-forest candidates in other polls held the same day. The former environment minister Marina Silva lost a bid for the Senate and Joenia Wapichana, a former head of Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, failed to win a seat in Congress. Out of 57 Indigenous candidates, only two won.
Flávio Bolsonaro is the heir to the political legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, a former army captain whose four years in power resulted in a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying 2bn trees.
If he wins, Bolsonaro has promised to free his father, who was imprisoned for plotting a military coup and attempting to annihilate democracy in Brazil. He has said that his father could have any position he wants in his administration.
Flávio Bolsonaro has shown that he will be just as willing as his father to dismantle protections for climate and nature and allow illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers to invade Indigenous territories. As a lawmaker, he backed a 2019 bill to eliminate requirements for landowners in the Amazon to conserve a proportion of native vegetation. In his manifesto, he completely ignored the climate crisis. And he has courted support from some of the most predatory landowners in the rainforest.
He is also part of a movement – Bolsonarism – that is geared towards maximising profits for extractive industries regardless of the environmental cost. Take its victorious candidate for the Amazonian state of Pará, Daniel Santos, who was fined $275,000 (£208,000) for deforestating 280 hectares (692 acres) of his land without authorisation and is now promising to waive such penalties. As a result of Sunday’s election, Bolsonarists now control seven of the nine states in the Brazilian Amazon, and could win an eighth in the runoffs.
Bolsonarist influence in the legislature, which is dominated by agribusiness interests, is also growing. Jair’s brother, Eduardo, and mother-in-law, Michelle, were elected to the Senate, while an uncle and brother won seats in the lower house of deputies. Even before the election, Congress had been pushing hard to weaken environmental protections. Now it will be almost impossible to stop, particularly given the current chaos in the supreme court, which has been a partial check on untrammelled expansion by miners, ranchers and monoculturalists. Against these forces, Lula would struggle to govern even if he wins the runoff.
As a result, it is not just the Amazon that is in peril, but all of Brazil’s biomes, its traditional peoples and the stability of the global climate. The question now is why voters paid so little heed to these concerns.
That inquest is already under way. Many focus on the influence of social media, which has been used far more effectively by the far right. During the Bolsonaro administration, his sons were part of the “hate cabinet” that spread fear and disinformation via WhatsApp groups and other online channels – Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos, was indicted by federal police for leading the group. Environmentalists were often the target.
Another factor is the expansion of US-style Pentecostalism, which is steadily supplanting Catholicism across Brazil, particularly in the Amazon. The political and environmental consequences of that religious shift can be seen by comparing the pro-nature treatise of the past two popes with the sermons of many evangelical preachers who encourage followers to seek wealth today as much as, if not more, than following moral creeds to ensure a good afterlife.
Lula, 80, has been slow to adapt. Although he is arguably the most iconic and successful Latin American politician of the 21st century, his messaging seems less attuned to the people than it was in his heyday. The Workers party has struggled in an era of weaker unions and in some ways been the victim of its own success – with education and social policies that raised millions out of poverty and created greater expectations for consumption and entrepreneurism; and huge subsidies to farmers, who now support the right wing because they chaff at environmental limits.
Tied into those explanations are the geopolitics of the climate and nature crisis, which is exacerbating great power rivalry between the US and China and amplifying extreme ideologies as much as extreme weather. In this light, the Brazil election is just the latest in a broader pattern of the far right taking control to expand extractivism despite growing evidence that the capitalist economy is breaking planetary boundaries. In the past two years, Donald Trump has ripped apart environmental regulations in the US and treated the rest of the Americas as his sphere of influence. Argentina was already onboard. Venezuela has been invaded for its resources, while in Colombia, Peru and Chile there has been a sharp shift to the right.
Will Brazil be the next domino to fall to Trumpism and its bonfire approach to nature? The Bolsonaro family certainly hope so. Jair went so far as to salute the US flag. His son Eduardo urged the US to apply tariffs on Brazilian people to “punish” the government for imprisoning his father. The Brazilian intelligence agency has warned that the US was trying to interfere in the election.
That election isn’t over yet. Lula stands a small chance if he can win over the many millions of voters who chose not to mark their ballots for either candidate. But the odds are stacked against him. Most of the eliminated candidates were on the right so their supporters are more likely to switch to Bolsonaro. No first round leader has ever failed to win the runoff of a Brazilian presidential election.
Voters, of course, are allowed to change their minds. Either on 25 October or, constitutionally, in four years’ time. But for how much longer will that be possible? If Bolsonaro wins, it won’t just be Lula that is finished, it could also be the Amazon and democracy itself.

Srinagar, Oct 7: Government Medical College (GMC) Anantnag has suspended seven MBBS students of the 2025 batch from academic activities and evicted them from the boys hostel following reports of alleged ragging on the intervening night of Sep 28 and 29.
The disciplinary action was ordered by the Principal, GMC Anantnag, on Oct 3 after the college’s Anti-Ragging Committee conducted an inquiry into the incident.
The Principal ordered that the students “shall stand suspended from all academic activities, including theory and practical classes, clinical postings and examinations, with immediate effect and till further orders.”
They “shall stand suspended from the Boys Hostel, GMC Anantnag” and “shall stand evicted from their hostel accommodation with immediate effect till further orders,” the order said.
The action was taken “in order to ensure a safe and secure environment for hostel residents,” it said.
The Anti-Ragging Committee “took cognisance of the matter” and conducted a “detailed, impartial and exhaustive enquiry,” affording the students “due opportunity” and acting “without prejudice to any party.”
The committee’s findings, submitted to the Principal GMC Anantnag, Dr Junaid Salam Wani established the involvement of the seven students, according to the order.
It does not detail the nature of the alleged ragging or the specific acts attributed to them.
Their parents or guardians have been directed to “accompany their wards” and appear before the Anti-Ragging Committee on Oct 12 at 2:30 p.m. for further proceedings.
Failure to comply “shall consequently result in initiation of further disciplinary action as envisaged under the extant National Medical Commission (NMC) Anti-Ragging Regulations and institutional statutes,” the order said.
A copy of the order was forwarded to members of the Anti-Ragging Committee, the Registrar Academics and the Chief Warden of GMC Anantnag. The Warden of the Boys Hostel was directed to ensure the eviction of the students from the hostel.
The finding is an internal disciplinary determination by the college and does not amount to a criminal conviction.
The action comes days after SKIMS Medical College Hospital, Bemina, suspended five MBBS students and interns for a week over a separate reported ragging case, imposing aRs 10,000 fine on each and summoning their parents before its Anti-Ragging Committee.
SKIMS Principal Prof. FazlQadir Parry had said the institution followed a “zero-tolerance policy towards ragging,” with the safety and well-being of students its priority.
Anti-Ragging Committees operate across professional and other higher-education institutions, and students are required to furnish anti-ragging undertakings as part of the admission process.
Under the Jammu and Kashmir Prohibition of Ragging Act, 2011, ragging is a punishable offence carrying up to two years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to Rs 10,000, or both.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) held a protest at Shivaji Park Maidan in Mumbai on 02 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. The protesters raised concerns over the alleged exclusion of voters during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanded greater transparency in the election process. Although Mumbai Police had denied permission for the meeting, hundreds of people took part in the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for violating the restrictions.
Against this backdrop, a video circulating on social media (here, here) claims to show footage of the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of CJP’s protest demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar at Shivaji Park ground in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The viral video is unrelated to the CJP protest in Mumbai. It is an old video showing a public meeting organised by AIMIM leader Asaduddin Owaisi at the Central Library Ground in Bhopal on 15 September, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same footage (here and here) from 18 September 2026, nearly two weeks before the CJP protest in Mumbai.
We found that the video was uploaded on Facebook and Instagram by a Bhopal-based content creator, Amin Siddiqui, on 18 September 2026. We also found several other videos showing the same scenes on his Instagram page (here, here, and here). These videos indicate that the footage is from a public meeting addressed by AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
News reports (here and here) also confirm that Owaisi addressed a public meeting at the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal on 15 September 2026, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly.
When we compared the visuals from the viral video with the location on Google Street View, we found that the surroundings match the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, confirming that the video is related to the Bhopal meeting.
To sum up, an old Bhopal public meeting video is being falsely shared as a CJP protest video in Mumbai.

Formula 1 stages its sixth and final Sprint event of the year this weekend to conclude the first flyaway triple header of the sport's busy 2026 season run in.
And, for the first time, the Sprint format is being used at the Singapore Grand Prix and its Marina Bay street track, home of the sport's original night race.
But on a track not known for its overtaking, what kind of weekend can we expect with two qualifying sessions and two races?

How the Singapore GP weekend will be different to normal
When the Sprint format was first introduced at three races for the 2021 season, the tracks selected - Silverstone, Monza and Interlagos - were ones deemed to be particularly good for racing so to justify the addition of a 100km race on the Saturday as an appetiser to the main Sunday Grand Prix.
That has generally continued to be the case in the selection of Sprint venues up to this year, with perhaps the inclusion of Imola in 2022 the surprise exception.
Street tracks, which by their nature traditionally aren't as overtaking-friendly as conventional permanent tracks, have generally not featured on that yearly list.
Azerbaijan did host a Sprint in 2023, but Baku's wall-lined street track features the longest straight on the calendar and so allows passing.
Singapore certainly falls more into the category of conventional street track - there are no long straights of note and overtaking opportunities are severely limited around the confined, twisty layout.
The floodlit race is instead most known for its physicality owing to the hot and humid conditions of the Asian country and the fact the 62-lap race pushes towards the two-hour limit around a 19-corner lap that features plenty of 90-degree turns.
So, holding a second race this weekend appears counterintuitive in one sense to the original purpose of the Sprint format. However, there are flip sides to the decision.
The first relates to qualifying. Given the lack of passing opportunities in the race, qualifying is always considered absolutely essential at Marina Bay and, like all street tracks where the walls are so close, the Saturday spectacle is often spectacular.
The circuit was the scene of one of the most famous qualifying laps in the sport's recent history when Lewis Hamilton surged to pole position for Mercedes in 2018, while numerous drivers have come a cropper against the barriers over the years when pushing for a decisive, grid-defining lap.
This year there will be two such sessions - Sprint Qualifying on Friday followed by Grand Prix Qualifying on Saturday - which means double the qualifying challenge and, therefore, double the jeopardy for drivers.
The Sprint format also means drivers and teams will have two-thirds less time to hone their cars' set-ups and settings for the competitive sessions given there is only a single one-hour session of practice running instead of the usual three.
Building up rhythm and confidence is crucial on a street track so drivers know they will have to shortcut that process this time in Singapore. However, that is clearly easier said than done, increasing the likelihood of mistakes in sessions that count and teams going down set-up cul-de-sacs.
A further potential twist comes in the scheduling of the sessions.
That sole practice takes place in the hours before sunset at 4.30pm local time (9.30am BST) whereas Sprint Qualifying is at 8.30pm (1.30pm BST) when the floodlights will be in full effect and temperatures will be a little cooler, creating a set-up conundrum for teams as cars, engines and tyres won't necessarily behave the same in different conditions.
Parc-ferme conditions mean teams can't then touch the cars again for Saturday's Sprint, which takes place during the late afternoon like practice.
A precursor to Monaco 2027
Next season the Sprint format is being expanded to 10 events and, when the full 2027 calendar was published last month, the surprise news came from the fact that Monaco had been selected to host one of them.
The Principality's street circuit is even narrower and harder to pass on than Singapore's, which has increasingly made qualifying the standout aspect of that particular race weekend as cars have become wider and more reliable.
Staging two races there next year therefore appears to be as counter-intuitive as it does in Singapore, yet the opposite thinking in terms of doubling up on qualifying and building in the potential for more unpredictability now appears to be a balancing factor.
It will be interesting to hear what drivers, who have mostly been supportive about bringing the Sprint to Monaco next year, make of the Singapore Sprint experience as it unfolds.
A four-team fight for Singapore victory?
Irrespective of how much unpredictability there is this weekend on Singapore's Sprint debut, the weekend promises to be competitive in the battle for victory at the front.
Max Verstappen's impressive win for Red Bull last week in Malaysia means F1's 'Big Four' teams have now all won at least one race in the first year of the sport's new regulations, with Mercedes' early-season dominance a thing of the past despite the Silver Arrows' continued command of both world championship races.
Marina Bay was actually one of only two races that Mercedes won last year although George Russell, who dominated that weekend, already knows his hopes of going back-to-back are effectively over thanks to a grid penalty for excessive engine usage that will send him to the back of Sunday's grid.
Russell will still hope to be a factor at the front in Saturday's Sprint, though, where the grid penalty does not apply.
But it is clearly championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who dominated Monaco but crashed in Baku qualifying, who will be carrying Mercedes' front-running hopes into Sunday on a weekend the team bid to get a handle on why their big aerodynamic upgrade brought to Malaysia did not deliver the expected step forward.
The in-form Verstappen will also likely be a factor at the front for resurgent Red Bull as he finally looks to win the Singapore Grand Prix - at the 10th attempt.
Marina Bay is the one long-standing track on the current calendar (Madrid, where Verstappen finished second last month, only joined the schedule this year) that the Dutchman has yet to win at.
Verstappen has qualified and finished second in each of the last two years, so has certainly been knocking on the door to do so. Red Bull will hope their recent performance gains elsewhere transfer to the unique demands of Singapore.
Then there is McLaren, who claimed dominant victories with Lando Norris on F1's last visits to high-downforce tracks in Hungary and Zandvoort but have hitherto not enjoyed great success across the first two legs of the Azerbaijan-Malaysia-Singapore triple header.
The absence of long straights is good news for Ferrari, who will hope the race pace that allowed Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to recover strongly from the team's disastrous slick-tyre strategy at the start of last Sunday's delayed Sepang race will transfer to the slower-speed streets of Singapore.

The ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 is a practical, performance-driven business laptop featuring a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, an exceptional keyboard, excellent port selection, and easy RAM/storage upgradability. However, its main drawbacks are mediocre battery life, a dim display limited to 45% NTSC, and an underwhelming webcam.
ASUS offers the ExpertBook series in many configurations. If you want the best business laptop Asus offers, consider the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra. If you are a business owner who wants a premium design without compromising essential business features, the ASUS ExpertBook B Series is worth considering. Finally, the ASUS ExpertBook P Series is for those looking for an affordable business laptop without paying a premium.
In that regard, the ASUS ExpertBook P3 is a sweet spot for people looking for an affordable business laptop. It doesn’t try to compete with the flashy, ultra-thin consumer aesthetics of the Apple MacBook Air or Dell XPS line; instead, it positions itself as an aggressive challenger to the Lenovo ThinkPad and HP EliteBook ecosystems, as well as other business laptop ranges.
I have been using the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 version (2026) for the past several days. Overall, it has been a solid business laptop. The model I am testing comes with a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 255H and delivers excellent performance, a reliable port selection, the best keyboard in its class, and plenty of business-focused features.
ASUS has also expanded the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G2 series, now offering more choices than before with both Intel and AMD configurations across different sizes, while also addressing some of the shortcomings we noticed with the earlier ExpertBook P series.
In this full, detailed review, I will share my experience with the ASUS P3 G1, compare it to the original P3 launched in 2025, and see how it stacks up against the recently announced ASUS P3 G2 series. By the end, you should have a better idea of whether the Asus P3 G1 still makes sense or is worth going for the latest generations instead.
Table of Contents
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review
Design and Build: Practical Over Premium
Asus ExpertBook laptops are easy to spot from miles away. Most models across the lineup look the same and follow a very similar design language, with an understated gray finish and a clean, minimal look.
Asus ExpertBook P3 G1 also follows the same design. It may not impress you with flashy looks or an ultra-slim profile, which is something the ExpertBook P3 isn’t trying to do anyway. This is a practical, business-first laptop.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 comes in two chassis variants. The 1A variant has a plastic chassis, and the 2A variant has a metal chassis for those who want an even sturdier, more premium build.
My unit comes with a plastic body, but it doesn’t feel cheap by any means. In fact, it is a step up from some of the older ExpertBook laptops I have reviewed in the past.
Although the chassis is plastic, the matte, grainy finish hides it and gives it a much more premium feel. I love minimal laptop designs, and the ASUS ExpertBook takes that approach even further with nothing but the ASUS logo on the lid. The matte, grainy finish is also fingerprint-resistant; as a result, smudges don’t show up, and it stays clean.
The same treatment continues when you open the lid. The hinge is now slightly stronger. The display is stiffer than ideal to position, but it still wobbles a bit when you type and change its angle.
The lid opens up to 180 degrees, allowing the display to lie completely flat on the surface. It can come in handy if you want to share your screen with someone across the table. One limitation, though: since this variant doesn’t have a touchscreen, you cannot really use the display while it is lying flat.
Build quality is stronger than last generation, but it still has noticeable flex, especially in the center of the keyboard and between the touchpad and the keyboard. Thankfully, I didn’t notice it while typing. The deck doesn’t bend much under normal use unless you press harder.
The rounded corners also make the laptop more comfortable to hold during longer carrying periods.
One thing Asus continues to get right is port selection. In a world where fewer ports have become the norm for a premium experience, Asus ExpertBook P3 supports all major ports, including one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, a full-size RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet port, HDMI 2.1 TMDS, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a Kensington Nano lock. You get pretty much every port you expect from a business laptop. That also means you can connect most everyday accessories directly to the laptop without carrying a separate dongle.
The chassis is also MIL-STD 810H tested across 24 procedures. The laptop should handle everyday wear and tear. Note that the laptop is not water-resistant.
The keyboard supports backlighting. This makes it easy to see and type in low-light conditions. The backlight also doesn’t leak when you’re looking straight at the laptop. It also has durable keys, and ASUS claims the keyboard is tested for up to 10 million keystrokes to withstand wear and tear over time.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 is available in both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. My review unit is the 14-inch variant with a WUXGA 16:10 display. The side bezels are fairly noticeable, and there is a rather large chin at the bottom that also houses the Asus ExpertBook logo. Above the display is a physical privacy shutter, which I truly appreciate for business-centric users who want better privacy.
Display: Good for Work, Not for Creative Use
The 14-inch display is a sweet spot if you want something compact without giving up too much screen space.
ASUS ExpertBook doesn’t get the kind of high-end OLED displays Asus offers on some of its high-end laptops or even more affordable VivoBook models. It is a 14-inch IPS-level display with WUXGA 1920 × 1200 resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, a 60Hz refresh rate, up to 300 nits of brightness, and 45% NTSC color coverage.
The display quality is decent and gets the job done, especially if you’re buying the ExpertBook primarily for office work. It is perfectly fine for browsing and using office apps like spreadsheets and documents, but if you work on photos or video editing, you will probably want something with better color coverage.
The display also has an anti-glare coating, which does a good job of cutting down reflections and makes it easier to use in bright environments. However, the trade-off is that a matte finish coating removes some of the visual punch you get from glossy panels. Colors aren’t as vibrant, although the text remains sharp.
Watching videos and content on this WUXGA IPS-level panel isn’t a pleasant experience, but as I said, for everyday tasks such as browsing, spreadsheets, and other office applications, it feels comfortable to use, and the text looks sharp enough to read clearly.
Performance: More Power Than Most Office Users Need
Performance is easily one of the ExpertBook P3’s strongest aspects. Asus offers it with either a Core Ultra 5 225H or Core Ultra 7 255H. My unit came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, paired with 16GB DDR5 RAM and a 512GB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD.
At the heart of the configuration is the Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, a high-performance processor with 16 cores, 16 threads, a maximum clock speed of 5.1GHz, and integrated Intel Graphics. In everyday use, this combination handles almost any task without breaking a sweat. Whether you’re using multiple graphics-heavy applications, running dozens of browser tabs, or switching between office apps all day.
Another advantage is upgradability. Asus ExpertBook P3 comes with two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, and the existing RAM isn’t soldered to the motherboard, so you can upgrade later if you want to, and it won’t cost you a bomb upfront, which is the case with most modern laptops.
It also has two storage slots: one M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 slot and one M.2 2230 PCIe 4.0 slot, giving you more room to expand the storage later.
One thing I did notice is that the laptop gets quite warm at the bottom even during something as basic as browsing the web. You can definitely feel the heat when using it in your lap. It is not entirely surprising, though, considering the Core Ultra 7 255H is an H-series processor designed for higher performance.
Keyboard and Trackpad: The Keyboard Is the Star
The keyboard is easily one of my favorite things about the Asus ExpertBook P3. It offers one of the best typing experiences I have had on a laptop after Mac. A lot of that comes down to the 1.5mm key travel, which delivers a great typing experience. The keys are also large and well spaced, giving your fingers plenty of room to move around. It didn’t take me long to get comfortable with this keyboard.
The trackpad is also large enough for daily use. The large surface area makes it easy to move the cursor and also use gestures.
I have no issues with the keyboard and trackpad, though some users may find the fingerprint sensor placement inconvenient because it is integrated into the power button. To prevent accidental presses, ASUS made the power button slightly firmer.
Battery Life: The Biggest Compromise
This kind of performance is always welcome, especially if you regularly handle high-demand tasks. The trade-off, though, is battery life. My configuration comes with a 50Wh, 3-cell battery, and the ExpertBook P3 takes a noticeable hit here.
Even for basic use, I was getting only about 8-9 hours. On medium to heavy gaming, the battery life dropped to 4 to 5 hours, which isn’t the performance you want if you plan to use it on battery power all day.
ASUS bundles a 65W USB-C charger in the box, and it can take your laptop from 0 to 100 in less than 2 hours. That’s fairly quick, but I really wish Windows laptop makers offered more travel-friendly options instead of big, bulky charging bricks and three-pin plugs.
Sound: Decent, but Nothing Special
The speakers are decently loud, but they don’t get particularly loud. ASUS uses two built-in speakers with Dirac audio support. Thankfully, Asus includes a built-in 3.5mm headphone jack, so you can plug in wired headphones or earphones directly without relying on the built-in speakers.
Windows 11 Home: Still Too Cluttered
I have never been a fan of Windows’ cluttered experience. If you’ve used Windows for years, you probably won’t mind much, but if you are coming from a Mac or Linux, you’ll have to deal with Windows’ cluttered experience first.
It took me more than three hours to set up the device, including the unwanted Windows updates I had to install during setup. Plus, the Windows update prompts never stop. Even Microsoft has promised to improve the Windows laptop experience by eliminating these unwanted distractions.
Since this is an ExpertBook, ASUS includes business-centric features, including AI ExpertMeet for meetings. However, this configuration lacks some useful Copilot+ AI features for those who care about privacy and want to run AI features locally on the device. The Core Ultra 7 255H delivers up to 13 TOPS of NPU performance, well short of the 40+ TOPS required for a Copilot+ PC. You may need to rely on cloud processing for more demanding AI features.
Camera: Still Needs Work
ASUS has been pretty good at improving the little things in everyday use, but the camera is still one area that needs work. My configuration comes with a 1080p FHD IR camera with Windows Hello support and a physical privacy shutter. Even on the maxed-out ExpertBook Ultra, the camera quality is rather underwhelming, especially on business laptops like this, where it matters a lot.
Even in good lighting, the camera adds plenty of noise, and in low light, it gets worse. However, you can always connect an external camera if camera quality matters to you. But this is something Asus needs to improve.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review Verdict: Powerful and Practical, but Battery Holds It Back
Overall, if performance is high on your priority list, then the ASUS ExpertBook P3 might be a better choice. Everyday tasks feel quick and responsive, plus it also has plenty of power for more demanding tasks. The excellent keyboard, with 1.5mm key travel, makes typing sessions comfortable, and the full selection of ports lets you connect any peripherals without constantly reaching for or using a dongle. The biggest advantage of the Asus ExpertBook P3 is plenty of room to upgrade later. It offers dual SO-DIMM slots for memory and dual M.2 slots for additional PCIe storage.
Among the pros are also some compromises. Battery life takes a noticeable hit when you push the processor harder, and while the laptop can handle some AI workloads locally, it cannot run the full set of Copilot+ PC features.

SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about the Season 4 finale of Apple TV‘s Ted Lasso, titled “Being Alive.”
If you thought the penultimate episode of Ted Lasso was packed with Mae’s shocking death, Keeley’s (Juno Temple) surprise pregnancy and Zelda’s (Tracey Ullman) unexpected (for some) deceit, you’d better buckled up for the finale.
The 56-minute episode featured a touching memorial for Mae, including a moving song by Niamh (Aisling Sharkey) and Siobhan (Rex Hayes); not one but two AFC Richmond manager shakeups with Roy Kent (Brett Goldstein) quitting the men’s team to take the helm of his old team Chelsea, signaling a possible exit for the fan favorite character; and Alice Chilton (Tanya Reynolds) promoted to head coach of the women’s team upon Ted’s (Jason Sudeikis) recommendation, with him and Coach Beard (Brendan Hunt) as her assistants.
And that was not all. The shareholder showdown offered a twist too, with Zelda’s henchman Hugo switching sides and securing the Milk sisters’ shares for Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), which, along with Mae’s 2% left to her in her will, gave the accidental football club owner an unassailable majority 51% ownership. Additionally, Ted told his son Henry about his father’s suicide. The finale also managed to squeeze in a marriage proposal as Rebecca spontaneously popped the question to long-term boyfriend Matthijs in her office.
Watch on Deadline
Hunt, who co-created the series and co-wrote the finale with Sudeikis, spoke with Deadline about the episode’s twists and how they set up a potential fifth season, addressing speculation that a renewal is imminent. He explained whether the finale marked the exit of Goldstein as a series regular (and Temple by association as Roy and Keeley are a couple again). Goldstein is the creator, exec producer and star of a new Amazon comedy series, Escorted, in addition to his duties on Apple TV’s Shrinking and his movie career.
Bad news for fans of Ted Lasso’s original Richmond men’s team who have been holding out hope for a larger presence of the players in the show’s new incarnation. The cameos by most of them in the Season 4 finale may have been the last we saw the team in a planned “passing of the torch” moment from the men to the women, Hunt said, explaining why Phil Dunster’s Jamie Tartt didn’t make the scene.
Hunt clarified how Ted’s conversation with Rebecca led to Alice’s promotion and how the new dynamic may impact Ted. He also cleared confusion over the title of the finale, originally listed as “The Departing Lass,” which changed to “Being Alive” when the episode aired.
Additionally, Hunt addressed the divisive character Zelda and whether Ullman would come back next season an shared the surprising inspiration for Beard’s new look in Season 4.
In separate parts of the interview published earlier, Hunt revealed that there was an idea for the late actor Anthony Head to be in the Season 4 finale and explained why the finale employed a cover of the theme song performed by Brandi Carlile and whether that the new version may be here to stay.
DEADLINE: I hear that Season 5 renewal is imminent. What do you say?
BRENDAN HUNT: Where did you hear that?
DEADLINE: I have my sources.
HUNT: Well, then that’s news to me. I certainly hope it happens, and I’m optimistic, but yeah, haven’t heard anything official yet. It would be nice though.
DEADLINE: And you don’t have a Season 5 writers room going, correct? My understanding is that the writers room will start after the green light.
HUNT: Yeah. As happened for Season 2, they can greenlight a room before they greenlight a season if they want, but neither has happened.
DEADLINE: There were two big manager changes at AFC Richmond in the finale, the most important for longtime fans being Roy Kent’s departure. We know how busy Brett is off-screen — he has a new show on Amazon, obviously Shrinking on Apple TV, movies. So, should we assume that he is leaving as a series regular?
HUNT: No, not necessarily. It is acknowledging that he’s a busy man and giving us some wiggle room I would say. But no, there’s no expectation of losing Roy and Keeley. But they are two very busy people, so wiggle room is a smart thing.
DEADLINE: So it’s possible that both Brett and Juno may not be series regulars in Season 5 and the Roy and Keeley storyline may not be as prominent?
HUNT: We have no idea. We don’t know if we’re coming back, and when we come back, we don’t know what’s going to be going on in their lives. But yeah, they’re both really busy. So yeah, the wiggle room.
DEADLINE: Ted’s line to Rebecca about wanting “to talk to her about the newly open manager position” came just after Roy had resigned, so I assumed that was for the vacated men’s team job, and Ted was pitching himself or Nate who had just resurfaced. Instead, we got Coach Chilton promoted. Are the two things connected?
HUNT: He doesn’t say the men’s manager position.
DEADLINE: But why did he say “newly open”?
HUNT: Because he’s coming in to let her know that he is no longer the manager of the women’s team.
DEADLINE: OK. Let’s talk about the decision to change that dynamic. It does make sense, Alice has proven herself, and it’s a women’s team, but Ted for the first time being a backup singer, how will that be? And will the show be called Alice Chilton next season?
HUNT: Yeah, I think Apple’s really excited about that (laughs). We just have to wait and see what is going to be the full impact of that dynamic. I’m certainly interested in finding out like, is this a bit pie in the sky for Ted to think he can just shift down to backseat and have someone telling him what to do and where to be and making demands of him? We’ll see how how he adjusted that. It might not be as easy as he thinks.
DEADLINE: What prompted him to do that? We didn’t get to hear his arguments to Rebecca.
HUNT: Well, he clearly is not spending enough time with his son, and he says to Henry in that previous scene, “I’m going to make some changes to make sure that I’m not missing as many of your games.”
DEADLINE: And the men’s team, is it now completely in the rearview mirror? Roy Kent was the only character that kept it in the picture even though we didn’t see any of their games or any of the players until the finale. Do we care about who the manager will be? Is there any chance for Nick Mohammed’s Nate to come back?
HUNT: I’m not sure that we do care. We do love Nick, though. The men showing up in that last episode was really meant to be a passing-of-the-torch moment, and I think that worked well. We’ve been very judicious with how much we see of the players this first season, and whether or not we’re coming back, we’ve taken the long view from the beginning.
Back in Season 1, we actually met the players just a very little bit, and a little more in Season 2 and Season 3. So if we’re able to come back, then yeah, we’ll certainly be able to start giving more time to these players now that we’ve gotten done a little bit.
DEADLINE: Speaking of the players, the two Irish twin sisters emerged as standouts at the end of the season with their hilarious telepathy pig bit in episode 9 and their touching performance at Mae’s memorial in the finale. Will we see more of that next season and more of Alice’s personal life? There was only one scene with her partner this season.
HUNT: We’ll have a lot to see but we like all these characters, and we’re gonna try to get into all of them, a little bit more now that we set the table with them. But in terms of the twins, Rex and Ash were just fantastic together. There were a few good nominees for the twins when we were casting, but in the end it was like, these are them, and the degree to which they are different and similar is fantastic. They’re so game for everything, and then to finally unlock that twin-telepathy thing towards the end was just really really cool.
DEADLINE: Did they sing that song themselves and how did that come about?
HUNT: That is a traditional Celtic song that gets sung at funerals a lot. It was actually first pitched by Declan Lowney, one of our directors, who is an Irishman himself. And yeah, they crushed it.
DEADLINE: Phil Dunster was not in the finale with the rest of the team. Was it just for logistical reasons because he has the HBO series Rooster?
HUNT: It was a logic thing. Jamie lives in Spain [He plays for Barcelona]. We’ve already seen him at that point, so we didn’t need to bring him back just to stand and applaud with the rest.
DEADLINE: Speaking of Jamie, your character Coach Beard underwent quite a transformation this season, and there was online chatter that Beard may have tried to copy Jamie Tartt’s look.
HUNT: I didn’t see that.
DEADLINE: Talk about Beard’s physical transformation. Is it simply a midlife crisis, or was there more to it?
HUNT: Yeah, he is going through a bit of a midlife crisis. First the Jane stuff, then trying to come back from the Jane stuff, and then getting the gut-punch of miscommunication on New Year’s. We were not specifically going for Jamie Tartt but what a compliment. I’ll take it.
DEADLINE: Was there inspiration for the look, though?
HUNT: Not specific to Jamie, no, the hair was more Hugh Grant in his Four Weddings and a Funeral days, and then went to the costume department and our designer Jackie Levy, and it was awesome. Like what trying-too-hard-to-look-like-a-young-person stuff do we have? Now maybe she had Jamie in mind. I can’t speak for her, but that was never discussed specifically.
DEADLINE: And the new look introduced at the end of the finale, was it Walter White-inspired?
HUNT: It’s just a bald head and goatee, Walter White didn’t invent that.
DEADLINE: Tracey Ullman’s character Zelda, I’m sure you’ve seen the discourse, she was very polarizing. Talk about her arc, and since Zelda technically is still a pretty significant Richmond owner, would you want her to come back?
HUNT: We love Tracey, and we love that character. Zelda has a stake but not a majority one. Again, the same with with Roy and Keeley, there’s wiggle room there. Hopefully we get the chance to have her come over for some more. But we’re not plot-obligated to have her around in every episode, and Tracey can go on with her life.
DEADLINE: The title of the finale changed last-minute to “Being Alive”? Why? Was “The Departing Lass” too British?
HUNT: Well, the change had been made a few weeks ago — it just apparently didn’t make it to whoever puts those titles up, so it was not as late a change as it seems. It had been “Being Alive” for the last like month at least. That was Jason’s call entirely. He didn’t walk me through his thought process entirely, what it did. I watched it last night, and when Hannah has her line about being alive, it was a nice little echo, frankly. So it is a little more than what the episode is about than just about the lass who has departed and a a cute little pun.
DEADLINE: I don’t think we ever find found out how the women’s team ended the football season, did they win the final game?
HUNT: They got promoted in the second to last episode, and then the win in the last episode is that they sold out. So the results of the game itself better than that.

Good morning. We’ve got a heartbreaking story from Jason Mast today on two friends with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Read that now, and if you need a pick-me-up afterward, read about our 2026 class of Wunderkinds.
Democrats go MAHA for the midterms
As the midterms approach, Democratic candidates including New York’s Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed are building agendas around issues like food and toxins that are important to the Make America Healthy Again movement. In some ways, it’s a rebranding of long-held progressive ideals, STAT’s Daniel Payne writes. Democrats are largely disregarding vaccine injuries, the signature issue of MAHA leader Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
“A lot of [the MAHA activists] really don’t believe that their fight is partisan,” Ocasio-Cortez said on a podcast in July, “and it’s not in many ways.” Read more from Daniel on the midterm push to woo MAHA voters, as well as what universal health issue still looms larger than the others.
83%
That’s the percentage of adults with health savings accounts and flexible spending accounts who would put that money toward oral care products like toothbrushes, toothpaste, floss, and mouthwash, if it were allowed. That interest is even higher among families and younger adults, according to a recent survey of 1,200 people by the Consumer Healthcare Products Association.
HSAs and FSAs usually don’t cover “general health products” like toothbrushes. But as sellers of these accounts beef up their lobbying power to expand the market, the distinction between what is and isn’t covered starts to sound silly. Internally, a few STAT staffers have closely followed the growing list of products that you can use your HSA to buy: mountain bikes, Meta glasses, saunas, radiation-blocking underwear … etc.
Worried about the plague? Read this
Infectious disease doctor Krutika Kuppalli’s new opinion column for STAT, ID Consult, is arriving just in time. In the wake of our collective Covid trauma, the recent death of a 28-year-old in Russia who worked at a lab that studies, among other diseases, the plague, has raised concerns around the world. (The WHO has said the case presents a “very low” risk outside Russia.)
Kuppalli offers some factual reassurance: There’s no evidence that this is the start of the next pandemic. Currently, we don’t even know what truly caused this person’s pneumonia. But as Kuppalli also explains, there’s historical context that requires transparency and independent verification here. Read more on why reports out of Russia deserve attention, not panic.
Two friends, one diagnosis, disparate outcomes
Yannick and Brecken became friends because of their diagnosis. Each boy, age 13 and 12 respectively, has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a rare, fatal muscle-wasting disease. But only Brecken has received a promising new drug to treat the condition. The medicine makes the cell’s protein-building machinery “skip” part of the gene, called an exon, behind Duchenne. But it won’t work for everyone — it has to be targeted to a patient’s specific mutation.
As Brecken grows, Yannick is losing function. This summer, the company that makes Brecken’s treatment delayed a clinical trial for another drug candidate that would treat Yannick. Brecken decided to write a letter to the company, his mom told STAT’s Jason Mast. “My friend Yannick is waiting to get the next Avidity therapy,” Brecken wrote. “He was so happy when I got it.”
Read Jason’s heartbreaking story about two friends with vastly different experiences and the regulatory landscape that has some parents taking matters into their own hands.
2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry awarded for research with an impact on pharmacology
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry this morning for “the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.” They solved a chemical mystery: Some molecules exist in the world that are mirror images of one another, a phenomenon known as chirality, from the Greek word from hand (as hands are mirror images of one another). Amino acids are among chiral molecules, and a living organism can only contain one of the versions. The other mirror molecule is found rarely elsewhere in nature, but prior to the laureates’ experiments, how such imbalance could occur was not understood.
Their research has an important impact in pharmacology, as more than half clinically employed drugs are chiral. For instance novrad, a cough medicine, and darvon, a painkiller, are mirror images of one another (hence their mirror names, too). — Annalisa Merelli
ER visits from people born outside the U.S. dropped after ICE raids
Amid mass ICE raids, dramatically increased arrests, and deadly encounters with federal agents, it’s long been clear that many immigrant patients are avoiding medical treatment. “There’s been a huge lapse in care,” a Minneapolis-based pediatrician told STAT’s Daniel Payne in February.
A study published Monday in JAMA Network Open puts some hard numbers to those claims. Researchers found that visits by people born outside of the U.S. to three Los Angeles emergency rooms dropped precipitously after immigration enforcement increased last year. At the same time, the number of hospital admissions among that population rose, suggesting that “heightened immigration enforcement may lead to avoidance of acute care among immigrant patients, with potential negative health and economic consequences for patients and the systems who care for them.”
A WUNDERful bunch of scientists
Today, STAT announced the 2026 Wunderkinds, an annual roster of ambitious, intelligent doctors and researchers at the beginning of their careers. This year, we’re spotlighting people working on important issues like “chain of thought” cognition, how immune systems talk to one another, and ethical debates in medicine. In their spare time, these scientists listen to house music, train for marathons, and hang out with the adorable 2026 class of Wunderkind pets.
Here’s a preview of some of the scholars in this year’s cohort, but I encourage you to take a spin through all of the profiles:
- Physician-researcher Andy Zeng was already interested in biology in college. But a visit to his grandmother, near the end of her life in China, planted the seed for his singular focus on understanding cancer. Today, he uses cutting-edge tools to illuminate how stem cells influence cancer.
- For years, Duke researcher Drew Schreiner observed rodents pressing levers to get rewards of cocaine, methamphetamine, and food. But all the while, he wondered about birds. “What makes us human is this ability to culturally transmit learning,” Schreiner told former STAT reporter Eric Boodman. Birds do this, too, in how they learn and teach their music. Now, he hopes his birdsong research will eventually help uncover how human brains learn, and how it could help treat diseases like Parkinson’s.
- Health policy researcher and surgeon Vishal Patel was driving and trying to queue up a new Taylor Swift album when he noticed he was drifting out of his lane. The experience inspired a widely discussed study that found traffic fatalities increase by about 15% on days with major music album releases.
