Bob Persichetti, a director of Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse, concedes that the audience bar is rising ahead of the third outing in the Oscar-decorated blockbuster franchise.
“Expectations are kind of limitless and we have to try to meet them,” he told Sony Pictures Animation President Kristine Belson with a grin during a panel discussion at the Crunchyroll Anime Future Forum.
Even though the chat took place at the Javits Center, where New York Comic Con will be held over the next few days, the point of the session was not plot teases or fan service. (Persichetti did show attendees the same work-in-progress footage from the film that screened at Cinema Con in April but Sony is holding back for now on an official teaser for the June 2027 release.)
The discussion instead focused on process and also, in keeping with the theme across other Crunchyroll sessions, about creating an animated work that draws on a multitude of influences but retains its originality.
Watch on Deadline
Belson asked Persichetti, who directs the films with Justin K. Thompson, about how things have changed since the first installment in 2018.
“There were all these questions of, like, ‘Wait, who is it really for?!'” he recalled. “Because it’s not an outright comedy. There’s going to be action in it and Spider-Man guys – what are you doing?! And I think it was at that moment when we were in the room together and we screened it. It was made very clear to us that, ‘Oh, we have been underestimating the general audience for a long time in terms of what the sophistication of an animated film can be.'”
The first film wound up winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature en route to a global box office haul of $395 million. The follow-up, Across the Spider-Verse, took in $690.5 million in 2023 and was nominated for Best Animated Feature, losing out to The Boy and the Heron.
Since the franchise left its unique mark, Persichetti said, “The animation industry is going, ‘Oh, you can make choices that seem unorthodox and still make money and still succeed.'”
In the sequel, he said, “we piled on like five different looks and wondered if it was working and people said, ‘not only is it working, but we want more,’” the director said. “What we learned is that the audience is fine with the image changing every shot. … That’s ultimately how we were able to do so many things in one movie. The narrative throughline was creating this incredible visual extravagance.”
Technology has evolved dramatically since a decade ago when the franchise began. The filmmakers and crew are “seeing more creative choices” at a preliminary stage of the process, Persichetti said. “We’re able to think about a movie, holistically, creatively, much earlier.”
The collaborative way of making the film revolves around keeping an open mind, with writer/producers Phil Lord and Christopher Miller in the mix and material taken from real-life experiences. For all of its visual energy, Persichetti said, the original film “was really a movie, in my eyes, that was about Miles and his family. It was also sort of a love letter to New York. It’s also a love letter to hip-hop music and, ultimately, a love letter to Spider-Man.”
The filmmakers have “never said no to an idea,” the director continued. “If it’s an idea we’re doing in the movie, it will be stress-tested repeatedly, and then maybe the real idea ends up being not that thing but pieces of the stuff, pieces of that idea might fall into place on something else.”
The breakthrough of the first film earned the directors considerable leeway, Perischetti said. “We are very fortunate because we’re now on our third movie. The first two movies were successful, and the studio trusts us to make these movies. So we get to explore, probably way more than others do. But I will say, even on that first movie, we were exploring things that nobody believed in, and at first we weren’t even sure worked.”

As Nandigram and Rejinagar constituencies in West Bengal go to the polls on October 6, several local journalists in Murshidabad district, where Rejinagar is located, have alleged that access to their news Facebook pages has been restricted in India. These outlets primarily covered Opposition parties and the limited campaigning they were able to carry out in the constituency.
The notices they received stated: “We repeatedly had to restrict access to content posted by you pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules… We have accordingly temporarily restricted access to your account for 7 days in India.”
Two Seats: Little in Terms of Electoral Contest
Byelections are being held in these constituencies because the elected representatives also won from other seats in the state elections earlier this year. The Nandigram assembly constituency has about 2.5 lakh people, with Muslims accounting for around 27% of the electorate. It is Suvendu Adhikari’s home constituency. In 2021, Adhikari defeated former chief minister Mamata Banerjee here by 1,956 votes. In the 2026 assembly polls, he won from Nandigram as well as Bhabanipur. He chose to retain the Bhabanipur seat where he defeated Banerjee, necessitating the byelection in Nandigram.
The Nandigram contest took an unexpected turn when the candidate of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress faction, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, withdrew her nomination on September 18. Banerjee then decided to support Congress candidate Milan Pradhan. However, within hours of Banerjee announcing her support for Pradhan, he was arrested in connection with old cases related to the 2007 Nandigram violence. Congress and the TMC questioned the timing of the arrest, while the BJP said the police action was based on pending cases and involved no political intervention. He was later granted interim bail by the Calcutta high court.
Rejinagar presents a different electoral landscape, with Muslims accounting for around 69% of its electorate. The constituency was a closely watched seat in the 2026 assembly election. Aam Janata Unnyan Party (AJUP) leader Humayun Kabir won both Nowda and Rejinagar and subsequently vacated the latter, where his victory margin was more than 58,000 votes.
The Rejinagar by-election has seen little campaigning by the main Opposition candidates, who allege police intimidation and interference by the ruling party. The Banerjee-backed Trinamool Congress faction has fielded former three-term MLA Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, who had considered withdrawing from the contest before Banerjee persuaded him to stay. The Congress has fielded Abdullahil Kafi, while the Democratic TMC faction has nominated Safiuzzaman S K and the CPI(M) Saeed Asad Ali.
Kabir has alleged that police arrested 15 of his workers in what he calls false cases, while others have fled the area. He was also questioned twice over a viral audio clip. He says he has therefore halted major campaigning and is reaching voters primarily through Facebook, while his son continues to visit some areas. Independent candidate Saiful Islam, who is close to the AJUP leadership, was arrested on September 19.
With arrests, alleged intimidation, and lack of opposition campaigning, the elections in both the seats appear to offer little in the way of a competitive contest.
Facebook Pages Reporting Local News Restricted
With the Opposition campaign already muted in both constituencies, the election is also unfolding amid allegations of censorship in Rejinagar. Local journalists who reported on issues critical of the government or law enforcement, or covered Opposition campaigns, suddenly found their Facebook pages, which were their primary outlets for publishing their work, restricted in India.
Alt News identified at least 12 such pages: Murshidabad Global Times run by Asif Roni; Hariharpara Times Bangla run by Jabbar Sheikh; Murshidabad Today run by Swapan Karigar; Murshidabad Shironam run by Rinku; Murshidabad News Time run by Baktar Sk; Reporter Press run by Rajib Sheikh; M News TV run by Muhaimenul Haque; Bartabahi News run by Aminul Islam; Hi News run by Saidur Rahman; BNS News Bangla; AN Bangla News run by Abdus Samad; and News Front Digital run by Abdul Halim.
Swapan Karigar’s Murshidabad Today, which had a following of around 7.4 lakh, was among those worst affected. A practising journalist with more than 26 years of experience, he now has a restricted account, limiting his ability to report on politics ahead of the election.
Karigar said the page had been reporting allegations of intimidation by police made by residents who support Opposition parties, including AJUP and the Congress. “A lot of common people, who have aligned themselves with opposition parties like AJUP and Congress, people who have, say, walked in political rallies, have alleged that their family members, especially women and children, are being intimidated and tortured by police officials. They (the police) have visited these houses with 12-14 cars, even. A child was also pulled by her hair, and a woman was physically assaulted. They have totally created an atmosphere of fear and intimidation before the election. We were covering these incidents, upholding the truth. That is probably why our accounts have been withheld,” he told Alt News.
We spoke to Asif Roni, whose Facebook page, Murshidabad Global Times, had around 4.47 lakh followers before it was taken down on the night of October 1 — the same day chief minister Suvendu Adhikari visited Rejinagar. Roni said the page had recorded 39 million views in the preceding 28 days. Law enforcement officials told him that the page would be withheld for seven days.
“This happened once around April, right before the assembly election,” he said. “I used to run a different page called AN Bangla. It still hasn’t been reactivated. They shut quite a few pages then, and those haven’t been restored either. So I had to switch to Murshidabad GT, which used to be a backup page.”
Roni said that after the earlier restriction, a senior police official had told him that the page would be restored “after the election”.
Jabbar Sheikh, who runs Hariharpara Times Bangla, told us that his Facebook page, which had around 4.39 lakh followers, was taken down on September 30, after it published a report on Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury. “More than thirty pages have been restricted. The main reason is that we covered news about the Opposition parties, especially Humayun’s campaign. So there was possibly a political motive. It’s the Indian government that did it. The pages don’t show in India, although they would show in other countries,” Jabbar said.
This was the first time Jabbar had faced such a restriction. He, too, approached police, but said officials told him they had not ordered the restrictions. “They told us that Meta itself had found guideline violations and restricted the pages on that basis, and that cyber crime had no hand in it,” he said.
For a lot of local journalists, publishing news content on Facebook was their only source of livelihood.
It took Swapan Karigar six years to build Murshidabad Today. “This has never happened before. This was my only source of income. I know nothing apart from journalism. I have another small page with around 14,000 followers, and I am posting non-political content from there now. I can’t give up my profession, but I’m cutting down on political content for the time being,” he said. The page had around 24 million views before it was restricted.
Roni said around 25 to 30 such pages had been restricted across the district. When we asked why these pages had been targeted, he said he was told that they had published news that could be perceived as anti-government. “Mostly they’ve closed those who give a bit more coverage to the Opposition political parties’ news. For me, they restricted it after I posted my report on Adhir Chowdhury,” he said.
Roni now publishes from another page, MGT, which has around 15,000 followers. Jabbar is similarly posting content from a second page with barely 2,000 followers.
“All of our pages were monetised. Good money came from it, and a lot of us were getting by. Educated, unemployed youth started this trend alongside other things,” Roni said.
They are not Journalists, Says Murshidabad SP
We spoke to Sachin Makkar, superintendent of police, Murshidabad, who first asked us to “read the notice carefully”.
“Does the notice mention the police or the cyber crime wing? You should contact Meta about this. Does it say that the police restricted the pages?” he asked. When we pressed further, he said, “I do not have a lot to say on the matter. And they are not journalists; they are not accredited journalists. Whatever action has been taken, we have not done it. You can talk to Meta about the rest…”
It is worth noting that the notices received by the administrators say the pages were withheld pursuant to legal requirements. This indicates that the restrictions followed a legal request or complaint concerning the content on these pages, rather than being solely the result of Meta’s own content-moderation process.
We have written to Meta seeking details of the requests it received and the reasons for restricting the pages. This article will be updated if and when we receive a response.

According to data provided by the state of Virginia, where the U.S. branch of PETA is headquartered, the figure is correct. The specific figure, according to Snopes’ own calculation of the data provided, is 66.7%. A spokesperson for PETA said via email that the statistics reflect it being the last shelter in its area to provide “free end-of-life services” for suffering animals, resulting in a high number of referrals from other shelters and vet clinics.
In October 2026, a rumor circulated online that animal welfare nonprofit organization People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals put down 67% of the animals it took in during the year 2024.
Social media users claimed that PETA euthanized 2,213 out of the 3,317 animals it took in that year.
The assertion appears to have originated from a popular Facebook page called Rack Junkies that focuses on hunting and fishing.
In short, the claim is true, according to data provided by the state of Virginia, where the organization is headquartered.
The Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services' database of animal custody record reports for PETA in the year 2024 shows a total of 3,317 companion animals taken in, including 1,374 dogs and 1,885 cats. Of the total number, the data shows 2,709 of the animals were classified as "surrendered by owner."
Of those 3,317 animals, 2,213 were euthanized, making the percentage of animals euthanized by PETA that year 66.7% (which rounds up to 67%).
Among the companion animals euthanized, 875 were dogs (63.7% of dogs taken in) and 1,299 were cats (68.9% of cats taken in). A separate figure for wildlife taken in throughout 2024 shows that 32 of 38 wild animals were euthanized (84.2%).
According to PETA's explanatory notes, also available in the report, the organization's shelter is "the last in the region to still provide free end-of-life services" and that "dozens of Virginians were referred to PETA for end-of-life help" for animals by most of the area's shelters and veterinary clinics, which the nonprofit says had a "significant impact" on the statistics.
The notes also say the euthanized wildlife animals "were critically injured/dying."
(Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services)
A spokesperson for PETA said via email that the organization is appreciative for "the opportunity to respond even though it's to a social media post that deliberately misrepresents PETA's work and is written by a man who makes a hobby and career of killing animals, which is what PETA works against every day," referencing Rack Junkies' hunting content.
Snopes contacted Stephen Ziegler — whose name is in the biography of the Rack Junkies Facebook account — for a response to the PETA spokesperson's comments. We will update this article if we receive a reply.
The spokesperson provided several examples of nearby pet owners and their companions who were referred to PETA for euthanasia, calling this "a small fraction" of cases. The spokesperson wrote:
PETA's services also span 260 localities across Virginia and North Carolina. So naturally, our intake—and by extension our euthanasia figures—will be higher than shelters that serve only their specific locality, because we are assisting exponentially more animals, including those from communities far beyond Norfolk's borders.
PETA's spokesperson reiterated the same points seen in the explanatory notes and added, "While other shelters in and around PETA's headquarters in Norfolk, Virginia, have adopted restrictive 'no-kill' policies aimed at keeping animals out of their shelters and often turn away animals, PETA takes in all comers without discrimination, without admission fees, appointments, waiting lists, or other obstacles."
PETA's intake policy notes that its "shelter does not have a waiting list or charge a surrender fee, and our staff is available 24/7, including to respond to after-hours emergencies and pick up and transport surrendered animals. We often take in aggressive or feral animals rejected by other shelters as unadoptable."
The policy further states that some of the "dangerous" canines who were euthanized had been previously adopted out by other shelters that later declined to take them back "when families attempted to return them due to aggression" and that "more than 100 behaviorally unsound, ailing, and even actively dying animals were referred to PETA by area shelters and veterinary clinics."
In 2012, PETA was the subject of an expose from news magazine The Atlantic, titled, "PETA's Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad History of Killing Animals." That article says that in 2011, the nonprofit's adoption rate was only "2.5 percent for dogs and 0.4 for cats."
A spokesperson for PETA reportedly told the outlet that "euthanasia is a product of love for animals who have no one to love them" and that animals sometimes "need the comfort of being put out of their misery."
Snopes has previously unpacked similar claims against PETA, including its founder's previous comments on animal euthanasia and reports of PETA workers stealing family pets and euthanizing them.

Several photos are circulating online purportedly showing a gold-covered statue depicting a naked U.S. President Donald Trump on display at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, in early October.
For example, a popular Facebook page that shared one picture of the alleged sculpture wrote (archived):
NEWS: A 2.5-meter-tall statue depicting a naked, gold-covered Donald Trump has been unveiled inside the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
The satirical sculpture, titled "Orange Plague" and also called "King of Injustice," shows Trump sitting on the shoulders of another man while holding an enormous golf club. It is reportedly covered in 23-karat gold.
Other photographs of the artwork are also circulating on X (archived) and Instagram (archived).
In short, the photos are authentic and the statue is real. Danish sculptor Jens Galschiøt created the piece and named it "The Orange Plague." On Oct. 7, a spokesperson for the European Parliament's press service confirmed via email that, as of this writing, it is on display at the parliament's Winston Churchill building in Strasbourg, France. Galschiøt said via email that it is set be taken down on Oct. 8.
The sculpture in the pictures shared online matches the piece that can be seen in photos that Galschiøt and reputable news agency Reuters have published. The photographs spreading online also show no signs of being digitally edited or created. Therefore, those photos are authentic and do truly show a naked statue of Trump on display at the European Parliament.
Snopes contacted the White House for comment and for Trump's take on Galschiøt's work. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Why Galschiøt created the statue
On his website, Galschiøt describes "The Orange Plague" as "a satirical out-cry against Trump and the U.S. assault on the green transition and the rule-based world order."
The artwork is 2.6 meters (approximately 8 feet, 5 inches) tall, made of copper and covered in 23 carat leaf gold, according to the sculptor. Danish author Hans Christian Andersen's "The Emporer's New Clothes" tale — in which an emperor parades naked in front of his subjects because he believes he is wearing the finest clothes — inspired Galschiøt to depict Trump as naked.
"The illusion — sustained by fear and flattery — endures until a child cries out, 'He's not wearing any clothes' — and the emperor becomes a figure of ridicule," Galschiøt's website says. The page adds that the gold on the sculpture also plays on this illusion, "Like Andersen's emperor, he [Trump] believes the gold makes him great. It merely makes his nakedness shine brighter."
Speaking via email on Oct. 7, Galschiøt said he initially approached left-wing Danish politician and European legislator Per Clausen MEP about displaying "The Orange Plague" at the European Parliament. The sculptor added that he was "astonished" the exhibition actually happened.
Galschiøt said he thought the European Parliament was the right place to display the piece because "it fits right into the discussion about whether the superpowers should have the right to bully smaller nations, and here Europe is the key player in standing up to them."
When asked whether the artist had heard any reaction to the sculpture from Trump or the White House, Galschiøt said he had not heard from the U.S. president but also had not "had time to look" for reactions to his work.
On Oct. 7, a spokesperson for Clausen said via email that the pair had been discussing displaying the statue at the European Parliament for a couple of years. The politician reportedly said of the sculpture:
I know some people think we shouldn't provoke Trump and therefore shouldn't exhibit a sculpture like this. To them, I have to say two things: First, we cannot accept living in fear and self-censorship. Second, if someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot handle this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no business on the world stage.
A European Parliament press service spokesperson said the office could not comment on individual cases but that, in general, its lawmakers, known as MEPs (Members of the European Parliament), could sponsor "two cultural events or exhibitions per parliamentary term." The spokesperson said:
The rules in place foresee that cultural events and exhibitions shall under no circumstances be offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded or likely to give rise to disturbances in the designated exhibition areas.
The spokesperson said all sponsored events must be approved in advance by the College of Quaestors, a political body "responsible for administrative and financial matters directly concerning Members and their working conditions."
A spokesperson for Clausen said the politician sponsored "The Orange Plague" exhibition at the European Parliament.
Before visiting Strasbourg, the piece was previously on display at the United Nations COP30 climate conference in Brazil. According to Galschiøt's website, the artwork is also set to be on display at the COP31 climate conference in Turkey in November.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other golden Trump sculptures, and statues the Trump administration coated in gold.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Gut microbes followed migrating humans across continents, new study suggests
The Hadza people are hunter-gatherers who have roamed northern Tanzania for thousands of years.
The indigenous Tsimane people forage, fish and hunt in the Bolivian Amazon, some 7,000 miles away.
These two rural communities, separated by an ocean, may appear to have little in common. But a new study shows that they share remarkable similarities when it comes to the bacteria in their guts.
For stories of life in our changing world, subscribe here to the global health newsletter.
Experts say the new paper in the journal Nature suggests this microbial kinship may have taken shape long ago, before human migration split these groups' ancestors apart.
The study, which relied on stool samples from both groups, also showed that both the Hadza and Tsimane microbiomes were markedly different from city folk, even those living nearby.
The findings suggest that some strains of gut bacteria have long coexisted with humans, possibly to their mutual benefit. It's an idea that some scientists say raises questions about the impacts of losing those microbes to modern lifestyles.
"If we were inhabited by very similar microbes over a long period of time, it suggests that our human genomes may have come to expect a certain set of microbes and functions," says Justin Sonnenburg, a professor of microbiology and immunology at Stanford University and the study's senior author. "When you start to lose biodiversity in your gut, there may be big issues for your human biology to adjust to and accommodate."
Other researchers not affiliated with the paper say the hypothesis is intriguing, but not yet proven — and that perhaps there's a reason these microbes tend not to appear in city dwellers' guts.
"Another alternative is that the industrialized microbiome profile may actually be adapted to an industrialized lifestyle," says Andrew Moeller, an associate professor of evolutionary biology at Princeton University. "From a health perspective, is it good or deleterious that industrialized humans have lost a lot of ancestral microbial taxa [groups]? We actually don't know."
Documenting what's been kept and lost is a step towards figuring that out, he says.
Microbes hitchhiked on migrating humans
Sonnenburg has previously contrasted the microbiomes of the Hadza with those of industrialized people. He and his colleagues wanted to compare these two communities with one another. "They're living a lifestyle that's much more similar to the lifestyle our ancestors lived, and so therefore is more hospitable to microbes that were handed down through many generations over the course of human evolution," Sonnenburg says.
Still, the major overlap was "startling," he says. In comparing the genetic material in stool samples from dozens of individuals collected by the Tsimane Health and Life History Project, with previous analysis from the Hadza community, Sonnenburg and his colleagues found they had around 1,200 of the same bacterial species living in their guts — a near-90% overlap.
In a typical gut microbiome, hundreds to thousands of species interact with each other — mostly bacteria, along with some fungi and viruses. "The microbes are helping us digest foods in our gut, secreting molecules that get absorbed into the bloodstream," Sonnenburg says. "And our blood, of course, circulates throughout our bodies."
The gut bacteria can influence moods, behavior, and the body's response to infections, affecting fundamental parts of biology and health, he adds.
Microbiomes are dynamic — which means they can also change quickly, depending on what foods we eat and what medicines we take.
So it's remarkable that the Hadza and the Tsimane — isolated communities living very far apart, eating different vegetables, fish and meats — have gut bacteria that are much the same, Sonnenburg says.
He and his colleagues think Hadza and Tsimane peoples' shared microbial profile goes back to their common ancestors in Africa, before some of those humans left the continent, passed through Eurasia and crossed a land-bridge that once connected Russia with Alaska, and eventually settled in the Bolivian Amazon. Later, as sea levels rose, the land bridge disappeared.
"Once the land bridge went away, we had a clear picture that it was going to be very hard for them to exchange gut bacteria through traditional human contact means," says Ben Good, a theoretical biophysicist at Stanford and a study co-author.
Using dating techniques based on the rates at which bacteria change, they determined that on average, the microbial strains likely shared a common ancestor about 17,000 years ago — with some dating much further back. "That is consistent with the idea that these populations in South America, Africa and probably in other parts of the world are not just acquiring microbes from their environment that match their lifestyle, so much as transmitting microbes over generations," Sonnenburg says.
Other researchers agree that the findings support the concept that large swaths of the gut microbiome migrated with humans — and likely evolved with them, too.
"If the bacteria and the humans had a shared history for many, many generations, there are more opportunities for selection," says Taichi Suzuki, an assistant professor at Arizona State University not affiliated with this paper, who conducts microbiome research. "We would expect more potential dependencies between [the co-evolved] gut microbes and our own genome, basically."
How the microbiome develops
Babies are born with a blank slate microbiome, and start acquiring gut bacteria right away.
"We first get our microbes from our mother's vaginal canal, mother's skin," says Suzuki at Arizona State, "Then as we develop, we get microbes mostly from other individuals in the household and the community."
This human-to-human transmission occurs through the fecal-oral route — ingesting microscopic particles of poo in the air and dust — and serves the important function of passing along microbes that are specific to humans, says Moeller at Princeton. "Something that might make that less disgusting is realizing how tiny these things are," he says, "They're a micron or less in length, and in principle, you just need one cell to found a new population."
The gut also picks up generalist microbes that exist in the environment by ingesting food, soil and water, Moeller says. For instance, E. coli — a bacteria that's found in many places, and thrives in the bodies of humans and many animals.
Some researchers hypothesize that the microbes that have co-evolved with humans may help protect human health — or at least do less harm. For instance, in a case study, those with African ancestry have been found to have a far lower risk of getting seriously ill from an African strain of H. pylori, presumably because their genomes developed alongside the bacteria, compared with those of other ancestries who are susceptible to developing a deadly stomach cancer. It's an example that shows the potential harms of a mismatch between gut microbes and the human genome, Suzuki says.
Around 60% of the gut microbes the Hadza and Tsimane people share are rare or absent from the guts of people who live modern, industrialized lives, according to the paper. "The microbes that inhabit my gut are very unlikely to be the microbes that were handed down through the generations from my great great grandparents," Sonnenburg, the Stanford co-author, says. "They are much more likely to be a product of my current lifestyle and the people that I've interacted with locally."
He thinks losing these ancestral microbes may be harming human health. While proving causation is tricky, "a lot of the arrows are pointing in the same direction, that our modern microbiome has changed in ways that may be propagating inflammation, may be unhealthy for us and leading to inflammatory diseases," Sonnenburg says.
Much scientific work will be needed to prove or disprove the theory. "With regards to the evolutionary questions like, which of [these] microbes have we co-evolved with? Which ones have we lost that would be beneficial to regain? It's still early days for that line of questioning," Moeller at Princeton says.
Still, he adds, determining which gut bacteria have been with humans for a long time helps move the field forward.

Asia shares subdued, bonds swamped by AI debt wave
SYDNEY, Oct 8 : Asian shares slipped on Thursday as strains in sovereign bond markets were aggravated by reports some major tech companies were seeking to raise billions in debt in direct competition for limited funding.
A fresh rise in oil prices added to the pressure on Treasuries, though a strong auction of US 10-year debt overnight did help pull yields off 24-year peaks.
While lofty yields underpinned the dollar, the euro slid to near 17-month lows as concerns over France's finances spread to Italian and Greek debt.
The steady climb in borrowing costs put equities on the defensive and Japan's Nikkei eased 0.9 per cent, with South Korea down 0.6 per cent. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dipped 0.1 per cent.
On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures were barely changed. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures, DAX futures and FTSE futures all edged up 0.1 per cent after sliding on Wednesday.
The Wall Street Journal added to media reports that SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle were looking to raise money to buy AI chips.
Broadcom was looking for $50 billion in financing, while SpaceX was planning to issue $30 billion in investment-grade debt and raise $10 billion in loans to buy chips from Nvidia, which is a major shareholder in SpaceX.
The news saw credit default insurance on SpaceX jump to record highs, while its shares and bonds lost ground.
Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, warned of a dangerous loop where Nvidia was bankrolling the very customers who buy its products, leaving global investors at risk if the expected profits failed to materialise.
"The AI build out started on cash," said Green. "It's increasingly running on credit, and credit changes the risk profile entirely."
"Debt has to be repaid on schedule, whether the revenues show up or not," he added. "And this debt is landing in the bond funds and pension pots of savers right around the world.”
SOVEREIGN BONDS VS CORPORATE DEBT
Still, the fact much of this money will be spent on AI equipment could be positive for earnings in the semiconductor and memory sectors.
Samsung Electronics on Thursday projected a 783 per cent jump in third-quarter operating profit to 107.4 trillion won ($80.17 billion), though its shares eased 0.3 per cent.
All this corporate debt is coming at a time when sovereign bond markets are being sorely tested by inflation fears, ever-widening budget deficits and rising cash rates.
Minutes of the Federal Reserve's last meeting released on Wednesday showed "most" members considered another rate hike likely by year end, though they would approach each meeting with an open mind.
Markets imply just a 19 per cent chance the Fed will move again this month, but are 80 per cent priced for a rise in December.
"We expect a second Fed hike in December, though we see a strong chance the Fed ultimately concludes further tightening is unnecessary," wrote analysts at Goldman Sachs in a note.
The prospect of a pause in tightening helped keep 2-year Treasury yields at 4.78 per cent, while 10-year yields nudged up to 5.298 per cent having hit a 24-year top of 5.326 per cent overnight.
Strains in the French bond market led Bank of France head Emmanuel Moulin to acknowledge the country's economic situation was serious, but he reassured investors it did not need help from the European Central Bank.
Investors reacted by dumping the euro, which was pinned at $1.1198 having lost 0.6 per cent overnight. A break of the recent low at $1.1161 would risk a retreat to $1.1065.
The dollar was the main beneficiary of the single currency's woes and its index rose to 102.22, near an 18-month peak. It was off 0.1 per cent on the yen at 157.90, with the Japanese currency protected by the threat of intervention.
In commodity markets, Brent futures rose 0.9 per cent to $101.14 a barrel, while US crude futures added 0.8 per cent to $89.02 a barrel.
Non-interest-bearing gold has suffered as yields climbed, leaving it at $4,105 an ounce and near two-month lows. [GOL/]

Honeymoon over as Pocognoli's Scotland suffer domestic disharmony
- Published
On a dismal night at Hampden when Scotland failed to ask enough questions of Slovenia, there are one or two that could be posed to new boss Sebastien Pocognoli and his players.
We knew Pocognoli was a disciple of three at the back - the issue being whether he was rigid or flexible in his philosophy, whether he was a bit of an ideologue or a coach capable of changing things on the hoof.
Well, he changed it, that's for sure. Maybe not early as he should have, but at 1-1, and then when Slovenia took a deserved 2-1 lead, Pocognoli switched formation and personnel, not out of design but out of desperation, you felt.
He hurled players on in a bid to take a point; strikers, wingers, kitchen-sink stuff. Indiscriminate and messy. Scotland never really got out of the blocks. They got what they deserved.
So to the questions. Where did this turkey of a performance come from?
As early as the 13th minute there were signs of a rough night when Slovenia got in behind and Adam Cerin's shot had to be blocked by Jack Hendry. Concerning.
It got a touch nervy as the visitors knocked it about, trying to work it into all the space that Scotland were affording them. Hampden was deathly quiet. Then Ryan Christie scored and it stirred, only to fall into a slumber again.
The trouble at the back was revisited soon after, Andy Roberton having to make a lung-busting effort to throw himself in front of a point-blank shot from Zan Vipotnik after Hendry was caught dozing.
The issues were obvious. Can the back three, so badly exposed by Slovenia, be long for this world when the opposition is decent? Why did all that acreage of space open out wide and through the middle? Slovenia were licking their lips for most of the night. They were clever and creative and should have won by more.
Why did Scotland's lauded midfield look so overrun? Seconds into the second half, Slovenia went straight through the middle again.
Was anybody taking note of the warning signs? Where was the intent and urgency? Where was the accuracy and the width? Where were the chances? Where were the bodies in the box supporting the frontman and the pressing game?
How could Slovenia go from being thoroughly outplayed by Scotland in the second half in Ljubljana to being so superior in Glasgow?
Aljosa Matko's equaliser started with a Scotland throw-in. Danijel Sturm's chance that should have made it 2-1 three minutes later came on the back of Ben Gannon-Doak staying miles up the pitch oblivious to Sturm's danger. Angus Gunn didn't exactly cover himself in glory, either.
The goal that we thought had made it 2-1 was disallowed - correctly - for offside, but the build-up was more of the same. Before Matko banged it past Gunn, Slovenia won one aerial duel and then another. Weak, weak, weak.
That second goal did come, as everybody suspected it would. Matko down the right, squared to Sturm. Easy. Luis Binks was caught this time. Soft, soft, soft.
Ramifications could stretch beyond this campaign
What does it all mean for Scotland's bid for second place in their Nations League group, a position that would give them a favourable pot two seeding for December's Euros draw?
That looks in jeopardy now. The ramifications of this defeat could stretch beyond the disappointment of a cold Tuesday night in Glasgow.
It was such a damaging evening for Pocognoli, a bolt from the blue, you sensed. He probably thought he was a little further down the road than he really is.
The air of dejection from him and his captain at the end was unmissable. It all sounded like some of the darker days under Steve Clarke.
There were giant empty spaces in the stands at Hampden but, at the end, there were enough fans left behind to deliver a lusty verdict on what they saw.
Going into this, there was positivity around Scotland's energy and the chances they'd been creating, about a burgeoning attacking style far removed from Clarke's supposed stodginess. All of that was badly undermined.
It wasn't so much that Scotland lost the game - bad enough in itself - it was how they lost. It was limp and lifeless for far too long.
Gannon-Doak played well as a wing-back last Saturday, but that was North Macedonia, not Slovenia. The youngster got targeted and exposed in a position he's not familiar with. Offensively, he was kept pretty quiet.
A back three that has looked impressive was hassled to distraction, calm replaced with confusion. Scotland's go-to leaders did not lead.
Robertson said his team was out-fought, which was a telling comment. Fight is the easiest part to get right, the thing that requires no talent.
On Saturday in Skopje, everything was easy for Scotland because North Macedonia were no good. They scored two and could have scored five and six.
Was there a sense of them believing in their own hype? Hard to imagine given that it was only North Macedonia they'd beaten, but there was a lack of edge about Scotland on Tuesday that begs that question.
Or can it all be laid at the door of the system? Slovenia did their work on that. Ripped it to pieces, in truth.
Pocognoli needs time, of course he does. He needs his most potent attacking midfielder, Scott McTominay, at the heart of things and needs more training sessions to drill his message into his players.
November is his next chance, away to Switzerland and home to North Macedonia. No real margin for error now. They had a big chance to make it a healthy seven points from four games and they blew it.
The head coach will need to nurse his wounds after this. He will have learned a lot about his players and has much thinking to do.
The honeymoon period is over. The reaction of the Hampden crowd at the end told you that the first marital row has now occurred.

Nearly 25 years after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the families of victims are still waiting for their long-running legal battle against Saudi Arabia to reach trial.
A federal appeals court in New York on Wednesday (October 7) heard arguments over whether the Kingdom should remain a defendant in a lawsuit alleging that Saudi government-linked individuals provided assistance to some of the 19 al-Qaida hijackers.
The three-judge panel did not immediately rule on whether the case can proceed. The hearing, however, gave the families a fresh opportunity to press their demand for accountability — and to call on President Donald Trump to put pressure on Riyadh.
More than 100 relatives of 9/11 victims attended the hearing in lower Manhattan, according to the accounts provided.
The judges asked “really meaningful questions” and challenged Saudi Arabia's lawyers, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the attacks, said after the hearing.
The civil lawsuits, first filed in 2004, involve hundreds of victims' relatives and injured survivors, as well as insurers and businesses.
At the heart of the claims is an allegation that Saudi government employees or officials knowingly assisted members of the 9/11 plot and helped create an environment in which al-Qaida could operate and develop.
The plaintiffs allege that individuals associated with Saudi Arabia provided support to at least two of the 19 hijackers who eventually carried out the attacks.
The lawsuits also allege that extremist religious figures in Saudi Arabia assisted the hijackers and that Saudi-linked charities helped funnel money and other support to people associated with al-Qaida.
Fifteen of the 19 hijackers were Saudi nationals. Saudi Arabia, however, has consistently denied that its government was involved in the attacks.
The attacks killed 2,977 people when hijacked aircraft crashed into New York's World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania.
Other defendants in the broader litigation, including Iran, the Taliban and al-Qaida, have already been found in default.
The latest legal battle centres on sovereign immunity — the principle that foreign governments are generally protected from being sued in US courts.
Saudi lawyers argue that the Kingdom should be dismissed from the case because it is a sovereign state and that the allegations do not overcome that immunity.
They have also pointed to the US-Saudi relationship in the 1990s, arguing that Washington and Riyadh were partners in efforts against terrorism and al-Qaida founder Osama bin Laden.
The plaintiffs' lawyers disagree. They argue that the evidence and allegations are sufficient for Saudi Arabia to face the civil lawsuit in a US court.
The appeals court hearing followed an August 2025 ruling by US District Judge George B. Daniels, who allowed the case to continue in federal court. Importantly, Daniels did not rule that Saudi Arabia was liable or that the allegations had been proven; his decision concerned whether the litigation could proceed.
The appeals court must now decide whether that ruling stands.
The judges did not indicate when they would issue their decision.
If Saudi Arabia succeeds, the Kingdom could be removed from the case before the families get their opportunity to take the allegations to trial.
If the families prevail, the litigation could move forward, potentially forcing Saudi Arabia to continue defending itself against allegations that its officials or agents assisted the 9/11 hijackers.
That would not mean Saudi Arabia had been found responsible for the attacks. It would mean only that the plaintiffs' claims could proceed through the US judicial process.
For the families, that distinction is important: after decades of litigation, they say they want the opportunity to establish the facts in court.
The families are also demanding action from President Donald Trump.
After Wednesday's hearing, relatives called on Trump to pressure the Saudi government to apologise and to support the victims' efforts to hold Riyadh accountable.
Aaron Sand, whose father died in the attacks, directly appealed to the president.
“President Trump, I love ya, but you are not doing enough,” Sand said.
He urged Trump to prioritise the families who lost relatives in the attacks and said Saudi Arabia's status as a US ally should not prevent the victims from seeking accountability.
Brett Eagleson, whose father Bruce was killed on 9/11, also questioned where the president and Congress stand.
“We are about a month from the midterm elections. Where are the members of Congress? Where is the president of the United States? Will he stand with the families or with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia?” Eagleson asked.
Strada similarly said the administration could intervene politically and called for the Kingdom to be held accountable.
“As an American, a patriot, I want to see the right thing done,” she said.
(With AP inputs)

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

The Jan Swasthya Abhiyan (JSA) and the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment have called for regulation of charges levied by private hospitals and ceilings on trade margins for medicines, medical devices and medical consumables, amid renewed scrutiny by the Supreme Court of pricing practices in hospital pharmacies.
The groups, in a statement issued on Monday (October 5, 2026), said patients continued to face high and arbitrary charges for treatment, medicines and consumables, with limited avenues to challenge hospital bills.
The Supreme Court has recently questioned steep markups on medicines sold through hospital pharmacies and practices that require patients to purchase medicines from hospital-linked pharmacies. The court has also asked the government to examine regulation of trade margins.
Pricing vs determining charge
“The problem extended beyond the pricing of individual medicines to the broader question of how private hospitals determine charges for procedures, services and consumables. Private healthcare has expanded enormously in India, but regulation has simply not kept pace,” said Abhay Shukla, co-convener, JSA. He added that patients often had little bargaining power at healthcare facilities.
The Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 provides a framework for registration and regulation of clinical establishments and envisages standardisation of services and charges. However, its implementation is not uniform across the country, and several States have their own legislation or regulatory arrangements.
The groups said the absence of a uniform mechanism to regulate hospital charges had left patients vulnerable to hefty bills, particularly for prolonged hospitalisation and procedures involving multiple medicines, devices and consumables.
They are now demanding that the Centre and States introduce ceilings on charges levied by private hospitals for procedures, services and treatment and establish accessible, time-bound mechanisms through which patients can challenge excessive or unjustified bills.
The groups have also called for regulation of trade margins on medicines, medical devices and other medical consumables.
K.M. Gopakumar, co-convener, Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatment, said that the maximum retail price (MRP) cannot become a licence to charge patients many times the procurement price.
The group has also cited earlier concerns raised by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) regarding margins in pharmaceutical sales and incentives created when hospitals or hospital pharmacies control the products patients are required to purchase.
Financial incentives for doctors
Raising concern over the effect of financial incentives on clinical decision-making, Gayatri Sharma, a community health physician and researcher, said revenue-linked incentives could put pressure on doctors to increase investigations or procedures.
“Doctors should be able to make treatment decisions solely on the basis of what is medically necessary for the patient,” she said, calling for the National Medical Commission (NMC) to examine incentive-linked remuneration practices for doctors.
The group, in its statement, has called for a stronger public healthcare system alongside regulation of private providers, including increased public health spending and strengthening of government hospitals to provide accessible care. The demands include immediate regulation of trade margins on medicines, medical devices and consumables; ceilings on private hospital charges; a competition-law review of potentially anti-competitive practices; and an independent and time-bound grievance redress mechanism for patients.

The clip as presented in some social media posts lacked context that made it clear Trump was not referring to his IQ when he mentioned the number 1,775 during a campaign rally speech. Rather, he was speaking about the "warrior dividend" his administration promised U.S. service members.
In early October, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump said his IQ was 1,775.
IQ, or intelligence quotient, is a measure of a person's relative intelligence. There are many different tests for IQ that usually assign the taker a number score. An IQ score of 1,775 would be remarkable, given that the Guinness World Records holder for highest IQ held a score of 228 before Guinness retired the record in 1990.
One Facebook user who shared the claim included a clip of Trump saying:
I'm a high-IQ person, unlike some other people I can tell you about. Very, the, among the highest IQs anywhere in the world, 1,775. And I said, you know, if we can scrap up $1 more we'll be at 1,776, and that's what we did.
The Facebook user captioned the video "Trump thinks his IQ is 1775."
The clip of Trump speaking and his purported claim about his intelligence also circulated on X (archived) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers contacted us, asking whether Trump really claimed his IQ was 1,775.
Trump did not claim to have an IQ of 1,775. Social media users appeared to misrepresent a portion of the president's campaign rally appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Oct. 3, where he talked about the $1,776 "warrior dividend" his administration promised U.S. service members in December 2025.
The clip was authentic, meaning not generated with artificially intelligence or otherwise edited; Trump did say he had a "very high" IQ and that it was "among the highest IQ's anywhere in the world," immediately followed by saying "1,775." However, the number referred to the amount federal officials initially suggested for the warrior dividend, not Trump's IQ. This was clear when watching that section of Trump's speech in full.
Therefore, we find social media users miscaptioned authentic footage.
Speaking in Vandalia on Oct. 3, Trump said (at 2:17:38, emphasis ours, archived)
And remember just recently, I, just to give you an example, just recently, I gave all members of the military $1,776. And everyone said that couldn't be done and I did it. And you know, Bernie, that, when they put the number I said, "What would be the right amount? What would be something we can afford for our great military?" They came back with 1,775 and they put it on my desk. "Sir, we can do 1,7—" Can you believe this? "We can do 1,775." they said. I said, "Wow." Nobody saw it but me, I'm very proud of this, very intelligent. I'm a high-IQ person, unlike some other people I can tell you about. Very, the, among the highest IQ's anywhere in the world, 1,775. And I said, you know, if we can scrap up $1 more we'll be at 1,776, and that's what we did, 1,776.
Considering the full context of Trump's speech, it was obvious he was not referring to his IQ when he said the number 1,775.
Though Trump often calls himself a "high-IQ individual" (in fact, he did so while telling the same story at a rally on Sept. 16) his actual IQ is unconfirmed. Snopes has previously debunked rumors that he scored 73 on an IQ test during his time at the New York Military Academy as well as an article claiming the president's IQ was 156.

An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.
Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.
On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.
Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.
Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.
“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”
The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.
Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.
The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.
More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.
The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.
The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human-rights record, but has largely kept the majority of funds flowing.
This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, read a state department memo revealed by Reuters.
While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”
Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.
Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.
Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsada2sh are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

We invest a great deal of time and thought into how we live on the outside. What we eat, where we live, what we wear, what we drive, what we achieve. And yet the quality of our inner life i.e. the thoughts we carry, the feelings we nurture, the mental habits we repeat without questioning, receives almost no deliberate attention at all. And it is precisely that inner life that determines the quality of everything else. Just as we decide what we will eat, where we will go and what work we will complete, let us also decide what we want to feed our mind. A few moments of gratitude in the morning. A peaceful thought before beginning any work. A conscious decision not to carry someone's harsh words throughout the day. A moment of silence before going to sleep.
How does this sound? These may appear to be small things. But small thoughts, repeated consistently, eventually become the architecture of our personality. And architecture, once built, is hard to ignore. The person who spends years feeding fear and resentment builds a life shaped by fear and resentment, often without ever realising it was a choice. Whereas the person who consistently feeds gratitude and courage builds something entirely different. Both are in same world, but have completely different inner life.
Let us therefore put something beautiful into the storehouse of our mind, the knowledge that expands us, thoughts that strengthen us, acceptance that frees us, gratitude that makes us content, and generosity that reminds us that life is not only about taking but also about giving. Remember, we may not be able to control everything that happens to us. But we can become more conscious of what we allow to happen within us. And perhaps that is what it really means to Think Right. Because when our thinking changes, our feelings begin to change. When our feelings change, our actions change. And when our actions change, the quality of our entire life begins to change. This is not a philosophy reserved for saints or scholars. It is available to every single person who is willing to pause, even briefly and ask: am I feeding my mind what it deserves? So let us not merely dream of living a "king-size" life by having more. Let us learn to live a king-size life by thinking better, feeling deeper, giving more and becoming lighter within.
