Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is among the most widespread of human viruses. More than 90% of adults are estimated to have been infected during their lifetime. Most people acquire the infection during childhood without developing symptoms. In some, particularly those infected during adolescence or adulthood, it can cause infectious mononucleosis. The virus then remains in the body for life.
A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates that about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. The analysis incorporates recent evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer and places EBV among the infectious agents responsible for a substantial cancer burden worldwide.
What is Epstein-Barr virus?
EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, belongs to the herpesvirus family. It spreads mainly through saliva, including through kissing or sharing drinks, food, eating utensils and toothbrushes.
According to WHO, many people infected with EBV have no symptoms. When illness occurs, symptoms can include fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and marked fatigue. Infectious mononucleosis generally improves within a few weeks, although fatigue can last longer.
After the initial infection, EBV remains in the body in a dormant state. In most healthy people, the immune system keeps the infection under control.
EBV is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen. It has established causal links with several cancers, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma. The latest IARC analysis also incorporates evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer.
Who is at risk?
Most people infected with EBV do not develop cancer. The infection is therefore not, by itself, an indication that a person will develop cancer.
People with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of serious EBV-related disease. This includes some people who have undergone organ or stem-cell transplantation and those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.
The cancers associated with EBV also vary geographically. Nasopharyngeal cancer, for instance, is particularly prevalent in parts of eastern and southeastern Asia. The development of EBV-associated cancer is thought to involve factors beyond the infection itself.
How is it diagnosed?
A person does not normally need to be tested simply because EBV is common.
When infectious mononucleosis is suspected, doctors may make a diagnosis based on the symptoms and clinical examination. Blood tests can provide supporting evidence. These include tests for heterophile antibodies and EBV-specific antibodies, which can help determine whether an infection is recent or occurred in the past.
In suspected EBV-related cancers or serious disease in people with compromised immunity, more specialised tests may be needed. These can include testing for EBV genetic material in blood or other samples and examination of tumour tissue for the presence of the virus.
A positive EBV antibody test does not mean that a person has cancer. Since infection is so common, evidence of past infection is expected in most adults.
What are the treatment options?
There is no treatment that removes latent EBV from the body and there is currently no vaccine against the virus.
According to WHO, treatment for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis is mainly supportive. Rest, adequate fluids and medicines to control fever and pain may be advised. Antibiotics do not treat EBV because it is a virus.
People with mononucleosis may also be advised to avoid strenuous activity and contact sports for a period, particularly if the spleen is enlarged, because of the risk of splenic injury.
When EBV is associated with cancer, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted treatment or a combination of these.
Can EBV be prevented?
There is currently no vaccine against EBV. Preventing transmission can also be difficult because infected people may spread the virus without knowing that they have it.
WHO advises avoiding the sharing of drinks, utensils, toothbrushes and other items that come into contact with saliva.
The development of an EBV vaccine is an important area of research. The latest IARC analysis adds to the evidence on the virus’s contribution to cancer and highlights the need for continued research into prevention.

What are emotions, really? And why do we have them?
Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought.
Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed.
Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in Science, in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions.
The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream.
In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished.
Stories hidden in blinks
In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli.
The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming.
Also read: Making the brain transparent
During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses.
As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”.
The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods.
The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns.
Enter: ketamine
Each puff causes a signal to be broadcast throughout the brain, like a “breaking news” alert, followed by a slower, more persistent signal. In this second phase, based on data from the electrodes in the brains of participants, scientists found that specific circuits in the brain were activated, which were linked to the generation of an emotional response in the individual.
To confirm this possibility, the scientists administered ketamine to some of these participants and had them redo the eye puff assay. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved ketamine’s use as an anaesthetic and at lower doses as an antidepressant. Ketamine also induces short-term dissociation: i.e. for a brief period, it alters subjective perceptions. By injecting it, the team could separate a person’s reflexive response from the emotional one.
The scientists found that being subjected to air puffs in the eye when a person was on ketamine changed neither the initial reflexive behaviour nor the initial burst of neural activity in the brain. However, it caused the subsequent slower brain response to dissipate much faster, so much so that the volunteers no longer described the experience as annoying but as a “tickling of the eyeball”.
Consistent with this ‘weaker’ subjective experience from ketamine, the participants’ behaviour also changed. They didn’t blink or close their eyes between consecutive air puffs. Instead, they held their eyes open even though they knew more puffs were in the offing.
Ketamine is known to block a sensor in the brain whose job it is to integrate signals coming from different corners. This means in the participants injected with ketamine, the brain may not have integrated the various signals into a coherent emotional response.
Of mice and men
Even though vertebrates have brains of vastly different sizes and complexity, the overall ‘brain plan’ is highly conserved. (The brain plan is akin to the building plan of a house or apartment.) To zero in on those systems responsible for emotions and which have survived evolution, Deisseroth’s team repeated their experiments with lab mice. The mice went through the eyepuff assay, had their brain activity measured with surgically planted electrodes, and had ketamine injected.
The team noticed the same patterns in mice as they had in humans. Injecting ketamine substantially changed the spiking activity in some neurons but not others. Only those neurons (or brain regions) coordinating the second phase — the slower response after the burst — were affected by ketamine. The initial burst didn’t change in any way, just as with the human participants.
The scientists could also study the neural activity following a puff in greater detail in the mouse model. They found that the fast/reflexive responses corresponded with a sharp rise in activity in some of the midbrain regions. This included the thalamus, where incoming sensory signals converge before being relayed onward, and the periaqueductal grey, which is involved in emotional behaviours.
They also found that the second phase of neural activity corresponded with activity in the brain’s emotional centres (described by the umbrella term ‘limbic regions’) and the frontal cortex. Again, as expected.
Then they dissected the brain activity patterns by stages, focusing on how quickly activity in brain regions shot up after the eyepuff and how long it took to fade away. They noticed that activity patterns in most of the pertinent regions increased at an explosive pace right after the eyepuff — but the rate of decrease was more interesting.
A pattern appears
The patterns in different regions slowed at different rates, fading first in the midbrain regions and last in the frontal cortex. The thalamus was active both in the first and the second phase. Considering the thalamus is the brain’s coordinating centre for all sensory signals, it makes sense that it would be active in the first phase. Incoming sensory signals go on to higher brain regions from the cortex. So it also served the role of handing off the baton, so to speak, and thus essayed a sort of bridging role across timescales.
The new study is the first to report this sort of differential pattern across different parts of the brain vis-à-vis emotions. At this point, it is not possible to say with any certainty what the implications are for the brain’s cortical and mid-brain areas.
With computational models of neuron firing activity in the mouse and the mouse’s behaviour following the eye puff assay, the team found that the timescale of neural activity was an important factor that shaped the emotional response.
Indeed, if the sensory signals dissipate before the brain has a chance to integrate the information, the person won’t be able to learn the lesson: “protect yourself from that obnoxious thing”. On the other hand, if brain activity is more strongly coupled to the fast and slow phases that Deisseroth & co. observed, such activity also lasts longer than normal, causing its own problems. Over-stabilised brain states have been correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder, all of which cause people to experience uninterrupted or mistimed thoughts and emotions.
Beyond the binary of health and disease, the fast and slow phases of brain activity highlighted in the study could reveal the fundamentals of information processing in the brain. People differ in how their brains process information about their environment — in turn a product of their genetic makeup and their upbringing in their formative years.
First steps
Why do we have emotions? For now it may be more gainful to flip the question: what would happen if we didn’t have them?
In the absence of an instinctive reaction that our emotions afford us, the brain’s response would be based entirely on risk-benefit analyses, which can be very time consuming. Over time we’d struggle to make decisions both big and small. What should I wear today? What should I make for dinner tonight? What should I study? Whom should I marry? Purely rational thought would turn such questions into never-ending decision-making exercises with no final answer.
The new study has revealed what happens in the brain in the first seconds when an emotion takes root. One hopes future studies will reveal the specific information encoded by this primal circuitry, how they encode different emotions, and how they evolve with time.
Dr. Reeteka Sud is a neuroscientist by training and senior scientist at the Center for Brain and Mind, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, Bengaluru.

'I've lost my peace' - Cape Verde hero Vozinha on newfound fame
- Published
Cape Verde's heroic World Cup goalkeeper Vozinha says he craves the "peace and tranquillity" of the life he led before he shot to fame.
The 40-year-old shot to global prominence in June when he almost single-handedly kept Spain at bay as Cape Verde drew 0-0 with the European champions on their World Cup debut.
Vozinha's follower count on social media sky-rocketed over the course of the game, from about 50,000 to more than one million.
But his fame shot up even further when Argentina needed extra time to beat Cape Verde in the round of 32.
Vozinha says his life was easier before his World Cup heroics.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he told the Observer., external
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.
"Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph. Or, worse, someone is filming me.
"That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
Vozinha's mother became part of the fairytale too. After he revealed that she had could not afford a visa to watch his World Cup debut, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced that the visa fee had been waived.
Now Vozinha has revealed that his mother is visited on a daily basis by fans wanting to talk or to take photographs with him.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," said Vozinha.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
His World Cup performances for Cape Verde, a West African island nation with a population of 525,000, earned Vozinha a nomination for men's goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or awards.
"It's nice to feel like a kind of ambassador, but I want to make it clear that what we achieved was a collective effort," Vozinha said.
"We made history and the best news would be if we could harness that momentum to develop our country and improve the living conditions of our people."

Quick Answer
Snapchat’s distinct navigation uses custom icons across its main features: the bottom bar accesses Snap Map, Chat, Explore, Stories, and Spotlight. In chats, color-coded arrows and squares signal message types (pink for audio-less snaps, purple for video/audio snaps, and blue for text chats), while outlined versions show opened status or screenshots.
Snapchat successfully positioned itself as “the social media platform for Gen Z”. With its ephemeral nature and best retention features such as Snapstreaks, Snapchat is one of the most popular social media platforms currently.
However, I took my time to understand the platform better and finally became a user. But still, I am far from being a snapper, a word I use for those who are obsessed with Snapstreaks, including my close friends.
Despite being a user for months, I still find the Snapchat interface harder to navigate. Part of the reason is that it is completely detached from the common interfaces used in other social media platforms.
Moreover, Snapchat uses its own terms, such as Planets, Best Friends, and Chats, which can confuse new users. So, as part of our icon explanation series, in this guide you will learn everything about icons and their meanings on Snapchat. For quick reference, here is the Snapchat legend, followed by various icons on each screen and what they mean.
Table of Contents
Snapchat Icons Legend
Snapchat Icons and Symbols and Their Meanings
Snapchat Bottom Navigation Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Open Snapchat > View the bottom navigation bar
Snapchat is still one of the apps that uses a bottom navigation bar, which lets you switch between different Snapchat core features such as Snap Map, Chat, Stories, Discovery, and Spotlight
- Snap Map: Snap Map is an interactive feature that lets you see your friends’ current locations and also locations with the most Snap activity
- Chat: The chat icon lets you switch to the Chats tab
- Explore: Using this icon, you can browse various Snapchat lenses and filter options
- Stories: Takes you to the Snapchat stories tab
- Spotlight: Spotlight is another name for the short video feed in the Snapchat app, just like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts
Snapchat Chat Screen Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon
Now, moving on to the chat feed, which many of us also spend more time on, you will find various icons and symbols. This screen can be confusing for the user with various symbols. Here is what each symbol means.
- Add Friends: This is the same add button that you see on other screens, where it lets you discover or add new friends
- More Options: This option opens additional chat screen options, including the ability to create new chats, create new groups, manage them, manage friendships, and also customize friend emojis and more.
- Viewed Snap Without Audio: This means you have viewed your snap without audio
- Snap Reply: If you see a reply, it means you can reply to a friend with a snap again
- Unopened Snap With Audio: If you see this icon, it means it is an unopened snap with audio
- Chat: The chat icon lets you start a new conversation with your friend.
- New Chat: The new chat icon lets you create a new chat with any of your friends
Snapchat Chat Status Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon
Snapchat also uses various colored arrows and squares to represent the type of snaps. If you see a pink arrow icon, it means you sent a snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means you sent a video snap; in other words, you sent a snap with audio or video.
If you see blue, it means the chat was sent; in other words, you sent a chat message. If you see gray, it means your chat is waiting for the person to accept you.
If the arrow turns into an outline pink arrow, it means the recipient has opened your Snapchat without audio. If you see purple, it means the recipient opened your Snapchat with audio or video, and it’s the same for the blue outline arrow.
If you see a square-shaped icon in pink, it means you received a new snap without audio. If you see a purple square box, it means you received a new snap with audio or video.
If you see a blue square-shaped icon, it means you received a chat message. If you see the outline messages, it means you have viewed all the chats and messages.
If you see a double-arrow outline pink arrow, it means someone took a screenshot of the snap without audio, and it is the same for the other arrow types, including video and chat.
If you see a reload symbol, it means someone replayed your snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means someone replayed your snap with audio or video.
Snapchat Chat Call Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation
Chat screens can be confusing initially with the various arrow and square icons, but it consists of a similar interface to other chat applications, such as the ability to voice call and video call, and also an input bar with various options to send a message
- Camera: It opens the camera to send a snap as a reply
- Voice Call: Snapchat also supports voice calls. Tapping on this icon, you can make a voice call to your friend.
- Video Call: Along with the voice call, Snap also supports video calls. You can tap on the video icon to start a video call with your friend.
Snapchat Chat Toolbar Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation
Snapchat uses different icons to represent various inputs for the message toolbar. Here is what each of the icons means.
- Camera: It opens your camera to send a snap quickly
- Voice Note: You can also quickly record a voice note and send it as a message
- Stickers: This is a sticker icon that lets you add stickers, Bitmoji, and other reaction options
- Notifications Off: If you see a bell icon with a cross, that means you have turned off notifications for the chat
- Photos: Lets you send your memories or camera roll photos to your friend
- Games: This icon opens the games you can play in the chat
Snapchat Chat Message Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation
More icons from the chat interface, and here is what each of them means
- Reply: You can reply to your conversation in a thread to a message in your friends’ chat
- Stickers: Lets you access stickers, Bitmoji, and other emoji reactions
Snapchat Friendship Profile Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation > Tap on your friend’s profile
Snapchat friends’ profiles can also be confusing for new users. It also consists of various icons similar to your profile page. Here is what each of them means.
- More Options: It opens more options for the friend you are viewing, including the ability to manage pin chat, manage location history, and much more
- Share Profile: You can share your friend’s Snapchat profile with others

- Chat: You can also initiate a conversation directly from your friend’s network profile
- Voice Call: You can also have a voice call with your friend by tapping on this icon
- Video Call: You can have a video call with your friend by tapping on this icon

Snapchat Snap Map Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Snap Map icon
Snap Map shows your friends list and snap activity visually. It also includes various icons that can confuse beginners, especially when it shows Ghost Mode and other map settings.
- Ghost Mode: If you see this icon, it means your location is hidden from friends on Snap Map. You can tap on the icon to allow or disallow your location.
- Map Settings: It lets you manage your location and see your location. It also controls whether Snapchat can access your location.
- Satellite View: Snapchat supports both heat map and satellite view. You can switch to satellite mode using this icon.
- Explore Layer: The Explore option lets you see Public Snap and Activity Hotspots
- Battery Status: The battery icon shows a friend’s phone battery status. Remember that they should enable this option from their settings.
- Compass: It is a digital compass that lets you check the direction and reorient the map
- Friend Finder: It lets you search for and find friends who are visible on a Snap Map.
Snapchat Camera Screen Icons
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon
The Snapchat camera is the default screen that opens every time you launch Snapchat. It consists of various icons and symbols meant for different purposes. - Search: This is a global search option that lets you search for your friends or groups. Recent search results also appear here.

Snapchat Camera Screen Icons
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon
Snapchat camera screen consists of various icons, so it’s hard to explain. In this part, let’s explore all the camera tools, which include the ability to switch cameras, control the flash, add music, HD mode, and much more.
- Profile: This is a global profile icon. Tapping on this takes you to your profile page.
- Notifications: Again, the same global notification icon that lets you see all your Snap notifications in one place

- Sounds: Let’s show you access various music options or sounds to add to your Snap

Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar is learnt to have warned his Cabinet colleagues to remain vigilant against possible sting operations, amid reports that private agencies could be secretly recording Ministers’ conversations, meetings, and movements.
Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara and Minister H.C. Balakrishna, who attended the Cabinet meeting on Tuesday (October 6, 2026), confirmed that Mr. Shivakumar, who also holds the Intelligence portfolio, had alerted the Ministers about possible sting operations.
“Since the Chief Minister holds the Intelligence portfolio, he cautioned us based on some information he had received,” Mr. Parameshwara told reporters.
Mr. Shivakumar is learnt to have raised the issue at the Cabinet meeting and shown the Ministers a “file” containing details of alleged ongoing sting operations. The file reportedly included the names of a few Ministers who were purportedly being targeted.
The Chief Minister is said to have advised the Ministers to exercise caution in the light of these purported developments. The Ministers were also reportedly advised to be cautious about meeting strangers privately or allowing themselves to be photographed with unfamiliar persons.
Political charge
Mr. Balakrishna, meanwhile, sought to link the alleged sting operations to Janata Dal (Secular) leader H.D. Kumaraswamy, accusing him of attempting to damage the Chief Minister’s political standing.
“Why did he not remember the NICE land issue and undertake a padayatra when Siddaramaiah was Chief Minister?” Mr. Balakrishna asked, referring to Mr. Kumaraswamy’s recent political campaigns against the Congress government.
The Minister alleged that Mr. Kumaraswamy had been using protests and padayatras since Mr. Shivakumar became Chief Minister in an attempt to undermine his position as a prominent Vokkaliga leader.
His remarks also referred to the State’s long history of political allegations involving purported CDs, pen drives and other forms of recorded material. About a decade ago, Mr. Kumaraswamy had claimed that he possessed CDs containing material relating to alleged corruption involving former Minister G. Janardhana Reddy, though the material was not subsequently made public.
The latest warning comes at a time when political activity is intensifying in Karnataka, with the major parties already positioning themselves for the 2028 Assembly elections.
This is not the first time Mr. Shivakumar has cautioned Congress leaders about possible action against them by investigating agencies. During the Enforcement Directorate searches involving the family members of Public Works Minister Satish Jarkiholi, he had claimed Congress MLAs and Ministers were under the agency’s scanner and urged party leaders to remain cautious.
The latest claims about alleged sting operations, however, have not been independently established.
Long history
The latest episode also revives Karnataka’s long history of political battles involving recorded conversations and purportedly incriminating material — from audio tapes in the 1980s to video CDs, sting operations, pen drives and, more recently, digitally recorded conversations and videos.
Such material has periodically been used as a political weapon, with allegations, counter-allegations, and demands for investigations often becoming part of electoral and intra-party battles.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Here's a core dynamic of our AI moment: Many of the people who are most worried about AI's power are also the people running the most powerful AI companies.
And that's always been the case, argues Kevin Roose. The veteran technology journalist says that many of the men leading the AI boom — most prominently Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman — have been rushing to build AI at least in part because they worried someone less responsible would beat them to it.
Some AI critics accuse the Amodeis and Altmans of the world of inflating apocalyptic AI worries in order to hype their own businesses. But that kind of concern is thoroughly commonplace in AI circles, Roose says. In San Francisco, he notes, it's not uncommon to find people in the tech scene who think the likelihood that AI will bring about doomsday at 50% or more.
Roose just left The New York Times to co-host a podcast for NPR. He's also out with a new history the AI industry: "The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence." It's jam- packed with backstories and biographies of the technologists who got us to this moment.
I talked to Roose about the impetus to build this tech, the Oppenheimer-like moment many AI leaders think we're in now, and if there's any way to slow things down on my Channels podcast. You can read an edited excerpt below. One note: We taped the conversation a day before Donald Trump hosted an AI summit with Altman, Amodei, Elon Musk and other tech bosses — and then announced that federal regulation wasn't necessary, because the industry would regulate itself.
Peter Kafka: A big tension in your book is that the people who raced to build AI were also very worried that AI could be an existential danger. So why did they want to build it?
Kevin Roose: I think the thing that they saw was that the technology was improving rapidly. There's this great Dario Amodei essay from 2017 called "The Big Blob of Compute Hypothesis," where he talks about how basically, if you want to make these systems smarter, the best way to do that is just to make them bigger.
And I think they saw that if this is just a simple recipe — put in more compute and put in more data, and train the model for longer, and out comes more intelligence — then someone's going to figure that out eventually.
And when people figure this out, there will be this race, and this technology will be so strategically important and will have so many economic and military and political benefits to whoever creates it, that everyone's going to join the race.
So if we want the world to be OK, we — "the good guys" — have to win the race, because otherwise it is only a matter of time before someone else wins the race, and that would be bad for all kinds of reasons.
I'm not saying that's the correct justification for racing, but that is their story that they told themselves for participating in a thing that they knew would be dangerous.
When people imagine AI going wrong, they might mean losing their jobs, or someone making a bioweapon, or machines replacing us altogether. What are the AI leaders worried about?
They're envisioning a whole continuum of potential outcomes. People often talk about P(doom) — the sort of viral statistic people like to share — which just encapsulates their probability that we'll all die.
But there's other Ps, right? There's P disempowerment. There's P pandemic. There's P everyone loses their jobs. These people are worried by nature and worried by temperament.
If the premise for the good guys is "We have to get there before anybody else, so we can handle it responsibly" — how would they manage that? People compare this to efforts to restrain nuclear weapons. But those weapons required resources that only a couple of countries had. That doesn't seem applicable here.
It could be applicable. We would just have to do it a lot faster, because the technology is proliferating much more quickly than nuclear.
You could imagine a whole inspections regime where you'd have something like the UN — some sort of standards body with inspectors that would go into the labs and inspect their training runs and see if the models are doing dangerous things.
There's already been some proposals along these lines for these so-called embedded evaluators who would sit inside OpenAI and Anthropic and would not work for them, but would have employee-level access to all their systems.
That would be step one. But to be clear, I think there's many things that could be done aside from that. Right now, there is essentially no regulation on these companies. The people who serve food in the OpenAI cafeteria have to go through more inspections and paperwork than the people training the models that could become self-replicating and destroy a lot of things.
That is a crazy, untenable situation.
It seems like we're going to be in that situation for a while. The president listens to people who say we should have essentially no regulation. Congress doesn't pass laws, and even if it did, Trump would veto them. Aren't we at least two and a half years away from meaningful federal regulation?
I want to push back on the premise. Things can change really quickly. Just in the last couple of weeks, public sentiment is really turning very rapidly on this. The saliency of AI is skyrocketing. People care a lot about it, more than they did just a couple weeks ago.
They're more worried about it. Voters are more worried about it. Politicians are sensitive to the concerns of voters. So yes, there's a cluster of people around Trump who don't think any of this merits regulation.
But there are other clusters who are part of the national security community who are more hawkish on China, who don't want to see things go sideways with AI. And I think those people may find more purchase as voters get more worried about this. It is not completely a given to me that we will have essentially no regulation from the rest of this administration.
What if things stay static? If you're Dario Amodei or Sam Altman and you're not going to get the government to do this, what can you do yourselves?
I think there could be some kind of an industry-wide pact to pace the frontier: slowing down the research, specifically on frontier models, the most capable models that can work for hours or days at a time with minimal or no human supervision.
I think there probably will be some kind of agreement between the labs at the head of the pack. Which is surprising considering these guys hate each other.
The reason Anthropic exists is because Dario hated Sam Altman so much he built his own company.
And the reason OpenAI existed is because Sam Altman and Elon Musk hated Demis Hassabis at [Google's] DeepMind so much they wanted to build their own company. The whole frontier is populated by people who dislike and mistrust each other.
But I think they are going to act in the absence of some kind of government regulation. They realize that they're probably not going to get some kind of coordinated, centralized mechanism out of this administration, so I think they will do something on their own.
Even if the big US AI companies really do slow down, what about everyone who isn't participating? Chinese models are copying existing models, and this stuff gets commoditized quickly. Isn't the genie already out?
It's possible, and that's why they're being very cautious about calling for a slowdown, because they don't want to unilaterally disarm. Because that could invite China or Meta, a company that is American, but that is not concerned with how fast things are moving, to race ahead.
I think China's AI position is sometimes overstated quite a bit. I think they still are quite dependent on American AI companies pushing the frontier forward so that they can then distill from those models to create their own models. They do have some of their own capacity too, and they're starting to get more hardware.
But I think for now, the big leaps in capabilities are coming out of the American labs that have all the compute and all the researchers and all the breakthroughs.
What's your personal P(doom)?
I usually say I'm at about 10%.
A 10% chance that it all goes super bad?
Yeah. Which sounds crazy to people in most parts of the world. But in San Francisco, that makes you an optimist. I know people walking around with 50%, 60%, 70% P(doom). I know someone who has a 99.9% P(doom).
Is that person putting money in their 401(k)? Why are they even in San Francisco? Why don't they head to New Zealand or wherever they think they can survive?
I do know people on the extremes who are liquidating their 401(k)s. I know a person who took up smoking because they thought "AI's gonna kill us all, so we might as well have some fun on the way out." I know someone who doesn't wear sunscreen to the beach anymore, because why bother?
I'm telling you this because in San Francisco, a P(doom) of 10% is like, "Oh, you think this will all go well?" It is jarring to hear people with P(doom) that low. So I say that because I think we still have some agency and some control over this.
We still could slow things down, pass some regulations, coordinate to pace the frontier. We could come out of this in a sensible way.
We have the narrow path to utopia available to us, and I'm more hopeful than I was even a month or two ago. Because paradoxically, everyone is talking about doom now — which makes me less worried about doom.

Prem* is a young mathematics graduate from a village in Jharkhand. He was known as an energetic and supportive young person. Children from the village often approached him when they had difficulties with mathematics. When he was selected for a job with the Indian Railways, it was expected to be a moment of happiness. But the thought of leaving his parents, friends, village and the life he shared with them was difficult for him.
In the weeks following the job offer, Prem began having sleepless nights, worrying about how he would cope with a new life and new responsibilities. Gradually, he stopped talking to his family. He began to feel helpless and worthless, lost interest in everyday life and reached a point where he attempted to end his life.
What helped was having people around him who could understand not only what he was going through, but also the world he was coming from. A neighbourhood facilitator working in a community-based organisation was able to sit with him, listen to his worries and share his dukh-sukh. They understood why leaving his parents, friends and village felt so difficult and gave him space to talk about the fears he was carrying.
The support was not about asking him simply to adjust or move on. It helped him think about what mattered to him, what he wanted for his future and how he could remain connected to the people and place that were important to him while taking up the new opportunity. He eventually wrote to the department asking for another opportunity to join. He was invited again and went to work, while continuing to receive support.
Prem’s experience highlights that what looks like a positive life event from the outside can sometimes become overwhelming. A suicidal act can often happen suddenly, during a moment of intense crisis. But the distress behind that moment may have been building for much longer.
For Adivasi communities, distress can be shaped by circumstances that may never appear in a psychiatric consultation.
When distress is accumulates
A recent study in Jharkhand examined psychosocial distress and help-seeking among Adivasi Ho adolescents. It found that distress was often linked to family conflict, pressure around education and work, financial hardship, violence, separation and loss, and difficulties in relationships. Some adolescents withdrew and stopped sharing what they were going through; for some, this included thoughts of self-harm or suicide
These accounts do not offer a single explanation for suicide among Adivasi communities. They show how distress can accumulate across everyday life — in family conflict, having to leave school temporarily or reduce schooling to help with agricultural or household work, substance use, untreated illness, violence, displacement, loss of livelihood, lack of mentorship, identity-related stigma and self-doubt, or the erosion of community and belonging.
When communities are disrupted
Belonging is an important part of suicide prevention. Stereotypes, exclusion, humiliation, discrimination and pressure to hide one’s identity can affect how people see themselves and how connected they feel to society. Historically, Adivasi communities stayed together. But modern development, alongside education and employment opportunities, have in some cases, uprooted Adivasi people from their culture. Mainstream schools do not teach Adivasi children in their own mother tongue; their history is woefully under-represented in the school curricula.
Sandip Sing, a radiologist from the Munda community practising in rural West Bengal and a first-generation learner, says, “There is a rapid transition in accessing and navigating educational and professional spaces, often amid gaps in resources, networks, and institutional familiarity. Bridging these gaps can be challenging, particularly with unfamiliar systems.”
Many educated Adivasis may also have had fewer opportunities to engage with their community’s history, culture, language and traditions, and may have complex or evolving relationships with their Adivasi identities. This matters for mental health because belonging itself is a source of strength. When people are uprooted without finding a new sense of belonging, distress can deepen.
This does not mean that development itself causes mental illness or suicide. The concern is what happens when rapid social change is accompanied by displacement, loss of livelihood, cultural disconnection and weakening social support.
Collective strength, mentoring
The strength of Adivasi life also lies in ways of expressing emotions and sharing knowledge. Songs and dances are not simply cultural performances; they are ways of expressing emotions, maintaining connection and making sense of life. The Adivasi dance itself is a powerful metaphor. People dance in a chain, holding one another. The village headman, Majhi Baba, dances alongside everyone else. An 80-year-old and an eight-year-old can dance together. There is no hierarchy; the strength is in the circle. For suicide prevention, this collective strength matters.
Young people also need places where they can be themselves without constantly having to explain or defend who they are. Lilibiti Saren, a medical officer from the Santhal community working in tribal areas of Bankura, West Bengal, notes that she often finds young people in these communities lacking direction. “There is a need for proper mentorship,” she says.
Locally organised Adivasi youth spaces can help. Such spaces can offer young people opportunities to speak in their own language, share experiences, learn from peers and elders and explore what Adivasiyat — identity, history, relationships and belonging — means to them.
Access and pathways in care
Clinical care remains essential. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts may need assessment for depression, substance use, trauma, psychosis, previous attempts, suicidal intent, access to means and immediate safety. Treatment and follow-up can save lives.
But access to mental health care is itself a major challenge in many Adivasi areas. Services are often limited, distant and unevenly available.
And even when services are available, the pathways into care may not be optimal. An Adivasi person with lived experience of mental healthcare says: “I felt like the psychiatrists and the psychologists were not speaking to me. They were judging me for what I had done and they were trying to find symptoms instead of trying to understand me, my pain and my situation.”
This raises an important question: are our mental health systems listening as carefully as they are diagnosing?
When formal services are scarce, difficult to reach, or experienced as unfamiliar or judgmental, people may seek support elsewhere—including from family, community networks, faith healers or indigenous systems. These spaces may offer something that the formal system does not: familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and a sense of belonging.
Adivasi mental health therefore cannot be treated simply as another category within rural health. Representation matters — from schools to healthcare institutions and policy making.
Models that could work
In Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, particularly among the Ho, Munda and Santhal communities, Madait refers to a tradition of voluntary help and collective support for someone who needs it or is in distress. It reflects an understanding that some difficulties are too large for one household to manage alone.
This may be a useful way to think about mental healthcare too. The question is not simply how services can be delivered to Adivasi communities, but how communities themselves can shape, participate in and lead the care they need.
The same principle can be seen in Dukhu-Sukhu Baithaki — community support group meetings where people experiencing mental health difficulties and their families can meet, share experiences and support one another. This model works in West Singhbhum, Jharkhand, where people living with mental health conditions come together each month. These spaces do not replace professional care. They bring community knowledge, relationships and mutual support into the process of recovery.
Education without a knowledge of one’s roots; development that comes with displacement and mental healthcare that does not see or hear the people who need help is no longer enough. For suicide prevention, we must ask not only, “What is wrong with the individual?”, but also, “ Where is the community support? Where is the system that understands them?”
Perhaps suicide prevention in Adivasi communities must begin there — not by doing things for Adivasis, but by doing them with Adivasis.

A common misconception I’ve seen with Googlebooks is that the Quick Insert and Google logo keys are new. They’re not, as they first debuted a couple of years ago on some Chromebooks. But there is something new for Googlebooks that’s ripped straight from Android phones circa 2014.
Android’s physical navigation buttons are back on Googlebooks, but not the way you think
An oldie but a goodie — and kind of a necessity-die.
On every Googlebook keyboard, the F1, F2, and F3 keys are the old triangle, circle, and square navigation icons that first debuted on Android 5.0 Lollipop. These were the back, home, and app switcher buttons long before everything went to gesture-based navigation, and they’re still built into phones on Android 17 as an alternative. On Googlebook OS, these keys do what you expect: the left-pointing triangle goes back, the circle goes “home” by minimizing all open apps, and the square tiles your open apps like Mission Control on macOS / Task View on Windows.
It’s useful to have these buttons, and to have them matched across all Googlebooks. The back button seems sometimes necessary when using Android apps that aren’t really optimized for a desktop interface or mouse controls. I just wish a second press of the home button brought all your apps back to where they were, but that’s another feature called desktop peeking that uses a different keyboard shortcut.
If you’re an Android nerd of yore, it’s kind of fun to see these buttons live on. But they’re also a reminder that you sometimes need a fallback when Android gets all Android on you.

NEW DELHI: Elon Musk has hit out at "certain oligarchs", who he alleged were "blocking" Starlink's entry into India.
The trillionaire's comments came on a day when Starlink, the company owned by him, said at India Mobile Congress (IMC) that it was ready to start service here as soon as "India is ready".
"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are... This is a crime against the people of India!" Musk said on X in response to a post, which said Starlink was needed here due to the large number of villages still not having broadband connectivity.
"Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable Internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all," Musk further said on X late Wednesday night.
Starlink has already built 20 gateway sites in India and developed India-specific security controls to keep Indian user data within the country, said Lauren Dreyer, VP of Starlink business operations, at IMC Wednesday.
Dreyer said Starlink hopes to start satellite broadband services in India "as soon as" all approvals are granted, amid buzz that Sunil Bharti Mittal-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Jio may get the green signal earlier, given the impasse in trade talks between the US and India.
"For years we have been setting the foundation for same type of relationship (that Starlink has in countries where it operates) here in India, establishing MoUs with Jio, Airtel and more, working closely with state govts to learn how Starlink might be able to serve best once it is authorised," said Dreyer. "Starlink can help reach places where the last mile is still the hardest mile, working alongside India's operators, govt and industry. As India works through the final approvals, our message is simple: We stand ready to serve India, as soon as India is ready," she said on X.
With the now-disbanded Digital Communications Commission (DCC) recently clearing Trai recommendations on satellite spectrum allocations, satellite service providers are likely to receive spectrum for five years and they will be required to pay a spectrum usage charge (SUC) equivalent to 5% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR). The greatest threat to the human brain today isn’t a virus, a tumour, or a traumatic injury. It is a lifestyle we’ve quietly accepted as normal.
We wake up to notifications, rush through deadlines, scroll through endless feeds, and fall asleep with glowing screens still inches from our faces. Somewhere between constant connectivity and relentless productivity, our brains have forgotten what it feels like to truly rest. Stress has become an accepted part of modern living. Students navigate academic pressure, professionals chase deadlines, and families juggle responsibilities in an increasingly demanding world. Although many dismiss mental fatigue as a normal consequence of a busy life, neuroscience tells a different story. Chronic stress alters the way the brain functions, influencing memory, attention, emotional regulation, and decision-making.
Unlike short-term stress, which prepares us to respond to immediate challenges, prolonged stress keeps the brain in a constant state of alertness. Elevated levels of cortisol,the body’s primary stress hormone which can gradually affect brain regions responsible for learning and memory. The result is a growing number of people who complain of brain fog, forgetfulness, poor concentration, and restless sleep despite having no neurological disease.
Every notification competes for our attention, quietly training the brain to choose distraction over deep focus. The result is a generation that feels mentally exhausted despite doing less physical work than ever before. Yet the brain is remarkably resilient. Through neuroplasticity ,its ability to rewire and form new neural connections,it can recover, adapt, and thrive when given the right environment. Regular physical activity, restorative sleep, meaningful social interaction, and periods of digital disconnection are not simply lifestyle choices; they are scientifically proven strategies that support brain health. Even a daily walk can improve blood flow to the brain, enhance mood, and strengthen cognitive function. Protecting the brain does not always require complex interventions. Often, it begins with simple habits practiced consistently.
The brain is humanity’s greatest asset, yet it is often our most neglected. Every choice we make either strengthens it or slowly wears it down. In the pursuit of faster lives, let us not sacrifice the very organ that allows us to think, create, love, and dream. The greatest investment we will ever make is not in technology, but in the health of our own brain.
Dr. Hina Gul, PT, Neuro Rehabilitation Specialist,

Zelensky condemns 'vile' large-scale Russian attacks that killed 24

At least 24 people have died in overnight strikes across central and eastern Ukraine, in what Volodymyr Zelensky has described as one of Russia's "most vile" attacks.
Ukraine's president said a residential building in Pryluky in the Chernihiv region was destroyed as a "birthday 'gift' to Putin", who turns 74 on Wednesday. Strikes also hit Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia and Oleksandriya.
Zelensky said Ukraine had struck targets in attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions in the past 24 hours, adding there was "also a response in the Black Sea", without providing further details.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest strikes.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelensky said, adding that 70 missiles were fired in total.
In a social media post on Wednesday afternoon Zelensky said 18 people, including four children, had been killed in one strike on a five-storey apartment building in Pryluky.
State Emergency Service of Ukraine says there had also been 50 people injured in the attack, including seven children.
Elsewhere two people were also killed and eight injured after Russian missile strikes damaged five apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, said Zelensky.
Two people were also killed in the capital, Kyiv, and two others in Oleksandriya, he added.
Ukraine's national police posted pictures online showing what it says is an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in the middle of a Kyiv district. BBC Verify has confirmed the images are genuine and the apparent missile fragments came down in an area of open land surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings.
A video posted by the police shows people digging through collapsed remains of a residential building in Pryluky. Another verified video shows damage to cars and what appears to be rubble and a fallen tree in an area surrounded by apartment blocks in Kremenchuk.
Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine, saying its military only managed to shoot down "some" of the missiles launched by Russia overnight.
According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was the country's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities.
In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.
"There is also a response in the Black Sea," the Ukrainian president wrote.
On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia.
The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued.
Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgaria's BTA news agency. No details of the crew are known, but Nikolov said it was assumed there were Syrians on board.
Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.
Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime.bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala.
As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued.
Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks.
It comes as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident.

- A rumor spread online in fall 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had formally denied protections for monarch butterflies under the Endangered Species Act until 2030.
- This rumor originates from a September 2026 settlement between conservation groups and the Fish and Wildlife Service over the federal agency's failure to finalize a policy proposal that would have protected monarch butterflies under the act.
- In December 2024, under then-President Joe Biden's administration, Fish and Wildlife formally proposed such a rule. Under the act, proposed rules must be finalized within one year. Thus, Trump's administration was supposed to make a decision by December 2025. It did not, which resulted in the lawsuit.
- The settlement specifies that the Trump administration must finalize the proposal to protect monarch butterflies by June 2030, meaning the administration could technically issue a decision anytime before 2030. However, the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said Fish and Wildlife "asserted that they do not have the resources to issue the final listing before the agreed upon date because of budget and workload."
- Given that we cannot predict the future, we have rated this claim as a mixture of truth and undetermined information.
In fall 2026, a rumor spread online that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had formally denied protections for monarch butterflies under the Endangered Species Act until 2030.
In other words, posts claimed that the government had refused to designate monarch butterflies as an at-risk species deserving of specific protections under federal law — and that the government would not consider the issue again until 2030.
The claim circulated on Facebook (screenshot) and X.
The claim is largely true, although it omits a few details. On Sept. 30, 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service reached a settlement with conservation groups, including the Center for Biological Diversity, over a delay on the federal agency's decision as to whether monarch butterflies should be protected under the Endangered Species Act.
The settlement requires Fish and Wildlife to issue a final decision by June 6, 2030. Technically, that means Fish and Wildlife could issue a decision anytime before that deadline. However, Center for Biological Diversity spokesperson Tierra Curry said Fish and Wildlife "asserted that they do not have the resources to issue the final listing before the agreed upon date because of budget and workload."
We reached out to Fish and Wildlife to confirm whether this is true and await a response.
It's also worth noting that Trump is due to leave office in January 2029, so it's possible that a future administration may prioritize making a decision on monarch butterfly protections before 2030.
Because we can't predict what the future holds, we have rated this claim as a mixture of truth and undetermined information.
Monarch butterfly conservation
Fish and Wildlife estimates that, by 2080, the probability of extinction for eastern monarchs ranges from 56% to 74% and for western monarchs the probability for extinction is greater than 95%. Threats to the species include loss of habitat, exposure to insecticides and the effects of climate change, the agency said on its monarch butterfly conservation page.
The Endangered Species Act allows the federal government to designate imperiled species as threatened or endangered. Each designation comes with its own protections and resources for conservation.
For more on the Trump administration's changes to the Endangered Species Act, see our explainer.
Background on conservation efforts
Conservation groups have fought to bring monarch butterflies and their habitats under Endangered Species Act protections since at least 2014, when three groups and a monarch scientist named Lincoln Brower filed a formal petition with the Fish and Wildlife Service. 
In December 2020, under the first Trump administration, Fish and Wildlife announced that protection for monarch butterflies was "warranted but precluded by work on higher-priority listing actions."
Fish and Wildlife's news release on the decision said 161 species were listed as higher priorities for formal protections under the Endangered Species Act ahead of the monarch butterfly.
"With this decision, the monarch becomes a candidate for listing under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), and its status will be reviewed each year until it is no longer a candidate," then news release said.
Under former President Joe Biden's administration in December 2024, Fish and Wildlife proposed an official rule that would have designated the monarch butterfly as a protected species under the Endangered Species Act:
We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to list the monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus), the iconic orange and black butterfly, as a threatened species and designate critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). We propose to list the monarch butterfly as a threatened species with protective regulations.
Under the Endangered Species Act, Fish and Wildlife is supposed to publish its final decision within one year of publication of a proposed rule, which would put the rule into effect and thus, in this case, officially list the monarch butterfly as an endangered species worthy of protection.
Trump took office January 2025. His administration did not meet that one-year deadline, which prompted the lawsuit from the Center for Biological Diversity and the Center for Food Safety.
What the settlement says
The settlement does not prevent the Trump administration from making a decision before 2030. Here's what it says on Page 2:
On or before June 6, 2030, the Service shall submit to the Office of the Federal Register for publication a final listing determination for the Monarch Butterfly, pursuant to the ESA, 16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(6).
Curry, the Center for Biological Diversity spokesperson, said in an email that, in effect, the settlement meant the denial of current protections would end in 2030 with a final listing. The Center for Biological Diversity's news release about the settlement called it a "bittersweet move for conservation groups."
In other words, it's not as if the Trump administration withdrew the proposal to protect monarch butterflies — rather, the settlement means Fish and Wildlife has until 2030 to make a decision on whether to finalize protections for the species.
There are also additional ways, per the settlement, that the deadline to make a decision could be extended. For example, if the government were to shut down due to a lapse in funding before 2030, the deadline would be extended for the number of days the shutdown occurred (see Page 2).

Four medical establishments in Hyderabad were issued show-cause notices after joint inspections by the EAGLE Force and TG SAFE found discrepancies in records concerning the purchase and sale of habit-forming medicines.
The inspections, carried out following inputs from Central intelligence, covered pharmacies in Masab Tank, Mallepally and Tolichowki. Officials checked compliance with requirements governing the purchase, storage and sale of regulated medicines, including Schedule H and H1 drugs.
At Al-Hamra Medical & General Store in Masab Tank, officials found that prescribed schedule registers had not been maintained and sale bills concerning certain habit-forming medicines, including Tapentadol, Alprazolam and others, were either not maintained or produced for verification.
At MM Medical and General Store in Mallepally, operating as MED24 Pharmacy and General Store, officials found deficiencies in prescribed registers and non-production of sale bills relating to Pregalyv 75. The Schedule H1 drugs register and sale bill book were also not produced.
A surprise inspection was conducted at First Step Drug Mart in Tolichowki following information about the indiscriminate sale and distribution of habit-forming medicines. Officials found several such medicines at the establishment, while the pharmacist was not present during the inspection. The Schedule H1 drugs register was also not produced, and discrepancies were noticed in records concerning the purchase and sale of the medicines.
At Hayat Pharmacy in Tolichowki, the prescribed Schedule H1 records and prescription register for habit-forming medicines were not produced. Officials also found deficiencies in the maintenance and production of sale bills for certain medicines.
Show-cause notices were subsequently issued to all four establishments, with further regulatory action to be taken under the applicable provisions and norms of the Drugs Control Administration.

Ex-Spurs player Vega set to run for Fifa president
- Published
Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.
The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, which has sparked a major backlash across football.
A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004.
"I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," he said.
Last month, Infantino said he was "fully committed to leading Fifa" despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit.
Vega considered running for Fifa's top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter.
Four years later he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of Fifa's 211 member federations.
"I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game," Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy.
"Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution.
"It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life.
"It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world's game.
"Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family.
"The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged Fifa's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating.
"Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better."
Vega concluded: "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. Fifa needs a new direction and fundamental reform.
"We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise Fifa's governance. This requires decisive change - not cosmetic adjustments."
