Forced to call him 'Dad': Sexual abuse of disabled residents that shocked South Korea
- Published
"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."
These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.
Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.
She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.
Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.
The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.
The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.
We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.
'I just endured it'
Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.
The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.
According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.
Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.
That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.
She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.
Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.
According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.
As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.
"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.
When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."
A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.
They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.
Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.
He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.
For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".
A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.
The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.
In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.
The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.
But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.
According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.
Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.
Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".
But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.
"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.
Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".
Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.
Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".
Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."
The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".
Public scrutiny and protests
The case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.
That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.
These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.
But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.
A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose.
The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.
Jo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns.
Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.
One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.
Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.
And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.
In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year.
In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022.
"The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."

Since the case came to light, South Korea's prime minister has ordered the formation of a cross-government response team, calling the incident "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".
In April, the government said it had inspected 1,507 residential facilities for disabled people nationwide and identified 33 suspected cases of abuse. So far investigations have been opened into eight of them.
The government also said it would strengthen targeted inspections based on risk factors, as well as joint inspections involving local authorities, police and disability rights advocacy agencies.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close and the local government has revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The local government has said it will draw up individual independent-living support plans for all 33 Saekdongwon residents. That process is still under way.
Saekdongwon has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence. It has yet to comment on Kim's conviction.
Asked what had changed most since leaving Saekdongwon, Seo said: "I just feel at peace. I'm happy every day."
She also said the best thing was being able to eat and sleep when she wanted.
What she wanted most now was "to cut ties with the director completely and never have anything to do with him again".
But, Seo added, people with disabilities still need somewhere they could feel safe.
"I hope there can be a facility without sexual violence, where disabled people like us can live in peace."

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday (October 1, 2026). They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The General Administration Department (GAD) has issued directives to departments to hold Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) meetings under the Madhya Pradesh Public Service Promotion Rules, 2025.
The directive says that if any unexpected vacancy arising in 2026 cannot be filled through the waiting list, a DPC meeting should be organised between September and November 2026 to consider expected vacancies for 2027.
Under Rule 6 of the promotion rules, a DPC meeting is required for every selection year. Such meetings should normally be held in the previous year between September and November to consider the eligibility of public servants for promotion against possible and unexpected vacancies available till noon on Dec 31 of the next selection year.
Earlier, after the rules came into force, a DPC was held for vacancies available till noon on Dec 31, 2025. On this basis, the promotion process for 2026 was undertaken or is underway.
The directive further says that departments that have not held meetings for expected vacancies within the stipulated period should do so. However, where action has already been taken within the prescribed timeframe, no fresh DPC meeting is required.

Amazon’s Prime Day is back for its fall edition, and Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?
There’s already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it’s whether the sales are a real discount or more of a mind game. That’s thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case for recommending it.
If you’re interested in Amazon’s device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I’ve got you covered. I’ve been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED’s resident Kindle expert, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here’s my full breakdown of all of Amazon's on-sale gadgets and which sales are best, whether it's an Amazon Echo speaker or a Kindle e-reader. Be sure to check out our guide to the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals for more great discounts.
Updated October 7, 3:52 AM ET: We've confirmed all of these deals are still live, and added a new deal on a Fire tablet , as we head into day two of Prime Day.
- My favorite Amazon Echo deal: Echo Spot for $55 ($55 Off)
- The cheapest Amazon Echo: Echo Dot (5th Gen) for $40 ($40 Off)
- A better version of our favorite Kindle e-reader: Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition for $170 ($80 Off)
- A great price for a color Kindle: Kindle Colorsoft for $190 ($100 Off)
- An art TV powered by Amazon: Ember Artline TV (55 inches) for $500 ($400 Off)
The Best Amazon Alexa Deals
Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you’re set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.
The Best Amazon Kindle Deals
If you’re shopping for a Kindle, this is the best time to buy since most were hit with price increases. You won’t get as good a deal anymore after Amazon raised prices across its e-reader lineup, but it’s much better to buy at a discount off the new price than at full price for the same product.
Just about every older Kindle (specifically the 2024 line) is on sale. Brand-new Kindles were announced just last week, but we don’t expect those to go on sale during this event. Here are the sales I’d recommend checking out.
The Best Fire TV Deals
If you’re shopping for a Fire TV or streaming device, look no further. Here are our favorites from Amazon’s lineup that are also on sale.
Best Amazon Eero Deals
If you haven’t already upgraded your home Wi-Fi router with a mesh system, then you’re long overdue. Amazon’s Eero system is one of the most popular for a reason, and Prime Day has a few versions on sale that we like.
Other On-Sale Amazon Devices We’ve Tested
Looking for a different device during Amazon’s sale event? We’ve tested several other Amazon Echo and Fire TV devices that are also on sale right now. Here’s what else you can consider, and what the discount looks like.
- Amazon Echo Dot Max for $80 ($40 Off): If you’re looking for a small speaker with bigger sound than the older Echo Dot, the Echo Dot Max has impressive sound for its size, plus a built-in smart home hub. Its price did increase by $20, though, so it feels like it’s just $20 off even if it looks like $40.
- Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $125 ($75 Off): While this model is on sale, I prefer the older Echo Show 8 (though it seems rarely available anymore) and the Echo Show 11 since both have better sound. It’s a good discount, even off the original $180 price tag, but I’d just spend $25 more and get the better Echo Show 11 if you’re set on a new Amazon Alexa-powered smart display.
- Amazon Echo Show 15 for $250 ($100 Off): The Echo Show 15 and Echo Show 21 are on sale and both double as a Fire TV device, with a massive screen, a flat back for mounting, and an included Alexa Voice Remote. I don’t love the TV experience, but it works, and the homepage fits a ton of widgets if you want to see multiple at once. Both sizes are discounted, but both models also cost more now, so it’s not as good as you’d think for the same device.
- Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max for $45 ($40 Off): If you love Amazon Prime as your streaming service, this is the favorite we’ve tested of Amazon’s Fire TV streaming devices. It’s not a crazy discount since it went up $25 in August, but it’s still a really affordable streaming stick during this same event.
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Kids for $170 ($60 Off): The Paperwhite Kids has everything we like about a Kindle Paperwhite, but adds a cover to protect it from any drops by your kiddo's hands and comes with six months of Kids+ content, which is like Kindle Unlimited but designed for kids. It’s a good device, but the discount isn’t as good as before; it used to retail for $180, so it’s really only $10 off what it used to cost. But you won’t find it new for cheaper.
- Amazon Kindle Kids for $123 ($57 Off): This is the cheapest Kindle Kids device, with a 6-inch screen similar to the cheapest Kindle, and it still comes with a colorful cover and six months of Kids+ content like the Paperwhite Kids above. It has the smallest discount out of the Kids devices, and it used to retail for $130, so it’s only $7 off the original price. The other Kids models are a better buy.
- Amazon Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $480 ($150 Off): The Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has one of the biggest discounts on an Amazon device for Prime Day, but for the most expensive Kindle ever. While I really like the Kindle Scribe system if you want both an e-reader and a digital notebook, for that price I’d recommend a reMarkable Paper Pro digital notebook, which comes with a ton more features and a color screen. Otherwise, stick with the more affordable Kindle Scribes. It is a much better price right now if you really want those features and color, but it’s hard for me to recommend over other options.
- Amazon Fire HD 10 for $73 ($82 off): Given the steep discount here, and the timing, I expect Amazon will be updating its tablet line this fall. However, given the price hikes for the rest of the company's products, whatever new Fire tablets are coming will likely be more expensive, which makes this deal more appealing, even if it is potentially outdated tech. The Fire HD 10 is the best of Amazon’s tablets and the one we recommend. It's certainly not the fastest tablet around, but when you can snag it on sale for around $100, it's a good deal. It has the best battery life of any Fire tablet, and a 1080p screen that has a lot of glare, but looks decent when you're watching a movie in the dark. You can even set it up to work like an Echo speaker. Turn on Show Mode and you can query Alexa til your heart's content. Realize this is no iPad, but performance is good enough for browsing the web and watching movies.
Which Amazon Device Prices Went Up?
Amazon raised prices across several of its device categories at the end of August. It’s not a shocking move, but it hit many affordable products and makes for a worse sale season since we’re getting discounts on a higher price tag for no other improvements. Here’s a quick breakdown of most of the price changes to help you navigate what sales are good and which are really just bringing you back to the old price.
Either way, I’d only buy an Amazon device on sale now, but it is unfortunate that the sales just won’t be as good anymore on these existing devices. I expect most, if not all, of these devices to go on sale at some point during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss as Spygate ban suspended
- Published
Tonda Eckert is free to continue as Southampton manager after being given a suspended ban for his role in the Spygate scandal.
A Football Association (FA) independent regulatory commission handed the German a six-week ban from all football, but suspended it until the end of next season.
Eckert has also been given a £28,000 fine and a reprimand but avoided a lengthy ban that could have cost him his job.
The FA had proposed a three-month ban, but the commission gave credit to Eckert for what they called "considerable mitigation in this matter, most particularly around the genuine contrition".
The governing body charged Eckert in July with misconduct, and a hearing took place at the end of last month.
Saints were expelled from the Championship play-offs in May after admitting spying on training sessions involving Oxford United, Ipswich Town, and Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.
They were also handed a four-point deduction for this season.
An English Football League (EFL) independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".
The 33-year-old apologised in June - claiming he was unaware the practice was banned and that it had no impact on his team's performances - but the FA took action.
Eckert has been sanctioned for three breaches of FA Rule E3.1. The six-week ban from all football activity would be triggered if he was found to be involved in any other spying between now and the end of next season.
Eckert was appointed permanent Southampton manager in December 2025 after taking interim charge when they were 21st in the Championship. They finished the season in fourth place.
Saints, who face local rivals Portsmouth this weekend, are 13th in the Championship this season with four wins from their eight matches so far.
They argued they had suffered enough as a result of the scandal.
Eckert told BBC Sport last month: "It's been a big, big punishment. Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports.
"I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly."
According to the EFL commission, the club employed "a particularly deplorable approach" by using junior members of staff to conduct the spying "at the direction of senior personnel".
An arbitration panel detailed how a junior analyst intern said he felt under "extreme pressure".
The FA did not charge Leeds United's former manager Marcelo Bielsa after the club were found guilty of spying on Derby in 2019, instead issuing a formal warning.
The EFL fined Leeds £200,000 - which Bielsa said he paid - and introduced a rule prohibiting any club from observing a rival's training session within 72 hours of a match between them.
The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year after opponents New Zealand were spied on.
Recap: What did Southampton do?
It was the morning of Thursday, 7 May.
Middlesbrough were at their Rockliffe Park training base preparing for the game against Southampton 48 hours later.
The spy - Southampton intern William Salt - is said to have parked at the golf club, then walked a couple of hundred yards down a road that leads to a raised area of ground.
Sources told the BBC that Salt stood pointing his mobile at the training session, while wearing in-ear headphones.
Middlesbrough staff believe he may have been live-streaming the session via a video call.
A member of Middlesbrough's staff approached, say BBC sources, but the person would not identify himself. He then quickly deleted some content on his phone before running into the golf club.
He jogged into the toilets, changed his clothes and hurriedly left the site.
Middlesbrough's photographer took photos and matched him to a photo on the Southampton website. One of those pictures was subsequently made public.
Boro were furious and quickly reported the incident to the EFL, which charged Southampton with breaking two regulations:
- EFL regulation 3.4, which requires clubs to act towards each other with the utmost good faith; and
- EFL regulation 127, which prohibits any club from observing, or attempting to observe, another club's training session within 72 hours of a scheduled match between the two clubs.
During the investigation, details emerged about the club watching training sessions involving Oxford and Ipswich, in addition to filming Middlesbrough as they prepared for the first leg of their play-off semi-final.
Southampton did not win any of the three games - they lost 2-1 at Oxford, drew 2-2 at home to Ipswich and 0-0 at Boro.
Salt has since been appointed to a permanent role at Saints in the club's academy.
Southampton told the BBC "he's been through a time time".
"When your photo is put out to the public, that is something tough to deal with," chief executive Phil Parsons told the BBC last month.
"A lot of people probably underestimated how that could have impacted a young lad so we've got a job to make sure that he's looked after in his early career. But he's a talented boy as well. I get good feedback and he's got a good role at the club."

According to statements from the Kennedy Center and Steinway and Sons, the center leases some of its pianos from a Steinway franchisee who is retiring soon. The leases on 16 of the center's Steinways are therefore expiring and the center needed to return them. Not all of its pianos were moved.
In October 2026, photos shared online appeared to show workers at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts moving Steinway pianos out of the Washington, D.C., center. The photos were accompanied by posts claiming the center was planning to sell all of its Steinways.
Because U.S. President Donald Trump — whose time as chair of the Kennedy Center Board has been tumultuous — announced in September that the facility had closed for renovations, the idea that the center was preparing to sell all its Steinway pianos seemed plausible to some online, and Snopes received several emails asking for a fact-check.
We contacted the Kennedy Center, the White House and Steinway and Sons for clarification on the matter. We heard back from the Kennedy Center and Steinway, both of whom provided statements disproving the rumor. As such, we rate the claim false.
The photos posted online showed workers in hard hats moving grand pianos through the center's hallways. One appeared to be wearing a shirt that said "Lewis" on it, which matched the name of a Washington-area piano moving company. We found no signs of generative AI or other tampering, meaning that the photos were real and the pianos were really being moved.
In its statement to Snopes and other outlets, the Kennedy Center said it was returning 16 leased pianos, not selling its collection. According to the statement, the center leases some of its pianos from a Steinway franchisee in northern Virginia who plans on retiring soon and is selling off his inventory. The leases on those 16 pianos, which were mostly located in "rehearsal rooms and dressing rooms," are expiring as a result, the statement said.
The center noted it was talking with Steinway's corporate office, which is taking over the local franchise, about new contracts. It also noted center still has about half of its pianos on site, some of which it owns.
Steinway spokesperson Anthony Gilroy confirmed those facts in an email to Snopes.
"The true story is that the owner of Steinway's dealership for DC, Maryland, and Virginia is retiring and closing by the end of the year," he said. "Sixteen Steinway pianos were leased by the Kennedy Center from that local Steinway dealer, who will be closing his store soon, and thus the pianos needed to be returned. That lease was done between the Kennedy Center and this local authorized dealer."
The claim emerged during a chaotic two years at the Kennedy Center. Trump has treated the center as a pet project of sorts throughout his second term, installing himself as the center's chairman and removing other board members, attempting to add his name to the center (a judge later ordered him to remove it) and closing the center for two years for repairs (then threatening to not complete those repairs unless his name is put on the building).
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous rumors about the Kennedy Center, including recent photographs of the president on Air Force One looking at a poster seemingly titled "Kennedy Center Demolition," suggesting that Trump may be thinking of tearing down the building.

3 dead, eight injured as 5-storey building collapses in Delhi's New Seemapuri
The Delhi Fire Service received a call about the building collapse at around 3:30 pm and rushed four fire tenders to the spot. A rescue operation is underway.
Three people, including two children, died after a five-storey residential building collapsed in Delhi's Seemapuri area on Wednesday afternoon, while 8 people have suffered injuries. The rescue operation is being carried out jointly by the Delhi Fire Services (DFS) and the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF).
The deceased include a 21-year-old woman, Gulafsa, who was around four months pregnant, and two children—a 12-year-old girl and another child whose identity is yet to be ascertained.
Eight injured people have been rescued and shifted to Rajiv Gandhi Super Speciality Hospital in Tahirpur for treatment. One of the injured is a toddler, while the other seven are adults. They have been identified as Momin Mirja, 56; Abdul Rehman, 28; Devruddin, 28; Salma, 50; Chote, 34; Sakina, 35; and Samad, 30.
The building, constructed on a plot of approximately 25 square yards, collapsed and partially damaged two adjoining buildings.

Eight injured persons, including a child aged around three years, have been rescued from the affected area while some are feared trapped.
The injured are being treated at the GTB Hospital emergency department, which is currently operational at the Rajiv Gandhi Hospital campus.
The Delhi Fire Service (DFS) received a call about the building collapse at around 3:30 pm and rushed four fire tenders to the spot.
Some people are feared trapped under the debris, an officer said. "Search and rescue operation is ongoing," a DFS officer said, according to PTI. The rescue operation is being carried out jointly by the DFS and the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), which was called in immediately.

According to people who spoke to Hindustan Times, the building is owned by Mohammed Anwar. His son-in-law, Mohammed Akbar, 33, said the family lived across four floors of the building and that he witnessed the structure collapse.
He said three family members, including his sister-in-law, remained trapped. Anwar's daughter Ameena told HT that an adjoining building had been undergoing demolition for the past five to six days using a machine, which she claimed had affected their house.
Another resident, 30-year-old Sameena, told HT that her 21-year-old sister Gulfisha, who is four months pregnant, was trapped under the debris along with her four-year-old daughter. Gulfisha reportedly called from under the debris and said she was having difficulty breathing. "She (Gulfisha) is four months pregnant. Her four-year-old daughter and owner's daughter are with her too. She said she is stuck inside and is facing difficulty breathing".
Ameena also told HT that the family had moved into the building around four months ago after it was newly constructed.
A resident of a street adjacent to the spot said there was a shop on the ground floor, while families lived on the four floors above it.
"Two-three people have been rescued by locals and police, multiple are still trapped," said Kulsum Khatoon.
Pankaj Luthra, Municipal Councillor from Jhilmil, who reached the spot, said, “We received information that an old building, around 40–50 years old, had collapsed…Four to five people have already been rescued from the debris. This comes a month after a boys' PG in Delhi's Satya Niketan collapsed on September 6 while repair work was underway. Seven people were killed and several others were injured in the incident.
Since the Satya Niketan incident, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has been conducting enforcement drives against dangerous buildings, unauthorised constructions and violations of the Master Plan of Delhi (MPD) and building bye-laws. Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital ‘who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her’

Christa Pike, an inmate who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday evening.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” the statement continued.
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her.”
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death nearly a week ago last Wednesday.
On Sunday, her lawyer, assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell, told CNN, “She's still in the hospital on a ventilator, critically ill. We don't really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days.”
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Asked by CNN if she’d regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Ferrell replied: “Not that I’m aware of”, adding that doctors were still trying to clear the high barbiturate dosage out of her system.
Pike's execution was delayed for more than eight hours Wednesday as the U.S. Supreme Court considered, and ultimately overturned, a federal appeals court ruling to halt her lethal injection so judges could thoroughly review whether the jury that sentenced her to death should have considered sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child.

Rathi Med Speciality Hospital, Chennai, launched a fresh meniscus allograft transplantation (MAT) programme as part of the Chennai Knee Course 2026 on Sunday (October 4).
The programme was inaugurated by IIT-Madras Director V. Kamakoti and Tamil Nadu Health Secretary Darez Ahamed, IAS.
The programme involves using a healthy meniscus from selected patients undergoing total knee replacement as a fresh graft for patients whose damaged meniscus cannot be repaired or reconstructed.
The hospital said it had received a licence from the Tamil Nadu government to perform fresh meniscus transplantation of the knee ), valid until December 2030.
The programme is led by N. Ragunanthan, Director, Head of Orthopaedics, and Consultant Surgeon of the hospital.
The conference, titled ‘The Meniscus 360° – From Repair to Transplant’, discussed meniscus transplantation and knee preservation.
The hospital also presented its Kinematic Knee Treatment and KPA Knee Preservation 360° approach for knee preservation in suitable patients below 60 years of age.

Maharashtra: SRPF jawan dies after venomous snakebite at Gadchiroli camp
SRPF jawan deployed in anti-Maoist operations in Maharashtra died on Tuesday evening after being bitten by a venomous snake at a camp in Regadi
A 37-year-old State Reserve Police Force (SRPF) jawan deployed in anti-Maoist operations in Maharashtra’s Gadchiroli district died on Tuesday evening after being bitten by a venomous snake at a camp in Regadi.
The deceased was identified as Police Naik Rahul Prabhakar Shingare, attached to the ‘F’ Company of SRPF Group No. 6, based in Dhule.
According to officers, the SRPF company was deployed to Gadchiroli about a month and a half ago, with personnel accommodated near the Regadi Police Aid Centre.
Shingare went to take a bath near a large water tank in the camp when a venomous snake bit his hand on Tuesday around 11am.
Fellow officers immediately took him to the Chamorshi Rural Hospital, located 40 kilometres away. As his condition deteriorated, he was transferred to the District General Hospital in Gadchiroli. Despite doctors’ best efforts, he died during treatment later that evening.
Shingare was reportedly also working as a snake charmer and was known to rescue them.
“A condolence salute was accorded at the police drill ground in Gadchiroli, where three rounds were fired in the air as part of state honours. Senior police officials, SRPF officers, and fellow jawans were present to pay their respects,” Gadchiroli Superintendent of Police (SP) M Ramesh said.
Following the necessary legal formalities and an autopsy, the body was handed over for final rites.
Meanwhile, in a separate operation on Tuesday, Gadchiroli Police and security forces recovered and destroyed a large cache of buried weapons, explosives, and Maoist material in the Koparshi forest area under the Bhamragad subdivision, near the Maharashtra-Chhattisgarh border.
The seized materials included one .303 rifle, two single-shot rifles, two country-made pistols, one Barrel Grenade Launcher (BGL), live cartridges, detonators, walkie-talkies, and Maoist literature.

Medicine and surgery are not the answer for overweight children, the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
Releasing its first guidelines addressing the sharp rise in obesity among children and adolescents, the WHO instead strongly recommended structured diets, physical activity and behaviour changes.
"WHO does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery (surgery that changes the stomach or digestive tract) or weight-loss devices for children aged 0-9 years," it said.
"For adolescents aged 10-19 years, treatment with approved medicines may be considered only when a supervised multimodal lifestyle programme has not achieved the desired results.
"Bariatric surgery may be considered under strict conditions for adolescents with severe obesity."
The recommendations for those aged 19 and under contrast with the UN health agency's guidelines for adult obesity issued in December 2025, following the surge in popularity of a new generation of appetite-suppressing drugs called GLP-1 agonists -- which includes blockbuster brands Ozempic and Mounjaro.
The WHO said the range of weight-loss and diabetes drugs could be used for tackling obesity -- in adults.
170 million affected
In 2024, some 70 million children aged five to nine were obese, as were 100 million adolescents aged 10 to 19 worldwide, according to the WHO.
Among 5- to 19-year-olds, the prevalence of obesity has surged globally, rising from two percent in 1990 to eight percent in 2024.
"The rise of obesity is observed everywhere in all regions," said Luz Maria De Regil, director of the WHO's nutrition and food safety department.
"It's growing in low- and middle-income countries," while some high-income countries are starting to stop the rise of obesity, without yet making reductions.
"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change," she said.
The recommendations also stressed the importance of addressing mental health alongside obesity.
Anxiety, depression and low self-esteem can contribute to unhealthy eating, physical inactivity and social withdrawal, the WHO said.
Children and adolescents living with obesity may experience stigma and bullying, the UN health agency added.
Maria Nieves Garcia Casal, a scientist in the WHO's nutrition and food safety department, told reporters that bariatric surgery may be considered during adolescence for cases of severe obesity accompanied by complications such as type 2 diabetes or hypertension -- if diet and lifestyle changes have failed.

Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Less than a month before the midterms, the price of fuel is becoming a powerful election issue.
This week, President Trump issued an executive order aimed at lowering costs for frequent diesel users by making a type of fuel called "dyed diesel" more accessible through the end of the year.
Could this lower the cost of diesel? Let's get into it.
Why is diesel so expensive right now?
Prices for all kinds of oil products have risen this year because fewer ships have been getting through the Strait of Hormuz and transporting crude to refineries worldwide — but the diesel supply chain has been uniquely hit. Ukraine's recent attacks on Russian refineries have taken many of them offline, and Russia has cut back on its diesel exports. China has, too.
It's added up to a limited supply of diesel — a fuel that powers much of the industrial supply chain.
So its price has soared; the U.S. average for a gallon hit a record of $6.52 a few weeks ago. The price has eased a bit since then, but a gallon remains about $2.60 higher than this time last year, according to AAA.
When diesel prices rise, inflation is likely to follow, analysts say. Diesel powers much of the industrial supply chain, from agricultural equipment to trucks transporting goods from warehouses to grocery stores.
What is dyed diesel?
The "dyed" part means: red dye. "Red-dyed diesel is diesel with red dye in it. That's it," said Will O'Neill, principal analyst at S&P Global Energy and a follower of all things diesel.
Chemically, this diesel is almost identical to the regular kind you'd find in most gas stations. But it's a different color because it's used, and taxed, differently.
Red-dyed diesel is only meant for off-road vehicles, mainly farm and construction equipment — like a tractor that's used in a field. It's exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon on commercial diesel.
Drivers aren't suppose to use it in vehicles that drive on highways. People who do are subject to an IRS penalty — either $1,000 or $10 per gallon, whichever is more expensive.
The red color makes it easier to catch someone who filled up their tank with the wrong stuff. Using the red-dyed diesel is "effectively a form of tax evasion," O'Neill said.
But the new executive order says dyed diesel will be allowed on highways through the end of the year. The IRS won't penalize anyone who uses it.
Will this save people money?
It could help farmers, truckers and other workers who count on diesel to do their jobs. The executive order said this move would put money directly into their pockets "to support their vital service to our Nation."
It essentially expands the ways in which workers can use dyed diesel, sparing them the federal tax. Imagine a farmer who usually puts dyed diesel in their tractor — now they can also legally use it to fill up their cargo van, get on the highway, and take their produce to market.
Plus, a handful of states have said drivers can use red-dyed diesel on their highways. On average, state diesel taxes run about 35 cents a gallon. Allowing drivers to use dyed diesel — and skip both federal and state taxes — could add up to a savings of about 60 cents a gallon.
But because the cost of a gallon of regular diesel is now about $2.60 higher than this time last year, drivers will still be paying a higher price overall
Will this put more diesel on the market?
Technically, this will increase the total amount of diesel that people could use.
But Jaime Brito, executive director of oil markets at Dow Jones Energy, points out that this doesn't mean most people can easily access dyed diesel. It isn't available at most gas stations. "When was the last time that you went to a pumping station and you saw that one of the stations gave you the possibility to feed red diesel into your truck?" he asked.
Instead, people would need to go to a special wholesaler — or might be able to find it at gas stations in rural areas.
In an email to NPR responding to these critiques, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers wrote that the president wants to see prices fall and is taking "historic measures" to alleviate oil supply disruptions.
Can the Trump administration do anything else to lower diesel costs?
Over the past month, some politicians have floated the idea of a diesel export ban. The idea was that if the U.S. stopped sending diesel to other countries, maybe that would temporarily increase the supply in the U.S., pushing down the price.
But bottom line: refiners pushed back. It would be bad business for them.
Refiners make money by selling diesel within the U.S. and exporting it around the world, said Jacques Rousseau, who focuses on oil, natural gas, and refined products as a managing director with Clearview Energy Partners.
If there was a diesel export ban, sure, that diesel would stay in the U.S. But then, refineries would wind up with a ton of extra diesel. "Then it'll start going into storage. And then once your storage gets filled, then you have to reduce the overall production of your refinery. So then you just start producing less of everything else too because you have nowhere to put this diesel," Rousseau said.
Ultimately, that could lead to prices for refined oil products, like gasoline — and diesel — going up.
President Trump said late Friday that he was not seriously considering an export ban, and that the U.S. didn't need one anymore, as Europe just released about 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from its own stockpiles.
Analysts told NPR that the only real fix will be ending the wars in Iran and Ukraine — until there's more oil flowing freely around the world again, they said, it's hard to see the price of diesel getting much lower. " There's no silver bullet," said O'Neill. "There's no way to snap your fingers and end up with $4 diesel before the election."
"Barring the rapid and credible conclusion of the wars," he continued, "I don't think that happens."

Trump swats away female journalist after she asks him to explain ‘take out’ LA and San Diego comment
President refuses to explain rally line that incensed California lawmakers

President Donald Trump swatted away a question from a female reporter at the White House when she asked him to explain his comment about Iran “taking out” Los Angeles and San Diego.
Addressing a rally crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, Monday, the president had been discussing the Iran war driving up gas prices due to the blockading of the Strait of Hormuz, which he said was “a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.”
He then continued: “They can take out a city – let ’em take, let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. That’s – this is a very small price to pay.”
The comments drew outrage, particularly from California Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom, L.A. Mayor Karen Bass and San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria, who accused the president of being “deranged and dangerous” and reminded him that American lives are not expendable.
As he appeared on the White House lawn the following day, a female reporter called out to Trump: “Mr President, what did you mean by your comments yesterday about San Diego and Los Angeles possibly being wiped out by Iran?”
He walked towards her as though he were about to answer before making a swatting gesture with his right hand and ignoring her. The identify of the reporter who asked the question is not clear.
Trump also refused to engage with queries about his meaning at an earlier event for Gold Star Families in front of the presidential mansion, at which he appeared with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The official White House “Rapid Response” X account subsequently posted a clip of that moment with the comment: “Some whiny Fake News loser spent the entire press gaggle shouting at POTUS about the ‘take out Los Angeles and San Diego’ hoax – which is so obviously a lie, even CNN debunked it. These people are sick.”
White House Communications Director Steven Cheung also lashed out on X, reupping the original clip of Trump speaking in Nebraska with the caption: “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality.
“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”
However, CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, who was part of the press gaggle, appeared on her network’s Anderson Cooper 360 Tuesday evening and told the host journalists had “tried to ask the president to clarify those comments, or explain what he meant” on three separate occasions throughout the day and he had repeatedly refused to do so.
“When you look at the transcript and the audio of what he said there, he obviously heard the questions,” Collins told Cooper, concluding that the president had simply “declined to answer them.”
Trump has a long history of clashing with female members of the press, notably snapping “Quiet, piggy” at Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey last year and telling Weijia Jiang of CBS News she would be “incapable” of “acing” a cognitive test as he claimed he had just done.
He has frequently sparred with Collins, urging her to smile more and calling her “stupid and nasty” on Truth Social.
Among the California legislators taking exception to Trump’s rally line were Marni von Wilpert and Jim Desmond, congressional rivals at next month’s midterms, who found themselves in rare agreement on the president’s words.
Von Wilpert, the Democratic candidate for the Golden State’s 48th congressional district suggested Trump’s remark was an impeachable offense while Desmond – her GOP rival, whom Trump endorsed – said he “vehemently” disagreed with the commander-in-chief.
“Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” he said.
“No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Welcome to the debut of ID Consult, a new STAT column from infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli about diseases, outbreak response, global health, and health policy.
A 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia develops severe pneumonia and dies. She worked at an institute that studies plague and other high consequence infectious diseases. At least one hospital is placed under quarantine with close to 200 contacts reportedly being monitored. Simultaneously Russian public health officials descend on the region.
It is not difficult to understand why this story has received attention. After everything we have lived through over the past several years, an unexplained pneumonia in someone who worked at a laboratory studying dangerous pathogens can quickly lead to speculation about a laboratory accident, biological weapons, or “the next Covid-19.”
But we need to slow down.
There are important reasons to pay close attention to what is happening in Russia. There are also legitimate reasons to ask difficult questions about transparency, laboratory safety, and Russia’s history of biological weapons research. None of those things means we should jump ahead of the evidence.
Based on the information currently available, there is no confirmation that this woman died from plague, despite widespread speculation, nor is it clear her illness was connected to her work. Nothing reported thus far suggests sustained person-to-person transmission.
Most importantly, there is no evidence that we are witnessing the beginning of another pandemic.
What we have is an unexplained death that deserves a thorough and transparent investigation.
According to reports, Daria Shipilova worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, an institution involved in research of plague, anthrax, tularemia, and other high-consequence infectious diseases. She was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with severe pneumonia and died approximately two days later. Early news stories suggested that Shipilova may have had pneumonic plague, but Russian authorities have described her illness as pneumonia of unknown etiology and said that testing has not identified a pathogen associated with her work.
Public health officials have undertaken an extensive response. At least one hospital has reportedly been quarantined, contacts have been identified and monitored, and senior public health officials have been sent to the region. Covid-19 and rhinovirus have been identified in a small number of contacts tested.
This picture is broadly consistent with the latest assessment from the World Health Organization, which said Russia has reported no confirmed cases of plague in Irkutsk and no evidence of further infections among the contacts being monitoring. The WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of Shipilova’s severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and whether a second employee also has pneumonia of undetermined cause, as media reports suggest.
The absence of confirmed plague or documented transmission is reassuring, but uncertainties remain. In particular, the cause of Shipilova’s illness has not been established publicly, and reports of a second employee with unexplained pneumonia require clarification. The combination of limited information, conflicting reports, and a unusually extensive public health response naturally raises questions. At the same time, suspicion is not confirmation, and monitoring contacts does not mean they are infected. Most importantly, a “pneumonia of unknown etiology” is not synonymous with the emergence of a new pathogen. It simply means that we do not yet know what caused the pneumonia.
Could this be plague? Yes — it remains a possibility that warrants careful investigation, particularly given where she worked. However, even if pneumonic plague is ultimately confirmed, that does not mean we are facing the “next Covid-19.”
Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium that has caused infection in humans for thousands of years. Pneumonic plague is serious because it affects the lungs and can spread from person to person though respiratory droplets. Without prompt treatment, it can progress rapidly and lead to death.
The reassuring news is that plague is not an unknown threat. We know how to diagnose it, and we have effective antibiotics to treat it. We also know how to identify and monitor contacts, provide post-exposure prophylaxis, isolate patients, and implement infection prevention and control measures to interrupt transmission. That is fundamentally different from the situation we faced when SARS-CoV-2 emerged, when we were confronting a novel pathogen with limited knowledge about its transmission, clinical course, or how best to prevent and treat infection. There is an important distinction between encountering a new pathogen and responding to a disease we have studied for more than a century.
The epidemiology of plague also differs substantially from that of SARS-CoV-2. Person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague generally requires close exposure to respiratory particles from someone who is actively ill, and asymptomatic transmission has not been documented.
That does not make pneumonic plague benign. Rather, it means we should understand the risk based on what we know about the pathogen rather than immediately comparing it to Covid-19.
There is, however, another reason the situation in Russia deserves close attention. Russia, and before it the Soviet Union, has a well-documented history with biological weapons research.
The Soviet Union operated an extensive clandestine biological weapons program despite being a party to the Biological Weapons Convention. That program included work with pathogens capable of causing some of the world’s most dangerous outbreaks, including Yersinia pestis.
There is also well-documented historical evidence of an accidental release from the Soviet biological weapons program.
In 1979, an accidental release of aerosolized Bacillus anthracis spores from a military biological facility in Sverdlovsk caused an outbreak of inhalational anthrax that killed at least 66 people. Soviet authorities blamed contaminated meat.
Years later, investigators reconstructed the outbreak and found that human cases and livestock deaths followed a narrow zone extending downwind from the military facility. Their investigation, published in Science in 1994, provided compelling evidence that the outbreak resulted from an airborne release.
What does any of this mean for today?
It does not mean the current situation is connected to a biological weapons program. There is no evidence at this point to support that conclusion. A laboratory exposure, an accidental release, and a biological weapons program are separate claims, and each requires its own evidence.
Nevertheless, this history matters and provides a legitimate reason to demand transparency and independent verification.
Sverdlovsk is a particularly important lesson. A biological event occurred. People died. The official explanation was wrong. It took years before the world understood what had happened.
That history gives us good reason to ask questions about what is happening now. The appropriate response is neither panic nor blind reassurance, but a clear demand for transparency and data.
What specimens were collected? What testing was performed? Was Yersinia pestis specifically excluded? What pathogens did this woman work with? Was there any evidence of an occupational exposure or laboratory incident? Have any contacts developed a compatible illness? What explains the scale of the quarantine?
Most importantly, will Russian authorities share enough information with international public health organizations and independent experts to allow their conclusions to be evaluated?
We may eventually get a straightforward explanation or we may never know.
The uncertainty is uncomfortable, but uncertainty is a routine part of outbreak response. Since Covid-19, we seem to be particularly bad at tolerating it. An unusual infectious disease event occurs somewhere in the world. Information is scarce. Within hours, social media fills the gaps. Suddenly it is “Disease X,” a laboratory leak, or “the next pandemic.”
That is not preparedness. Preparedness is detecting unusual events early, investigating them quickly, sharing information transparently, and having the expertise and infrastructure to determine whether a signal represents an isolated event or something more serious.
There is a difference between vigilance and alarmism. But it is important to recognize that at a time when we need strong systems capable of detecting biological threats around the world, the United States is weakening parts of its own public health and scientific infrastructure.
Public health surveillance is not just about counting cases. It is part of national and global security. Laboratory networks, genomic surveillance, epidemiologists, infectious diseases experts, international partnerships, and relationships with scientists and public health officials in other countries all help us recognize when something unusual is happening.
Weakening those systems does not make biological threats disappear. It makes us less capable of seeing and understanding them. It also makes us more dependent on information provided by governments whose conclusions we may need to independently evaluate.
This should concern us far more than speculation on social media about whether an unexplained pneumonia is “the next Covid-19.”
There are developments that would change my assessment of the situation in Russia. Confirmation of Yersinia pestis or another high-consequence pathogen would be important. Additional unexplained pneumonia cases among contacts would matter. Evidence of person-to-person transmission, cases outside the immediate contact network, or credible evidence of a laboratory exposure would all raise the level of concern.
We do not have evidence of those things right now.
One of the most important things we can say in an outbreak investigation is also one of the hardest: “We don’t know yet.”
For now, we need more information from Russia. Until we have it, we should ask questions, follow the evidence, and resist the temptation to fill in what we do not know with what we fear.
Krutika Kuppalli, M.D., is an infectious diseases physician and former World Health Organization medical officer whose work has focused on vaccines, emerging infectious diseases, and outbreak preparedness and response. She served as medical director of an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola epidemic and has supported outbreak and vaccine efforts in Africa and globally.

Cisco is bringing a new agentic framework to its Webex enterprise platform
It's called Dialog and promises to turn "fragmented interactions into continuous customer relationships."
Cisco is updating its Webex cloud collaboration platform to better accommodate AI agents. Perhaps the biggest bit of news here is a new toolset called Dialog, which is an "agentic harness" that directs AI to handle customer interactions.
The company says that Dialog tasks various agents with keeping the consumer happy, as they'll "keep working on the customer's behalf after a conversation ends." This means that agents under Dialog's umbrella have the ability to coordinate "across people, agents and backend systems."
The platform also allegedly speeds up the onboarding process, treating "AI agents like new teammates." This means they'll be given the opportunity to peruse existing employee handbooks, knowledge bases and operating procedures.
Cisco promises a safety-forward experience via a collaboration with a data analysis company called Splunk, but this is a new feature and you never know what issues are gonna pop up. Agentic AI is gonna agentic AI. The company does suggest that the Dialog platform "continuously refines agent performance with every interaction." However, that's kind of the promise with all AI agents. We'll have to wait and see.
As for employees, the updated Webex will let anyone in a workspace directly invite AI agents into "spaces, meetings and calls to execute complex, multi-step work" across the platform and in third-party applications. Cisco gives an example of an agent quickly pulling up statistics during a presentation and updating a PowerPoint on the fly. That could be extremely useful, assuming it works.
"The numbers remain dismal. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University found earlier this year that even the best-performing AI agent, which was Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro at the time, failed to complete real-world office tasks 70 percent of the time."
A 70% failure rate is w i l d
— Matthew Noe (@noethematt.bsky.social) 2025-12-04T03:01:49.232Z
To that end, multiple studies have indicated that AI agents are still prone to mistakes which lead to cascading failures. The failure rate sits somewhere between 60 and 70 percent with regard to multi-step tasks. This is because all it takes is one single mistake during one step of the process to throw the whole thing off. Even an agent with a 95 percent per-step reliability rate will only succeed around 36 percent of the time when dealing with a 20-step workflow.
This will likely improve over time, but we aren't quite there yet. Even a 99 percent per-step reliability rate seems incredibly risky when money and a company's reputation is on the line.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

On September 23, the nominations for the 54th International Emmy Awards were announced and, in a significant achievement for India, the SonyLIV series Real Kashmir Football Club bagged a nomination in the Best Drama Series category. The recognition came as a pleasant surprise for the team, who are understandably on cloud nine. Our skin, hair and nails require adequate protein, energy, vitamins and minerals for growth, repair and normal functioning. When deficiencies are significant or prolonged, some may become visible. But many of these signs also overlap with hormonal disorders, chronic illnesses, dermatological conditions, stress, poor sleep and other factors. So when and how do you know if there is a nutritional deficit?
What the signs can indicate
Iron deficiency, particularly when it progresses to anaemia, can cause pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, and may be associated with diffuse hair shedding. Spoon-shaped nails can also occur with iron deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles, as well as changes in the tongue and oral mucosa.
Zinc deficiency can affect skin integrity and hair growth, while inadequate protein intake can affect hair structure and growth and, in severe cases, cause marked changes in the skin and hair. Vitamin C deficiency can result in bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Dry or scaly skin may be associated with inadequate vitamin A, essential fatty acids or zinc.
Cracks at the corners of the mouth can occur with iron, vitamin B12, zinc or riboflavin deficiency. A smooth, red and sore tongue, or glossitis, can be associated with deficiencies of vitamin B12, iron, folate or niacin.
Ramya Subburaj, senior clinical dietitian and head of the department of dietetics, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said these signs should be viewed as clues rather than proof of a deficiency. “There is considerable overlap between nutritional and non-nutritional causes,” she said, noting that a person with hair loss should not assume that poor nutrition is necessarily responsible.
What ‘ferritin face’ really means
Terms such as ‘iron-deficiency face’ and ‘ferritin face’ circulating on social media are not recognised medical diagnoses. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia and pallor, but there is no specific facial appearance through which low ferritin can be diagnosed.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and its level is used to assess the body’s iron stores. Low ferritin can occur before iron-deficiency anaemia develops. However, it does not produce a distinct facial appearance.
Pushpa Gnanaraj, senior consultant, dermatology, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, said pallor associated with anaemia may be visible in the skin, lips, gums or inner eyelids because of reduced haemoglobin. But dullness, dark circles or changes in facial appearance are not specific to low iron stores.
Vinitha Krishnan, chief clinical dietitian, nutrition and dietetics, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, said any changes associated with depleted iron stores are generally subtle and non-specific. Similar features can occur with inadequate sleep, stress, dehydration, allergies, ageing, thyroid disorders or other nutritional deficiencies.
A proper history and clinical examination are therefore important. Depending on the symptoms, investigations may include a complete blood count, ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Thyroid testing, zinc assessment or other investigations may be considered when clinically indicated. Dermatological conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, fungal infections, autoimmune disorders and pigmentary diseases may also need to be ruled out.
Correcting deficiencies
When a confirmed nutritional deficiency is responsible for a symptom, correcting it can lead to improvement. The timeline, however, depends on the nutrient involved and the severity and duration of the deficiency.
Pallor and some symptoms associated with iron deficiency may begin to improve within weeks of appropriate treatment, while mouth ulcers and glossitis can also improve after the underlying deficiency is corrected. Hair shedding and thinning generally take longer to recover because hair grows slowly; improvement may take several months. Nail changes can similarly take months to grow out.
Reshma Aleem, senior clinical dietician, Rela Hospital, Chennai, said the extent and speed of recovery depend on whether the deficiency is mild, moderate or severe and on how effectively it is corrected.
Fixing the basics
A varied diet remains the foundation. Adequate protein, pulses, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with eggs, dairy, fish, lean meat or fortified foods according to dietary preference, can provide a range of nutrients.
Experts caution against taking supplements based only on a social-media checklist. Excessive intake of some vitamins and minerals can itself cause adverse effects and may interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other nutrients. More importantly, treating an assumed deficiency can delay the diagnosis of the actual cause.
The appropriate approach is to investigate persistent changes, confirm a deficiency where indicated and then correct it with dietary measures or supplementation under clinical guidance.

Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.
“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month and moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.
“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases. If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.
Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.
Medical officers said this year, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.
The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.
According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.
The fact that the KMSCL owes over ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.
He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL
According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.
