Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.
- 'They aimed to kill' - BBC identifies security forces who shot Kenya anti-tax protesters 
  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park demanding accountability from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleged voter deletions, and transparency in the electoral process. Despite Mumbai Police denying permission for the gathering, thousands attended the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for allegedly violating restrictions on the assembly (here, here, and here).
In this context, two videos are circulating on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The videos show the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The videos do not show the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026. The first video was recorded at CJP’s protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, while the second video shows the Tiranga Vijay Rally jointly organised by Shiv Sena (UBT) and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) at Shivaji Park on 26 July 2026 . Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
Upon closely reviewing the viral videos, we noticed ‘Delhi Police’ written on the barricades. This indicates that the videos were recorded in Delhi, not Mumbai, as claimed in the viral posts.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to the same video uploaded on the Facebook page ‘Indian Sawarn Samaj News’ on 08 August 2026. The video was uploaded with a caption stating that it shows a CJP protest in Delhi demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. This confirms that the viral video predates the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
We also geolocated the high-rise building visible in the viral video to Jai Singh Marg, Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, Delhi. A comparison of the building in the viral video with its appearance on Google Maps Street View can be seen below.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) began its protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 06 June 2026, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in NEET-UG 2026. The protest continued for several weeks and was called off on 25 July 2026 following Pradhan’s resignation and government assurances on some of the protesters’ demands.
Video 2
We conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to the same video uploaded on the Facebook page ‘Mumbai Explore’ on 26 July 2026. The caption states that Dadar celebrated a memorable victory with grand celebrations. This confirms that the viral video predates the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
According to reports, the Tiranga Vijay Rally was held at Shivaji Park on 26 July 2026, one day after Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. It was jointly organised by Shiv Sena (UBT) and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS), led by Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray. The rally was originally planned as a Tiranga Morcha demanding Pradhan’s resignation, but after his resignation on 25 July 2026, it was turned into a victory gathering celebrating the student movement. Thousands of people attended, carrying the national flag and posters (here, here, and here).
We found multiple posts (here, here, and here) on the official Shiv Sena (UBT) social media handle featuring the rally. The stage, banners and other visual elements seen in these posts match those visible in the viral video, confirming that the viral video shows the Tiranga Vijay Rally held at Shivaji Park in July 2026, not the CJP protest held there on 02 October 2026.
To sum up, none of these viral videos shows the CJP protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026.

McKenzie starts at flyhalf for first Bledisloe test after Mo'unga injury
Oct 8 : Damian McKenzie will start at flyhalf for the All Blacks against the Wallabies in the first Bledisloe Cup test at Eden Park on Saturday after Richie Mo'unga was ruled out by an injury suffered in training.
• Coach Dave Rennie's preferred starter Ruben Love has been sidelined by an ankle injury so Mo'unga had been expected to start until he suffered a calf injury on Tuesday.
• Former captain Scott Barrett returns to the team for the first time since last November, starting in the second row with Josh Lord.

When India takes to the field for a T20I on October 22, it will be exactly three years and 11 months since Bhuvneshwar Kumar last took to the field for India.
There is, however, every chance that the streak will end before it can hit four years, with the 36-year-old named in the squad for India’s upcoming T20I series against New Zealand, marking the culmination of a remarkable turnaround for a bowler who seemed nowhere near national contention even this time last year.
The player himself had made his peace with not representing India. At a select media interaction during IPL 2026, he said, “I had made peace with it the day after I was dropped from the national team. It didn’t take me much time to think [on how to proceed]. With all these T20 competitions, there is enough in a year to be in touch with cricket.”
Comeback through the IPL
Bhuvneshwar has forced his name back into contention almost entirely through his performances for Royal Challengers Bengaluru across the last two seasons of the Indian Premier League (IPL).
He exclusively plays the shortest format of the game, with all of his appearances since February 2025 coming in T20s either in the IPL, Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, or UP T20 League.
ALSO READ | Gujarat Giants enters WPL 2027 mini-Auction with “least work to do”
His exclusive focus on short-format cricket has done little to affect his form, and he has arguably been the outstanding bowler across the last two seasons of the IPL. He is the leading wicket-taker since the start of IPL 2025 with 45 dismissals. More impressively, he is the only pacer in the top 20 of that list with an economy rate below nine (8.55), even as scoring rates rise higher by the season.
His effectiveness has translated across phases. He is the leading wicket-taker in the PowerPlay across the last two years (25 wickets), but he is also the joint-highest wicket-taker between overs 16 and 20 (18 wickets), level with Prasidh Krishna.
Central to his prolific wicket-taking has been his control of length. He has dominated the traditional ‘Test match’ lengths, the good-length and back-of-a-length areas, claiming 29 of his 45 dismissals from them.
“The length ball trend is back, but that is not for everyone. If there is help in the wicket, the length balls are effective,” he reflected. “The younger generation doesn’t care who is bowling or what the wicket is; they just go for it. They are being rude to seniors.”
His ability with the new ball was particularly devastating, allowing him to end matches almost on his own, as Delhi Capitals and Mumbai Indians found out to their detriment in IPL 2026.
A complete skill-set
But the 36-year-old is far from a one-trick pony. A look at his bowling patterns across the last two seasons indicates that while he has stuck to Test lengths during the PowerPlay, he has been far more adaptable in the closing stages of the innings, able to go both full and short to keep batters guessing.
His ability to vary his length is complemented by a repertoire of change-ups, including cutters, the knuckle-ball and, in the right conditions, reverse-swing. He noted that being a full-time T20 player meant that he was able to call on those skills more easily, saying, “The variations are always there when I practice. When I used to play other formats going from Tests to T20, there used to be a transition or it needed few net sessions to bring yorker and slower ball into practice.”
The variations not only made him a more adept death bowler but also gave him extra tools to counter aggression once the new-ball movement had worn off in the PowerPlay.
A multi-format option for India
Bhuvneshwar’s recall to the Indian team comes at an interesting time, given that its white-ball focus is currently on the 50-over format with the ODI World Cup next year.
A recall to the 50-over side seems unlikely, given that he has not played a List A game since December 2023. But his multi-phase excellence gives the T20I side flexibility as it looks to blood players before the 2028 T20 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand.
ALSO READ | WPL 2027 Retention: How Perry’s return complicates RCB’s top order
Many of the bowlers India has invested in, including Prasidh Krishna, Harshit Rana, and Gurnoor Brar, tend to operate with the older ball, and having a bowler who can reliably cover across phases gives it the chance to expose them to different situations with a safety net behind them.
But beyond his value for India, Bhuvneshwar’s comeback is testament to a bowler who has put in the hard yards to reinvent himself and stay relevant in an increasingly batting-dominated era of T20 cricket. In the process, he has perhaps become the standout bowler in the IPL.

Russian missile strike in Ukraine's capital kills at least 2
Russian missiles and drones have pounded Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, killing at least 21 civilians, including four children, and wounding around 60
KYIV, Ukraine -- Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into Wednesday, killing at least 21 civilians, including four children, and wounding around 60 in Moscow's latest devastating barrage, Ukrainian officials said.
Ukraine had anticipated the attack, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warning the previous day that intelligence services had concluded that Russia was building up for a “massive” strike.
Although Ukraine knew about the looming attack, which coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday, it couldn’t fend it off completely.
The deaths and damage illustrated the difficulty Ukraine has in countering Russia’s ballistic missiles and the new jet-powered drones used in Moscow’s escalating bombardments. Without ammunition for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukraine can’t stop Russian ballistic weapons. It is racing to develop a new generation of interceptors fast enough to catch Moscow's high-flying jet-propelled drones.
Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a long-range aerial war as their armies remain largely deadlocked on the battlefield, more than 4 ½ years after Moscow’s all-out invasion of its neighbor. The unrelenting aerial attacks are hurting Russia but could be ruinous for smaller Ukraine.
U.S.-led peace efforts appear unlikely to bring any short-term relief, with the possibility of holding low-level technical talks still under discussion. Putin, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with the invasion in the belief that Ukrainians will buckle under the pressure and Kyiv’s Western supporters won’t stay the course, Western analysts say.
“Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. “Trying to make daily life impossible for Ukrainians who want to live in peace.”
A Russian strike destroyed an apartment block in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, killing 15 people, including four children, and wounding about 50, authorities said.
Deaths were also reported in three other Ukrainian cities, including the capital Kyiv, according to Zelenskyy.
“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian leader said on social media.
Ukraine is looking worldwide for available Patriot missiles, which are in short supply due to the Iran war.
“Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelenskyy said.
In Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region, two people were killed and seven injured, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the regional military administration, and a rescue operation was continuing.
“That is exactly what the enemy is counting on. For us to be afraid to fall asleep. To let our children out of our sight. To plan anything. So that everyone thinks: next time it could be my address,” he said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said the military carried out a massive strike overnight targeting industrial facilities involved in the production and storage of missiles and drones across Ukraine. The ministry said that port and ship repair facilities in the southern Odesa region and ships carrying cargo for the Ukrainian military were also hit.
Ukraine has hit back at Russia by launching long-range drones and missiles at oil refineries and storage depots.
Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Ukraine targeted two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions of Russia.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.
Zelenskyy also indicated that Ukraine had struck in the Black Sea. He posted images of a fire said to show an oil tanker burning in the water near the Russian city of Sochi.
It was not possible to independently verify the images.
Some Russian online media late Tuesday also posted the images. Unconfirmed media reports said it was carrying oil from Novorossiysk to India and was attacked by Ukrainian sea drones.

Amazon thinks Thomas Gryta really likes beef jerky. He doesn't really know why.
"I've ordered more energy bars and vitamins than jerky," Business Insider's interim corporate editor wrote in Slack. He added that his Amazon "About You" customer profile "feels like a judgy accusation from a nutritionist."
That was just one of the messages that blew up Business Insider's Slack on Wednesday morning after I reported that people online were having a field day looking up their own Amazon "About You" page. People noticed the shopping profiles making bizarre — sometimes unflattering — judgments, like telling one Amazon user they have "flat buttocks" or another that their husband has "skinny legs."
The e-commerce giant launched About You in May. The page acts a bit like a customer dossier, pulling information from customers' marketplace searches, purchase histories, saved lists, product reviews, and conversations with Amazon's Alexa for Shopping assistant. Amazon says the goal is to connect customers with products that better fit their needs, and shoppers can update or remove details from the profile.
Naturally, Business Insider's nosy newshounds with semi-voyeuristic relationships with the internet wanted to share what we found out about ourselves, whether brutally accurate or laughably off base.
Per our own Slack channels, we found that Amazon typically made 30 to 45-ish observations for each subject. Those inferences frequently got the transactions right, but the human conclusions were sometimes a little off.
"My wife and I share an Amazon account, so our 'About You' profile was a bit warped," wrote Paul Squire, our deputy editor of homepage and programming, noting that Amazon correctly gleaned that he has a cat and a MacBook. "But it missed the mark by not realizing our second cat, Sylvie, even exists. 'Has one cat'? Try again, Jeff Bezos."
For Taylor Rains, a partnership editor, Amazon got a little personal about her taste in movie actors.
"One of mine is: 'used to like Ryan Reynolds, but not so much anymore,'" she wrote on Wednesday. "How does it know?"
Still, the majority of Amazon's judgments from our very unscientific newsroom poll proved correct.
Correspondent Madeline Berg said Amazon properly clocked that she was a stereotypical Brooklynite who prefers glass food storage and organic produce.
Deputy executive editor Taylor Berman said his account is optimized for "bathroom safety," a finding likely tied to his need for a shower chair after he tore his Achilles tendon last May (he asked me to make sure readers knew that his other purchases were "very cool").
Another editor, who has young kids, said Amazon reported that she frequently buys waterproof sheets.
Debbie Strong, deputy executive editor, said the system clocked her as a "boy mom" after it said she prefers Hot Wheels toy cars.
Other big themes: Amazon is very good at recognizing where we live (no surprises there), what kinds of groceries we frequently buy at Whole Foods, and if we have pets. Apparently, Business Insider's staff likes to buy a lot of books and Pokémon cards, too (many said the cards were for their kids. Sureeeeee.)
Amazon's crystal ball was less good at deciphering family size. Several people said their About You page incorrectly identified how many kids they had. Some relationship specifics were off too. It incorrectly said one editor had a girlfriend named "Barry."
As for yours truly, who knows what Amazon knows about me — I haven't had an account for years. Like my colleagues, I will be uncomfortably forthcoming with my results if that changes.
Do you have a funny story or screenshot to share from your Amazon "About You" page? Send it to bshimkus@insider.com and we might include it in an upcoming story!

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

Lime CEO Wayne Ting needed brain surgery to survive a serious stroke. Less than two years later, he's navigated his e-scooter company to a $1.7 billion IPO.
When he was in the hospital last year, Ting said he couldn't find examples of other CEOs who had publicly spoken about their stroke recovery. Now, he wants to be someone people can go to for help and guidance, he told Business Insider's Katie Roof at Tech Insider: Growth Mode, sponsored by Fidelity, on Wednesday.
"In Silicon Valley, you want to be hardcore," Ting said. "You can't be pumped; you have to be super pumped. Showing weakness and showing that you're a human is frankly the image that not a lot of CEOs want to portray."
Ting tied his fight to the tumultuous road that Lime took to its IPO this July. The company fought for years with scooter rivals like Bird in the infamously tough micromobility industry, and weathered a 95% drop in revenue during the pandemic.
He said that financial improvement, like stroke recovery, required getting "1% better" every day.
Lime used to have to replace its entire fleet every month, he said; now the company's redesigned e-scooters and bikes last more than five years. And adoption takes time, Ting noted: the mature market of San Francisco is now growing 100% year-over-year, he said.
Ting, a former chief of staff at Uber, also touted the need for sustainability, something he said he had hammered in under Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. When Khosrowshahi joined Uber, Ting said he overhauled a culture in which employees thought "there was no line that we're not willing to cross."
Now, as Ting sees it, "Win-at-all-costs is an insane idea."
"If you're not doing the right things, you can win for a long time, but things will ultimately catch up to you," Ting said.
Uber owns about a fourth of Lime and lets users book its scooters on its app, providing a boost that's helped Lime emerge as a victor of the 2010s' so-called "scooter wars." Lime raised around $167 million in its IPO. The company's stock price swelled higher in the late summer and has since dropped back to around its listing valuation of $1.7 billion.
Chief rival Bird, which was once worth more than Lime, filed for bankruptcy in late 2023.
Ting said that questions about Bird popped up again and again during Lime's IPO road show. Lime's size, its improving unit economics, and its financial growth convinced Wall Street this summer that the company could succeed where Bird failed, Ting said.

Yes, there are fancier milk frothers on the market (like the Subminimal Nano Foamer, which is also on sale, for $40), but WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane and I both own this Zulay frother and can't say enough good things about it. Mine has been through all manner of abuse, from espresso drinks and protein shakes to falling in the sink and being mostly submerged in a too-tall glass, and after a year and a half of near-daily use it's still going strong.
If You’re More of an Energy Drink Person

There’s been something of a change in the world of motorsport over the past few years. It has to do with where the money comes from. In the old days, it was tobacco and, to a lesser extent, booze. Today such things are mostly banned, and when you look at a racecar covered in sponsor logos, you’re likely to see something crypto-, cyber-, or AI-related.
This makes sense—an ever-larger share of our GDP is wrapped up in those segments. They’re the ones with all the money, and it takes money to go racing. So at the amateur level, we’ve seen tech CEOs replace dentists as the privateer of choice: This past weekend’s Petit Le Mans included co-founders of GitHub, CrowdStrike, Shopify, and the creator of Ruby on Rails, to name a few.
But this is an instance where a sponsor can provide tangible benefits to their motorsports partner beyond a bank transfer, as Chip Ganassi Racing (CGR) and OpenAI have been showing in IndyCar this year.
Ganassi’s might not be the most well-resourced team on the grid, but it is the most dominant; its drivers have won the championship 13 times in the past two decades. First that was Dario Franchitti, then Scott Dixon. But today the man bringing home the big trophies is Álex Palou, who this year sealed his fifth title in six seasons. And at some races, it’s his car that has worn OpenAI’s colors.
The 2026 season was a harder one for Palou than some, winning a mere third of the 18 races IndyCar held. But that was still twice as many as anyone else. Eight poles were far better than anyone else could achieve, either. And it turns out that OpenAI and one of its researchers have been working with CGR and Palou on optimizing car setups. That collaboration is the subject of a documentary series on YouTube, and the second episode just went live this morning. (The longer Part One is here.)

A decade ago, actor Deepika Padukone said in an ad campaign: ‘My body, My choice.’ But, in reality, when it comes to older people, society often wrests that agency from them. Last week, as the world observed both International Day of Older Persons (October 1) and Gandhi Jayanti (October 2), Mumbai-based Sumira Roy’s documentary film Bhangaar (Obsolete), raised the question of dignity in death and the right to die for the elderly.
The yet-to-release Marathi film, which won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film last month, was screened by the Kriti Film Club in Delhi NCR.
Bhangaar trains the lens on Narayan and Iravati Lavate, an octogenarian Maharashtrian childless couple, who petitioned for active euthanasia in 2018. Iravati succumbed to cancer in 2023, Narayan lives in an old-age home. His eyesight and memory, too, have deserted him. After the news of the National Award came in, Roy wanted to share the moment with Narayan. She rang up Prakash Joshi, the brother of Iravati, who also appears in the film. Joshi told her that due to Narayan’s present old-age health and impediments there of, nothing would register with man.
While Nilesh Maniyar and Shonali Bose’s documentary A Fly on the Wall (2024) is also on the same subject and travels with Chika Kapadia to Switzerland for his last days, Roy’s documentary shows how only privilege can afford that right.
Monisha Advani, Bhangaar’s producer and partner, Emmay Entertainment, calls the film personal, “My late mother was a Maharashtrian and while growing up, the frugality of my maternal grandparents’ lives somewhere was mirrored in the Lavates. Sumira has given me the opportunity, in a private way, to pay tribute to my familial pedagogy."
Excerpts from an interview with director Roy:
You are from an advertising background; how, when and why did you transition into filmmaking and documentary films at that?
Since I’ve been a student, I’ve been passionate about films and documentary films and had even sat for the FTII entrance examination. But the women in my family were against me going to Pune and feared the casting couch in the film industry. Years later, when I went to Japan for work, I did a postgraduate course in Japanese cinema, theatre and painting. I was just hooked on when I saw [films by Yasujirō] Ozu and all the greats there. So, I thought, there’s a roundabout way to do films through advertising films. There’s a great amount of discipline in ad films; you shoot minimally and you have only 30-40 seconds to tell your story. Ad films [at Ogilvy and JWT] also gave me a lot of exposure to a lot of things that you need in documentaries. For instance, understanding human behaviour. And then, in documentaries, I learnt how to listen… to people’s stories. I went on foreign location shoots and for post-production. All that’s helped me now. In 2011, I left advertising and started two agencies, mainly for production. I was a little bit jaded and cynical, trying to do these falsehoods to make people buy things they didn’t need.
Did the Central Board of Film Certification raise any objections in Bhangaar?
Only to the title. The censor board didn’t like the word bhangaar [obsolete] and called it insulting. I had to keep going back to explain to them that the word is what Narayan uses [in life and in the film]. It’s his, not mine. After some time, they agreed but asked me to carry a disclaimer in Marathi at the start of the film that this is the character’s interpretation of the title. That was fine by me.
There seems to be a thematic continuity between your documentaries Last DaysLast Shot (2017) and Bhangaar. Tell us about the earlier film.
I have an idea, and then I make a film. I don’t just go and make documentaries, because I’m not an activist or an investigative filmmaker. As Narayan says in the film [Bhangaar], the day you’re born is the beginning of death. He echoes the Myth of Sisyphus when he says there’s no purpose to life; it’s absurd. I am drawn to existentialism, and like diving into the interior of minds.
For my earlier film, I was interested in exploring the philosophy of moksha and nirvana. I went to Banaras [Hindu] University, and walked around in the gullies and ghats. People would pop out from the woods to say, ‘Come listen to my poem.’ There, I found a Bengali poet-artist who had gone to Japan and become famous. He returned to Varanasi with his Japanese wife [they ran the Kumiko Guest House]. By the time I shot him, he looked like Rabindranath Tagore. He was about 80 or 81. He told me his idea of moksha: to dissolve the ego. Then I met a 26-year-old Dom in Harishchandra Ghat cremation ground, who [told me he] hardly got a chance to light the fire, and couldn’t make money with it. So, he bought a camera and started shooting the relatives of the dead. He said from his experience that a good person’s corpse burns faster than a sinner’s.
What drew you to Iravati and Narayan Lavate’s story?
It’s a personal reason. My long-widowed mother was quite active in life. She’d drive, have a social life, her body and mind intact. A year before she passed away, she started saying, ‘I want to die with dignity.’ I was a documentary filmmaker, but I never listened to her nor asked her what she meant. I was petrified of her dying. [After] she passed away, I was stricken with grief and regret. I came across the Lavates’ story in Mid-Day; they asked for the right to die together with dignity. That struck me, and I went to meet them in their 12x12 room in a Mumbai chawl, to get closure for what I hadn’t done with my mother. They taught me so much about Marathi literature and theatre. Narayan looked like Picasso to me. He knew the Constitution by heart. I asked, how could they want to die. He said, ‘It’s time to go.’
They had this fixed spiel they would rattle to the media/news channels. They would do the same during our initial days of shoot. I just told them not to look at the camera and go about their days. I had to be a fly on the wall and filmed them over four years. Afterwards, they forgot there’s a camera. My DOP is brilliant because it was a boot camp for her, with no lights, no space to set up the camera. The aerial shot of them playing cards was shot from atop a washing machine.
In India, the elderly population is growing rapidly even as the birth rate declines. What did your research throw up about ageing and caregiving?
The elderly are growing three times faster than the population of the youth. Palliative care exists only for the rich. There’s no geriatric care and no focus on what is going to happen to the elderly population. All of us are in some stage of caregiving. We are either watching our parents or grandparents.
Gandhi spoke of self-rule. Swaraj is not just political self-rule but also the rule/autonomy over oneself. Does that idea of self-determination versus duty get complicated when it comes to an older person’s choice to die?
Loss of personhood and loss of autonomy, which older people fear, is exactly why they [Irawati and Narayan] asked for it [active euthanasia]. We do not connect with our families. Our conversations revolve around whether they have taken their medicines, if the oxygen tank is running low, if the nurse administered the injection. That’s our only conversation with them. The elderly feel like they are [outdated] machines. We have moved away from joint families to nuclear families. As a society, we have forgotten how to respect someone who has lived longer than expected. We keep talking about Gen Z and loneliness, but loneliness is far worse among the older generations. We hardly talk about it. Even our films don’t.
We’ve read about the Aruna Shanbaug case. This year, the Supreme Court gave its landmark judgment permitting passive euthanasia for Harish Rana who was in a vegetative state for over 13 years. What has been the impact of the Lavates’ petition?
Narayan and Iravati are the pioneers of this, at least in our country, or in South Asia. The courts are getting more and more petitions since. The press doesn’t cover many of these.
Bhangaar (Obsolete) screens on October 1 at the India Habitat Centre, Delhi, and on October 4 at Museo Camera, Gurugram at 4.30 pm.

Kenya has recorded its first confirmed Ebola case, a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and arrived in Nairobi on Saturday, the health minister, Aden Duale, has said.
The patient has since died, and 28 contacts have been identified so far including family members and health workers, Duale told a press conference.
DRC has been battling its largest-ever Ebola outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May but may have started months earlier and has so far resisted containment efforts, with the central African country recording more than 8,000 cases and over 4,000 deaths.
The outbreak spread to Uganda, which reported 20 cases and two deaths, but the World Health Organization declared Uganda free of the disease in August.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of infected people, living or dead. It can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

Zydus Lifesciences has launched in the U.S. market Riociguat tablets, in multiple strengths, developed and manufactured by MSN Laboratories.
The two companies are the first to launch the product, which is a generic version of Bayer’s Adempas. Approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as a generic equivalent of Adempas tablets, in all five strengths, Riociguat tablets are indicated for treatment of persistent or recurrent chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after surgical treatment, or inoperable CTEPH; and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
“Being first to market with generic riociguat is a milestone for our U.S. business and for patients with pulmonary hypertension. It reflects the strength of our complex-generics pipeline, our ability to execute day-one launches in specialty categories and the strength of our partnerships that complement our commercial reach in the U.S.” Zydus Lifesciences Managing Director Sharvil Patel said in a release on Monday.
MSN Laboratories founder and CMD MSN Reddy said “Riociguat is a technically demanding molecule and bringing the first generic to the U.S. demonstrates the depth of MSN’s integrated API and formulation R&D and the scale of our manufacturing. Together with Zydus’ established U.S. commercial platform, we are confident of delivering consistent, high-quality supply of this important therapy.”
Thus far, Riociguat was available in the U.S. only as the branded product. Sales of drug are not reported by IQVIA. According to Bayer’s annual report 2025, the global sales of Adempas were around Euro 745 million (approximately $850 million) in 2025, Zydus said.

Throughout 2025 and 2026, YouTube channels posted videos online (archived) claiming that Buzz Aldrin, one of the first two astronauts to land on the moon, broke down in tears during an interview and said, "The moon is not what you think."
At least three other popular videos (archived) on YouTube (archived) make the same claim (archived). Snopes readers sent emails asking if the claim was true.
Snopes could not find evidence that Aldrin ever said this in any interview he has ever participated in. Therefore, we've rated this claim as an incorrect attribution.
We reached out to Aldrin through his website's inquiry form to ask if he has ever said such a quote, or anything akin to it. We'll update this story if we receive a reply.
Searches for the "The moon is not what you think" quote and Aldrin's name on Google, DuckDuckGo, Bing and Yahoo did not find any videos or transcripts of the interview in which Aldrin supposedly said the quote, or the full interview in writing. The searches did not reveal any credible news reports that quoted Aldrin saying these words. Considering one YouTube video claims Aldrin said the moon quote in interviews and another referred to the quote as Aldrin's "famous warning," it's unlikely that there'd be no credible references to this quote outside of these YouTube videos.
Each of the four videos linked above tells a different story, and three of the four center the story around the moon quote Aldrin allegedly said. The fourth video, despite having a title about Aldrin apparently saying "The moon is not what you think," is not about Aldrin. That video focuses on Michael Collins, another astronaut on the Apollo 11 mission alongside Neil Armstrong and Aldrin, and does not even include the quote "The moon is not what you think."
The three videos that actually focus on Aldrin use the same commonplace artificial intelligence-generated voice for narration. In fact, two of these videos include YouTube's "AI" label just under the videos' titles.
The narrator, instead of Aldrin himself, says the quote in all three videos. None of the videos use footage from the interview in which Aldrin supposedly said it, even though one of the videos claims the interview took place in a television studio. One of the other videos changes Aldrin's quote to "You are mistaken about the moon" in the middle of the video.
Each video assigns a different meaning to the quote in its conclusion. One video says Aldrin's apparent quote was referring to the moon as the beginning of humanity's exploration. Another video refers to the quote as a reference to the moon's earthly origins. The third video suggests the quote means that no amount of data or knowledge of the moon can replicate the experience of being on the moon itself.
A search for the quote itself does show it has been used as a title for YouTube videos and social media posts. Snopes could not find any evidence the quote has ever been associated with Aldrin or any other astronaut.
This claim may have originated with an older video also narrated by an AI voice. A 2023 YouTube video titled "Apollo Astronaut Breaks In Tears: 'The Moon Is NOT What You Think!'" (archived) focuses on Michael Collins. The quote "The moon is not what you think" does not appear anywhere in the actual contents of the video.
None of the channels that posted the videos included publicly available contact information on their YouTube channels.
For further reading, we've previously collected 15 of our fact checks related to the moon.

Paramount Skydance completed its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery today, after a last-ditch effort to block the deal was rejected by Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan.
The post-merger company is called Skydance, taking the name of a firm that Paramount bought in a separate deal last year. The new Skydance combines two of the largest movie studios, streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max, CBS, CNN, “and a portfolio of live sports including CBS Sports and TNT Sports, as well as a deep programming library and expansive collection of brands and franchises,” Skydance said today in a press release announcing completion of the deal.
The merger was delayed a bit by a lawsuit filed by California and 11 other states. In July, US District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in the Northern District of California ruled that the combination would likely reduce competition substantially and violate antitrust laws.
California settled the lawsuit last month, and the other states involved went along with the compromise. A coalition of free speech and media advocacy groups urged the judge to reject the settlement, saying it will give residents of the states that sued Paramount “virtually nothing.”
Martínez-Olguín approved the settlement on September 30, saying the deal “represents a reasonable factual and legal resolution of the dispute.” She wrote that a typical settlement “does not fully remediate an alleged violation or even necessarily resolve the ultimate factual and legal issues of a case.” It “reflects a compromise of the claims short of full adjudication—compromise that may leave some dissatisfaction for both sides and the public but a compromise that saves the risk, time, and expense of litigating through trial.”
The settlement addresses the lawsuit’s complaints about film distribution “by requiring certain minimum thresholds of investment and release of domestic films,” and addresses complaints about licensing of basic cable channels with “requirements for continued, separate negotiations of distribution for the two entities’ basic cable holdings,” the judge wrote. Objections based on “hopes and desires for the proposed consent decree to reach farther—to achieve more—do not rise to the level of legal violations upon which the Court can reject the parties’ negotiated resolution,” she wrote.

At the United Nations High Level Meeting (UN HLM), in New York in September 2026, India made official remarks on the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention Preparedness and Response (PPPR). The Declaration is part of the emerging global legal regime on pandemics led by the WHO-Pandemic agreement (PA).
Shaping the framework
The PA was adopted by 124 member-states in 2025, including India. No country voted against it, while 11 abstained, reflecting alignment across high-, middle- and low-income countries (HICs/LICs/LMICs). The negotiations hinged on how to balance national sovereignty with international cooperation and solidarity, exposing the fault lines between the Global North and the Global South. Key issues included whether a global treaty can set binding targets for measures such as ‘One Health’ without securing funding for countries with fragile health systems. Or whether national pandemic regulations can be harmonised through global frameworks. And whether private manufacturers can be required to share vaccines in real time at affordable prices.
The PA is not yet open for ratification because negotiations are still ongoing for an annex concerning the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system. PABS could help ensure that, during a pandemic, LICs and LMICs receive a fair share of vaccines, medicines and other therapeutics.
Even without ratification, the PA has created a first-of-its-kind global legal regime for the PPPR. Operationalisation requires countries such as India to balance interests of the HICs, LICs and LMICs. This will determine whether the PA will further entrench the inequities of the COVID-19 pandemic or make global health governance truly inclusive.
Editorial | Landmark agreement: On the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement
At the UN HLM, India succeeded in enshrining the multilateral components of the PA within the principle of national sovereignty. India reiterated its commitment to strengthen global pandemic preparedness but stressed that effective pandemic management requires that international coordination is demonstrated. The first is equitable access to drugs, vaccines and therapeutics and the creation of global public goods, such as digital infrastructure (which admittedly align with its own national priorities).
The second is a respect for national sovereignty and the primacy of member-states in shaping global policy interventions according to national circumstance. As a contrast, the United States rejected the Declaration, calling the PABS and WHO’s role in declaring pandemics as a challenge to its national interests.
India’s line
In its remarks, India has acknowledged the concerns of the Global North and the South. Both sides have upheld national sovereignty as paramount in several provisions. The African countries did not give consent to commitments to monitor the human-animal-environment interface, a key source of pandemic outbreaks, without significant funding, which was not guaranteed by the Global North. Similarly, countries in the Global North did not want binding targets with regard to technology transfer (and other similar provisions).
But as India said at the UN HLM, ‘Global Solidarity must be demonstrated through action’; India must be an active player in the finalisation of the global PPPR regime. India is already actively engaged in the PABS negotiations and must lead the Global South in the post-PABS context. India can consider three options. First, developing partnerships on technical areas of the PA (One Health, surveillance, health workforce strengthening) to build trust with other countries in the Global South, and a ‘store’ of operational solutions to tricky national sovereignty problems.
Second, leveraging its leadership role within existing global political groupings. For example, the H20 summit (a health and development G-7 and G-20 partnership) will take place under the United Kingdom’s G-20 leadership at the end of 2027; pandemic preparedness is one of the core health agendas. During India’s G-20 presidency in 2023, India launched the Global Initiative for Digital Health and holds considerable influence within the platform’s health initiatives. Another is ‘Partners for Multilateralism’, which was launched in 2026 by the European Union (co-sponsors are Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya).
Third, strengthening and aligning domestic policy and regulatory architecture around its own priorities for the PA. Global leadership always rests on domestic strengths. India must ensure that its national policies on PPPR such as regulation of access to biological material and distribution of the benefits uphold the highest standards of equity which India can then demand at the global level.
A South-South health role
An equitable global regime on PPPR is in India’s interests as much as a responsibility towards the Global South. India is the pharmacy of the world, manufacturing one of the largest shares of vaccines in the world in terms of volume. Yet, it needs an equitable global vaccine distribution regime. The patents for the vaccines that India manufactures are held by global pharmaceuticals. India is also import-dependent for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs).
India needs access to the latest technology from the Global North to strengthen the manufacturing of high-grade personal protective equipment and medical devices. At the same time, India needs to lead South-South Cooperation and share its technological strength with other countries in the Global South.
India’s health system has a continental scale, and as India’s Health Secretary stated at the UN HLM, its interventions in digital health infrastructure, laboratories networks and One Health are valuable as global public goods. An effective PA needs an engaged India, and a strong PA will strengthen India’s own pandemic management.
Priyadarshini Singh is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). This article is based on a forthcoming CSEP working paper on the Pandemic Agreement.

Veteran actor Nana Patekar has passed away at the age of 75 after suffering a severe cardiac arrest at his residence in Goa. He was declared dead at 5:20 AM on Thursday, October 8. Doctors attempted to revive the actor through continuous CPR for around 45 minutes, but he could not be saved.
Nana Patekar passes away at 75 after severe cardiac arrest at Goa residence
Dr. Shekhar Salkar, Chief of the Oncology Department at Manipal Hospital, confirmed the news and said that a medico-legal case (MLC) has been registered. Further details regarding the circumstances of his death are expected following the post-mortem examination.
“Veteran actor Nana Patekar passed away at 5:20 AM today after suffering a severe cardiac arrest at his residence. Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived. A medico-legal case (MLC) has been registered, and a post-mortem will be conducted,” Dr. Shekhar Salkar said.
Nana Patekar’s journey in cinema
Nana Patekar began his film career with the 1978 film Gaman. While his early years in cinema were gradual, he went on to establish himself as one of the most distinctive actors in Hindi and Marathi cinema.
His performances in films such as Salaam Bombay! and Parinda brought him wider recognition. Salaam Bombay!, directed by Mira Nair, was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. In Parinda, Patekar played a gangster, a performance that earned him the National Film Award and Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.
The making of Parinda was also physically demanding for the actor. He suffered serious burns while filming a real-fire sequence and spent months recovering in hospital. Earlier, he had also been stabbed during the shooting of Salaam Bombay!.
Patekar later moved behind the camera with Prahaar: The Final Attack, which he directed and starred in. For the 1991 film, he underwent training with the Territorial Army.
Patekar remained active on screen in the years leading up to his death. His most recent released film was Subedaar, the Amazon Prime Video action drama starring Anil Kapoor. The film premiered on March 5, 2026, with Patekar making a special appearance as Lance Naik Nana Waghmare.
Before that, he had a substantial theatrical role in Vishal Bhardwaj’s O’Romeo, which released on February 13, 2026. He played Ismail Khan, the chief of the Mumbai Intelligence Bureau, in the film starring Shahid Kapoor and Triptii Dimri.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Chisora, 42, to fight in December after deciding against retirement
- Published
Derek Chisora says he is not retiring and will fight again in December.
The 42-year-old Briton lost to Deontay Wilder in April in what was billed as his 50th and final fight.
However, Chisora has since refused to confirm his retirement. Speaking at a news conference on Tuesday, said he believed he would fight in December against Murat Gassiev.
"December will be me versus Gassiev," Chisora said.
"We're going to decide where, either in London or Manchester. We're going to put two belts on the line, I believe, the IBA and the one Gassiev holds.
"What people have to understand is that what the IBA does is unbelievable. I believe this goes deeper than that we're doing here right now.
"I believe it's going to get better and better. In December we'll be fighting."
Gassiev is currently the WBA 'super' heavyweight world champion, but his status is unclear after reports claimed Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua would be fighting for his world title in their contest on 11 December.
The Russian said on Tuesday he was unsure if he remained the WBA's world champion.
Chisora's news conference was hosted by the IBA, the body that was stripped of its status as amateur boxing's governing body by the International Olympic Committee in 2023 and has since been staging professional bouts.
Gassiev's recent bouts have been under the IBA's banner and he was upgraded to the WBA's 'super' champion in June after Oleksandr Usyk relinquished the belt.
Several of Chisora's recent bouts have been billed as farewell fights and there have been repeated calls from people within the boxing community for the veteran to retire because of his age.
Chisora has 36 wins in 50 fights and defended his decision to continue fighting.
"I never said I was retired. They (the organisers) said '50 last dance'," he said.
"This is why you've got [films like] Rush Hour 1, Rush Hour 2, Coming to America 1, coming to America 2. You understand?
"So this is the Last Dance 3. Listen, trust me, I'm a seller, I sell. That's my job."

Wealthtech startup Zomint has raised ₹36 Cr (about $3.7 Mn) in a seed funding round from Lightspeed and Prime Venture Partners. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to strengthen its technology and investment capabilities, expand its team of wealth and investment experts, and grow its content-led distribution across new formats and regional languages. Founded in 2025 by Aman Mittal and Shavir Bansal, Zomint is a wealth management platform targeting working professionals and families building long-term wealth. It pairs customers with dedicated wealth experts, supported by investment research and AI tools. Mittal, the startup’s CEO, previously held product leadership roles at Flipkart and Pine Labs. Bansal, its COO, also founded personal finance content platform Bekifaayati, which claims to have more than 50 Lakh subscribers. Zomint allows customers to start with a monthly SIP of ₹25,000 or a lump sum investment of ₹5 Lakh, positioning its services beyond the high-net-worth individuals (HNIs) traditionally served by wealth managers. The platform provides a dashboard to track investments, while its experts review portfolios and recommend actions based on customers’ goals and fund performance. Its technology brings together portfolio information, financial goals, past conversations, and investment research to flag issues and track agreed actions. According to its website, Zomint operates as an AMFI-registered mutual fund distributor. Its listed offerings span equity, debt, hybrid, gold and silver, and global funds, including GIFT City funds. The startup said it plans to broaden its services beyond domestic mutual funds to address other investment and financial needs. Zomint claims to have acquired its entire customer base organically, led by Bekifaayati’s presence on YouTube and Instagram, without spending on paid customer acquisition. The startup said it has retained 97% of its clients since launch, while nearly one in three clients made additional investments through the platform within three months of their initial engagement. Each relationship manager currently serves more than 250 families, supported by investment specialists and AI tools, it added. The fundraise comes amid investor interest in startups offering wealth management, investment research, and portfolio tools. The broader segment includes platforms such as Centricity, Novelty Wealth, Tijori, and StockGro, although their offerings and target customers differ. Inc42 reported yesterday that IPO-bound StockGro has raised ₹110 Cr as part of its ongoing Series B round. This follows earlier tranches comprising ₹150 Cr from Param Capital founder Mukul Agarwal and $13 Mn from existing investor BITKRAFT Ventures.

Quick Answer
Meta Muse is a powerful AI agent that can handle emails, purchases, bookings, and more. But its need for deep access to personal data, combined with Meta’s privacy record and early reports of Muse ignoring user permissions, makes trust its biggest problem.
A few days ago, Meta hosted its annual hardware/software event, Meta Connect, at Menlo Park, California. The event was dominated by new hardware launches, such as the new Meta Ray-Ban glasses, new VR glasses, and camera-free Ray-Ban glasses (audio only), but swimming beneath the surface of all these was something that was actually introduced earlier. Meta had introduced Meta Muse in early September, but announced the rollout of the Muse AI agent on its Meta wearables and Meta Muse Charm at the event, and for us, that was easily the real highlight of Meta Connect.
After investing heavily in recruiting AI talent, Meta finally had something to show: an AI agent, which will basically make your dreams of having a robot butler come true. Not surprisingly, it has been making massive tech waves ever since. Since Meta Connect and its rollout, Muse has been topping app store charts, and its early numbers are being compared with ChatGPT, with many pointing out that it is far ahead of OpenAI’s chatbot’s numbers.
While this may paint a very rosy picture for Meta Muse, the reality may be a trifle thorny.
What those numbers do not tell – the “Threads” deception
These numbers, impressive as they are, do not necessarily mean Muse is a runaway success. There are a few reasons for this. Topping app store charts is more of a temporary phenomenon, often influenced by what is trending in a particular week, and does not represent real industry trends. Also, Meta has billions of users across different social media and messaging platforms, which makes it easy for the tech giant to get a few million users quickly without too much trouble. But the adoption rate might not match the number of downloads or sign-ups.
We have seen this happen with Meta’s X rival app, Threads, as well. It has more “active users” as per the numbers than X, which means it must be more used and popular than X, but that is mostly because of Threads’ integration with Instagram and Facebook, which gets the app most of its “active users.” However, the time spent on the app is not nearly the same as its other two sibling social media apps. Similarly, early ChatGPT comparisons with Meta Muse signups may not be fair, because ChatGPT was not launched or advertised as a tool for the masses when it was first launched. It did not have the sort of subscriber base and reach that Meta has, and back then, AI chatbots were not too common either.
Definitely a big deal
That does not mean Muse does not represent a big tech leap. So far, AI chatbots have generally been used for queries, information, help with work, and even personal advice, but that’s mostly about it. All of these chatbots are more about helping you with your queries, with no bar to the nature of the query. While useful in this regard, many are not able to perform actions that have an impact on your day-to-day life. That is where Meta Muse differs.
As we said earlier, Muse is actually the robot butler that the future always promised us. It can get tasks done and help you with managing your digital and even real life. Once you give it access, the AI agent can go through your mail, find messages, draft new messages, reply to emails, all without too much intervention. That might not sound too impressive, as most AI agents and virtual assistants can do the same with a simple command. But Muse goes a step further – it can even make purchases, make reservations, book appointments, and more, across different devices and platforms. In fact, if allowed, Muse can basically make deals on Facebook Marketplace or book you a table at your favorite restaurant or even call you a cab, all without needing any major intervention. Proper butling!
Muse has power and potential, but does Meta have our trust?
As impressive and life-altering as it may sound– some are calling it the biggest tech innovation since the iPhone – Meta still has a massive hurdle that it would have to cross to make Muse the AI butler it wants it to be. And that is the lack of trust in Meta.
For all its innovation and massive subscriber base, Meta has been in a number of controversial situations when it comes to security and privacy. Zuckerberg’s brand has been accused of and even found guilty in cases that range from rigging elections, pushing agendas and ads, to exposing young children to adult content and potential groomers, to monopolizing social media and personal messaging space and using unfair means and practices to kill competition. Its recent hardware “hit” the Meta glasses have also got into a privacy mess, and have been (in)famously christened pervert glasses, following reports of their being used to record people without their consent.
Now, Muse requires even more data and access to private information to actually deliver on its promises. For instance, to be able to draft emails, it needs access to your email account. To be allowed to send messages, it needs permission to read, understand, store, and reply to messages, and needs access to your contact list. To make a reservation, it needs to know your location; to order things online, it needs to have your bank details and also your address. Basically, it needs to have complete access to all your information to act like the magic help that Meta is claiming it can be.
Why I am not A-Muse-D
And that is where my beef with Muse really comes in. Had this been any other company– if Apple had managed to deliver on its intelligent Siri promises or Google had delivered Gemini with such prowess, I personally would have felt less apprehensive in handing over the keys to my digital life, but to give Meta even more access to my data than it already has just feels scary.
Even though I have come to terms with the fact that we are all under passive surveillance from brands at all times, it will take some time for me to give complete control of my data over to Meta without any struggle.
Some of the recent headlines Muse has made do not help its cause. Recently, the AI agent not only made a deal for its user on Facebook Marketplace but even shared his address with the buyer. All without consent. The user, a tech YouTuber, Matt Robb, mentioned how the AI agent accepted low offers and even pretended to be the user while chatting with the buyer, calling the buyer to his address when he was not home at all. Once Matt realized what was happening, he specifically instructed Muse to not share his address. He then asked his friends to send him messages on Facebook Marketplace to see if the agent shares the address. Rather disturbingly, it did: multiple times, and even accepted low offers, all without consent. In another report by Apple Insider, alleged that Muse accessed and uploaded past and present Apple Messages even though the user said he had not granted it permission to do so. All this despite Meta’s claims that Muse has strong privacy and security protections.
All of this does not take away from the fact that Meta has created something really powerful with Muse. It has managed to deliver a finished, capable AI agent which can manage your digital lives, if you let it. Unfortunately, it may also steal your data, force specific ads, and make conversations on your behalf by pretending to be you. And therein lies the problem. The AI Agent is not just about technology, but also about trust. Meta has delivered on the first front with Muse, but until it delivers on the second, I refuse to be A-Muse-D by it. Pun intended.
