An under-the-radar procurement program led by the Department of Defense has been granting special statuses to would-be defense contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos that must be no longer than five minutes.
It’s part of the Pentagon’s desperate bid to inject competition in a market the United States military itself destroyed.
The initiative, known as Tradewinds, is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO.) Companies can submit videos describing how their AI products address one of several different “strategic focus areas” that the government periodically updates. At least once a month, a panel of judges review submissions and decide whether to accept them into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, where the videos can then be viewed by government officials.
If accepted, the pitched products are considered “post-competitive.” Many procurement regulations include competitive requirements. The status can let government buyers check off that box and potentially help shave months off of award timelines. A DOD official says that in several instances, the department has been able to make awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google declined to comment for this story.
Though the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace has been around since late 2022, the Trump administration has been far more vocal than its predecessors about the military buying and operationalizing AI. It also hopes to have more money than ever to throw around: As part of its 2027 budget request to Congress, the White House asked for $1.5 trillion for the Department of Defense, citing “historic investments” in AI as a priority.
This year, the military is seeking video pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and those that can “unleash” AI-enabled agents that can assist in the joint targeting process, including so-called kill chain execution.
No longer as relevant? Pitches for products that promote “a culture of responsible AI” and provide guardrails for AI development and use—requests made during the final Tradewinds submissions cycle under the Biden administration. A DOD official says that the 2026 topics were selected to align with a January 2026 AI strategy memo.
“There has never been a better time to build for the Army,” wrote then-sitting US Army secretary Daniel Driscoll as part of a pitch for more defense tech startups included in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 wishlist of companies to fund. (Driscoll has since resigned from his position and returned to the private sector. He did not respond to a request for comment.)
Opaque Transactions
Acceptance onto the Tradewinds marketplace—and the special “post-competitive” status that comes with it—lets government buyers more easily cut deals using special types of contracts such as “other transaction” agreements, or OTs, which aren’t subject to certain federal acquisition requirements. By law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million dollars on a single OT without having to notify Congress.
Procurement experts say that OTs are considered fast and flexible, which can be appealing to startups that don’t want to gamble on whether a months-long procurement process will result in a contract. However, not all agencies publicly report their OT spending, and even when they do, they’re difficult to find on government-run sites that track federal spending, like USASpending.gov and SAM.gov.
“While OTAs offer opportunities to attract new procurement partners and reduce red tape, numerous reviews have raised red flags,” US senator Joni Ernst of Iowa tells WIRED. “These include questionable costs, mishandling of restricted information, a lack of oversight, reduced accountability and transparency, and an inability to track and access OTA outcomes.”
Ernst recently worked to pass the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, which will require the Department of Defense and other agencies to report OTs to the public. They’ll have three years to get into compliance.
According to public records, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with the Pentagon’s CDAO. According to a DOD official, Tradewinds was leveraged along with market analysis and research as part of the department’s AI acquisition strategy, but the three companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for the specific agreements WIRED identified.
Armed Forces Meet Market Forces
One of the key goals of Tradewinds is to bring “nontraditional” players into the defense industry, says Will Roberts, a former acquisition lead for the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, CDAO’s predecessor, who helped launch the effort. In some ways, it’s an effort to swing the pendulum back to where it was in the past.
Following the Cold War, the Pentagon encouraged defense companies to merge during a now-infamous meeting called the Last Supper, since Congress was preparing to slash defense budgets. Even though it may seem like only having to deal with a few large companies might make things easier, “it actually had a huge impact on market competition,” says Roberts.
Around the same time, explains Sharon Weinberger, a national security reporter and author of the book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War, the personal computer boom meant that Silicon Valley was able to make its own money and with that, set its own research priorities without being beholden to the funding and influence of the military.
Roberts and other defense professionals brought up the military’s historic role in funding—and shaping—technologies like the Internet and GPS. With those investments also came leverage, says Roberts. “We've sort of lost that leverage because there's billions of dollars in AI being invested by companies themselves.”
Weinberger says this has given Silicon Valley titans an immense amount of power over the Pentagon’s technological future. “The amount of money that the Pentagon can put into AI, compared to what venture capital can invest? It's like a drop in the bucket,” she says. “And that's really frightening for the Pentagon. What happens when they can't drive the direction of technology anymore?”
Publicly, this can play out in dramatic and confusing ways. Weinberger points out, for example, that the recent legal battle over Anthropic’s status as a supply chain risk could be seen as the government trying to figure out what legal mechanisms it has to flex its authority over AI companies.
Silicon Valley sensibilities have also been a roadblock in the past, albeit briefly. Roberts recalls how Google employees got “super paranoid” in 2018 about the company’s involvement with the Pentagon’s Project Maven, which eventually led to Google pulling out of the effort. Roberts says the Pentagon spent years trying to “appease” Google with less politically charged projects like those focused on humanitarian aid and veteran health.
Google declined to comment on whether that telling was accurate. One of the Google solutions listed as “awardable” on the Tradewinds site is called “Google for Military Health - Tradewinds,” and in July 2025, the company announced a $200 million deal with CDAO to utilize its frontier AI technology. In a press release, Jim Kelly, a vice president at Google Public Sector said that the company was “committed to advancing the deployment of innovative technology across the defense ecosystem.”

In 2025, India recorded 55 deaths by malaria, 131 deaths by dengue, and 27 deaths by kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis or black fever), according to Union Health Ministry data, whereas there is no single comparable and comprehensive national measure of its annual human rabies mortality, even as the country looks to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by the year 2030.
While a community-based study led by researchers from the Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Epidemiology (ICMR-NIE) and published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases recently estimated that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year, the Health Ministry’s Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme-Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP-IHIP) system reported 21 deaths by rabies in 2022, 50 in 2023, and 54 in 2024.
In contrast, the Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022, and 271 in 2023. The MCCD system, however, covers only medically certified deaths and does not capture all registered deaths.
These figures are not directly comparable — the IDSP-IHIP is a disease surveillance system, while the MCCD captures medically certified causes through civil registration. At the national level, the MCCD covered 22.3% of registered deaths in 2022, and 22.0% in 2023. Neither system, therefore, provides a complete national count — underscoring the gaps in India’s rabies mortality surveillance.
The government table, sourced to IDSP-IHIP, had recorded one death in January 2025 but did not provide a figure for all of 2025. The government’s published table, labelled ‘Human Rabies cases (Death)’, gives the source as IDSP-IHIP.
ICMR for its study surveyed 3,37,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States and estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including about 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers used the community survey, laboratory data, and a probability decision-tree model to estimate the number of people who progress from an animal bite to rabies and die. The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual deaths, and not a count of deaths recorded in hospitals or by government surveillance.
The difference between the two datasets is substantial. The 54 deaths reported through government surveillance in 2024 is less than 1% of the study’s estimated annual toll of 5,726.
“The two figures, however, are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. The figures therefore highlight a large gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality,” a senior Health Ministry official said.
“Lack of consolidated data is a challenge in rabies eradication. Very often cases and deaths occur in areas of the country where they are not measurable. Vaccination of stray dogs, stringent post-exposure vaccination for humans, and disruption of the rabies chain is essential to curb the problem,” Nirmal Kumar Ganguly, medical scientist, public health expert, and former ICMR chief, speaking exclusively to The Hindu, said.
The National Centre for Disease Control itself says efforts are continuing to make human rabies a notifiable disease across India, and that all States have been asked to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
The Health Ministry has also acknowledged the surveillance challenge, with deaths occurring outside the formal health system posing an additional difficulty in capturing the full burden of disease.
Meanwhile, the Lancet study found important gaps even after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received the anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
Rabies is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear, with infected dog bites causing most human transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that domestic dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies transmission. Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths every year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia.
The WHO estimates that India accounts for 35% of rabies deaths globally and 59.9% of rabies deaths in Asia, underlining the country’s significant contribution to the global burden. Children are particularly vulnerable. The WHO says 40% of people bitten by suspected rabid animals are children under 15 years. Rabies is entirely preventable through timely vaccination of dogs and prompt post-exposure care.
The ICMR-funded study states that although there has been a substantial decline in human rabies deaths over the past two decades, India needs to fast-track its actions to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 by adopting a focused ‘One Health’ approach — integrating human and animal surveillance, ensuring timely administration of the full course of post-exposure prophylaxis, and accelerating dog vaccination across the country.

Sport is a kind of conquest. Rulers often get one significant, special coronation that cements their legacy before their followers. Sport, though, offers that sensational feeling of ‘taking over the horizon’ on a platter, again and again, patiently allowing those who persevere to have their fill.
The Indian women’s cricket team knows the feeling, with two such anointments in the span of a week, when it was undisputedly crowned the best in Asia — a record-extending eighth Women’s Asia Cup title in Dubai and a savoured gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan, both against the same opponent: Sri Lanka. Two summit clashes, two similar submissions to authority.
A marauding top order headlined India’s unopposed quest for glory, both in Dubai and Nagoya. The tempestuous youngster in Shafali Verma has well and truly given way to a wiser allrounder, hungry to contribute to a win in every way possible.
Smriti Mandhana rose to the zenith of international cricket, leaving behind names who had influenced her in the sport. Sree Charani’s incredible year kept getting better as she hacked down a number of records while reigning supreme in the T20I rankings.
ALSO READ | Smriti Mandhana breaks record for most runs in women’s T20Is
Nothing came in the way: be it feeble attempts at a fightback from weaker opponents, an unforgiving travel itinerary that barely gave the team breathing space between the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, modest accommodation provisions or threats of a Japanese typhoon that ultimately steered clear of the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin City.
Mismatch aplenty
Take away the passions of sporting merit from the consumption of these two tournaments, and the chronology and character pools are nearly identical. The traditional Asian top four — India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh — are paired against starry-eyed gladiators emerging from the Qualifiers. Valiant campaigns and campaigners come up against the Full Members, akin to bringing a knife to a gunfight, and eventually get found out.
In the Asia Cup, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong China and UAE asked the occasional tough question but were ushered out of contention without much mercy. One’s heart beats and breaks for the underdogs and keeps you invested long enough before you realise how every competition day across editions feels the same — lopsided contests, a glaring mismatch in resources and infrastructure, and a tape growing increasingly stale in an impatient consumer market where sport is primarily produced for broadcast.
The story was no different at the Asiad. While the big four — courtesy of some continuity gathered over their travels across the continent — found their rhythm, Thailand was the only constant among the rest, with Malaysia, China and Japan completing the pack. These are not random draws; qualifying tournaments guarded the gates to these stages. But as much as things change, teams improve or find their footing in the global game, the overall imbalance between the Associates and the Full Members stays the same.
ALSO READ | India wins first gold medal of Asian Games 2026 after women’s cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final
Asian teams are playing more fixtures, a welcome change from years of calendars filled with blots of emptiness. The focus now is on the quality of opponent one can afford to face.
Within the Asian fold itself, a tiered system operates where the likes of India, in particular, barely face Associates. So regardless of how futile a pampered cricket fan might think these tournaments are, they are, so far at least, the only avenues for teams to experience a top-class global opponent.
The knowledge transfer, by itself, becomes the biggest takeaway for so many of these teams. Images of Hong Kong players flocking around India’s senior players and Japan and China players lining up for photographs with women they had only watched in videos or heard about in lore passing over from the subcontinent made for heartening visuals. Hong Kong China’s Marina Lamplough’s videos through the Asia Cup, in which she showed glimpses of how the team took notes from the Indian openers’ style and strategy, are one such example.
But that’s as deep as the engagement goes. India’s ‘responsibility’ to democratise its presence in the Asian circuit now has the hurdle of a packed calendar standing before it.
In the Asian Games and Asia Cup, the eastern cricketing wave doesn’t realise what it has, Netherlands skipper Babette de Leede pointed out, highlighting Asia’s advantage over other continental groupings.
“You know how Asia has the Asian Games and the Asia Cup? We don’t have any of that in Europe. It would be great because you get more games. Look at the difference between the number of games we play and the number Australia or India play. We do have entities like the European Cricket Network... the T10 tournament they organise. Those numbers are developing. And now there’s the European T20 Premier League too. If there was something like that for us in Europe, it would be quite cool,” she told Sportstar on the sidelines of the T20 World Cup earlier this year.
ALSO READ | How Japanese women prepared for a moment of blossoming
The wish for integration isn’t random. With cricket making the Los Angeles Summer Games, the ecosystem hopes this is the start of a long stay in the Olympic roster. In 2028, six teams each will compete in the men’s and women’s events, with rankings deciding the majority of the slots and qualifiers filling the gaps. The Asian Games is no different: an eight-team tournament that begins at the quarterfinal stage in a continental showpiece involving 46 countries.
In Aichi-Nagoya, China didn’t even get to play, despite making the cut, after rain washed out its quarterfinal against Bangladesh, the latter advancing due to higher seeding. Cricket’s intense weather vulnerabilities leave teams on the bigger stage of amateur sport short-changed when months of preparation and dreams can drown in a downpour.
Work at the roots
The International Cricket Council, especially after the recent FIFA World Cup, has made its intention of expanding cricket to counter football, covertly and overtly, known. Development initiatives with Associates, infrastructure assistance and advocacy have spruced up since the turn of the decade.
The Indonesian ecosystem is a direct beneficiary, having landed Asian Cricket Council membership a few years ago. Cricket chief Abhiram Singh Yadav credits the role of former ACC president and incumbent ICC chair Jay Shah for making room for Indonesia at the high tables of Asian cricket.
“Mr. Shah thinks quite broadly about the game. He sees the potential of global markets. Indonesia is a country with a population of over 200 million. We are a G20 member. That recognition also came through in Mr. Sanjog Gupta’s (ICC CEO) visit. Both are working towards developing emerging markets and looking at non-traditional cricketing nations. With the sport now in the Olympics, this is the only way we can make cricket inclusive,” Yadav told Sportstar.
“Cricket wants to work towards becoming bigger than FIFA, and that requires looking deep into different international markets. As an Associate member, we want to support that vision. Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Japan and Korea are promising markets, and we want to be a model for others to follow,” Yadav added. UAE, too, has a promising women’s side drawing heavily from the expat Indian population in the Gulf. While the national side benefits from their quality, the Emirates Cricket Board has been trying to foster an interest in the sport among natives too.
ALSO READ | Asian Games 2026: Shafali Verma scores her maiden T20I century during Bangladesh semifinal
“I won’t say that it’s a challenge,” Emirates Cricket Board COO Subhan Ahmed told Sportstar. “If you look at the overall demographics of this country, about 80 per cent of the population is expat. So it’s natural that the sports that they have played back home and that culture travels. The infrastructure here has grown because of it. We have 62 grounds across the seven states in the Emirates. There are some Full Members who do not have that kind of base. The local Emirati population is always a part of our plans. We don’t envisage a complete takeover by the local population, but we do anticipate greater participation given how much it can do for overall community unity here,” he added.
Indonesia, too, faced the same predicament of leaning entirely on the diaspora, but Yadav underlined that the setup is on a war footing to ensure cricket can become a 100 per cent localised sport.
Sports tourism has emerged as a way to galvanise smaller boards, as Yadav pointed out earlier, allowing them to tap newer markets within cricket. Sanjog Gupta has also identified China as a potential cash cow, hoping to convert at least some of its 1.4 billion people into cricket fanatics.
The ICC pumped USD 1.5 million into cricket in the nation, broadcast World Cup games in Mandarin to whet the appetite for the game, and has also seen the cricketing system build three top-level cricket venues, including a new 1,500-seat stadium in Taicang that is primed to host domestic and international matches and provide a training base for the national teams. The Marylebone Cricket Club has chimed in with support, saying it will send a women’s team there for an overseas tour next year.
The women’s national team, made almost entirely of homegrown players, has climbed 10 spots in the rankings over the last two years, which only underlines why that faith isn’t misplaced. That Asiad washout stings that much more now, right?
Dissonance at the top
The one-sided nature of this fairytale Asian romp was known to all before the curtains rose. But even for the world’s most successful team, backed by the world’s richest board and cricketing circulatory system, multi-sport events bring with them nostalgia and old-time achievement.
Indian skipper Harmanpreet Kaur, for instance, grew up in Punjab, where tales of legendary Olympians were often served alongside a child’s daily meals. The Games — of the Asian, Commonwealth and Olympic kind — hold a special place. It’s why her creaking knees want to carry on till she makes it to Los Angeles 2028, till that Olympic gold finds its way to her neck.
ALSO READ | Asian Games a teaser to 2028 Los Angeles Olympics: India Women’s head coach Amol Muzumdar
While parallels can be drawn between India’s comfort and dominance here and what might lie ahead at the Olympics, that would be an oversimplification. At the end of the day, Olympic cricket — as it stands — is still a T20 knockout tournament, the sport’s most fickle format. It cares not for past laurels. Fortune only favours the brave here, as India learned at the Birmingham CWG when it watched Australia don gold while it made do, grudgingly, with silver.
For all the expansion, the view from the top remains fairly myopic. Players being dragged into the political theatre of handshakes and trophy tug-of-war took the sheen off what is, in theory, one of the most promising learning opportunities for teams on the fringes of the power core. If one wants to be doggedly apolitical, two high-importance tournaments in 2026 without television referrals and held at a single venue are no vote of confidence in the efforts of the custodians of the sport. The ICC can’t wash its hands off either, as the inaugural Women’s Champions Trophy — taken away from Sri Lanka due to political interference in administration — is due to be held across just two Tier 2 Indian venues.
While the prosperous continue to prosper, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh face tumultuous transitions within and outside the team. Outside India, franchise cricket is not a reality or a liberating financial avenue for any other Asian nation. FairBreak Global, an ICC-based independent initiative that brought several Asian Associate nations much-needed game time with stars from SENA countries, is now defunct.
Indonesia, for all its ambition, still played the Asia Cup without a shirt sponsor, while a Full Member nation like Afghanistan is still being shielded from accountability for failing the cardinal principle of said membership — mandatorily fielding a women’s team.
Hierarchy masquerades as competition in Asian cricket, with one crown after another for those already on top, while the rest are left arguing over scraps of legitimacy. Showpieces without follow-ups, expansion without equity and Olympic ambition without Olympic-standard competitiveness will only widen the gap the game is desperate to bridge.

Ring's smart lock has a hand crank so it works even if the power's out
You can generate power by twisting the front latch back and forth.
Ring founder Jamie Siminoff thinks smart locks aren't popular because users are worried about what happens when they run out of power. Say what you like about keys, but you don't need to recharge them once every few months, and they have worked without power for millennia. That issue is what drove him to develop the Ring Smart Lock, which solves the no-power issue with a hand crank. On the front of the unit, there's a wheel for the latch that, if you turn it back and forth three or four times, generates enough power to run the lock for 30 seconds.
Tucked inside the hardware is a small motor and a supercapacitor that, after a few strong turns of the wheel, will generate around three volts. That gives the unit enough power to run fully, rather than in any sort of compromise low-power mode, for about half a minute. That should be long enough to use the fingerprint reader, keypad, access the Ring app or ask Alexa. After all, as a Ring product, it integrates seamlessly with the rest of Amazon's smart home ecosystem.
This focus on the worst-case scenario, as Siminoff explained, is meant to address would-be buyers' fears about losing access to their home. But he sees plenty of other arenas where this sort of technology would work well, such as buildings you don't access regularly. If you can generate power on the fly to run the lock, it'll work equally well for cabins in remote locations. But this should be a once-in-a-blue-moon instance, since the lock's built-in battery should last a full year on a single charge. You may never need to use the crank at all, but it may offer you some degree of peace of mind.
The company isn't set on a launch date beyond the first few months of 2027, but Siminoff hopes to release the product closer to January than March and you can register your interest now. Ring says the lock will launch for $249. We also know it'll be available in three finishes: Black, Silver and Brass, and the company promises it uses a single-cylinder deadbolt and needs no additional wiring.
Updated cameras
At the same time as rolling out the new lock, Ring is also busting out a whole suite of updates for its cameras, too. After launching its first range of Retinal 4K cameras this time last year, it's now launching four more, including the Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus and Indoor Cam 4K. As the name implies, each one offers Retinal 4K, with the usual features attached depending on where in your home you're installing them. It's also wheeling out a new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K, where the powered base will turn a full 360 degrees and tilt 175 degrees, and will intelligently follow motion when it detects it inside your home. All are available for pre-order today, with pricing varying by your chosen spec and region.

The India-Canada relations hit rock bottom following then Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's allegations in 2023 of a potential Indian link to the killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar.

On August 1, 2026, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari claimed that of the 27 lakh people whose names were deleted from the voter list after adjudication due to ‘logical discrepancy’, only seven lakh had filed appeals before the court-appointed appellate tribunals seeking inclusion in the electoral rolls.
Speaking at the launch of the Census self-enumeration exercise in Kolkata, he said, “Out of the 27 lakh people who were given an opportunity to approach the SIR tribunal, around seven lakh had applied. The rest have not submitted any application or appeal so far.”
The figure was reported by multiple media outlets which quoted the chief minister (1, 2, 3). Adhikari went on to link the failure to appeal with questions of citizenship, and citizenship with access to welfare, saying, “Until the entire process was completed, it would not be possible to determine whether those who had not made any claim as voters would later seek recognition as Indian citizens.” He added, “If someone is not a citizen of the country, they will not get benefits of any social scheme.”
Five days later, The Telegraph published the same seven-lakh figure, this time attributing it to an unnamed senior official of the West Bengal government. According to the report, the official said, “It has been found that only about 7 lakh of the 27 lakh voters excluded by the adjudicators for ‘logical discrepancies’ have appealed before the tribunals.” The official said the figure had emerged from a compilation of reports from various districts, and that the state authorities had no idea why the remaining 20 lakh had not appealed before the tribunals.
The Figure was Unverifiable at that Time
In August, the seven-lakh claim could not be independently verified against any official source because the Election Commission’s own disclosure did not provide a separate breakdown of appeals filed against the exclusion of voters. An RTI reply that disclosed the total number of appeals carried a footnote clarifying that the figure included both appeals against the inclusion of names in the electoral roll and appeals against exclusions.
The RTI was obtained by Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP from Dakshin Malda in West Bengal, and placed before the Supreme Court on August 24, 2026, during the hearing of a petition filed by Prasenjit Bose of the Congress and Derek O’Brien of the Trinamool Congress against the Election Commission of India.
During the hearing, Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed that the break-up of the appeals mattered since “it was exclusion which was causing an immediate violation of a person’s rights.” The bench consequently directed the ECI to provide a separate account of the appeals, specifying how many were pending before the tribunals and segregating appeals relating to voters who had been excluded or included, as well as cross-appeals.
The ECI submitted this segregation on September 16.
ECI Numbers Refute Adhikari’s Claim
According to the latest affidavit filed by the ECI before the Supreme Court on September 16, 2026, of the more than 38.31 lakh appeals filed, over 22 lakh were filed against exclusion by voters whose names had been excluded or deleted, while more than 16 lakh were filed against inclusion.
Of the more than 38 lakh appeals filed, only 1.26 lakh had been decided by that date. Annexure R/1 to the ECI’s affidavit provides a district-wise break-up of the total appeals submitted to the appellate tribunals and is reproduced below.
It must be noted that the total number of appeals filed, as mentioned in the ECI’s affidavit (38,31,429), does not match the total number of appeals submitted in Annexure R/1 (38,29,926). The discrepancy is 1,503 appeals. Nevertheless, the outcome-wise data provided in the annexure shows that 8,649 appeals resulted in exclusion from the electoral roll, while 1,13,943 resulted in inclusion. In other words, nearly 93% of the appeals that had been decided resulted in the elector being included in the electoral roll.
Did the Claims Accumulate after the CM’s Statement? No
One may argue that the chief minister spoke on August 1, while the Commission filed its figure in the Supreme Court on September 16, leaving enough time for appeals to have accumulated in the intervening period. The available data, however, allows this possibility to be tested directly, because appeal totals are available for both dates. On August 7, 2026, six days after the chief minister’s statement and a day after The Telegraph report, the tribunals already had 38,10,620 appeals, according to an RTI response from the ECI to Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP for Dakshin Malda. By September 10, 2026, the figure stood at 38,29,926, according to the district-wise report annexed to the Commission’s affidavit. Thus, the total number of appeals increased by just 19,306 across the entire state during this period.
In the light of the latest revelations made by an Indian Express investigation, which have raised serious questions about the functioning of the Election Commission of India and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the seven-lakh claim takes on an even greater significance.
To sum up, Suvendu Adhikari’s claim on August 1 that out of some 27 lakh electors placed under adjudication and subsequently excluded from the electoral roll, only seven lakh had appealed against their exclusion is difficult to reconcile with the data that was already available at the time. The ECI has made it clear that the number is around 22 lakh. The discrepancy assumes greater significance given that Manoj Agarwal, the then chief electoral officer of West Bengal who oversaw the SIR process, is now the Bengal’s chief secretary.

Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections
- Published
A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week.
Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time.
Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed.
His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued.
A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported.
Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay.
Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register.
Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report.
"I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.
His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.
Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.
Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.
“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”
Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.
Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”
Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.

As part of its ongoing bid to more tightly regulate international students, the Trump administration on Wednesday announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience.
The Department of Homeland Security said the fee would help combat alleged fraud and abuse in the work program, known as Optional Practical Training, which allows students to get hands-on work experience related to their field of study while still on a student visa. The department also said the restrictions would help U.S. citizens compete against international applicants in the job market.
“Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” said a department spokesperson in a press release. “American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
An additional $30,000 fee would apply to students looking to participate in Optional Practical Training beyond one year; many science students remain in the program for three years. Academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee for each student they recommend for the work authorization program, and DHS estimates that it would collect $12.4 billion annually if the fees are finalized. The department plans to publish the proposed rule to the Federal Register on Thursday, though an unpublished version is already accessible, and DHS has said it will accept public comments through November 9.
Experts are already raising concerns that the proposal is yet another attempt by the Trump administration to close its doors to international students and scholars, who make up about a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates and 60% of postdoctoral researchers. The nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, which is currently suing DHS over a separate attempt to place time limits on the kinds of visas used by postdocs and graduate students, warned that the new proposed fee was misguided.
“Imposing this new fee structure on Optional Practical Training is the latest in a series of developments that creates deep uncertainty for international students. OPT enables international students to gain the same hands-on experience as their domestic peers while filling labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields and generating jobs for U.S. workers on U.S. soil,” said Fanta Aw, NAFSA’s CEO, in a statement. “The research is clear: international students don’t take opportunities from Americans, they create them.”
To participate in Optional Practical Training, often known as OPT, international students need an administrator at their school to recommend them for the program before they apply for authorization from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, a division of DHS. Students then have 90 days to find a job.
This program is often a bridge for students looking to work in the U.S. long term. OPT authorizations for STEM graduates have risen from nearly 27,500 in 2015 to more than 95,000 in 2024. But DHS argues that with these growing numbers have come increasing reports of students, employers, and school administrations “engaged in schemes to exploit the current OPT regulations for fraudulent purposes.”
In its unpublished version of the proposed rule, the department alleges that there has been “widespread” use of OPT as an unlimited employment benefit with little to no connection to a student’s area of study. DHS cited a 2020 incident in which federal agents arrested 15 foreign students charged with fraudulently using OPT to stay in the U.S. The department also cited a more recent investigation that it says identified more than 10,000 international students working for “highly suspect” employers, which in some cases included empty or non-existent worksites.
DHS estimates that the new policy could lead to $4 billion a year in opportunity costs due to students losing out on work experience, employers losing productivity if they’re unable to replace international workers, and academic institutions losing international student enrollment. But the agency also stated that the benefits of protecting U.S. workers and the integrity of the OPT program outweigh any potential costs.
The work authorization program, which was formally created in 1992, has been a major draw for foreign students. A NAFSA survey conducted last year found that 54% of current graduate students and postdocs would not have come to the U.S. if OPT did not exist, though the survey did not ask about the impact of program fees.
It’s not the first time the Trump administration has sought to use steep fees to cut off internationals from the U.S. workforce. Last year, Trump issued an executive order that would impose a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas, used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as engineering and biotech. Federal courts have blocked the fee for now, though DHS has reintroduced it as a proposed rule.
The administration is also seeking to put four-year caps on how long students and postdocs can remain in the U.S., alleging that a longstanding policy allowing these scholars to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training has incentivized fraud. A federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction preventing the time limits from taking effect; the order notes that plaintiffs opposed to the policy are likely to ultimately succeed in an ongoing lawsuit.
Even though many of these new policies have yet to take effect, current students and immigration experts say the Trump administration’s efforts have created a climate of fear and uncertainty that will turn students away from the U.S. There’s some evidence that is already happening. A survey this summer by the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications dipped 21%.

The Keralam government’s announcement that it will make private health care more “affordable” through consultations with the private health sector, and that a Bill in this regard was in the offing, should be seen against the State’s seven-year legal battle before the Kerala High Court upheld the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, throwing out all objections raised by private hospitals.
The KCE Act was the first ever attempt made in the State to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework.
But the Act was systematically opposed and its implementation stalled at every turn by the private health sector in the State.
It was in November last year that the Kerala High Court threw out all objections raised by the Kerala Private Hospitals’ Association (KPHA) and the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and upheld the validity of the Act.
Contentious area
Unlike the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (Central Act 23 of 2010), which attempted to cap the treatment/procedure/diagnostic rates charged by the private health sector by fixing a price range, the KCE Act had not touched this contentious area at all.
The KCE Act just insisted on mandatory registration of all clinical establishments under all systems of medicines (including hospitals, clinics and laboratories) and that every establishment maintain certain minimum standards based on the category in which they fall. It also said that hospitals display their rates for various procedures openly so that there is transparency.
However, the private health sector argued that it violated rights under Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Appeal in SC
Even after the High Court specifically held that KCE Act’s Section 16 (mandatory registration of clinical establishments), Section 39 (display of fee rates and package rates for services) and Section 47 (obligations concerning life-saving treatment/emergency care and safe transfer of patients) were constitutionally valid and gave directives to the government to implement the Act without delay, KPHA went in appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has not stayed the KCE Act, but granted members of the petitioning associations interim protection against coercive action by the government.
Yet to register
Kerala Clinical Establishments Council, which is responsible for the implementation of the Act, maintains that the registration process is continuing and that even now, many clinical establishments are yet to register themselves under the council.
Small hospitals with up to 15 beds have been given some concessions by the council, trimming down the checklist for assessment to just basic and essential points, so that at least the basic registration brings these establishments too within the regulatory framework.
The government’s efforts to draft a new Bill to bring in a regulatory framework that “protects patients’ interests while taking into account the operating costs and practical difficulties of private hospitals” is well-intentioned, but the fact remains that the private health sector is still holding out against the KCE Act at the Supreme Court.
Questions are also being raised whether a new legislation is in order or if the costing regulations can be incorporated into the KCE Act itself.
‘Entirely welcome’
Meanwhile, public health activists like B. Ekbal have stated that any attempt by the government to regulate the treatment expenditure in the private sector and save people from catastrophic health expenditure is entirely welcome.
Dr. Ekbal said that though private hospitals are an essential component of the health system, health care cannot be left entirely to market logic. It is the government’s responsibility to regulate the sector adequately so that patients are not exploited.
In a statement here, Dr. Ekbal said that the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) should be insisted on and that the government initiate a scientific cost evaluation of various medical and diagnostic procedures and treatments so that a rational and transparent rate list suited to the State can be evolved.

Enterprise software major ServiceNow is betting that its next leg of growth in India will come not just from digitisation of IT functions, but from enterprises putting AI to work across business processes, even as the rush to adopt the technology creates a parallel challenge around governance, security and identity. At its World Forum in India on Tuesday, October 6, ServiceNow announced AI Workflow Factory and Autonomous Engineer, two products aimed at helping enterprises identify where AI can improve work and then build, run and extend AI-powered workflows across the organisation. The launches come at a time when Indian enterprises are moving beyond AI experimentation, with CIOs increasingly looking at how to deploy the technology across customer experience, employee operations, software development and business processes. For ServiceNow, that creates an opportunity to move beyond its traditional identity as an IT service management company and position itself as the layer through which enterprises orchestrate AI across their existing technology stack. But the company is also betting that as AI becomes more deeply embedded into enterprises, security and governance will become inseparable from the adoption story. ServiceNow’s India AI Push Moves Beyond Pilots ServiceNow’s India strategy rests on three interconnected opportunities: domestic enterprises, global capability centres (GCCs) and its large technology partner ecosystem, ServiceNow India tech and business centre head Sumeet Mathur said in an interview with Inc42. The company has been expanding beyond its traditional strength in IT service management, with ambitions to become an “enterprise operating system” spanning IT, HR, customer service, finance, supply chain, legal and workplace operations. AI is now becoming the connective tissue across these functions. The company is seeing a growing willingness among Indian CIOs and CISOs to explore disruptive AI use cases rather than simply run small pilots. “The willingness is very high, and once you start to open your mind that I want to use this piece of technology in 10 different ways, then of course the problems are very visible,” Mathur said. That appetite, however, is running ahead of the governance structures needed to deploy AI safely. A ServiceNow AI maturity assessment cited by the company found that only 22% of Indian enterprises have AI testing, auditing and risk-assessment processes in place. Amit Zavery, president, COO and chief product officer at ServiceNow, said on the sidelines of the event that governance cannot become an excuse for delaying AI adoption but needs to be built into the process early. “It just slows you down enough to run faster later. If you’re going to run faster without any kind of brakes around it, it will crash,” Zavery said. The distinction is becoming increasingly important as enterprises move from individual AI experiments to multiple deployments across an organisation. The question is no longer simply whether an AI application works, but whether it can be governed, monitored and scaled without creating new operational or security risks. From IT Workflows To An Enterprise Operating System ServiceNow’s pitch is that enterprises do not need another standalone AI application. They need a layer that can connect AI models, existing applications, data and workflows. AI Workflow Factory is designed to help enterprises identify opportunities where AI can improve workflows and then build and operate those workflows. Autonomous Engineer, meanwhile, brings more autonomous capabilities into software development, including planning, building and testing. The proposition addresses one of the biggest problems emerging as companies scale AI: fragmentation. Enterprises building AI applications often have to stitch together different models, data sources, applications and workflows. They also have to manage changes when models are updated or prompts and underlying systems change. AI Workflow Factory brings more of that lifecycle onto a common platform, including building, deployment, governance and ongoing management. The broader ambition is to make ServiceNow the operating layer through which enterprises can introduce AI into existing business processes without having to rip out their existing technology infrastructure. This is also where ServiceNow believes it can differentiate itself from hyperscalers and model providers. Microsoft, Google and AWS can provide infrastructure and AI models, while companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic provide frontier models. ServiceNow, however, wants to sit one layer above these technologies, connecting them to the enterprise systems where work actually happens. AI Agents Create A New Identity Problem That strategy becomes more complicated as enterprises move from generative AI assistants to autonomous AI agents. Today, many enterprise agents still operate on behalf of a human. But as agents begin interacting directly with email, CRM systems, databases and other enterprise applications, the identity and access problem becomes significantly more complex. An AI agent could initiate another agent, access sensitive data and execute an action without a human manually intervening at every step. “The hardest problem I believe for agentic AI to become a reality is identity,” said Tarun Thakur, cofounder and CEO of identity security startup Veza, which ServiceNow acquired earlier this year. Veza was founded around the problem of understanding not just who an employee is, but what that identity can actually access across an enterprise’s applications and systems. Its Access Graph maps identities, permissions and relationships across enterprise systems, giving security teams visibility into effective permissions rather than simply relying on roles and groups. ServiceNow historically had extensive visibility into enterprise assets through its configuration management database (CMDB), but lacked the same depth of access context. The Veza acquisition brings those two pieces closer together — what an enterprise has and who or what can access it. That becomes particularly important as the definition of an “identity” changes. “Agent identity is ephemeral — it comes and goes,” Thakur said, pointing to a future where enterprises could have large numbers of temporary machine identities being created and removed as AI agents perform specific tasks. ServiceNow has also integrated Veza into its broader security portfolio, while using its AI Control Tower to help enterprises discover and manage AI agents across their technology environment. The company believes AI security could eventually become a significant new cybersecurity category as enterprises move towards more autonomous systems. The India AI Opportunity The AI opportunity also gives ServiceNow a broader opening in India than its traditional IT-service customer base. India is home to more than 2,100 GCCs employing around 2.35 Mn people, according to Mathur. These centres are increasingly responsible for technology, product development, cybersecurity and global technology decisions for their parent companies. For ServiceNow, that means the India opportunity can extend beyond selling to Indian businesses. GCCs can also influence technology decisions made for global organisations. The company’s partner ecosystem further strengthens that position. Mathur said around 30,000 engineers are working on ServiceNow in India across major system integrators including Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG and EY. BFSI remains among the company’s strongest verticals in India, while healthcare and life sciences, consumer and retail and the public sector are also important markets. Interestingly, in July, ServiceNow’s venture arm invested $40 Mn in Delhi NCR-headquartered BUSINESSNEXT, which sells software to banks, insurers and other financial institutions. Betting On The Orchestration Layer The larger strategic question is whether ServiceNow can establish itself as the control and orchestration layer as enterprises adopt AI from multiple vendors. The company is not trying to own the underlying AI models. Instead, it is building an open platform that can work with different frontier, open-weight and domain-specific models. Zavery said customers ultimately care about the outcome rather than which model powers a particular task. ServiceNow therefore tests different models and can route workloads depending on the task, performance and economics. That model-agnostic approach could become increasingly important as enterprises seek to avoid being locked into a single AI provider. ServiceNow is also competing in a market where Microsoft, Google, AWS and Salesforce increasingly position themselves as orchestration or control layers for enterprise AI. According to Mathur, ServiceNow’s advantage comes from its existing position across enterprise workflows. “ServiceNow was always a platform company,” he said, arguing that its role is to coordinate different systems and business processes rather than own every underlying technology. That positioning is increasingly extending into cybersecurity as well. ServiceNow’s security business was already generating more than $1 Bn in annual contract value globally before its recent acquisitions, according to Mathur, and the company is now seeking to build a much larger cybersecurity franchise around identity, vulnerabilities, incident response, OT/IoT and AI security. The Veza acquisition therefore fits into the same broader thesis: as more AI agents enter the enterprise, ServiceNow wants visibility into not just the applications and workflows they interact with, but the identities and permissions behind them. For Indian enterprises, the next phase of AI adoption could therefore shift the question from what AI can do to what AI can do inside their organisation, especially at scale. That is the gap ServiceNow is betting its India strategy can fill.

Ranbir Kapoor has been appointed as the Brand Ambassador of Pune-based real estate developer Mantra Group. The actor will be the face of the Group as it enters a new phase of expansion and brand evolution across residential, commercial and retail segments.
Ranbir Kapoor becomes the new brand ambassador of Mantra Group
As part of the association, Ranbir will feature in a new brand film alongside Rohit Gupta, Managing Director of Mantra Group. The partnership comes as the company looks to strengthen its presence across existing markets while exploring new opportunities in India and international markets.
Founded in Pune in 2007, Mantra Group has grown from a first-generation entrepreneurial venture into a larger real estate group over nearly two decades. While Pune continues to be an important market for the company, its portfolio has expanded across different segments and geographies.
In recent years, Mantra has also entered new areas of business. The Group expanded internationally through its entry into branded residences in partnership with luxury brand Jacob & Co. Its entry into Mumbai has opened opportunities for large-format developments, while its presence in Pune has continued to grow across residential and luxury real estate.
The company has also built associations across design, architecture and luxury. Its luxury vertical Burgundy has worked with designer Manish Malhotra, while Ganti Associates is among the names associated with its developments.
The partnership with Ranbir is based, in part, on similarities in the journeys of the actor and the Group. Both began their respective journeys in 2007 and have since developed identities of their own. While Ranbir has taken on varied roles during his career, Mantra has expanded across markets, formats, design and development.
Rohit Gupta, Managing Director, Mantra Group, said, “When we started Mantra in 2007, our focus was on building a strong business in Pune and earning the trust of the families we served. Over the years, that foundation has given us the confidence to think beyond individual projects and look at what we can build as a Group. Today, we are at a very different point in that journey. We have expanded into new markets, entered new categories and built relationships with some of the most recognised names across luxury, design and lifestyle. Ranbir comes at a time when we felt the brand needed a personality who could represent this evolution. There are several parallels in the journeys we have taken, from starting out in the same year to building our own identities and constantly evolving. We are delighted to have him as the face of Mantra as we enter this next phase, with several important milestones ahead.”
Ranbir Kapoor said, “What appealed to me about Mantra is that it has built its journey over time, but has also continued to evolve. There is a clear ambition to grow, explore new markets and think differently about the spaces and experiences it creates. I also found the journey interesting because there are some parallels in how we have both built our identities over the years. Mantra has strong roots, but it is also looking ahead and creating its own space. I am happy to be part of this next chapter and look forward to what we build together.”
The association will be accompanied by one of Mantra's larger brand and consumer campaigns, titled ‘The Festival of Choices’. The campaign will bring the Group's portfolio together under one platform, with inventory opening across its projects and a range of consumer benefits across Mantra and Burgundy.
For Ranbir, the association adds another brand partnership to his portfolio, while for Mantra, his appointment comes at a time when the company is looking to expand into new markets and micro-markets. The Group is also continuing to develop its premium and luxury portfolio while exploring categories including hospitality and branded residences.
With Ranbir as the face of the brand, Mantra Group will now focus on communicating its next phase of growth while building on the foundation it has established since its launch in 2007.

Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
- Published
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol with a big collective gasp, then followed by a minute of silence.
It is in this square in the centre of Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing.
On Wednesday, it became the place to pay tribute to her.
People lit dozens of candles around the square in a small improvised vigil that glowed with a warm light on a dry and warm autumn night.
Other candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners next to the candles read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then took to the streets that connect Puerta del Sol with the Spanish Congress, just 500m away, in an improvised protest.
During the march people chanted: "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
The police had set up barriers to block the march. There was not a big police presence, and there was the tension that protests sometimes have.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
Wednesday night's march has finished, but the camping, already on its 12th night, will continue "as long as necessary" one of the protesters told the BBC.
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences to Maricarmen's loved ones, as he said on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

A ‘Wall of Hope’, a youth-led initiative by the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) and its Department of Youth Mental Health, was unveiled at the IIT-Madras Research Park in Taramani on Saturday, a press release said.
With young people facing increasing mental health challenges and suicide remaining concern, creating spaces for expression, connection, resilience, and help-seeking is vital.
The mental health campaign, which began on October 10, 2025, encourages young people aged 10-25 to express, share, and reflect upon their personal reasons for living, through brief messages of hope.

Chhattisgarh professor abducted on evening walk, Rs 1 lakh extorted through UPI
A college professor in Raigarh was allegedly abducted during an evening walk and forced to make UPI transfers at knifepoint. Police rescued him within 24 hours and are probing the digital money trail and other suspects.
In a case that combined kidnapping with digital extortion, a college professor in Chhattisgarh's Raigarh district was allegedly abducted during an evening walk, blindfolded, held captive at knifepoint and forced to transfer nearly Rs 1 lakh through UPI transactions.
Police rescued the professor within 24 hours of the incident and have arrested one suspect, while efforts are underway to track down the remaining accused.
ABDUCTED WHILE ON EVENING WALK
The incident took place in Jakela village under the Pusaur police station area of Raigarh district.
According to police, Kapurchand Gupta, a professor at a degree college, was out for an evening walk between 6 pm and 7 pm on October 5 near Deepapara and Shobha Rice Mill. Feeling tired, he stopped to rest on a milestone near a roadside pond.
It was then that two men allegedly approached him, dragged him towards the pond, blindfolded him and threatened him with a knife.
The accused later transported him on a motorcycle to Pandripani village in the Bhupdevpur police station area, where he was allegedly confined inside a room.
MOBILE PHONE BECAME THE TARGET
Police said the kidnappers assaulted the professor and forced him to reveal the password to his mobile phone. They also obtained access to his Google Pay and BHIM accounts.
Investigators believe the accused then contacted a woman and obtained her QR code, which they used to transfer money from the professor's bank account.
According to police, the transactions continued until the account's transfer limit of around Rs 1 lakh was exhausted.
FAMILY GREW SUSPICIOUS
To avoid raising alarm, the kidnappers allegedly forced the professor to call his family and tell them he was safe.
However, relatives became suspicious and began tracing his location on their own. Their search reportedly led them to Pandripani village.
When the accused realised family members were closing in, they fled the spot, leaving the professor behind.
The family then informed police.
PROFESSOR RESCUED, SUSPECT ARRESTED
Acting on the information, Pusaur Station House Officer Harshvardhan Singh and his team reached the location and rescued the professor safely from the room where he had allegedly been held captive.
Raigarh Senior Superintendent of Police Shashi Mohan Singh ordered an immediate operation to identify and arrest those involved.
Police said Sunil Sarathi, a resident of Jakela village, was arrested within 24 hours of the incident. During questioning, he allegedly admitted involvement in the kidnapping and the conspiracy to transfer money through UPI transactions along with other accomplices.
Authorities said the identities of the remaining suspects have been established and raids are underway to apprehend them.
PROBE INTO DIGITAL MONEY TRAIL
Police have also launched an investigation into the digital transactions linked to the case.
The woman whose QR code was allegedly used to receive the money has been contacted, and the transferred amount has been secured, officials said.
Investigators are now examining her connection to the accused and whether the bank account or UPI ID was used in any previous criminal activity.
A case has been registered under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and further investigation is underway.
The incident has drawn attention to a growing trend in which traditional crimes such as kidnapping are increasingly being combined with digital payment fraud, allowing criminals to extort money directly through mobile banking and UPI platforms.

The image is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump’s account. The sentence about Musk did not appear in Trump's original post.
In October 2026, a screenshot of an alleged post from U.S. President Donald Trump's Truth Social account spread online, showing Trump seemingly thanking billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing Republican votes ahead of the November 2026 midterms.
The purported post (archived) stated:
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool—Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dummods with massive turnout! THANKS TO THE GREAT ELON MUSK EVERY REPUBLICAN VOTE COUNTS AS 3 VOTES! SO IMPORTANT - PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE, AND MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President Donald J. Trump
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The above post is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump's account. The yellow highlighted line about Musk was edited into the post. As such, we rate this image as fake.
On Oct. 3, 2026, Trump wrote (archived) the following post on Truth Social. The fake highlighted line about Musk was added after "we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout!":
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool — Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout! SO IMPORTANT — PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP
swampthevoteusa.com/
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The post in the screenshot is clearly edited, based on the nonsense phrase "Dummods" which appears to be a garbled version of "Dumocrats."
Snopes also looked up variations of the phrase on Trump's Truth, a website that archives his posts "every few minutes" and makes it easier to find them — including deleted posts. There was no evidence of Trump thanking Musk on Truth Social for making "every Republican vote" count as three votes.
Trump has been speaking at campaign rallies nationwide, trying to drum up support for Republican candidates ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.
For further reading, Snopes has debunked numerous posts falsely attributed to Trump over the years.

Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s statement at a recent function about avoiding unnecessary angioplasty seems to have stirred a hornets’ nest with many doctors objecting to the “generalised statement,” while some lone voices pointed out that Mr. Satheesan was 100% right and that unnecessary procedures had become the norm.
In a Facebook post, Rajesh Gopalan Nair, Professor and Head of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, had appreciated Mr. Satheesan “for pointing out a truth.” But it set off an avalanche of comments from the doctors and public, with the latter narrating their harrowing experiences in hospitals and appreciating Dr. Rajesh for calling a spade a spade, while many doctors expressed disappointment at Dr. Rajesh’s stand.
Dr. Rajesh, however, made it clear in his post that a person coming into the emergency with a suspected heart attack should in no way distrust the doctor, for the situation may call for an immediate angioplasty.
Second opinion
He also explained clearly the situations when one could afford to wait and seek a second opinion, if angioplasty was suggested to a patient. He also cautioned the public against looking at every doctor or hospital with suspicion. Angioplasty should definitely be done when it is clinically indicated and these situations are clearly documented, he said.
Even though much of the medical fraternity expressed their displeasure at the “unsubstantiated” statement of the Chief Minister and the support that unexpectedly seemed to have come from one of their own, Dr. Rajesh refused to be cowed down. He maintained that he stood by his position that some of the angioplasty procedures done in hospitals were indeed not warranted.
On Monday, the Interventional Cardiology Council of Kerala (ICCK) said in a statement here that public’s apprehension over “unnecessary” medical procedures should not delay life-saving treatment during a heart attack emergency.
Responding to the Chief Minister’s remarks on avoiding unnecessary investigations and angioplasty, the council said it supported evidence-based and ethical medical practice and the principle that every intervention must have a clear clinical indication.
ICCK president Rajesh T. said that public discussion on angioplasty should clearly differentiate between elective intervention in stable patients and primary angioplasty during an acute heart attack, where treatment is highly time-sensitive.
What the data show
According to Statewide ICCK registry data presented at the council’s last annual conference, more than 70% of angioplasties performed in Kerala involved acute and emergency clinical situations.
He said the council welcomed any discussion aimed at strengthening evidence-based care, transparency and public confidence in the health-care system. “In stable patients, there is usually greater scope for detailed evaluation and for deciding whether medicines, further assessment or intervention would offer the greatest benefit. In an acute heart attack, however, delay can have serious consequences,” ICCK said.
However, the council cautioned that a general atmosphere of mistrust surrounding cardiac procedures could have unintended consequences, particularly when a patient develops severe chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of a heart attack.
