Eradicating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection early could become an important strategy for preventing gastric cancer, Nobel laureate and gastroenterologist Dr. Barry Marshall said, stressing the need for wider testing, appropriate treatment and confirmation that the infection has been cleared.
Dr. Marshall, who shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren for their discovery of H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, said the bacterium should no longer be regarded only as a cause of ulcers.
“H. pylori is much more than an ulcer organism. If the infection persists for many years, it can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and increase the risk of gastric cancer. That gives us an opportunity because this is a potentially preventable cause of cancer," Dr. Marshall told PTI.
Dr. Marshall was in India to attend the World Congress of Gastroenterology (WCOG 2026) in the national capital.
Held in India for the first time, the four-day event, which concluded on October 3, brought together around 3,000 delegates from 61 countries to discuss the changing global burden of gastrointestinal and liver diseases, including H. pylori infection, gastric cancer prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.
His comments come amid renewed global focus on population-based H. pylori "screen-and-treat" programmes for gastric cancer prevention.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has recommended such programmes in populations where the benefits are expected to outweigh potential harms.
Dr. Marshall said the priority should be to identify infected individuals and ensure they receive effective eradication therapy.
"If we can find the infection before there has been extensive damage to the stomach, we have a much better chance of preventing the chain of events that can eventually lead to cancer," he said.
However, rising antibiotic resistance is emerging as a major challenge to this approach, he highlighted.
A 2026 review in Gastroenterology noted that increasing antimicrobial resistance is threatening the success of established H. pylori treatment regimens, while concerns also remain about the effects of repeated antibiotic exposure on the microbiome.
"We cannot simply keep giving the same antibiotics and expect the same results. Resistance varies between countries and even between regions, so treatment needs to take local resistance patterns into account," Dr. Marshall said.
The IARC guidance similarly emphasises antibiotic stewardship, treatment based on local resistance patterns and follow-up testing to determine whether eradication has been successful.
Dr. Marshall said India, where H. pylori infection is common, has an important role to play in generating evidence on local bacterial strains and antibiotic resistance.
"India has a very large population with H. pylori, so it is an important setting for research. We need to understand which strains are circulating, what antibiotics are still effective and how we can make testing and treatment accessible," he said.
According to the IARC guidance, Indian recommendations have included bismuth-containing quadruple therapy in areas with high clarithromycin resistance, highlighting the importance of regional resistance patterns in treatment decisions.
Dr. Marshall also stressed that successful treatment should not be assumed simply because symptoms improve.
"Treating the patient is only half the job. We should confirm that the bacterium has actually been eradicated. Otherwise, the patient may continue to carry the infection and remain at risk," he said.
He said non-invasive testing could make detection easier and help expand screening.
Dr. Marshall has also invented PYtest, a C14 urea breath test that provides a 15-minute, non-invasive and quantitative method for detecting current H. pylori infection using a breath sample from the patient.
The patient-friendly test could help Indian doctors detect active H. pylori infection through a quick diagnostic procedure.
PYtest is available in India through Pylorium Diagnostics, part of Trimed Australia, founded by Dr. Marshall and headed by Bhanu Rahoni in India.
The need for prevention has gained urgency as gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, with the highest incidence concentrated in several Asian regions.

Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League
- Published
Senior figures within English football are concerned that Manchester City could play in the Champions League next season even if they are relegated from the Premier League for breaching financial regulations.
It centres around the possibility that City win the Champions League, which would provide qualification for the competition as titleholders - regardless of their status in the English domestic pyramid.
BBC Sport has been told that there is no automatic mechanism to remove City from a European competition they qualify for on sporting merit.
An independent commission found City guilty of all charges related to inflating sponsorship revenue by £830m by using sham contracts, as well as hiding other expenses worth an additional £90m.
Without this, the independent commission said, City would have failed the profit and sustainability rules in all nine seasons between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
City continue to strenuously deny any wrongdoing, calling the outcome a "Premier League conspiracy". Last week the club lodged an appeal against the verdict.
No grounds for City to be denied a licence
BBC Sport has spoken to a number of senior figures within the game in recent days who are concerned about the prospect of City qualifying for the Champions League next season.
The feeling is that if City do not win their appeal and are therefore handed a strong sanction, then being allowed to compete alongside Europe's elite, and receiving the financial rewards which come with it, would not be acceptable.
The immediate issue surrounds the Uefa licence, which every club needs in order to play in Europe.
One source said the issue of City's licence "had been raised" and that a solution "would require the sort of joined up thinking that's been a bit lacking so far".
The licences are issued by the Football Association, though the process itself is delegated to the Premier League.
The licences are based upon current information which does not take into account sanctions or breaches related to historical offences.
If a club fulfils all minimum criteria required for admission, the licence cannot be refused.
The key reasons a club may fail relate to overdue payables to other teams, players or outstanding tax liabilities.
Match-fixing convictions within the last 10 years, or an integrity conflict related to multi-club ownership, are considered but would not apply to City.
A source added that "licences are awarded on the basis of current financial performance, so the grounds to refuse one are unclear".
If the verdict is upheld by the appeal board it is likely City will face severe sanctions, which could include heavy points deductions, a large fine and transfer embargoes.
The sanctioning hearing, which will determine the level of punishment City must face, is yet to be scheduled.
While a points deduction could rule City out of qualifying by league position, it might still be achieved through cup competitions.
Expelling City from the Premier League immediately is also an option which remains on the table.

  - Published29 September
- Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market? 
  - Published4 days ago
Uefa may choose to open a disciplinary case
Senior figures both in the English game and in European football are aware of how bad the optics would be if City face strong sanctions yet still play in the Champions League.
It is exacerbated by doubts that the whole process - including an appeal against the sanction - is not guaranteed to be completed by the end of the season.
The Premier League added new clauses to its regulations to set time frames around disciplinary processes and appeals in the summer.
If applicable, this would mean a judgement on the sanction must come no later than January. But there is no confirmation this applies to the City case.
It is not just about City winning the Champions League, however. If they were to win the FA Cup or Carabao Cup - they play Brighton in the fourth round on 28 October - that would provide a place in the Europa League or the Conference League respectively.
European football's governing body cannot take any action while the Premier League disciplinary process plays out, but it is understood that potential scenarios are likely to be discussed by the Uefa administration and the Uefa club financial control body (CFCB).
The Premier League case found City guilty of five charges of breaching Uefa's profit and sustainability rules.
Uefa may open a case in accordance with the disciplinary regulations to find a way to remove City's eligibility.
But this does not provide certainly as City's offences are historical.
In 2020, City successfully overturned their two-year ban from European club competitions handed down by Uefa.
Uefa issued the ban after ruling City had committed "serious breaches" of financial fair play regulations between 2012 and 2016 - with the same period as the Premier League's investigation.
But the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned the ban because the offences were "time-barred" under Uefa's rules.
If City are not successful in their appeal and win the Champions League, the CFCB will have to find a disciplinary measure to remove the club from next season's competition.
Yet with City already having won against Uefa through Cas once before, there is the concern they could do so again.

The Maharashtra government has reportedly directed all bike taxi aggregators, including Rapido, Uber and Ola, to transition to an all-electric fleet by July 2027. According to the Indian Express, the state transport department, earlier this month, wrote to the aggregators to phase out petrol-powered bike taxis in a phased manner in the next nine months. Following directions from chief minister (CM) Devendra Fadnavis, the platforms have been told to switch to electric bike taxis before the deadline. Under the proposed plan, ride-hailing platforms will initially be given six months to comply with the EV mandate. However, bike taxi operators, which have applied for provisional or temporary licences under the Maharashtra Bike Taxi Rules, 2025, will receive an additional three months to meet the requirement. This comes a month after the Maharashtra Bike Taxi Welfare Association (MBTWA) reportedly wrote to CM Fadnavis, state transport minister Pratap Sarnaik and transport commissioner over the EV transition. In its letter, the gig worker body had sought a deadline of one-and-a-half years for aggregators to comply with the EV mandate. “Most bike taxi riders hail from middle or lower-middle-class backgrounds, making it difficult for them to undertake a significant investment to purchase an EV bike at once. The lack of EV charging infrastructure and the smaller life of an electric vehicle also makes this decision more difficult,” MBTWA president Amit Gawde reportedly said. Meanwhile, sources reportedly said that ride-hailing platforms had also sought an extension until 2030, citing the need for more time to transition their fleets. The state government, however, appears to have granted them only nine months to switch to EV fleets. The development comes four months after Sarnaik said that the Maharashtra government would impose a temporary daily fee of ₹5 on bike taxi services operating illegally in the state. He had also said that aggregators would also be required to contribute 2% of fare of every ride to a welfare fund for bike taxi drivers. It is pertinent to note that bike taxis officially became legal in the state in July last year when the state government notified the Maharashtra Bike-Taxi Rules 2025. At the time, local authorities granted provisional 30-day licences to Ola, Uber and Rapido to transition to electric bike taxis. The rules mandated that only electric two-wheelers painted yellow and marked as bike taxis could operate commercially. However, the platforms allegedly failed to comply, leading the state government to revoke their licences in March this year. Afterwards, officials began undertaking enforcement action against aggregators for operating unauthorised petrol-powered bike taxi services. Local authorities collected fines totalling ₹16.25 Lakh for illegal bike taxi operations between April 2025 and March 2026, and another ₹2.31 Lakh during April and May 2026.

Mayor of Turkish opposition stronghold defects to Erdogan's party
A stronghold of Turkey’s opposition has fallen to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling party for the first time
ISTANBUL -- The mayor of Turkey’s third-largest city defected to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan ’s ruling party on Wednesday, giving it the mayoralty of the opposition stronghold for the first time.
Izmir had been led by the opposition Republican People’s Party, or CHP, for more than two decades until Mayor Cemil Tugay joined Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party, or AKP, at a ceremony at its headquarters in Ankara.
In a brief speech after Erdogan pinned a party badge on his lapel, Tugay described the AKP as the “voice of the voiceless” and pledged to revitalize and rebuild Izmir as the western port city’s first AKP mayor.
Tugay, who won the 2024 election with 49% of votes, resigned from the CHP in June after the party was hit by a legal case that removed its leadership.
The court’s decision in May saw droves of CHP members leave, with many joining the New Party established by deposed CHP leader Ozgur Ozel, which surpassed the CHP as the largest opposition party. Tugay, however, remained as an independent and denied plans to join the AKP.
Izmir’s municipal assembly remains under the control of a New Party majority.
Police set up barriers in Izmir’s main square Wednesday after the opposition called for people to protest Tugay’s defection.
Since 2024, when the CHP strengthened its grip on many major cities, including the capital Ankara and Istanbul, municipalities held by the party have been targeted by waves of criminal investigations that have seen hundreds of CHP members jailed.
The most prominent is Ekrem Imamoglu, the metropolitan mayor of Istanbul and the opposition’s favored challenger to Erdogan in the next presidential election. He has been behind bars since March last year.
Imamoglu faces several legal cases, with the main one alleging corruption within the Istanbul municipality. If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 2,300 years in total.
While critics claim the court cases are politically motivated and aimed at weakening the opposition, the government insists the country’s judiciary is independent and free from political influence.

Greetings from Lahore, Pakistan, whose high court offers an oasis for chatter and chai
I'm always eager for an excuse to visit the Lahore High Court in the British-built quarters of Pakistan's second-largest city.
To me, the high court is a near-perfect specimen of British South Asian colonial architecture: Mughal in its curly arches that frame porticos, the Gothic detail that emerges through the red brick baked on the city's outskirts in pluming kilns.
Within, it's a sea of busy, flapping penguins: Pakistani lawyers in their uniforms of white shirts and black suits rushing between courtrooms.
They take a rest in the main square, all chatter and chai under the banyan trees that still shade the men and women of law.
It's a contrast to the wheezy, heavily polluted city. Lahore has far fewer trees outside its elite quarters — a signal of a broader crisis in Pakistan, where there's one standard for the masses and another for those who hold power.

EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe.
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.
Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda.
The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.
Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars, which were not subject to tariffs.
Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.
It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.
On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.
In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.
The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.
Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.
Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”
Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.
Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.
Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.
“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry
STOCKHOLM — Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."
Kagan, born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai, 95 years old and born in Japan, with the Tokyo University of Science.
The so-called "Soai reaction" is named for the scientist's experiment.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.
Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.
This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.
The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the government’s ₹10,000 Cr SME Growth Fund (SGF) to offer growth credit capital to small and medium enterprises. Announced in Budget 2026-27, the fund will invest in high-potential SMEs across manufacturing, services, technology, innovation-driven sectors and strategic value chains. A majority of the allocation of the fund will go towards manufacturing-focused enterprises. The initiative aims to widen access to equity and liquidity for MSMEs and help promising Indian businesses scale into globally competitive companies. The SGF is meant to fill the gap in growth capital for SMEs, as most existing funds focus on early-stage and micro enterprises. Under the framework, the government will commit ₹10,000 Cr to alternative investment funds (AIFs), that will subsequently invest in high-potential SMEs. This will help businesses expand operations, increase manufacturing capacity, adopt new technologies, enter international markets and integrate into global supply chains. Centre's MSME Funding Push The SGF is part of the government’s wider push to support the MSME sector via credit, digitalisation, ease of doing business, public procurement and other initiatives. The fund will also support SMEs in industrial clusters across Tier II and Tier III cities, with the aim of strengthening local supply chains and creating jobs. As part of the ‘Creating Champion MSMEs’ strategy announced in Budget 2026-27, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman had also proposed an additional ₹2,000 Cr for ‘Self-Reliant India Fund’ to support micro enterprises and provide them with access to risk capital. The Budget also proposed several measures to improve cash flow for MSMEs through the Trade Receivables e-Discounting System (TReDS). This includes making TReDS the settlement platform for purchases from MSMEs by central public sector enterprises (CPSEs). The government also proposed a credit guarantee mechanism through CGTMSE for invoice discounting on TReDS, linking the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) with TReDS and allowing TReDS receivables to be used as asset-backed securities. As per the Economic Survey 2025-26, India's MSME sector accounts for approximately 35.4% of manufacturing, around 48.58% of exports, and 31.1% of India's GDP. With over 7.47 Cr enterprises employing over 32.82 Cr persons, the sector holds its position as the second-largest employer after agriculture. "With India’s manufacturing sector positioned for greater global integration, MSME sector’s role is critical in enabling effective supply-chain participation, fostering local value addition, and supporting inclusive regional growth," the Survey said.

Michael Stuhlbarg didn't know what to expect when he got to the set of "Digger." He just knew he had to be there.
The production of Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu's new movie with Tom Cruise was shrouded in mystery, even to its star-studded cast, which was kept on a need-to-know-basis about what kind of movie they were making.
Still, Stuhbarg and the rest of the cast, which includes John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, and Jesse Plemons, wanted answers.
"Our rehearsals allowed us that kind of time to ask as many questions: 'What have you heard?' 'What can we expect?'" Stuhlbarg told Business Insider over the phone, describing the cast as a "repertory company" that filmed over seven months. "We were all in the same boat of learning about the movie at the same time."
Those who haven't seen Iñárritu's provocative, twisty new climate-change satire have been kept similarly in the dark. Here's what I can tell you: Tom Cruise plays an oil tycoon named Digger Rockwell who has a lot of explaining to do when one of his wells explodes. Riz Ahmed plays an environmentalist on Rockwell's team, John Goodman plays the president of the United States, who is leaning on Rockwell to fix the problem, and Stuhlbarg plays his sheepish vice president.
Stuhlbarg's performance matches the movie's satirical tone as he delivers perfectly timed comedic reactions, often without dialogue, as the situation becomes increasingly dire. He attributes that talent to his training as a child under the iconic mime Marcel Marceau.
"It was one of those things where silence and thought was captured in a large scale," he said. "Every beat, every moment, every breath, every gesture needed to be registered by Alejandro's orchestration."
It's just the latest top-notch performance from Stuhlbarg, who broke out playing the lead in the Coen brothers' 2009 drama "A Serious Man" after decades in theater. Since then, he's had memorable roles in everything from "Boardwalk Empire" to "Call Me by Your Name."
For the latest interview in Business Insider's Role Play series, Stuhlbarg spoke about playing Timothée Chalamet's dad in "Call Me by Your Name," getting blindsided by Woody Allen's directing tactics on "Blue Jasmine," and the unique way Daniel Day-Lewis connected with him on the set of Steven Spielberg's "Lincoln."
On learning the movie business from the Coen brothers and getting acting tips from Woody Allen
Business Insider: You got your start on the stage, appearing in over 35 productions playing everyone from King Richard II to Hamlet, before you got "A Serious Man." At that time, were you content to be a stage actor the rest of your life?
Michael Stuhlbarg: I hadn't really thought about it, to tell you the truth. Theater was where I was initially most comfortable, so to get to work with Joel and Ethan [Coen] for an extended period of time in front of the camera for the very first time, it was absolutely a learning experience.
I remember speaking to Joel before we started and he said, "Do you want to look at what we're doing?" And I was like, "Nah, you let me know if you need me to see something, but otherwise I'll do it and you tell me if it's working or not working."
What was it like to be the star of a Coen brothers movie? You were the face of that movie, on the poster, all over the trailer, the award campaigns. For someone from the stage, was it daunting?
I was ready for it when it happened to me. I had built my sea legs enough; I felt like I was the right guy for that moment. And the rest of it was a delight. It was a remarkable welcome into a craft that, even though I knew very little about it, I felt like I was ready to listen and apply what I needed. And I had the best people in the business to guide me.
That's quite the understatement. By 2013, you had worked with the Coen brothers ("A Serious Man"), Martin Scorsese ("Hugo"), Barry Sonnenfeld ("Men in Black 3"), Steven Spielberg ("Lincoln"), and Woody Allen ("Blue Jasmine"). Would you say working with Woody Allen on "Blue Jasmine" was the project where you had the most restrictions put on your performance?
He knew what he wanted, and I think I just went along for the ride. There were some cases where he would basically go through it himself, being the actor that he is.
Meaning, you're standing there watching him act out the scene as you?
Yes. If I wasn't giving him what he needed, he would jump in, give it a go, and then I would jump in and try to provide the color that he was asking for.
As an actor, do you just think, OK, this is the gig? Or is there a shot to your ego? Hey, look at my resume! Why did you hire me?
I don't really mind, to be honest with you. I'm there to help a director achieve a vision. Very rarely am I so imprinted with a role that I know deep in my bones that what I have to offer is the right answer for something, because I never know how it's going to be captured —from what angle? I might be just part of the frame; who knows how things will be captured. So that's a part of cinema. I choose my battles very carefully. I'll say that.
On going down mobster rabbit holes for 'Boardwalk Empire' and working with Timothée Chalamet
You said you got obsessed with playing infamous Jewish Mob kingpin Arnold Rothstein on the HBO series "Boardwalk Empire." How obsessed did you get?
When you're given a real person to inhabit, like I was, obsession can be helpful in terms of learning as much as you can, which was simply my objective. Gambling, I had a tutor for, and billiards, I also had a tutor for. And there was a biography about him that gave me a lot of things to apply to my performance as well.
He was a historical character in a historical fiction story, so his real life provided the background. And that then led to the imaginative leap that we all have to take in storytelling.
Your performance as the father of Timothée Chalamet's character in "Call Me by Your Name" is a career highlight. How do you go about working with younger actors, and did working with Chalamet change at all when you did "Bones and All"?
We all meet each other where we are. So I don't think of it as young and old, I think of it as individuals meeting and sharing energy together. With "Call Me by Your Name," I felt naturally drawn to want to share as much as he would want to share with me. He was so dynamic and fun. It was fun to engage with him at that time in his life, and then we got to meet up again a couple of years later. His experiences had been remarkable to him, and that was reflected in his energy. You throw your energies together and hope for good things.
On battling Daniel Day-Lewis in 'Lincoln' and exchanging grins with Tom Cruise
Compare and contrast acting opposite Daniel Day-Lewis, as you did in "Lincoln," and Tom Cruise in "Digger."
The circumstances dictate how behavior is manifest. With Daniel, we were all so delighted to get to be in that world of President Lincoln: 1860s in America. It was part of that adventure for all of us to remove all anachronistic items from our persons when we entered these rooms so we were absolutely in the world. And Daniel was as welcoming as anyone has ever been, and open to play. Generous. Wonderfully weighty in his bearing down upon my character, as his character is trying to get me to vote his way, and I enjoyed very much being a barrier to that.
And when you mean weight with Daniel, you mean literal.
Yes! He came over between one take and kind of took his elbows and leaned from behind on my shoulders, so it was the physical manifestation of how his character was trying to apply pressure to my situation. It was both wonderfully unique to him and really generous, because it gave me something to play off of. I hope to get to play with him again.
With Tom, this experience has been unlike any other, and the world in which we are creating is huge and full of dynamic energy and ideas. To see his enthusiasm, which is so infectious, and his delight, generosity, and support to all of us to find our way and make us feel comfortable so we can provide what was needed, it was really fun.
I remember in the Situation Room scene where we are all watching what is happening on a screen, he looked over to me between takes, and he had a big old grin. He said to me, "I really enjoy playing with you!" And I was like, "Me too, let's do it some more!" It was a lovely moment.
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
"Digger" is in theaters now.

Two icons, a glorious farewell and a potentially bitter ending
- Published
On a night where one football legend received a grand farewell from his country, about 6,000 miles away, another released a lengthy statement discussing all the ways in which he had been wronged by his national team coach.
Argentina great Lionel Messi took the adulation of the crowd in Buenos Aires as his glittering international career ended with a goal against Benin on an emotional night.
Meanwhile, Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo released a statement on social media, accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" while admitting he should be held accountable for his own actions.
The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.
Portuguese journalist Jose Delgado says "things will never be the same again" for Ronaldo and Portugal - so is this the beginning of the end?
Jesus has said the door is open for Ronaldo to return to the national team, but is it? Or will this saga continue, potentially closing the book on the international career of one of the greatest players of all time?
BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international careers of two football greats.
What is going on with Ronaldo?
The Ronaldo saga has been rumbling on for some time, with many fans critical of former Portugal boss Roberto Martinez's insistence on starting Ronaldo at this summer's World Cup.
At 41 years old, Ronaldo is not the dynamic player he once was and many suggested his presence hindered the team rather than helped.
However, things came to a head on Sunday when Ronaldo was an unused substitute in the Nations League win over Norway. The player subsequently left camp after finding out he would not start against Denmark in November.
On Tuesday, Ronaldo released an almost-2,000 word statement on Instagram in which he said Jesus had twice "broke his word" and accused him of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media.
Ronaldo apologised to fans and team-mates for leaving the camp and said the consequences of that must be "assessed and punished" while also dismissing any suggestion that he had played his last match for Portugal.
"We will have one or more farewell matches, there will be time for that," the statement said.
Manager Jesus said on Sunday the door remains open for Ronaldo to return if he chooses to, but many are suggesting the damage is already done.
- Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring 
  - Published18 hours ago
Portuguese football journalist Delgado told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I don't think there is a way back. In the statement, Ronaldo says he will return to the national team but at the same time he calls Jesus a liar three times.
"In the polls in Portugal made about this issue, only 15% of the Portuguese were on Ronaldo's side and people think we owe him a lot but his time is already done and he must understand it.
"The problem is that Ronaldo does not understand it, he wants to keep playing as if he was 24, not 41.
"Things will never be the same again. No matter what happens, no matter if he plays again or if you have a game to say goodbye to Ronaldo things will never be the same.
"What Ronaldo did for Portuguese football is unique and incredible and we must thank him for all the service he gave to Portugal. But at 41, he has no place in the best XI of Portugal."
Manager Jesus has reportedly said that he had not seen Ronaldo's statement as he was watching the Portugal under-21 game.
Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.
It seems unlikely that Ronaldo will voluntarily retire from the national team before he hits the elusive 1,000 goal mark he is chasing for club and country - he currently has 979.
But have his actions made the situation untenable?
When it comes to fans, opinions appear to be split.
On several billboards in Lisbon posters have been put up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.
They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain.
"Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."
At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.
What next for Messi?
In stark contrast, Messi brought the curtain down on his illustrious Argentina career, where he has won one World Cup and two Copa Americas, in front of an 85,000-strong sellout crowd inside the Monumental in Buenos Aires.
The 39-year-old announced his retirement from international football in August after Argentina finished runners-up at the World Cup and following the death of his father Jorge.
Messi marked his final appearance for La Albiceleste with a goal before addressing the adoring fans in a speech lasting nearly 10 minutes.
Some of his team-mates were in tears as Messi admitted he did not want to leave the field.
"There are so many emotions going through me right now," he said. "I'm surely forgetting many things I would like to say because this is a very difficult moment for me. The first person who comes to my mind is my dad.
"I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything."
- Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends 
  - Published1 day ago
Messi departs as the record appearance-maker and goal-scorer for Argentina but will continue his club career with Major League Soccer team Inter Miami.
It seems the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner wants to enter the world of football club ownership and is making moves to do so.
He already owns two clubs - Spanish fifth-tier side UE Cornella and second-tier CD Eldense - as well as being a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa, which plans to open five branches in Catalonia.
Messi also has a lifetime deal with Adidas and a collection with drinkware brand Stanley as well as investing in the property and hotel industries.
Football expert Guillem Balague said: "Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.
"Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.
"Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game."

Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
- Published
"I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."
Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.
The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.
However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.
Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.
Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.
"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, BBC Sinhala.
The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.
Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.
The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.
His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.
The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.
In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.
"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, MP, told BBC Sinhala.
Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased.
"My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."
In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.
Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.
In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations.
"The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.
Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.
There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.
Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.

The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), an umbrella forum representing Christians from different denominations in West Bengal, on October 5 formally submitted complaints to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the West Bengal Human Rights Commission (WBHRC) and the National Commission for Minorities, alleging a pattern of targeted violence against the Christian community, including attacks, vandalism and desecration of small house churches and prayer gatherings across the state.
A public hearing was also held on the same day at Christ the King Hall on Syed Amir Ali Avenue in Park Circus, Kolkata, where pastors, victims and eyewitnesses recounted alleged incidents of attacks and intimidation before representatives of prominent human rights and civil rights organisations, including the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR) and Banglar Manabadhikar Suraksha Mancha (MASUM). Civil society figures, including retired IAS officer Jawhar Sircar, were also present to hear the testimonies.
The gathering was held amid a series of reported attacks on Christian communities, mostly in the hinterlands of Bengal. Alt News has previously documented at least 35 such incidents of violence and intimidation between July 1 and September 20, 2026.
Based on the testimonies of victims, the BCP, which is the eastern chapter of the All India Christian Council, formally submitted its complaints to the rights bodies alleging recurring patterns of targeted violence and intimidation, as well as institutional and governmental negligence in responding to the incidents.
The BCP identified four key concerns:
1. Systematic attacks on peaceful prayer gatherings – According to the BCP, small house churches and local Christian congregations conducting prayer services have repeatedly been targeted over the past three months. The organisation alleged that the intruders had assaulted worshippers, vandalised places of worship and desecrated religious symbols and objects. The BCP also criticised the efforts to downplay the attacks, saying, “Regrettably, some public figures and local leaders have characterised these lawless disruptions as “public protests” while remaining silent on vigilante groups taking the law into their own hands.”
2. Disinformation and manufactured narratives – The BCP alleged that several incidents followed similar “scripted patterns”, in which aggressors forcibly entered private prayer gatherings to disrupt services, “engineer chaos” and “record selective footage”, which was subsequently circulated on social media in edited form. According to the organisation, the videos were then used to make allegations of “forced conversion through inducement”, allegedly fuelling communal tension. BCP founder Herod Mullick said, “These edited videos are subsequently circulated online after false allegations of forced conversion to mislead local authorities and justify vigilante actions”. The organisation further alleged that such videos were presented to local district magistrates (DMs) and sub-divisional officers (SDOs) as evidence, and used to promote what it described as false narratives. The BCP rejected the allegations of forced conversion as “unfounded”, saying that “peaceful believers gathered for routine prayer are being falsely framed as perpetrators.”
3. Discriminatory police action and non-registration of complaints – The BCP further alleged that police responses to the incidents had been inconsistent. It said alleged aggressors were often allowed to leave the scene without immediate action, while injured believers and pastors who reported being victimised were taken to local police stations, “subjected to late-night questioning” and allegedly intimidated. Of the dozens of reported incidents, the BCP said FIRs have been registered in only 13 cases, and only “after extraordinary effort and legal intervention”. “In all other instances, local police authorities have displayed severe reluctance to accept formal written complaints from the victims,” the BCP added.
4. Institutional apathy and unaddressed concerns –The BCP also alleged that repeated appeals to local administrative authorities had failed, with officials “consistently declined to engage in dialogue with state church leaders or representatives of our organisation”, the organisation said. It further alleged that “no independent or impartial inquiries have been instituted to verify the authenticity of these viral video clips”. According to the BCP, “this persistent administrative apathy creates a climate of impunity for vigilante groups and deprives minority worshippers of equal protection under the law.”
Citing violations of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 14 (Equality before Law), Article 19 (Freedom of Speech and Assembly), Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty), and Article 25 (Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice, and Propagation of Religion) of the Constitution of India— the BCP urged the NHRC, WBHRC and NCM to direct the West Bengal Government and the director general of police (DGP) to conduct a high-level independent investigation of all the recent incidents of violence targeting the churches and prayer gatherings.
The organisation also sought an investigation into alleged cyber disinformation and circulation of edited videos allegedly intended to portray worshippers as perpetrators of violence. Additionally, the council pleaded for clear directions to the police and administration to immediately register FIRs in all pending cases and ensure prompt legal action against those responsible.
The BCP further requested the commissions to direct district administrations to provide police protection to vulnerable house churches and congregations during weekly prayer services, and to ensure that victims are not harassed, intimidated or pressured by law-enforcement authorities under alleged influence from vigilante or extremist groups.
After attending the public hearing, former Union culture secretary Jawhar Sircar shared a post on Facebook describing the recent attacks on Christian churches and communities in West Bengal as “tragic and unprecedented” and condemned the attacks as “dastardly”. Sircar expressed his support for the Christian community and their right to practice their faith peacefully.

Ahead of COP31 next month, what has India committed to and what does it expect?
COP31 will take place from November 9 to 20, 2026 in Turkiye, with Australia serving as the president of negotiations
India is heading into the UN climate conference in Turkey’s Antalya next month with a strengthened set of climate targets for 2035, but is arguing that COP31 should be less about announcing new promises and more about delivering those already made -- particularly on climate finance, technology transfer and adaptation.
On Wednesday, at the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC pre-COP31) meeting in Fiji, Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav said the success of the Antalya conference should not be measured by new targets or declarations, but by whether implementation is accelerated, support reaches countries that need it and existing solutions are taken to scale.
“The long-term objectives and goals are already set,” Yadav said, referring to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, including the ambition to limit global temperature rise to 1.5°C. He called for greater focus on closing gaps in understanding, fulfilling existing commitments and accelerating implementation.
COP31 will take place from November 9 to 20, 2026 in Turkiye, with Australia serving as the president of negotiations.
What India has committed so far
Since last year’s COP30 in Brazil in November last year, India’s latest climate commitment has come through the updated Nationally Determined Contribution for 2031-35, approved by the cabinet in March. Under it, the country has committed to reducing the emissions intensity of its GDP by 47% by 2035 from 2005 levels, increasing cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil fuel sources to 60%, and creating an additional carbon sink of 3.5-4 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent through forest and tree cover, compared with the 2005 baseline.
The NDC also included qualitative targets on sustainable lifestyles, strengthening adaptation capacity and following a cleaner development pathway as India pursues its Viksit Bharat @2047 goal.
Also Read: COP31 success is about delivery, support and scale, not new targets: Bhupender Yadav
India’s earlier 2030 targets included reducing emissions intensity by 45% from 2005 levels and achieving about 50% cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources. India crossed the latter milestone in June 2025, five years ahead of schedule. As of June 30, 2026, the non-fossil share had risen to 54.18% of installed electricity capacity. The country’s longer-term commitment remains to achieve net-zero emissions by 2070.
But India’s ask at COP31 is implementation
Yadav’s intervention in Fiji makes clear that India does not see another round of headline targets as the central outcome it wants from COP31. He called for parties to fulfil their existing commitments under the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement “in true letter and spirit”, while ensuring that countries have the means to meet them.
He also called for greater capacity building and for countries to demonstrate concrete examples of high-impact mitigation, large-scale adaptation and effective delivery of climate support.
India has also called for equal attention to mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation, arguing that there cannot be a one-size-fits-all approach to climate action and that equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) must remain central. CBDR-RC is a core rule in global climate agreements that gives countries different duties to fight climate change based on their wealth and past pollution.
Climate finance remains the biggest fault line
Climate finance is likely to be one of India’s major demands in Antalya. India has repeatedly argued over the past year that the new climate finance goal of mobilising $300 billion annually by 2035 is inadequate for the needs of developing countries, and has backed the Baku-to-Belém roadmap aimed at scaling climate finance towards $1.3 trillion annually for developing countries.
At COP30 last year, Yadav had said adaptation finance in particular needed to increase in both quantity and quality and should be provided through grants rather than debt-creating instruments. India has also argued that developing countries face major barriers in accessing finance, including complex approval procedures, slow disbursement and limited flexibility.
This demand is closely linked to India’s wider position that climate action cannot be separated from development needs. At the Bonn climate talks in June, India said developing countries needed adequate carbon space to eradicate poverty, expand energy access and meet sustainable development goals, while developed countries should take the lead through accelerated emissions reductions.
India also wants technology and capacity support
Technology transfer and capacity building are another recurring part of India’s negotiating position.
At Fiji, Yadav called for greater capacity building and for climate solutions that are already working to be taken to scale. In June, India and Japan adopted rules for implementing their Joint Crediting Mechanism under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, designed to facilitate investment, technology transfer and capacity building around low-carbon technologies in India.
India’s position is therefore that developing countries should not simply be given emissions targets, but also access to the finance, technology and institutional capacity needed to meet them.
The BRICS position: no CBAM, no one-size-fits-all energy transition
The September BRICS summit in New Delhi added another important layer to India’s COP31 position.
The New Delhi Declaration opposed “unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures” such as carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM) – already in place across the European Union, arguing that such measures could undermine developing countries’ efforts to address climate change and improve adaptation and resilience.
Also Read:Climate action needs cash. Where is it?
The declaration had also taken a firm position on energy security. It said fossil fuels would continue to play an important role in the global energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies, while backing “just, orderly, equitable and inclusive” energy transitions and lower greenhouse gas emissions.
So what does India want from COP31?
Taken together, India’s public positions have pointed towards clear expectation from countries around the globe – faster implementation of existing Paris commitments; greater and more accessible climate finance, particularly for adaptation; technology transfer and capacity building; recognition of equity and CBDR-RC; and protection of developing countries from unilateral climate-linked trade measures such as CBAM.

The day has finally arrived. Jaguar began its long road to electric reinvention in November 2024 with a firestorm of a rebrand featuring no cars. Just a month later, it revealed a prototype: the Type 00—a car so polarizing it practically broke the internet’s automotive enclave. Some loved it; others hated it so much that Jaguar’s own staff were targeted for supposedly betraying the company’s 90-year history.
Since this chaotic but undoubtedly viral launch, major departures have followed, including Jaguar Land Rover’s (JLR) chief creative officer Gerry McGovern, the notable car designer who signed off on Jaguar’s divisive all-electric design and the no-car ad campaign.
Jaguar’s managing director, Rawdon Glover, is a brave man. Through this shitstorm, and a frighteningly long period of selling no new cars whatsoever, he’s remained unflappable; utterly confident that, when people see the final car—the finished version of the luxury four-door GT that is “like no other”—everything will make sense. That moment is here. The company finally revealed the Jaguar Type 01 at an event in New York City on Tuesday—the finished version of the Type 00. (Jaguar Land Rover paid a portion of WIRED's travel expenses so we could attend the launch.)
“A bold grand tourer that never arrives unnoticed, like all the best Jaguars of the past,” Jaguar’s press material says. This is most certainly true: you will see this thing coming. The low roofline, short front and extended rear overhangs, long hood, and huge 23-inch wheels all remain from the prototype, just as promised. The cab-rear design hides a 50–50 weight distribution, and the huge surfaces make it hard to square the fact that this is the most aerodynamic Jag ever, with active vanes, a deployable spoiler, and airflow trickery delivering a drag coefficient of 0.23 Cd.
Crucially, the production model’s extra doors make more sense of the design, shifting the Type 01’s look away from Thunderbirds territory to more familiar ground. The front has been softened ever so slightly as well, which again is preferable to the prototype’s exceedingly bluff nose. The rear, however, is where the exterior design really shines with hidden-until-lit, full-width lights embedded in horizontal strikethroughs.
Let’s get the specs out of the way: the Type 01 is the most powerful Jaguar road car, with up to 1,030 Pferdestärke (PS) and 1,365 Newton-meters. It goes from standstill to 62 mph in 3.2 seconds. Justifying the tagline of “power in reserve,” the car can rocket from 62 to 112 mph in a further 4 seconds. I’ve been driven in it, and it feels like the acceleration never ends thanks to the tri-motor setup of a 260-kilowatt (kW) front motor paired with twin 310-kW rear motors.
It stands 5,235 mm long and 1,403 mm tall, but all-wheel steering makes it feel much smaller on the road. The 850-volt bespoke Jaguar architecture and 118-kilowatt-hour usable battery supposedly deliver an EPA range of up to 400 miles (450 miles on WLTP), with a “sustained highway speed” range of up to 320 miles. Drivers can add up to 200 miles of range in 13 minutes using 350 kW rapid DC charging. So the TL;DR? It’s huge, fast, aerodynamic, powerful, and, most definitely, unique.
Inside, a dramatic central spine runs the full length of the cabin, creating a zone for each occupant. Lots of “brass-inspired” finishes are intended to underline the luxury message. A panoramic glass roof with adjustable virtual blinds brings in the light, but there’s no rear windscreen. Instead, a digital “ClearSight” rearview display is embedded centrally in the full-width panoramic soundbar at the base of the windscreen to show what’s behind. Cleverly, the feed from this rear-facing camera is positioned at the same height as the door mirrors, supposedly reducing the annoying focal adjustment these systems usually demand.
Ahead of the driver is a 24-inch OLED screen that extends toward the center of the car. A central 7-inch smartphone-style display sits between the driver and front passenger for common controls such as climate and audio, operated entirely by touchscreen with (sadly) no physical switchgear in sight. “Hot stone massage effect” seats, whatever those are, are also electrically adjustable in 12 different ways. Cabin air purification removes allergens, toxins, and particulates, and a fragrance diffuser offers a choice of scents—which seems to be the pinnacle of what Western auto companies think a luxury car interior needs these days.
As a grand tourer, luggage space is important. The Type 01 offers 450 liters of load space, expanding to 1,000 liters with rear seats folded. And then there are the production stories: Jaguar built more than 150 prototypes, drove 700,000 miles, and filed more than 360 patents while developing the car.
Jaguar is most proud, and rightly so, of its “impossible panel.” It's a single, unbroken panel that runs more than 3 meters from the A-pillar to the rear of the Type 01. Pressing this huge piece with five different acute angles in it was deemed not possible by Jaguar's modeling system. After roughly 22 weeks and 1,500 hours of development (supposedly requiring someone to come out of retirement), Jaguar realized this “impossible” panel.
Pricing of the Type 01 is possibly the most important thing Jaguar has to nail. Starting at around $170,000 (or £130,000—no confirmed pricing yet), this puts the Jag well below Ferrari Luces, electric Merc G-Wagens and Lamborghinis, and even the new Bentley Torcal, exactly where Glover wants to sit. Jaguar thinks it has a sweet spot in luxury EVs, a Goldilocks zone where buyers are eager to part with cash for electric cars that aren’t astronomical but priced high enough above the premium sector to be legitimately highfalutin.
No one has really succeeded with the luxury EV market. Porsche has tried. So has Lamborghini. Mercedes has had a very tough time. Now Bentley is having a crack at it. Glover thinks that the Type 01 has a shot.
“One of us is going to break through the glass ceiling and make a success of EVs at elevated price points,” Glover tells me. “The best way to do that is not to play into the tropes of EVs. You’re not going to get there because it’s an electric car. You’re going to get there because the car itself looks a certain way, feels a certain way, drives a certain way. If you can do all of those things, [it doesn’t matter] whether it’s combustion or electric. Just being an electric car was enough for such a short period. Cars have got to earn their right in somebody’s garage.”
Glover has openly said the Type 01 will have to earn its place with “almost an entirely new client base,” one that is supposedly younger, more affluent, urban, independently minded, creative, and wishing to “carve their own path.” We shall see very soon exactly what kind of person signs on the dotted line to reserve a Type 01. Will they look like the youthful, vibrant characters in Jaguar’s initial launch campaign, or like traditional Jaguar, Lotus, and Aston owners with gray hair, flannel shirts, and bad shorts?
“We’ve got to make sure that new audience comes along," Glover says. “But I don’t want to alienate anybody.” The Chinese do well with that youthful audience. “I’ve driven some of the Li Autos. I’ve driven some of the XPeng cars. They’re impressive in terms of the amount of technology in them. The quality of fit and finish is increasing at a pace.”
But Glover still thinks a big gap exists between Chinese cars and established Western autos; though with Xiaomi’s achievements after only a few years of making cars, it’s hard to see this view staying true for long. “They’re playing in a commodity space," he says. "It’s about how many features, how much tech, how much range, and how can I do it at the lowest price. I’m not saying we’re immune to all of that, but it certainly validates us getting out of the volume premium market.”
Like Bentley, Jaguar is leaning into its heritage to look for things the Chinese will find harder to emulate. But it could be argued that the Type 01 lacks any obvious heritage. The pioneering spirit is there, for sure, but this is an EV very much looking forward, not back. With that in mind, what does, say, two years of success look like to Glover for this electrified rebirth of the brand?
“Success will be we’ve established ourselves at the [new] price point,” he says. “People are saying, ‘Yep, Jaguar is worth paying more for.’ I know what volumes we need to achieve. I’m not going to articulate those, but just under that we need to generate a certain level of volume to create that critical mass.”
For Glover, this level of volume requires customers to see Jaguar as a more current, culturally relevant brand, and to be genuinely interested in what the company will do next.
“Is it just the man in the bad shirts and bad shorts, or have we actually been successful in attracting a new audience?” Glover says. “We start seeing that in the first two years.”
