Centre moves SC to scrap Jharkhand DGP appointment
The application has challenged the legality of appointments made under the “Selection and Appointment of Director General and IGP, Jharkhand (Head of the Police Force) Regulation, 2025”
The Centre has moved the Supreme Court seeking a direction to declare as illegal the appointment of the incumbent Jharkhand director general of Police (DGP) Tadasha Mishra, contending that the state government’s 2025 regulations governing the selection of police chief are contrary to the top court’s binding directions in the past.
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant agreed on Wednesday to list the Centre’s application for hearing on Thursday, after Solicitor General Tushar Mehta mentioned it.
The application, filed in the long-running Prakash Singh case, has challenged the legality of appointments made under the “Selection and Appointment of Director General and Inspector General of Police, Jharkhand (Head of the Police Force) Regulation, 2025”. The Centre has asked the court to direct Jharkhand to implement its directions in the Prakash Singh case and, alternatively, declare DGP appointments made under the 2025 regulation illegal.
The Prakash Singh case relates to the Supreme Court’s monitoring of police reforms, in which the court has issued a series of directions since 2006 aimed at insulating the police from undue political interference and ensuring transparent, merit-based appointments and fixed tenures for senior police officers.
Also Read: Chandigarh: PGI eyes parking project revival after SC ruling
In the present plea, the Centre has particularly objected to the manner in which the Jharkhand government amended its regulations to facilitate Mishra’s appointment as DGP on December 30, 2025, a day before she was due to retire. According to the application, a December 29 resolution removed the requirement of six months’ residual service for appointment as DGP, paving the way for Mishra’s appointment under the 2025 regulations.
This, the Centre has argued, runs contrary to the Supreme Court’s directions in the Prakash Singh case, under which recommendations for appointment of a DGP are to be made from officers having at least six months of residual service before retirement. The court had clarified in its March 13, 2019 order that the requirement would apply to the UPSC’s recommendation and preparation of the panel.
The Centre has also questioned the very framing of the 2025 regulations. Jharkhand notified the regulations on January 8, 2025, providing for a state-level nomination committee for selection of the DGP. The application says the state framed the regulations without obtaining the Supreme Court’s permission as required by its earlier directions.
Also Read: Supreme Court decision to allow green fire crackers may still push pollution to 2025 levels
The Centre’s challenge comes against the backdrop of an earlier appointment made under the same regulatory framework. Jharkhand appointed Anurag Gupta as DGP on February 2, 2025, for a two-year tenure despite his having only around three months of service left before superannuation. The Ministry of Home Affairs subsequently wrote to the state on April 22, May 3 and May 23, 2025, opposing the appointment and pointing out that Gupta had retired on April 30, 2025.
After Gupta subsequently sought voluntary retirement, Jharkhand appointed Mishra as DGP on December 30, 2025. The Centre says its January 6, 2026 communication asked the state to cancel both the 2025 regulations and Mishra’s appointment, since she was due to superannuate the following day, and to initiate a fresh appointment process in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directions. The state, however, continued with the appointment process, the application alleges.
The Centre has also brought to the Supreme Court’s notice that a PIL challenging the 2025 regulations and Gupta’s appointment, which was pending before the Jharkhand High Court, was transferred to the Supreme Court on August 18, 2025. The top court had, in an order of May 19, 2026, also noted that an acting DGP was functioning in Jharkhand and sought a compliance affidavit from the state.
The Centre has contended that Jharkhand cannot selectively rely on the Prakash Singh judgment to claim a two-year tenure for its DGP while departing from the mandatory selection requirements laid down by the same judgment. “The directives of this Hon’ble Court are required to be implemented in toto in true spirit and not in a selective or partial manner,” said the application.
The Prakash Singh directions require the state government to select the DGP from among the three senior-most officers empanelled by the UPSC on the basis of length of service, very good record and experience, with the selected officer ordinarily having a minimum tenure of two years irrespective of the date of superannuation.
The Centre has now asked the Supreme Court to direct Jharkhand to abide by its directions in the Prakash Singh case and to declare DGP appointments made under the state’s 2025 regulation illegal.

Riyadh: Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were targeted in two separate attacks on October 6 and 7, resulting in a total of three fatalities and 36 injuries, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said.
According to GACA, two people were killed and 28 injured in the attack on Abha International Airport. The deceased were female residents of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, while the injured included Saudi citizens, a Bangladeshi resident and a Filipino resident. The injuries ranged from minor to critical.
At King Khalid International Airport, one Sudanese resident was killed, and eight people were injured, GACA said. The injured included five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents and one Pakistani resident, with injuries ranging from minor to critical.
"All injured individuals were transported to hospital for appropriate medical care," GACA said, adding that the two attacks also caused some property damage.
The authority said emergency response teams and relevant authorities responded immediately in accordance with established protocols and applicable emergency response plans.
"GACA is working in coordination with the relevant authorities to assess the damage, verify the safety of the facilities, and take the necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and maintain the security and safety of operations within the Kingdom's civil aviation system," it said.
Meanwhile, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jassim Mohammed al-Budaiwi strongly condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's Abha and King Khalid airports, describing them as "systematic crimes" targeting civilians, Al Jazeera reported.
Al-Budaiwi said in a statement that targeting civilian airports and "endangering the lives of travellers, workers and civilians represents a dangerous escalation and a flagrant violation of international laws and norms".
He added that the GCC countries stand united with Saudi Arabia, as reported by Al Jazeera.
The developments come amid continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and an escalating conflict in Yemen.
Earlier, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday (local time), citing the ongoing security situation in Saudi Arabia and public threats by the Houthis against airports and airspace across the Kingdom.
"Due to the ongoing security situation in Saudi Arabia and Houthi public threats against airports and airspace across Saudi Arabia, the U.S. Mission reminds all U.S. citizens to exercise heightened vigilance," the embassy said.
The US Mission said the Houthis had engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks against civilian airports, and warned that the military conflict had the potential to escalate.
"U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions," it said, advising citizens to check flight departure status directly with their airline and the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen also said it destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform used in an attack on Riyadh earlier in the day.
"The destruction operation took place in Yemen's capital of Sanaa during preparations for an imminent attack against the Kingdom," coalition spokesperson Colonel Turki al-Maliki said.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted 11 groups of Yemeni government forces with ballistic missiles across Yemen in the past 24 hours, Al Jazeera reported.
Saree claimed the internationally recognised government's forces were targeted along key routes near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including Ras al-Ara, al-Mudarabah and al-Saqiya, by 11 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis. He claimed the attacks resulted in dozens of casualties, including military commanders, and destroyed several vehicles.
Saree separately said the Houthis targeted the Saudi Arabia-backed Giants Brigades with a ballistic missile, killing and injuring more than 30 people, according to Al Jazeera.
In a separate development, Syria's Ministry of Information denied rumours on X suggesting that Damascus could become involved in the Yemen conflict.
"Syria's policy in the region is focused on stability, peace and cooperation, not opening new fronts," the ministry said, adding that any involvement from Syria would come only through official channels and existing bilateral frameworks.
"Syria's position is clear: we stand firmly with Saudi Arabia against threats to its security and stability. At the same time, Syria's policy in the region is focused on stability, peace and cooperation, not opening new fronts," it said.
The ministry added that Syria's priority was rebuilding the country, strengthening its institutions, working with partners on reconstruction and improving the lives of Syrians.
"Any military cooperation with partner countries would take place only through official channels and existing bilateral frameworks," it said.
Earlier, Houthi military spokesperson Brigadier General Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for a series of missile and drone attacks targeting sites in Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Rabigh.
In a statement on Telegram, Saree said the group carried out "three qualitative military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones".

క్లెయిమ్: 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్ మైదానంలో సీఈసీ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలంటూ CJP చేసిన నిరసనను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.

ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి, అంటే CJP ముంబై నిరసన ప్రదర్శన కంటే రెండు వారాల ముందు నుంచే ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం.
ఈ వీడియోను ఫేస్బుక్, ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్లలో అమీన్ సిద్ధికి అనే భోపాల్కు చెందిన కంటెంట్ క్రియేటర్ 18 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న మరిన్ని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా అమీన్ సిద్ధికి తన ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియోలు మధ్యప్రదేశ్ రాజధాని భోపాల్లో జరిగిన AIMIM అధ్యక్షుడు అసదుద్దీన్ ఒవైసీ బహిరంగ సభకు సంబంధించినవిగా పేర్కొన్నారు. వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, మధ్యప్రదేశ్ అసెంబ్లీ ఆమోదించిన యూనిఫామ్ సివిల్ కోడ్ బిల్లుకు వ్యతిరేకంగా భోపాల్లోని సెంట్రల్ లైబ్రరీ గ్రౌండ్లో 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న ఈ సభను నిర్వహించారు.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే దృశ్యాలను గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పోల్చి చూడగా, ఈ వీడియో భోపాల్కు సంబంధించినదిగా స్పష్టమైంది.
చివరిగా, ముంబై శివాజీ పార్క్లో CJP నిరసన దృశ్యాలంటూ భోపాల్కు చెందిన సంబంధం లేని వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

New Zealand Cricket (NZC) said on Wednesday it had considered a range of expert opinions before deciding to launch a domestic T20 competition amid criticism of its handling of a Deloitte report that favoured joining Australia’s Big Bash League.
After NZC announced in March that NZ20 would replace the existing Super Smash provincial competition, cricket great Richard Hadlee and former NZC President Lesley Murdoch criticised what they said was a lack of transparency in the process and the body’s refusal to share the Deloitte report with stakeholders.
NZC Chair Diana Puketapu-Lyndon said the governing body should have done a better job explaining the decision when it announced its plans.
The Deloitte report was just one of four expert reports considered by the board in making the decision, alongside analyses of community cricket, high-performance pathways and fan engagement, she added.
“Its analysis favoured exploring the Big Bash opportunity further, for reasons including financial upside and governance, but it also said weighing the options was for the board and encouraged us to continue exploring both options,” Puketapu-Lyndon said in a statement.
The board had also considered feedback from the country’s six Major Associations and the New Zealand Cricket Players Association, both of which supported NZ20 ahead of seeking to put a New Zealand team in the established Australian league.
“When all of that was considered, alongside the board’s own due diligence, the board voted unanimously, 7-0, to support NZ20 as the preferred option,” said Puketapu-Lyndon.
NZC said it would not release the full report, citing confidentiality.
“This is the biggest change to domestic cricket in a generation, and we know not everyone agrees with it,” she said.
“NZ20 is genuinely aspirational. It has the potential to revolutionise the game of cricket in this country and ensure a sustainable future from the grassroots to the elite.”
NZ20 organisers had initially planned to launch the six-team competition this summer but NZC postponed the tournament until the 2027-28 home season to allow more time to establish the privately owned franchise league and accommodate the international schedule.

This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles.
"To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo, a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
Many of these fossils wind up at the nearby Paleontological Museum of Liaoning, a facility that Luo and his colleague, Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn, visit each year to examine new finds. A decade ago, a specimen in a thick slab of shale caught their eye.
It was the fossilized bones and soft tissue impressions of an ancient mammal that lived some 165 million years ago. "Early fossil mammals — in fact, they are exceedingly rare," says Luo.
This animal, which the team named Megacauda sungei and have described in the journal Nature, was a prize discovery. The remains were so intact that it was possible to determine that it was likely capable of chewing food and then swallowing it, and also suckling — traits that are shared by mammals.
Luo and his colleagues conclude that these evolutionary innovations — and their presence among our ancient mammalian relatives — extend deep into the past to at least the middle Jurassic.
"It's all there in one remarkable fossil," says Luo.
A chihuahua-sized chimera
The fossil was about the size of a chihuahua, but somewhat hard to discern from the rock surrounding it.
"The fossil itself is actually very dark," explains Luo. "The bones are black, the slab [is] dark. And it's kind of difficult to have beautiful photographs."
One of his collaborators, Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong University of Science and Technology, snapped a different kind of vivid image using a technique called X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. "It would make this bone pop out in different colors," says Luo.
The resulting image rendered the skeleton a bright yellow and it showcased a curious combination of characteristics. The back end, which includes the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail, resembles a modern-day platypus.
These features suggest that this animal was likely semi-aquatic and foraged in the water. "The big tail is good for swimming," says Luo.
"However," he continues, "its teeth and the jaw would be very different from platypus. So the head is very much of a predator." Indeed, Luo and his colleagues found a smattering of small salamander bones inside the fossil that they suspect the animal had eaten by first cutting and shearing with its sharp teeth.
A lot to swallow
There was something else that Luo instantly noticed about the fossil. "My eyes zeroed in on these tiny hyoid bones," he recalls.
The human hyoid bone sits in the throat, half an inch or so above the Adam's apple, and supports the backside of the tongue.
The team later CT scanned the fossil, including the underside of the skull, which exposed a delicate roof of the mouth as well as a series of bone hooks and ridges.
With this combination of rarely preserved features, "we are able with great confidence to reconstruct the whole muscular skeletal machinery," says Luo.
This reconstruction revealed that the animal was likely capable of doing two things that are unique to mammals.
The first is swallowing food after chewing it. Other vertebrates tend to bite and gulp. But mammals "chew down all the food with our teeth," Luo says. "And then we swallow one bolus of food down to our esophagus at a time."
Consider, for a moment, a carnivore that chews meat, an herbivore that crunches on vegetables, and an insect-eater that chomps bugs. This diverse array of foods all get chewed up and then swallowed down a mammalian throat in a similar way.
Secondly, this fossil appears to have been capable of suckling, which embodies something even more fundamental.
"That ability to suckle mother's milk literally defined our biology," says Luo. "And that's why our group is called mammals. We're named after the mammary glands."
This is some of the oldest fossil evidence of an animal with both these key mammalian abilities.
Small but varied
"It's a fascinating specimen," says Jessica Theodor, a paleontologist at the University of Calgary who wasn't involved in the research. "The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals."
Theodor would like to see some of the images in greater detail, but she says a fossil like this tracks the evolution of lactation, which she likens to a kind of dietary and hormonal conversation between mother and baby.
"The conversation is beginning very far back in the Mesozoic — in the Jurassic and Cretaceous," says Theodor. "That's amazing to me that it's this old and this fundamental."
For Luo, this fossil is the latest evidence of how new ways of feeding have helped mammals and their predecessors diversify — even back when they were the little guys on the proverbial block.
"Mammals, they're never dominant in the age of dinosaurs," he says. "But nonetheless, they hold out relatively well compared to all other vertebrates."
By the time of the Jurassic period, there were already proto-mammalian gliders, swimmers, land-dwellers, tree-dwellers and diggers. Each one was making a living in its own distinct way — all united in their shared ability to chew, swallow and suckle.

Google's AI detection website is now available
SynthID Detector will flag content created with AI tools from OpenAI, Google, Apple and other companies.
Google is making SynthID Detector, its web tool for identifying AI-created and AI-edited content, available to everyone. The web-based tool is able to flag images, video and audio clips created with AI tools from Google, OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao. It's free to use, but does require users to log in with a Google, OpenAI or Apple account.
The website will also be one of the first AI detection tools that will be able to identify images created with Apple's AI features, like Image Playground. Google says support for images created and edited with Apple Intelligence is coming "soon."
Google has been working on SynthID Detector for more than a year, and previously made versions of it available to journalists and other "media professionals." Now, anyone can visit synthid.com to check whether a piece of content has a SynthID watermark. The company has other methods for detecting SynthID watermarks and C2PA content credentials, including its "Circle to Search" feature and the Gemini app itself. But creating a dedicated website for detection makes these capabilities a bit easier to access, especially for people not already using Google's AI tools.
As with all AI detection features, there are some limitations. SynthID Detector can't detect all AI-generated content, since many companies rely on different standards for watermarking. Watermarks can also be stripped from content in some situations. And Google's website doesn't distinguish between content that was entirely AI-created and content that was merely edited with it. So it won't provide specific details about how a particular piece of content was created or which aspects might be synthetic.
While SynthID Detector is a step in the right direction, verifying AI-generated content is still far from foolproof. AI detection tools like SynthID Detector rely on a patchwork of different standards so there's no such thing as a universal checker. Meta, for example, has been experimenting with its own web tool, which can identify images created or edited with its latest Muse Image models, but not those from other companies or even its own prior models.
But it does seem likely Google will get more companies to sign on to SynthID over time, The company previously said that ElevenLabs had committed to adding support for the watermarks. On its website, Google notes that it's "continuously working on extending our partnerships to allow detecting more generated media."

What is the pneumonic plague?
The ancient word "plague" is back in the headlines.
NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes reported this week on what we know about a Russian researcher working in a lab studying the plague who died from pneumonia of an unknown origin last week.
Maynes reports that the employee was a 28-year-old woman who worked in a lab in Siberia, some 2,500 miles from Moscow. An investigation by Russia's consumer health watchdog concluded that no pathogens in her body were connected to her work with infectious disease.
But local media have raised concerns about the spread of pneumonic plague, which NPR has not independently confirmed.
It's one of the diseases studied at the lab in Siberia. It's airborne and can be fatal.
While noting that 200 "contacts" were in quarantine, Russia has denied that there are cases of plague in the area. But questions loom. In a press conference Wednesday, the head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said these Russian assurances were — at the very least — incomplete: "We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment."
In the meantime, here's what we do know about the bacterial disease of plague — and the variant known as pneumonic plague.
Plague variations
The plague comes in several versions, depending on which body part the bacteria invade. When a flea bites a person, the individual typically develops what's called bubonic plague. In this case, the telltale sign is one or more swollen and painful lymph nodes, known as buboes. (The word "bubonic" comes from the Greek boubon, which means groin, because some people have swollen lymph nodes in their groin.) Doctors can diagnose the disease by taking a sample from the person's blood or lymph nodes and then submitting the sample to a lab for testing.
But when the bacteria spread to the lungs, this can cause what's called pneumonic plague. In this case, there's often no telltale sign of the plague, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
This version is much more dangerous, says medical entomologist Adelaide Miarinjara at Emory University. "It transmits pretty easily between people because it spreads through droplets, almost like COVID spreads."
And people can die more quickly with pneumonic plague than other forms, she adds, because the disease progresses more rapidly. "The key here is early diagnosis. If people aren't expecting it or don't seek treatment, they can die."
Treatment involves antibiotics, often administered by IV infusion.
In 2017, Madagascar suffered a large outbreak of pneumonic plague when a person from a rural part of the country brought the disease to the coastal city of Toamasina. That city hadn't seen a case of the plague in nearly a century, says Miarinjara, who was in Madagascar at the time. "A person transmitted the disease on public transportation," she says.
The country recorded more than 2,400 suspected cases, including nearly 1,900 cases of pneumonic plague. One study estimated that about 25% of people with confirmed cases died in this outbreak.
The history of quarantine
As for the reports of Russian "contacts" of the lab worker under quarantine — that reflects a long-standing response to sicknesses like the plague.
The idea of isolating, or quarantining, sick people dates back at least 3,000 years. The Book of Leviticus in the Bible mentions how to isolate people with leprosy.
The word "quarantine" itself arose during the Black Death, when the city-state of Dubrovnik, now part of the country of Croatia, enacted what is likely the first state-imposed isolation.
At the time, Dubrovnik was a wealthy merchant city along the coast of the Adriatic Sea. City leaders wanted to keep the bubonic plague out. So they began to force visitors to wait for 40 days on a remote island outside the city before coming ashore.
They called the wait quarantino, from the Italian word for "40."
"The first quarantine was pretty much improvised," Ivana Marinavić, the head of educational programs at the Lazarettos of Dubrovnik, told NPR in 2021. The Lazarettos were the first buildings ever constructed for the sole purpose of quarantining.
If you broke the quarantine during the plague, the consequences were severe. "Torture, or cutting your nose or your ears off," Marinavić told NPR.

Britain's George Russell will start from the back of the grid in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix.
The Mercedes driver has received a power-unit penalty from a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday.
The 28-year-old qualified in eighth but was heading for a podium finish before an engine failure forced him to retire from third place with five laps remaining.
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has confirmed that Russell needs to take a new power unit this weekend, putting him over the limit on several components and meaning he will be penalised in Singapore.
Russell's retirement last Sunday meant Kimi Antonelli, who finished second behind Max Verstappen, took a big leap towards his first Formula 1 world title as the Italian is now 84 points ahead of his Mercedes team-mate.
There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs for Qatar and Abu Dhabi, in the context of the war in the Middle East.
"[Russell's penalty] is particularly frustrating given the way he drove last weekend and the result he deserved to be fighting for," said Wolff.
"Unfortunately, these things are part of the sport and our focus now is on giving him the best possible car and opportunities to fight back through the field."
Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix last month having taken a similar penalty, while this is the latest setback in a season of frustrating mechanical issues for Russell, who won last year's Singapore Grand Prix.
Extra points are on offer this weekend as Singapore hosts the sixth and final sprint event of the season. Russell's penalty will apply to Sunday's Grand Prix and not the sprint race on Saturday.
"We have spent the days since [last Sunday] working hard to understand why our performance was not where it should have been," Wolff added.
"Singapore gives us an immediate opportunity to continue that work.
"We need to keep learning and score the strongest result we can with both cars."

India seeks update from Russia on 69 Indians in Russian military
India said on Wednesday it has sought an update from Russian authorities on the whereabouts of 69 Indian nationals still serving with the Russian armed forces
India said on Wednesday it has sought an update from Russian authorities on the whereabouts of 69 Indian nationals still serving with the Russian armed forces, even as it reiterated the “grave danger” of taking up offers of military jobs against the backdrop of the conflict in Ukraine.
Fifty-one Indians, including men who were fraudulently lured into accepting jobs in the Russian Army, have died so far while serving on the frontlines of the conflict in Ukraine, according to information provided by authorities in the past. Reports of Indians being inducted into the Russian Army continue to emerge despite Moscow saying it has halted such recruitment.
External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a regular media briefing that a total of 259 Indian nationals are believed to have been recruited into the Russian armed forces so far, and India has pressed Russian authorities for their release.

“Of these, through our efforts, so far 139 Indian nationals have seen early discharge from the Russian Army,” Jaiswal said. “We are following up with the Russian authorities for updates on the whereabouts of 69 Indian nationals who are reportedly with the Russian Army.”

The issue continues to be one of the rare irritants in the otherwise robust India-Russia relations, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi has personally raised the matter at several meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The figures provided by Jaiswal on Wednesday were higher than numbers provided by foreign secretary Vikram Misri after a meeting between Modi and Putin in Kyrgyzstan in August. Misri had said 227 Indians had been recruited into the Russian armed forces and 51 had been killed.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

The MRP debate, which has been recently triggered where a hospital purchased a product for ₹11 and billed it for ₹325, is misplaced and lacks the context we need to understand the issue properly.
Hospitals rightly point out that the gap between procurement and billing is not all profit: storing supplies, maintaining sterility and ensuring availability carry costs. But patients are entitled to ask a more basic question. How did ‘maximum’ become the price they routinely pay?
Understanding maximum retail price
MRP was designed as a ceiling to protect consumers. In healthcare, it can, however, also conceal how a price is built. The printed figure tells a family little about the manufacturer’s returns, the margins taken along the supply chain, or whether the product offers any advantage over a cheaper alternative. A patient in an emergency cannot shop around. When choice disappears, a ceiling risks becoming the default charge.
This is a serious problem, and price controls can help. In 2019, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority applied trade-margin rationalisation to 42 non-scheduled cancer medicines. The government estimated that this could save patients 200 crore annually. But the wider lesson is not that every medicine and device should have the same permitted margin. It is that India needs to decide what each margin is paying for.
Different products, therapies
A standard syringe sold by multiple suppliers does not justify the same return as a therapy developed for a rare disease after years of research and clinical trials. Nor should a familiar medicine acquire an innovation premium simply because it has a new brand name and a large marketing budget.
India needs a differential profit and margin strategy. Routine, high-volume products should have modest, transparent distribution and hospital margins, informed by comparable procurement prices. Bulk purchasing should benefit patients, insurers and public programmes. Genuine costs of stocking, safe handling, wastage and round-the-clock availability should be recognised openly, rather than recovered through an inflated price for the item itself.
Companies that take substantial scientific risks deserve a different approach. Those investing in original research, rare and neglected diseases, or products that demonstrably improve outcomes while reducing hospitalisations and total care costs should be able to earn higher profits. Fair returns give investors a reason to fund difficult work. But the premium should go to the organisation creating the clinical value, not automatically to every intermediary between the factory and the patient.
Science must earn
‘Novel’ must not be a label a company awards itself. A claim for a higher return should be tested against existing treatments: Does the product help patients live longer or better? Does it prevent complications? Is it safer or easier to use? Does it lower the total cost of treatment, even if its purchase price is higher? A product that costs more upfront but prevents repeated admissions may be better value than the cheapest item on the shelf.
Societal impact should count too. Research into diseases affecting small or neglected patient groups, reliable supply in underserved areas, and meaningful differential pricing for vulnerable patients merit consideration. These commitments must be specific and measurable. A patient-assistance scheme that reaches a handful of people cannot excuse a price that excludes everyone else.
India has an institution on which to build: Health Technology Assessment already evaluates clinical effectiveness, costs and equity to inform public decisions. Its evidence could help distinguish genuine advances from claims designed to justify a higher price.
Margins under microscopes
The government should establish an independent Healthcare Pricing and Value Panel with clinicians, scientists, health economists, patient representatives and pricing regulators. It should assess products against published criteria: clinical benefit, research risk, development investment, disease burden, total health-system cost and access for those least able to pay. Its members should disclose conflicts of interest, explain decisions and provide an appeal process.
A higher return would come with obligations. Companies seeking one should submit evidence and relevant costs for independent review. Premiums should be reconsidered as products mature or competitors enter the market. Where promised benefits remain uncertain, agreements could link part of the payment to observed outcomes. Concessional access for eligible patients and public programmes should be enforceable, rather than left to goodwill.
The panel must also separate manufacturer profits from trade and hospital margins. Otherwise, a policy intended to reward research could simply enlarge the amount captured downstream. Regulators need visibility into invoice prices, rebates and patient charges. Patients need itemised bills showing the product charge and any separate handling fee. Small and rural pharmacies, meanwhile, need viable returns to keep essential products available. A pricing policy that closes the last-mile supplier has failed its patients.
Profit, but not profiteering
MRP should remain a shield against overcharging, but it cannot be our entire definition of fair price. Companies should be able to make a profit, but not profiteer. India can protect a family buying an IV set and reward a company developing a breakthrough for a child with a rare disease. To do both, we must ask what the price rewards, what benefit the patient receives, and who can actually afford it. In healthcare, margin should follow proven value and access, and not bargaining power over a captive patient.
(Dr. Rajendra Pratap Gupta is the chairman of Health Parliament, a global executive think tank on healthcare, and former advisor to the Health Minister, government of India. founder@parliament.health)

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.

An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

NAMSCON 2026, the 66th annual conference and convocation of the National Academy of Medical Sciences (India), will bring together medical professionals, researchers and academicians from across the country in Chennai from October 8 to 11.
Hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, the conference will focus on the theme ‘Synergy of Science and Technology in Healthcare for a Healthier Tomorrow’.
Tamil Nadu Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar will inaugurate the conference as the chief guest.
The four-day programme will include pre-conference workshops, symposia, keynote addresses, National CME sessions, and oral and poster presentations.
The scientific sessions will cover antimicrobial resistance, CAR-T cell therapy, biosimilars and biologics, senolytic therapies, rare genetic disorders, emerging infections, pandemic preparedness and the Indian diabetes phenotype. Discussions will also focus on medical education, robotics in surgery, organ donation and transplantation, and evolving approaches to tuberculosis management.
Eight workshops on October 8 will cover trauma care, neonatal resuscitation, AI in clinical research, spine surgery, endoscopic gastroenterology, palliative care, diagnostic reasoning, and physician entrepreneurship.
Among the speakers are Shekar C. Mande, president, Indian National Science Academy; Abhijat Sheth, Chairman, National Medical Commission; Mohan V., Chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai; Mohan Kameswaran, Managing Director and Senior Consultant, Madras ENT Research Foundation; Vivekanand Jha, Executive Director, The George Institute of Global Health, India; and Gobardhan Das, Member, NITI Aayog.
M. Srinivas, member (Health), NITI Aayog, will deliver a plenary lecture on ‘Good Governance for Transforming Medical Institutions in India and Quality Research during Residency’. He will also interact with undergraduate and postgraduate students on research during residency.
Founded in 1961, NAMS is a non-statutory body that advises the Government of India on health policy and planning. NAMSCON 2026 will be the first annual conference of NAMS to be hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre.
The conference is being organised under the leadership of R. Jayanthi, Organising Chairperson and Dean, SRM MCH&RC, and Melvin George, Organising Secretary and Head, Centre for Clinical Pharmacology and Clinical Trials Research, with Rajarajan Swaminathan as State Convenor.

Veteran actor 
Nana Patekar
 has passed away at the age of 75 after suffering a severe cardiac arrest. The National Award-winning actor was among the most respected and distinctive performers in Hindi and Marathi cinema.
Actor found unconscious at Goa home
The actor was found unconscious at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa. He was subsequently rushed to a hospital, but the doctors declared him brought dead. According to ANI, Dr. Shekhar Salkar, Chief of Oncology Department, Manipal Hospital has shared that despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, the actor could not be revived. Further, a medico-legal case (MLC) has been registered, and a post-mortem will be conducted.
The news has shattered the industry, with the film fraternity members and fans trying to process the loss.
Nana Patekar built a career spanning several decades across films, theatre and television. With powerful screen presence, intense dialogue delivery and the ability to portray complex characters with remarkable restraint, the actor made a unique place for himself in Indian cinema.
About Nana Patekar
Born as Vishwanath Patekar in 1951, in Maharashtra, Nana Patekar’s journey into the world of acting started in the late 1970s. 
'Gaman' was his debut film; following it, he gave one performance after another to establish himself in the industry.
Some of his most loved cinematic pieces include, 'Parinda', 'Prahaar', 'Angaar', 'Krantiveer', 'Agni Sakshi', 'Yashwant', 'Ab Tak Chhappan', 'Apaharan', 'Welcome' and 'Natsamrat', among several others. His performances frequently moved beyond conventional hero and villain roles.
The late legendary star was honoured with the 
National Award
 thrice. In 1989, he received the National Award for Best Supporting Actor for 'Parinda' and got the Best Actor title for 'Krantiveer in 1994. Then in 1996, he was again honoured with the National Award for Best Supporting Actor in 'Agni Sakshi.' Further, he was honoured with the Padma Shri for his contribution to the arts in 2013.

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.
Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.
“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.
New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.
“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said.
The report finds that as the climate heats, glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said.
Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume.
“We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said.
Greenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.
“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said.
Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress.
Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans were warming 34% faster than the global average which has been linked to mass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scale fish standings and penguin deaths.
The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.
The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places.
Severe storms, including Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods in 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs.
New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said.
“Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”

Clemens is an accomplished baseball player, but he’s also been plagued with scandals, including allegations of steroid use

Donald Trump has announced that he will honor former MLB star Roger Clemens with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying that the Baseball Hall of Fame has cheated him.
Trump listed Clemens' impressive stats at a rally in San Antonio, Texas, Wednesday night, where the one-time superstar pitcher introduced Trump to the stage. The president has been traveling to red states to boost GOP candidates’ chances in the midterm elections as Democrats gain ground. Clemens has been a vocal Trump supporter for several years.
Clemens was a two-time World Series Champion with the New York Yankees and won seven Cy Young Awards, the highest honor for MLB pitchers, during his career. But he has also been mired in controversy over allegations of extramarital affairs and steroid use, which he has denied.
Trump recalled playing a round of golf with Clemens, during which he said, “It's a ridiculous thing that you're not in the Hall of Fame with that kind of a record.”
The president then said, “Forget about the Hall of Fame,” and announced that he was going to give him the Medal of Freedom — the highest civilian honor.
Trump then welcomed Clemens back on stage, and the former baseball player told a crowd of the president’s supporters that he was “stunned.”
“This supersedes anything that obviously I've done in my playing career, and to get it from this man, this president, there wouldn't be another president I'd want to get it from,” Clemens, who is now based in Texas, said, adding that Trump was a “winner” too.
“I can't thank you enough. That's a huge honor,” Clemens told the president.
Clemens will join the likes of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. and the Apollo 11 astronauts when he receives the Medal of Freedom.
Trump’s announcement comes more than a decade after Clemens’ former trainer, Brian McNamee, claimed that he injected Clemens multiple times with steroids and human growth hormones from 1998 through 2001.
It was also reported by the New York Daily News in 2008 that Clemens had a decade-long affair with the now-late country music star Mindy McCready.
Clemens has been married to his wife, Debbie, since the 1980s, and they have four children together.

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.
Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.
Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

New Delhi: India and the UK have agreed to explore ways to boost cross-border investment and Indian firms’ access to international capital, including through equity and bond listings via Gujarat International Finance Tec-City International Financial Services Centre (GIFT IFSC), according to a finance ministry statement. The agreement was part of the joint statement adopted after the fourth UK-India Financial Markets Dialogue, held in London on 29 September. The dialogue was led by senior officials from the finance ministry and HM Treasury, with participation from financial services regulatory authorities from India and the UK. The Indian participants included the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), Reserve Bank of India (RBI), International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA), Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai). The UK side included the Bank of England (BoE) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The finance ministry said participants exchanged updates on reforms in their respective jurisdictions and reaffirmed their shared ambition for sustainable economic growth, resilient and open financial markets, and increased bilateral trade and investment. The discussions covered capital markets, insurance and pensions, asset management and fintech. The finance ministry said Sebi shared how India is transforming global investor participation by streamlining market entry and operations, while RBI highlighted the significant ease of overseas access to sovereign and corporate debt. The participants discussed the growing role of GIFT IFSC in mobilizing international capital into India and agreed to continue regulatory cooperation and knowledge-sharing to support its development as an international financial centre, the ministry said. The two sides also agreed to identify priority areas to explore for future capital markets cooperation ahead of the next Economic and Financial Dialogue, according to the joint statement. The finance ministry said the UK outlined recent updates to its insurance regulatory framework as part of its Financial Services Growth and Competitiveness Strategy, as well as developments in its pensions and annuity markets. India outlined its ambitions to expand coverage, investment and market capacity, the ministry said. Both sides agreed on the importance of the Insurance and Pensions Workplan established in 2023 to support market development, bilateral trade and investment. The participants recognized the value of competitive and resilient markets, access to specialist expertise, diverse pools of capital and reinsurance capacity in managing complex risks and supporting long-term domestic development, according to the finance ministry. The two sides also discussed opportunities in reinsurance arising from India's evolving regulatory framework and from deeper cooperation between the London market and Indian insurers and reinsurers. Participants exchanged experiences on regulation, governance, coverage and long-term savings reform. They discussed measures to increase participation and support productive long-term investment and agreed to explore knowledge sharing in areas aligned with their domestic priorities, the ministry said. The UK set out work on its regulatory framework for alternative investment fund managers, while India provided an overview of key reforms undertaken by Sebi and the IFSCA. Both sides welcomed continued regulatory cooperation on asset management and discussed how mutual understanding of reforms, investor requirements and market conditions could support increased cross-border investment. The two sides also welcomed further internationalization of the Indian rupee and recognized London’s role as the leading offshore rupee trading hub, the ministry said. Participants discussed the importance of credible sustainable finance frameworks, high-quality disclosures, global standards and investor confidence in mobilizing private capital for the low-carbon and climate-resilient transition. The finance ministry said participants also reviewed progress under the India-UK Financial Partnership asset management workstream and recognized the value of industry evidence in identifying practical opportunities for deeper participation by the UK and Indian asset managers in each other’s markets. On fintech and innovation, India shared its experience on scaling fintech adoption and financial inclusion through digital public infrastructure, including digital identity, digital payments, central bank digital currencies and data exchange frameworks, according to the joint statement. Both sides agreed on the importance of supporting responsible innovation and competition without compromising regulatory oversight. They also exchanged perspectives on the potential opportunities and the risks of artificial intelligence in financial services and agreed on the value of continued bilateral exchange and coordination through relevant international fora. India shared its digital onboarding process for retail financial services and committed to further sharing its experiences, the finance ministry said. The two sides also noted risks posed by the criminal adoption of new technologies to financial crime, including the use of artificial intelligence to commit fraud on an industrial scale in so-called “scam compounds” operating in foreign countries, as well as risks to cybersecurity, data protection and operational resilience. Participants shared their experiences using technology and regulatory innovation to detect and prevent financial fraud and agreed to continue cooperation among the relevant authorities, according to the ministry. On cross-border payments, both sides reaffirmed their support for the G20 Roadmap for Enhancing Cross-Border Payments. They discussed practical priorities for reducing frictions, improving transparency and facilitating greater efficiency in cross-border payments aligned to the G20 Roadmap. The two sides also updated each other on developments in their retail payment infrastructures and recognised the work at the G20 to continue promoting interoperability and interlinkages among electronic payment infrastructures. The finance ministry said India and the UK welcomed the constructive discussions and reaffirmed the important role of the Financial Markets Dialogue in supporting their shared ambitions for sustainable growth, deeper trade and investment, and resilient financial markets. Both sides welcomed the contribution of the India-UK Financial Partnership in identifying practical and potential solutions to deepen financial services links. The participants also reflected on a strengthened relationship, particularly in the context of the launch of Vision 2035, and the importance of driving implementation of the UK-India Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, which entered into force on 15 July 2026, according to the joint statement. The two sides agreed to drive progress across the workstreams, with updates to be reviewed through the relevant bilateral mechanisms and at the next UK-India Economic and Financial Dialogue, the Ministry of Finance said. On September 30, Inc42 hosted the inaugural edition of the CTO Summit 2026 at JW Marriott, Bengaluru, bringing together 200+ senior technology leaders as delegates and speakers to discuss how India’s technology ecosystem is building and scaling in the AI era. The summit brought together CTOs, engineering, product, data, and AI leaders from India’s leading tech startups like Meesho, Swiggy, Flipkart, and Rapido for conversations around AI adoption, engineering productivity, infrastructure, architecture, and the systems needed to build at India’s scale. Across 10+ sessions, the discussions went beyond AI experimentation to examine what happens when the technology moves into production, from the economics of running AI workloads and the quality of data powering applications to verification, resilience, and the changing role of engineering teams. Speakers explored how AI is reshaping products and the way users interact with them. Swiggy’s CTO Madhusudhan Rao joined the summit to share his views on how the listed food delivery platform is using AI agents to take commerce beyond its app, while Flipkart CPTO Balaji Thiagarajan discussed the shift from keyword-led product discovery towards systems that can understand consumer intent. The conversations also moved into the engineering organisation itself. As AI-assisted coding increases the amount of software teams can generate, technology leaders discussed how design, review, testing, and verification are becoming increasingly important, while exploring how AI could make systems thinking more important as routine coding becomes increasingly automated. Building for India’s scale emerged as another key theme. Leaders discussed the challenges of building AI products for users across budget smartphones, multiple languages and patchy connectivity, while keeping infrastructure and inference costs under control. The conversation highlighted the need for technology teams to account for these constraints when designing AI systems for a market as diverse as India. The summit also featured three technical demos that offered a closer look at AI being applied in real-world systems. Dushyant Garg, lead, strategy & enterprise growth at Nugget (by Zomato), showcased how Zomato’s experience operating AI at India scale is being translated into enterprise systems through specialised agents, real-time intelligence and governance layers. Srivatsa Katta, CTO at Rapido, walked through how the company has adapted its engineering organisation and infrastructure for the AI era, including its use of coding agents, an LLM Gateway and AI Catalyst. Prabu Ram, SVP, Engineering at Razorpay, showcased Slash, the company’s autonomous engineering agent built to combine company context, connected tools and workflow triggers to execute engineering tasks. The summit also examined the infrastructure and data foundations behind these systems. Discussions around architecture focused on capacity planning, resilience and preparing for failures beyond a company’s own technology stack, while leaders from PhonePe Payment Gateway, OceanBase and Fibe discussed data quality, access controls and the need for reliable data foundations for AI applications. PhonePe Payment Gateway’s CTO Srijon Biswas shared how fintech is using AI across internal workflows, with more than 200 AI agents being used by around 1,600 employees daily. He discussed examples of AI-driven efficiency gains, including around 22 person-days saved per app release and audit processes that were reduced from four days to three minutes. As AI takes on more routine engineering work, Biswas said, “You need more people who can make stronger decisions and get them correct more often.” Oracle’s Palanivel Saravanan also underlined how companies are bringing AI models closer to their data. “Everybody is looking at how they can get the models much closer to their data, so that the model can learn better and respond to the user better,” said Saravanan. From AI agents and product discovery to engineering productivity, infrastructure resilience and data governance, the conversations reflected a technology ecosystem moving from asking whether AI should be adopted to figuring out how it can work reliably and economically at scale. But none of these conversations would have been possible without the support of our sponsors and partners, who helped bring the inaugural Inc42 CTO Summit to life. At the Inc42 CTO Summit 2026, PhonePe CTO Srijon Biswas joined Inc42 CEO and cofounder Vaibhav Vardhan for ‘How PhonePe Is Combining DPI And AI For 720 Mn+ Users’, where they discussed how the company is using AI to improve efficiency and build more personalised financial experiences at scale. Palanivel Saravanan, head of infrastructure cloud engineering at Oracle, participated in the session ‘The Architecture Of 10X: Engineering For India’s Next Scale Curve’, alongside Vikas Goyal, cofounder & CTO, Kuku; Noel Curtis, CTO, BookMyShow; and Prabu Ram, SVP, engineering, Razorpay.
