She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news on the midterms.
Ellen Allen has mixed feelings about the check from the U.S. Treasury and letter from President Trump that arrived at her house near Charleston, W.Va., on Monday.
"I just can't believe it; I mean, that's crazy," says Allen, who's the executive director of a small nonprofit called West Virginians for Affordable Health Care. She says, in her opinion, sending out these checks is a "political stunt."
NPR first spoke to Ellen Allen in the summer of 2025. She was 63 years old at the time and knew she needed coverage from Healthcare.gov even as generous federal subsidies for her premiums were ending. She has a serious eye condition and needs expensive drops to preserve her vision. She advocated for the Republican-controlled Congress to extend the subsidies. It didn't. She ended up using retirement savings to pay $1,967 every month for her premiums from January through August, 2026.
Then her birthday came; she turned 65 and was eligible for Medicare. "I was ready at midnight — the first day I could apply, I did," she laughs.
A second check on the way?
Allen chose traditional Medicare, which means she could soon be getting another check from the U.S. Treasury. Last week, President Trump announced that $90 checks will be sent to 20 million people enrolled in Medicare.
"The $90 is — I mean, that's just nothing," Allen says. In her work, she talks to people about healthcare costs all over West Virginia. "People aren't going to be fooled by this," she predicts. "People are hurting. People are feeling the cost of healthcare all year long."
"If they wanted to do something meaningful, they would work on affordable healthcare instead of just sending out checks every now and then," Allen says.
Both checks are directed to select groups. The $500 checks mailed by the Trump administration last week were only sent to people who live in one of the 30 states that use Healthcare.gov for their insurance marketplace. They also make more than $64,000 annually for an individual, which is too much money to qualify for subsidies. These are people, like Allen, who were likely to be hard hit when Congress failed to extend the extra financial help put in place under President Joe Biden.
The $90 checks that will be sent to Medicare beneficiaries are only going to certain people enrolled in Medicare Part B. People in Medicare Advantage plans, which are managed by insurance companies, will not get checks.
Can Trump do that?
The checks are hitting people's mailboxes just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The text of a letter sent along with the money touts the Trump administration's efforts on health policy and criticizes the Biden administration.
"This reads like electioneering," says Kathleen Clark, professor of legal and governmental ethics at Washington University law school in St. Louis, Mo. "This reads as though it's intended to influence votes. That is prohibited by law."
Specifically, it would violate the Hatch Act, "the statute that prohibits using federal power and money to influence partisan political elections," she explains. It may also be a use of funds that's unauthorized by Congress.
The money for Healthcare.gov enrollees is from fees insurance companies paid to participate in the marketplace, and the money for Medicare beneficiaries is from a general improvement fund. Neither of these funds has been used for direct payments to enrollees before.
"It looks like a pretty desperate effort to, in essence, bribe the recipients of this letter to vote in gratitude to Trump in the upcoming midterm elections," she adds.
An empowered executive branch
The checks and letters are arriving in people's mailboxes, whether they're legal or not. Clark notes the Supreme Court has enabled Trump's illegal actions many times in the past. "So, of course, he feels empowered to go ahead and do this," she says.
The White House did not respond directly to NPR's questions about electioneering, whether the action is a violation of the Hatch Act or if it is a "political stunt," as Allen put it.
"This is an out-of-touch criticism," Trump administration spokeswoman Allison Schuster wrote in an email. "Americans were overcharged for the operation of the Obamacare exchange, and President Trump returned their hard-earned money. This President will never stop enabling Americans to take control of their health by implementing policies that put money back in their pockets."
'Half a tank of gas'
Some Republicans in recent years have advocated for giving more money directly to people rather than to health insurance companies, although the party has yet to settle on a particular approach.
In any case, sending these checks is unrelated to that effort, says Joseph Antos, senior fellow emeritus at the conservative think tank American Enterprise Institute. There's nothing that requires people to use this money for their health.
"From the perspective of the average senior citizen, when they get a $90 check, it's money," he adds, referencing the forthcoming checks for Medicare beneficiaries. "You can go out to McDonald's and buy probably two hamburgers and a shake for $90 [and] maybe buy a half a tank of gas."
A widening trust gap, poll says
A few weeks from the midterm elections, voters say they are struggling with health costs and want candidates to address them, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonprofit health research organization KFF.
"The cost of healthcare is what's going to be front of mind as they're casting their votes in November," says Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology for KFF. "And what we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all voters on which party voters trust to handle healthcare, but they also have the advantage among independent voters, and that's a really important voting bloc for midterm elections."
She says there is "a widening gap" between the Democratic Party and Republicans when it comes to which party voters trust to handle health costs. "It was just a 10-point margin back in April, and now we're seeing it to be a 20-point margin," she says. The poll found 22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42% who trust Democrats.
Where's the credit for GOP candidates?
Antos, of AEI, calls the Trump administration's decision to send out these checks "inexplicable." He describes the move as politically strange, since a Republican administration that disparages Obamacare is investing more money into it, and "unreasonable from a fiscal standpoint," because of the growing national debt.
He also notes that most Americans won't be getting these checks. "How about the average, lower-income worker who has employer coverage?" he asks. "They're not getting anything. Why is that? Is that fair?"
He is doubtful the move will have a political benefit for Republican candidates. "For one thing, Trump is not saying that your local congressman did this for you, Trump is saying he did it for you," Antos says. "I don't get it, and I don't see any advantage to anybody, including Donald Trump."
Despite her mixed feelings, Ellen Allen of West Virginians for Affordable Health Care is planning to deposit the $500 check she just received. "I'm not going to send it back," she says. "I'm going to put it in my health savings account and keep working towards healthcare for all."

The first Atlantic hurricane of the season is forecast to reach the US Gulf Coast Friday, threatening damaging winds, flooding and potential disruptions to energy production after an otherwise quiet storm season for the region.
Tropical Storm Isaias is expected to grow into a strong Category 2 hurricane in the coming days, with top winds of 110 miles per hour, the US National Hurricane Center said in an 11 a.m. New York time advisory. The current forecast takes the storm well east of major oil platforms and natural gas pipelines off the coast of Louisiana and Texas.
That track is partly based on guidance from newer, AI-enabled storm models. But more conventional models, typically based on physics equations, have shown the system tacking toward eastern Louisiana, said Brian McNoldy, a hurricane researcher at the University of Miami. That trajectory would put the storm closer to energy assets near New Orleans.
“There’s a little bit of wiggle room,” McNoldy said.
Risk modeler Chuck Watson of Enki Research said in a blog post Wednesday morning that effects from Isaias could extend eastward to Pensacola, Florida, and Eglin Air Force base in the western Florida panhandle before the storm collapses. If that comes to pass, Watson said potential damages and economic impacts could exceed $6 billion.
The storm is poised to undergo rapid intensification in the next day or so as it runs through near-record-warm water and moist air. Though the storm could weaken again before landfall, NHC forecaster Eric Blake wrote Wednesday that it will likely grow in size — putting more communities in the path of damaging winds and rains.
Isaias arrives at a precarious time for oil markets. Amid strain from the war in Iran, there’s little cushion for disruptions to diesel production, the workhorse fuel used by trucks, trains, industry and for heating. A shift westward could bring more offshore production and Gulf Coast energy infrastructure into the storm’s path.
As of late Wednesday morning, hurricane watches and storm surge alerts had been posted from Mississippi to Florida. As much as 7 feet of water could push inland on top of high tide, the center said.
Chevron Corp. is evacuating non-essential personnel from its Gulf platforms as a precaution. No changes to production or operations are expected at this time, the company said.
As of Tuesday, roughly 9.24% of Gulf oil production and 3.36% of natural gas production had been shut in ahead of the storm, according to data published by the federal Marine Minerals Administration.
Forecasters have warned that the risk of damaging winds is rising along the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. Heavy rains are expected to extend for miles, bringing a threat of urban flooding and isolated river flooding in the US Southeast.
Isaias was situated 540 miles south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River Wednesday morning. By Thursday, it’s expected to grow into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season — a milestone normally reached in the second week of August.
This Atlantic season has lagged well behind the usual pace, with eight named storms, none of which became hurricanes. By early October, an average season typically has produced about 11 named storms, including five hurricanes and two major hurricanes.
Strengthening El Niño conditions have increased wind shear that helped suppress activity across the basin. Shear occurs when winds change speed or direction at different altitudes, disrupting a storm’s structure.

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Kenya's Health Ministry on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) confirmed the country's first imported Ebola case from Congo.
Health Minister Aden Duale said a Kenyan citizen who arrived in the country on Saturday (October 3, 2026) from Congo, via Uganda, had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital.
The patient tested positive for the Ebola virus after developing symptoms associated with haemorrhagic fever. The patient died late on Monday (October 5, 2026) while receiving treatment.
Health authorities have placed the country on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Mr. Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who had cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers who had travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced.
The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days, and will be released after testing negative for the virus, Patrick Amoth, the Ministry's Director, said. The patient will be buried within 24 hours, in accordance with recommended public safety protocols.
Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda recorded 20 cases, and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August.
This is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned it could become the deadliest, as it continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.
The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Vaccine and treatment trials are under way in Congo's Ituri province, the outbreak's epicentre.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Chief Minister Mohan Yadav has said that Madhya Pradesh is the only state in the country where deities are offered liquor and where tigers and cows drink water from the same river.
Speaking on the inaugural day of the four-day 7th edition of the Madhya Pradesh Travel Mart (MPTM 2026) at the Kushabhau Thakre International Convention Centre (Minto Hall) on Wednesday, he highlighted the state's cultural heritage and wildlife conservation efforts.
Reflecting on conservation milestones, he credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision for reintroducing the cheetah to India decades after its extinction, adding that he had just returned from releasing cheetahs into their third habitat in the state.
“In four months, we will launch India's largest pumped hydro storage facility, located near the Gandhi Sagar Dam in the Mandsaur-Neemuch region of MP, which falls within the broader Chambal River basin,” Yadav announced.
During the event, 12 strategic MoUs and agreements were signed, covering skill development, rural and adventure tourism, film and media promotion, smart tourism, and heritage conservation.
A historic Rs 848.40 crore mega-investment agreement was inked between the MP Tourism Board and M/s ARM Foods Pvt Ltd to construct an international-standard golf course, golf villas, a wellness resort, and a luxury hotel at Ramgarh in Sehore district.
The flagship project is expected to generate 920 direct jobs along with hundreds of indirect opportunities.
Letters of Award totalling Rs 252 crore were formally handed over for 14 major projects, including hotels, wellness resorts, luxury tented camps, eco-tourism units, and wayside amenities across three key tourism highways. A new MP Tourism website and a coffee table book were launched.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) held talks with Cote d'Ivoire's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Niale Kaba on strengthening bilateral ties, with a focus on trade, infrastructure, agriculture and healthcare.
The Minister arrived in Cote d'Ivoire from Ghana on the second leg of his three-nation tour of African countries, which also includes Ethiopia.
Mr. Jaishankar said he had "comprehensive discussions" with Kaba in Abidjan on advancing India-Cote d'Ivoire partnership, "including in trade, investment, infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare and people-to-people ties".
"Underlined that our people-centric cooperation will be driven by the priorities of Cote d'Ivoire," he said in a social media post.
The two sides also discussed deepening their engagement in multilateral fora, he said.
Earlier, in Ghana, Jaishankar received from Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa the country's Instrument of Acceptance for the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA).
IBCA is an India-led global initiative aimed at conserving seven major big cat species — tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma — and their habitats.
India launched the IBCA in 2023 to mark the 50th anniversary of Project Tiger.
The alliance seeks to bring together countries that are home to big cats as well as others interested in supporting their conservation, with cooperation envisaged in areas such as research, knowledge-sharing, capacity building and wildlife management.
Mr. Jaishankar also paid tribute at the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial in Accra, honouring Ghana's first Prime Minister and later president Kwame Nkrumah, a key figure in Africa's independence movement and one of the leading advocates of pan-Africanism.
Nkrumah, who led Ghana to independence from British colonial rule in 1957, played a prominent role in promoting solidarity among newly independent Asian and African countries.
He was also closely associated with the Non-Aligned Movement and the broader idea of South-South cooperation.

Drones sank two cargo ships and damaged a third in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries for the first time, killing at least two sailors. The attacks represent a notable escalation as Black Sea commercial shipping has increasingly come under attack during the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with Russia also being accused of carrying out “hybrid warfare” incidents across Europe.
The Togo-flagged cargo ship Alfa Watan sank, and the Palau-flagged cargo ship Able was set ablaze after being attacked by multiple sea and aerial drones about 80 miles (128 kilometers) off the coast of Bulgaria on October 6, according to the Associated Press. In an interview, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described the incidents as “an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone” and “a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”
The fate of the Alfa Watan’s crew was not immediately known after the vessel sank. A Bulgarian ferry managed to evacuate the 18 crew members of the Able, with two severely injured mariners being flown to a hospital in the city of Varna.
This comes one day after drones struck the Turkish-owned cargo ship named Royad Mammadov within Romania’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on October 5. That ship caught fire and eventually sank, with 11 crew members rescued by Romanian ships and helicopters while one crew member remains missing, according to Euronews. Two crew members were killed.
European Union president Ursula von der Leyen described the drone strikes on the three vessels in the Black Sea as “increasingly concerning” in a post on X. But she also cautioned that the circumstances of the attacks are “still being established” without naming a probable attacker.
“Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable,” Leyen wrote. “We stand in full solidarity with our Member States on the Eastern flank.”
By contrast, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described a joint investigation with Bulgaria’s navy as finding that the latest strikes represented a “Russian combined attack using both sea and aerial drones,” Reuters reported. Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine’s military was not conducting operations in that part of the Black Sea.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) asked the Centre to consider a representation a petition seeking standard operating procedures for police and rapid action force personnel to use ‘always-on’ body-worn cameras during crowd-control and protest-management duties.
The court asked the government to communicate its decision to the petitioner within six months, while disposing of the public interest litigation (PIL).
The court was hearing the PIL, filed by advocate Chahat Raghav, seeking direction for constitution of an expert committee to formulate a binding SOP, making the use of body-worn cameras mandatory and continuous (always-on) for every member of Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force deployed on crowd-control, protest-management or dispersal duty, from the commencement of deployment until stand-down.
The plea also sought a comprehensive regime governing the storage, integrity, retention and evidentiary use of footage recorded through such cameras.
During the hearing, the court asked how the absence of body-worn cameras affects the rights of public at large.
To this, senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing the petitioner, said when violence occurs there are allegations and counter allegations of violence and the issue pertains to accountability as to who is perpetrating violence and the use of excessive force by police.
He said there has to be some way for fixing the accountability.
Mr Sibal said cameras are being used by police officials but they are used in a very sporadic way. He said use of cameras was essential because allegations of excessive force used by police or protestors running and doing violence keep surfacing.
“We need a system so that the allegations are not left to private persons who are videographing,” Mr Sibal added.
Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma submitted that there were guidelines for organising protests in which videography aspect was taken care of.
The petitioner said the plea has been filed in the backdrop of the July protests at Jantar Mantar involving the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk.
The plea said in the July protests, the use of force by Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force (RAF) upon student protesters was documented almost entirely through unofficial mobile-phone footage recorded by bystanders.

The story so far
The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.
A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.
And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?
It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.
Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?
A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.
This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?
Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water
Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities
Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic meningoencephalitis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?
To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.
Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

CrowdStrike says China-based suspect used AI tools in South Korean bank hacks
SEOUL: The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea's financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China's Guangdong province who used a Chinese-developed AI agent tool called ARTEX and Anthropic's ClaudeCode, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said.
In a report published on Wednesday (Oct 7), CrowdStrike said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analysing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign targeting South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October.
The case is likely to intensify concerns over the rise of AI agents and whether organisations are prepared to defend their systems against them.
Australia said last month that an OpenAI autonomous agent breached a government health statistics portal in June, marking one of the first known instances of an AI agent hacking a government system.
CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models such as Claude.
"While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated," it said.
"This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts."
BANK HACKS
CrowdStrike said the individual also asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and sought assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups.
In another session, the person also asked Claude to create a security researcher resume, which included details such as a Telegram account, age, educational background and a location in Maoming, a city in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, which CrowdStrike said likely belonged to the attacker.
A man who answered a phone number provided by CrowdStrike in its report said he had no knowledge of the matter.
Anthropic, South Korean police and China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
ARTEX is an open-source AI agent for automated penetration testing that was published on GitHub this year by a Chinese security engineer with the handle Autumn. It is not a standalone large language model but connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in networks.
The tool’s GitHub page says it is intended for personal learning, code research and local technical verification and should not be used to conduct real-world testing against online systems or websites.
At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or have been reported by local media as having been targeted by cyberattacks since late September, prompting South Korean police to launch a probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures.
Shinhan Bank said last week that the personal information of about 25,000 of its customers was compromised, while KB Kookmin Bank said that the personal information of 119 of its customers was leaked.

In a significant move aimed at reforming the language used in cases involving custody of a child between couples in conflict, the High Court of Karnataka has directed all family courts and courts dealing with guardians and wards (G&WC) cases henceforth to use the term “parenting time” instead of “visitation,” observing that no parent should be treated as a mere “visitor” in a child’s life.
Justice Lalitha Kanneganti, who was hearing a child custody case, issued the direction while pointing out that it is time for a small change in the language employed in judicial proceedings.
Pointing out that courts often use the word “visitation” to describe the time the child spends with a parent, who is a non-custodial parent, the court said that the word “visitation” is familiar, but “it carries an unfortunate suggestion that one parent is part of the child’s life while the other merely visits.”
“A child should not be made to understand the relationship through the word visitation, which is used for someone who arrives and leaves as a guest. Children read the conduct of adults and sometimes the words of courts to understand where they belong. Calling it parenting time recognises a simple truth that no parent is a visitor in the life of a child,” the court said.
Though a change in terminology does not decide questions of custody, when a court imposes restrictions on the access to the child, the word “parenting” is more humane, Justice Kanneganti said.
Also, the High Court directed the Registrar of General to issue a circular to all courts in this regard on the use of “parenting time” while also directing that even in the applications for child’s custody the word “parenting time” should be used instead of “visitation.”

Relative humidity is a simple concept as weather phenomena go – but it has significant, far-reaching consequences for how we must take care of ourselves on a hot or wet day.
Letting the wind flow freely is the secret to cooling our cities
Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3. The second is specific humidity, equal to the mass of the moisture divided by the mass of air. It is expressed as a dimensionless number (but sometimes also as grams per kilogram, among other similar units.)
The third way is relative humidity: it is important because it factors in the amount of vapour that air can hold at different temperatures. Determining its value is a bit more complicated: it is the vapour density of the air divided by the saturation vapour density at the dry-bulb temperature.
Why does relative humidity matter?
On a hot day, our body uses sweat to cool itself. Sweat is released via our skin to the surface. There, the liquid evaporates. When water changes phase from liquid to vapour, it absorbs heat from the surface on which it lies. So when sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat from the skin, cooling it.
The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more. This means that the sweat on your skin can’t evaporate. At the same time, the body keeps sweating because it is still expecting to cool itself.
As a result, if the relative humidity is high, you can sweat on a hot day even when you are sitting still – while your body also keeps accumulating heat. This can quickly become dangerous.
A relative humidity of 30-60% is generally considered to be comfortable. Environments that have lower levels than this typically use humidifiers to increase the humidity. When the level is higher, a fan will help move the air around you and help sweat evaporate better.
In both cases, drinking water is important.
What does relative humidity imply physically?
Warmer air can hold more moisture than cooler air. So at the same absolute humidity, the relative humidity of warmer air will be lower than that of cooler air. It is like saying two vessels can hold the same amount of water – just that the bigger vessel will be less full than the smaller vessel.
This is why, for example, while Chennai had an absolute humidity of 70% at 2.30 pm on April 23, its relative humidity was lower, around 60%, because it had an ambient temperature of 32 C.
The change in the capacity for moisture as the air warms is also non-linear, meaning it doesn’t increase by the same amount as the air warms. For example, the difference as it warms over 20º C from -20º C to 0º C is small, but there is an enormous improvement in its vapour-carrying capacity as it warms over 20º C from 30º C to 50º C.
How do you measure relative humidity?
There are a few ways to measure relative humidity. One is to conduct a simple experiment with household items; another is to use maths; a third is to use an app or device.
Experiment
For the experiment, you need two mercury thermometers, some cotton, rubber bands, and access to cold water.
First, make sure both thermometers show the same reading, say, under a fan. Next, soak some cotton in cold water and wrap it around the bulb of one of the thermometers with a rubber band. Hold this thermometer under the fan, such that water from the cotton evaporates, and record the thermometer reading after five minutes. Hold up the other thermometer in the air and record its reading after five minutes. You will thus have the wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures, respectively.
Next, subtract the wet-bulb temperature from the dry-bulb temperature to get the temperature difference. Finally, use the relative humidity chart (see below) to get the relative humidity value. For example, if the difference was 6 C and the dry-bulb temperature was 28 C, the relative humidity would have been 59%.
A psychrometer is a device that has two such thermometers plus a chart to get the final reading. Modern, electronic psychrometers can calculate the relative humidity directly.
For a rough sense, the lower the wet-bulb temperature, the drier the air is, and the less relatively humid it is.
Mathematics
There are two mathematical ways (among others) to estimate the relative humidity, one simpler and one a bit more involved.
The first way is to divide the actual vapour pressure by the saturated vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is the amount of moisture that air contains. The ‘saturated’ value is the maximum possible amount. The formula (below) requires the dew point (Td), which you can obtain from a weather website.
RH = (e/es)*100
e = 6.11 x 10((7.5 x Td)/(237.3 + Td))
For es, use the same formula but replace Td with T, the actual temperature.
The second way is to calculate relative humidity starting from the specific humidity, pressure and temperature, using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
App
If you prefer software: Search for “hygrometer” in your phone’s app store to locate some options. (A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity.) Note that the app will only work if your phone has a sensor that can sense humidity.
If you like hardware, psychrometers and devices called hygrometers are available in physical as well as online stores.
Why does the wet-bulb temperature matter?
This said, a more direct way to understand the implications of the relative humidity for your wellbeing is in the form of the wet-bulb temperature (a.k.a. the adiabatic saturation temperature). It is the lowest temperature a surface – like your skin – can reach when water evaporates from it. The wet-bulb temperature is equal to the dry-bulb temperature when the relative humidity is 100%.
A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
The climate crisis is rendering heatwaves more common, more frequent, more spread out, and more potent over the Indian subcontinent. As a study published in May 2022 put it:
“Whether today’s most impactful heatwaves could have occurred in a pre-industrial climate, traditionally a central focus of attribution research, is fast becoming an obsolete question. The next frontier for attribution science is to inform adaptation decision-making in the face of unprecedented future heat.”
One way to adapt is to keep an eye on the relative humidity, drink lots of water, and cool yourself.

- The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more.
- A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)

Amid increasing state-sanctioned censorship of digital content across platforms like Meta and X, activists, journalists, cartoonists, artists, opposition politicians and others critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government and its policies have faced sweeping content restrictions and takedowns in the last few months. The latest to face such censorship are those raising concerns over the establishment of large-scale data centres in Visakhapatnam.
The port city in Andhra Pradesh is witnessing a massive digital infrastructure push, with investments of up to ₹1.25 lakh crore planned over five years (2026–30) and more than 2,000 acres of land earmarked for data centre projects. In October last year, Google and Adani formally announced an AI hub project in Visakhapatnam. By December 2025, 308 acres at Tarluvada, 120 acres at Adavivaram and 160 acres at Rambilli had been identified for the project. In January this year, reports indicated a much larger expansion involving Google, Sify, Reliance and CtrlS.
In April, the state government and Google laid the foundation stone for the Google Cloud India AI Hub at Tarluvada village. The facility, spread across 266.6 acres, is expected to draw 1 GW of power and is reportedly Google’s largest data centre outside the United States.
The projects are expected to make Visakhapatnam a major eastern data and subsea-cable hub, providing direct routes for Indian data to the US, South Africa, Singapore and Australia. Officials say this could reduce reliance on existing routes through Chennai, Kochi and the Red Sea, while shifting high-value technology activity from expensive metros to other cities.
But local influencers and journalists have raised concerns about the environmental and ecological impact of this rapid expansion of data centre infrastructure in Visakhapatnam and beyond.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Why the Data Centres are being Opposed
The Stop Dirty Data Centre campaign, led by over 60 individuals, formed to “oppose the setting up of 6.5 GW of AI data centres”, lists over 10 proposed data centres spanning across over 2,500 acres of land in Visakhapatnam. Besides the Tarluvada facility, the list mentions two other major Google-Adani Hyperscale data centers: At Rambilli village consuming 1 GW of power across 174.8 acres, and at Adavivaram-Mudasarlova consuming 512 MW of power across 165.40 acres of land. All three are currently under-construction.
It is important to note that Adavivaram-Mudasarlova is around 120 metres from the Mudasarlova reservoir — a critical drinking water source for the city; it also lies near the Kailasagiri-Kambalakonda forest landscape. The Tarluvada site is located 1.53 km from the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary and about 450 metres from its notified Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) while the Rambilli site lies on the Anakapalli coast and is surrounded by forests.
As most of these sites lie on coastal regions, close to wildlife sanctuaries, forest areas and ESZs, opponents of this expansion project have flagged the disproportionate energy and land usage, large-scale hill cutting, deforestation, and further water depletion in an already water-scarce zone — Visakhapatnam’s water demand already exceeds supply by around 70 million litres per day. They also cite the massive impact on climate, biodiversity, wildlife sanctuaries, coastal ecosystems, and residential areas as serious detrimental effects.
“If fully built, the proposed AI data centers capacity could consume as much as the entire electricity currently used by the state of Andhra Pradesh,” states the campaign website. “Vizag is already severely water stressed and cooling these data centers could take up almost half of city’s supply based on estimates; the proposed land allocation is roughly equivalent to more than 700 cricket grounds, and is present in eco-sensitive regions; hyperscale AI facilities can significantly increase regional greenhouse gas emissions through backup Diesel Generator (DG) sets, solid waste, and more,” it adds.
Critics also highlighted the lack of transparency and public awareness around the setting up of these data centres, demanding that these projects be undertaken in consultation with locals and not unilaterally by the state and corporations. “In a brazen act of environmental lawlessness, forest land at the site [for the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova data centre] was cleared by the project proponent over several months even before environmental clearance was obtained,” alleges a petition initiated by the campaigners.
Citizen Movement Flagging Environmental Concerns Blocked
Against this backdrop, on September 19, the Instagram account of the Stop Vizag Data Centre campaign was banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
One of the founders, Deeksha Vanguru, told Alt News that they did not receive any prior notification. While the account was restored on September 27, nine of their posts critical of the data centre expansion, which were restricted over the last two months, remain unavailable in India.
“Our page was apparently blocked due to a local government request, we appealed to Meta and it was restored due to that request being either expired or reversed. However, our reach has been affected and posts are getting shadowbanned. We had to open a backup account in the meanwhile because we did not want to stop our fight. We are still fighting for the restoration of our nine posts,” Vanguru said.
“We started this as a citizen group in July this year. Most of us are born and brought up in Visakhapatnam and we couldn’t sit and watch the destruction of our home. We wanted to ensure that voices of the farmers, fishermen, villagers, and common citizens are heard. Initially, there was a small-scale mobilisation of citizens, but it needed more youth anger, therefore we turned the campaign into a social media project,” she added.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
“A big concern around AI data centres globally is the consumption of fresh water, and India is already going into a phase of water scarcity. The 10 data centres together are going to consume 200 MLD of water, which is 50% of the city’s daily water supply. The DGs will require constant air conditioning because they claim to be using advanced air cooling, thus the energy strain on the grid will be extremely high. Due to the constant running of generators and ACs, there could be overheating. The whole thing is going to be concrete, which will increase the land surface temperature and reduce night-time cooling. The average night-time temperature in Visakhapatnam has alreadt gone from 23-24 degrees to around 28 degrees,” she said.
Vanguru alleged there was no transparency while these data centres were being set up.
“The government hasn’t held any public consultation with either the farmers or the people of Vizag living close to these sites. In fact, environmental clearances for a 600-acre project, now broken up to escape scrutiny, was given within nine days. On April 9, the environmental clearance request was filed and it was received on April 18. There was no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) because these projects haven’t been categorised as Category A projects (considered to have greater potential environmental impacts and are appraised by the Union environment ministry and require an EIA) but as Category B2 projects, which means buildings and construction. The way the government has gone about this is as if they’re building malls,” she said.
Further, Vanguru claimed that these data centres had nearly nothing to offer to the locals, even in terms of job creation, which she said was one of the upsides of an industrial construction. “When we checked the environmental clearances, the number of permanent jobs being created was only 1,725. The rest are all construction jobs and temporary jobs. These temporary and construction jobs are being positioned as skilled jobs, but in India, the government definition of skilled means blue-collar jobs. So it keeps people in the same worker or employee cycle and doesn’t really help uplift people from poverty,” she added.
Original Reportage on Dalit Displacement Blocked
After the Tarluvada data centre’s construction began, independent journalists Shamsheer Yousaf and Monica Jha began reporting the ground realities of the construction in early January, as part of the Dirty Data project undertaken by the Environmental Reporting Collective (ERC).
A 2-minute long Instagram reel posted by ERC in collaboration with Yousaf, which features interviews of Dalit farmers in the village who are faced with imminent displacement, was blocked in India on May 22 under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act with no prior notice. In the reel, which garnered 2.6 million views and 46,000 shares, several farmers say that they were granted the land over 50 years ago by the Congress government and have since cleared forests to build homes and farms, which is their only form of subsistence — all under threat as the same land has been allocated to the Google-Adani data centre.
View this post on Instagram
The reel formed part of a 5-minute-long video published on Dirty Data’s website alongside the report, ‘As data centers arrive, India’s poorest face displacement, health risks’ by Yousaf and Jha. Yousaf wrote to the Union ministry of electronics & information technology (MeitY), seeking the blocking order, reasons for the action, restoration of the reel and a personal hearing in order to appeal or respond. He also wrote to Meta’s grievance officer in India.
ALSO READ: Meta restricts posts by Indian Youth Congress, AAP, Opposition leader
Upon not receiving any response from either authorities, on June 30, Yousaf and Jha moved the Delhi high court with a writ petition. A month later on July 23, the petitioners were given access to the blocking order which revealed the authority behind the restriction as the director general of police (DGP), CID, Andhra Pradesh.
‘Procedural Lapses, Unconstitutional Takedown’
In a report, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), whose lawyers are representing the petitioners, highlighted certain procedural lapses in the blocking order and claimed that the takedown was “unconstitutional”. The order names one Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, alleging that the video “spread misinformation” against him. However, this individual does not feature anywhere in the reel or any of the journalists’ reportage on the data centre issue; he is also not known to either of them.
IFF had then sent a legal notice to the principal secretary, home department and the DGP-CID, Andhra Pradesh, flagging this discrepancy and violation of the provision of the IT Rules, 2021. “…there have been several procedural lapses which violated Rule 14 of the IT Rules, 2021..the Petitioners were not served with any notice…never afforded an opportunity to submit a response/defend themselves…provided with a copy of the blocking order…[the takedown] directly affected [the petitioners] right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution,” the report read.
On September 10, the reel was restored. Yousaf found out through a notification this time, that the restriction was lifted as the “local legal requirement or government request that has now expired or been reversed” — similar to Vanguru’s case.
Local Influencers, HRF Silenced
In the same vein, several local influencers reported that their reels critical of the data centres were being arbitrarily taken down. Malla Gnanesh, who runs the page @vizag_blogger, told News Meter, that a reel he posted on May 28 titled ‘Vizag Welcoming Google Data Centre — At What Cost?’ was restricted in India on May 31. In the reel, Gnanesh spoke about the massive loss of green cover due to the construction of the data centre at the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova region.
Another account, @vizagmowa, also posted a reel on the negative environmental impact of the same data centre such as massive deforestation and water depletion due to its proximity to the Mudasarlova reservoir. This reel was withheld in India on May 30 with the same Section 79(3)(b) notification. Both reels remain restricted till date.
Human Rights Forum on June 1 published a statement condemning the rampant restrictions. Four of HRF’s own Instagram posts were blocked in India on May 31 and June 25, again under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
Speaking to Alt News, Vijayawada state coordinator of HRF, Rohith Gutta, stated: “We have moved the Andhra Pradesh high court with a writ petition against the unlawful restriction on September 28, demanding the blocking order, the reason for the action and the immediate restoration of our posts,” he said.

He mentioned that all four posts were critical of the date centre expansion. The two posts blocked on May 31 publicised an online petition seeking transparency and accountability regarding the proposed data centre projects; demanded an immediate stoppage of all ongoing site activities at the proposed sites in Adavivaram and Mudasarlova villages of Visakhapatnam Rural mandal.
The next two blocked on June 25 showed a protest in the city against the construction of all three data centres; questioned how the Adavivaram data centre received environmental clearance despite being located within an ESZ, close to the Mudasarlova reservoir. One of the these posts directly asked: “Should a Resource-Guzzling, Intensely Polluting Data Center be Located near a Reservoir? On its Catchment?”
“The restrictions imposed on HRF content by Instagram do not appear to be isolated incidents but form part of a broader pattern,” the Forum wrote while highlighting the restrictions imposed on Yousaf and Jha’s work with the ERC. The Forum also put out another statement condemning the restriction of the Stop Vizag Data Centers account.
Speaking about the ordeal, Rohith told Alt News, “The restrictions have not deterred us from speaking up against the data centres, however, it is a painful experience. We received no prior notification all four times and when we searched for the reason, it was only a vague message repeated word for word four times. It feels like you are legally violated because your work is banned without explanation. Now, blocking of posts is akin to being arrested digitally. We are living through times of ‘social media arrest’ and they [the authorities] have blocked all means to fight it.”
Alt News has reached out to Meta’s grievance officer in India and Kumar Vishwajeet, the principal secretary, home, Andhra Pradesh government. This article will be updated if and when we receive a response.
It is worth noting that the opposition to the projects has also spilled onto the streets, with residents, activists and environmental groups staging protests in Visakhapatnam over concerns around water consumption, deforestation, displacement and the environmental impact of the projects.

Australia opener Travis Head has taken to task former Test players turned critics whom he accused on Wednesday of “putting a bullet” through the current team, which starts the first Test against South Africa in Durban on Friday.
Head did not single out any pundit directly, but his strong remarks at a press conference came the day after Matthew Hayden, one-time holder of the record for the most runs in a Test innings, accused selectors of “promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket”.
The reference, made in a podcast, was about the recall of Nic Maddinson, who has been out of Test cricket for nearly 10 years but who joined the squad in South Africa after Josh Inglis fractured his finger and Cameron Green suffered a stomach injury.
READ: The focus on developing red-ball skills, says India U-19 coach Yere Goud
“I think it’s unfairly judged a fair bit from a group of past players, pretty much that put the bullet through a lot of players, which I think is unfair,” Head said.
“But that’s what they’re paid to do. Some of them need a job, so they go after us, and that’s totally fine.
“This group is strong enough to deal with those sorts of things. That’s how it is. It’s unfortunate sometimes to have some of that feedback from a generation of players that we have huge respect for, but that’s the caper.”
Selectors accused of disrespecting cricket
Hayden accused the selectors of “disrespecting first-class cricket”, asserting that batters should have an average of 45 runs or more before being considered for Test selection.
But Head praised Maddinson’s abilities and the benefits of choosing experienced players for Test cricket despite the 34-year-old replacement having a first-class average of 37.11.
“We need mature guys that know what they need to be doing,” Head said. “And I think that revolves back to why we’ve been so good over a period of time and why Australian cricket was so good back then in that era, because you’d bring in the Mike Husseys of the world, who are 30, who are tried and tested and know what they need to do.”
Former Australia captain Allan Border suggested that the 32-year-old Head would face his toughest test as an opener against the South African bowling attack and would perhaps be better batting at number five.
“I have laughed at a fair bit of it because if a traditional opening batter had pushed out the same sort of numbers in his first 20 innings, I think he’d be pretty safe and not talked about in the way that it has been talked about,” Head said. “It’s a lot of headline stuff.”

While the funding trends in the Indian startup ecosystem have been showing signs of stability over the past few months, investor appetite for startups operating across different sectors and stages is varying significantly. Although Indian startup funding in the July-September quarter increased 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn across 210 deals, the startup investment story is increasingly turning into one of growth stage capital rather than late stage backing. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, capital deployed at the growth stage jumped 46% YoY to $1.1 Bn during the quarter. Meanwhile, funding lapped by late stage startups remained flat at $994 Mn. Beyond the headline funding numbers, investors seemed to be more active in evaluating startups at the Series B and C stages as compared to late stage ones. During the quarter, growth stage deal count rose 38% to YoY 90, whereas late stage deals declined 10% to 27. The divergence is also visible in cheque sizes. The median growth stage ticket size rose 4% to $8.3 Mn, while the median late stage check dropped 18% to $18 Mn. The data points to a funding market where capital is flowing more readily into startups that still have substantial growth ahead, while investors are becoming more cautious about committing large sums to mature startups. Investors highlighted a combination of factors behind this shift, including a growing pool of early stage capital, more inflated valuations at the late stage, greater scrutiny of business fundamentals and exit visibility, and a changing sector thesis. Why More Capital Is Flowing Into Growth Stage Startups One explanation lies in the expansion of India’s startup ecosystem, which now comprises about 2.5 Lakh businesses. A growing pool of investors backing startups at their earliest stages is creating a larger pipeline of businesses seeking subsequent rounds. Vikram Gupta, founder and managing partner at IvyCap Ventures, said the number of early stage and micro VC funds in India has increased substantially, helping create this pipeline of capital as startups progress towards Series A and Series B rounds. “If the number of early stage funds has increased, very naturally you will see a growth in the early to growth stage investments,” Gupta said. The changing sector mix is also reinforcing this trend, with investor interest broadening beyond ecommerce, fintech and consumer internet startups towards frontier technologies such as AI, deeptech and cleantech. AI emerged as the top funded sector in Q3 with $438 Mn, up 265% YoY, followed by cleantech at $433 Mn, up 267%, and deeptech at $290 Mn, up 176%. In contrast, fintech funding declined 11% and ecommerce funding fell 31%. The quarter also saw some of the largest funding rounds concentrated in these newer categories. AI startup Emergent raised $130 Mn, EV startup River raised $120 Mn and spacetech startup Pixxel raised $100 Mn. Gupta said the newer sectors — AI, spacetech, EVs — have longer gestation periods, meaning investors often wait for technology validation, customer adoption and other milestones before committing larger sums. However, the growth of these newer segments doesn’t necessarily translate into investors shying away from more established segments like fintech, ecommerce or consumer companies, said Apoorva Ranjan Sharma, cofounder of Venture Catalysts. “Those are now more mature sectors and investors expect stronger numbers from them.” Why Late Stage Capital Pool Remains Thin Even as more startups reach the growth stage, the pool of investors capable of funding them at scale remains relatively small. IvyCap's Gupta believes that India has a limited number of investors capable of writing large late stage cheques. Prior to the funding winter, India's late stage ecosystem relied heavily on global investors such as SoftBank, Tiger Global, Insight Partners and Sequoia Capital, which were among the most active sources of large growth stage cheques. “The larger dollar capital comes from the US and other geographies,” Gupta said, adding that changes in US policies and market conditions have made overseas deployment more difficult. He said US government securities have also become more attractive as a lower-risk investment, making it harder for funds to raise and deploy capital in markets such as India. While family offices, high-net-worth individuals and government-backed funds have stepped in to bridge some of the gap, Gupta said India would need at least $100 Bn of capital to become globally competitive. This has created a funding asymmetry. India now has a growing base of early stage investors backing startups through initial rounds, but a much smaller pool of capital available when those companies need substantially larger cheques to scale further. Why Late Stage Investors Are Holding Back The availability of capital is only part of the problem. Investors active at the late stage are also becoming more selective. According to Venture Catalysts’ Sharma, Series A and B investors can assess a startup's product, revenues, customers and execution while the business still has significant room to grow. By Series C and beyond, valuations are substantially higher, leaving investors with less room for error and making the potential return harder to justify. Several startups that raised capital at high valuations in earlier rounds are still working to deliver the business performance needed to justify the premiums, Gupta said. This is particularly relevant for deeptech companies, where technology development and commercialisation may take longer. “If an investor is putting in $30-50 Mn, there has to be a clear plan for how that money will be used and what the company will achieve,” Sharma said. “Growth continues to be important, but growth alone is no longer enough.” The shift is also changing how late stage rounds are structured. Gupta said investors may commit less capital upfront and release additional funds only when startups meet specific milestones. An investor capable of writing a $25 Mn cheque, for instance, could invest $15 Mn initially and reserve the remaining $10 Mn for a later tranche. Similar structures of investment deals are also seen at early and growth stages as well. For instance, Fireside Ventures committed ₹100 Cr capital to Arovia Consumer, a new ecommerce rollup venture by ex-Soulfull MD Prashant Parameswaran, with investments flowing as and when the startup closes acquisitions. Founders, meanwhile, are becoming more cautious about dilution and raising only what they need, Sharma said. What Could Unlock The Next Funding Wave? The current funding mix could eventually help narrow the late stage gap. The startups attracting Series A and B capital today — particularly in AI, deeptech, climate and manufacturing — could become a larger pipeline of companies seeking Series C, D and pre-IPO funding as they prove their technology, build markets and demonstrate commercial traction. Gupta said AI-funded companies are now entering a phase where investors will be able to assess how much of the sector's promise translates into actual business performance. Some could emerge as major winners, while others may struggle to justify their valuations. Deeptech companies are also moving towards commercialisation, with recent public-market milestones providing investors with evidence that some of these businesses can scale beyond the venture stage. The bumper IPOs of SEDEMAC and ESDS Software Solution, along with Skyroot's progress towards its next funding round, point to a broader pipeline of deeptech companies moving towards larger capital requirements. The number of companies requiring late stage capital is also on the upward trajectory. Inc42's investor survey found that 72% of investors have late stage startups in their portfolios that are at some level of IPO readiness. But IPO readiness does not necessarily mean these companies will need another large private round. Sharma said mature startups can instead raise smaller amounts, facilitate secondary transactions or move towards public markets. Gupta said greater visibility on a public market exit can itself unlock late stage investor interest, as investors become more comfortable when a company has a clearer path to an IPO. Successful listings could therefore become an important catalyst for the next phase of late stage funding. Gupta expects more capital to return as investors see successful outcomes, while Sharma said stronger profitability, more realistic valuations and successful IPOs will be important for rebuilding confidence. The bigger question is whether the companies now raising Series A and B capital can build the scale, profitability and exit visibility needed to attract the much larger pools of capital required at Series C, pre-IPO and beyond. As China and the EU begin crunch trade talks, optimism is in short supply
Observers on both sides are braced for more turbulence – and mainly hope Beijing and Brussels can avoid a full-blown trade conflict
As China and the European Union began a fresh round of trade talks in Beijing on Thursday, observers on both sides appeared to agree on one thing: a big breakthrough was unlikely.
Chinese firms based in Europe said they hoped the talks could achieve some “limited progress” to help stabilise the trade relationship, while European analysts remained cautious about the potential outcome.
“They’re bound to get some results,” said a Chinese source with knowledge of the talks, adding that EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic “will not go home empty-handed”.
The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU called on both sides to make full use of the Trade and Investment Consultations (TIC) mechanism to manage differences, push for solutions and send clearer signals to businesses.

25 years, many slogans: Modi's journey from 'Acche din' to 'We will do it'
The BJP’s spectacular win in the 2014 Lok Sabha elections was largely credited to Modi’s leadership, oratory and governance model in Gujarat.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has coined a new slogan to give impetus to his ambitious plan for a developed India by 2047: "We will do it".
On Wednesday, he completed 25 years in public service and as head of government, first as the chief minister of Gujarat and since 2014, as the premier of India. To mark the occasion, he dwelt on the past, summarised the present, and came up with a catch phrase for the future.
The PM used the slogan to nudge people to take on the challenge of bringing about changes from the economy to the manufacturing sector. He also listed several sectors where India needs to be the leader – from artificial intelligence to the space sector, and from the environment to exports.
Deep Dive
After he was named as the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)’s prime ministerial candidate in 2013, his political journey from the state to the national capital was pivoted on the catchy “Abki baar Modi sarkar” (this time, a Modi government) and the hope-inducing “Acche din aane wale hain” (good days are coming) slogans.
The party’s spectacular win in the 2014 Lok Sabha elections was largely credited to Modi’s leadership, oratory and governance model in Gujarat. However, opponents also saw it as the victory of a Hindu nationalist sentiment fostered by the BJP and its ideological fount, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
Modi then came up with the slogan of “Sabka saath, sabka vikas” (together with all, development for all), which sought to instill a sense of confidence that the government would be egalitarian and non-discriminatory. He added “vishwas” (trust) to the slogan when he returned to power for his second term in office in 2019, winning with a bigger margin and number.
In its first tenure, the Modi government set itself the task of weeding out outdated laws, meeting deadlines for infrastructure development, and ushering in economic and social reforms. For this, it chose the slogan of “Minimum government, maximum governance”.
The underlying message was cutting the bureaucratic red tape.
He even relied on slogans and catchphrases to introduce and implement policy decisions. Take for instance, the "Swachh Bharat abhiyan", to drive home the need for cleanliness and sanitation or the "Make in India" tagline for giving impetus to indigenous manufacturing. To check the country’s gender imbalance and prevent female foeticide, the PM came up with the “Beti bachao, beti padhao” (Save the daughter, educate the daughter) campaign.
Key phrases and catchlines have now become central to his style.
The “Atmanirbhar Bharat” (Self-reliant India) and “Vocal for local” (to promote Indian made goods) taglines were used to deliver the message to cut down on imports and drive domestic manufacturing and consumption during challenges imposed by the global pandemic in 2020. These taglines were reinforced when the West Asia crisis caused havoc in supply chains and sent prices of crude, gas and other essentials skyrocketing.
Difficult political decisions that led to disagreements and disruptions in Parliament and sharpened the divisions between the political class were also padded with slogans. A case in point being the proposal to synchronise Lok Sabha and assembly elections, popularly known as “One Nation, One Election”.
As the third term nears completion, the PM who once referred to himself as the “chowkidar” (guard) and reassured the electorate with the “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” (Modi makes it possible) tagline, has now set the agenda for 2047.
