Turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward, despite the remarkable progress in recent years ranging from self-driving cars to large language models. Systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
Vision-based systems, for example, hold promise for improving safety, monitoring health and aiding rehabilitation. For example, a camera-based system could help a clinician assess a patient’s gait or rehabilitation progress.
In the future, an assistive robot in an older adult’s home might need to recognise when the person is struggling to stand or reaching for an object. But a major challenge is ensuring these robots perform reliably beyond the lab, particularly in messy, unpredictable or low-visibility conditions.
As a computer scientist who studies AI systems designed to understand human behavior – especially through visual cues like body movements and interactions with objects – I see three main challenges to taking AI from the lab to the real world: generalisation, human behavior and resources.
Challenge 1: The generalisation gap
Most AI vision systems are trained on well-lit, high-quality images, often from curated sources like motion capture studios or daytime recordings. But when these systems are deployed in real-world settings, such as in a dimly lit home, hospital room or nighttime street, they often struggle. This is not because the technology is flawed, but because the data used to train it cannot fully represent the enormous variability of the real world.
Take human pose estimation, for example. This task involves detecting key points on a person’s body, such as joints, to understand how they’re moving. The result resembles a digital skeleton that represents the positions of a person’s arms, legs and other body parts. Pose estimation has been studied for health and rehabilitation applications, including measuring a person’s gait, monitoring rehabilitation exercises and assessing movement patterns associated with the risk of falling. In well-lit environments, modern AI models do this with impressive accuracy. But in low or uneven lighting, performance can drop sharply. That’s because the model has learned from clean, consistent data and isn’t prepared to generalise to tougher conditions.
Would collecting more nighttime training data solve the problem? More labeled data would certainly help, but collecting it is especially difficult. When a person’s joints are hard to see in an image, they are also hard for a human annotator to label accurately. Low light can also obscure visual information rather than simply make an image darker, and nighttime conditions vary with cameras, shadows, glare and other sources of noise. Collecting and manually labeling examples that cover all these conditions is therefore difficult and expensive.
We’ve been working to close this gap by developing AI systems that perform better in low-light scenarios. One method we use is unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model trained on well-lit, labeled data is adapted to handle low-light settings, without needing manual body-joint labels for the low-light images. This helps bridge the “domain gap” between clean training data and the messier world where these systems are actually used.
In our 2026 study on low-light human pose estimation, we generated realistic low-light training images and designed the system to balance uncertain visual evidence with its learned knowledge of human body structure. The method substantially improved performance on two low-light benchmarks, although the broader challenge is far from solved.
Challenge 2: Human behavior
Another major hurdle is the sheer variety of human behaviors, especially when people interact with objects. In computer vision, this is known as human-object interaction detection. Teaching an AI system to recognise actions like cutting a tomato or passing a basketball requires not just object detection, but an understanding of context and intent.
The real challenge is scale. The number of objects is large, and the ways humans interact with them are even greater. You can sit on a chair, carry it, drag it or stack it. Each is a distinct interaction. A cup might be used for drinking, washing, pouring or handing something to another person. An assistive robot would need to distinguish among these actions to respond appropriately. It’s simply not feasible to collect and label data for every possible combination.
In my research, we study how an AI system can detect interactions it has never seen during training. Researchers call this a generalisation-to-unseen-classes problem, and it’s a key challenge for building models that don’t just memorise patterns, but can adapt to new situations. Our work has explored how foundation models can help recognise previously unseen interactions. In a more recent study, we used large vision-language models, models that combine computer vision and natural language processing, to identify the parts of an object that support particular actions, without training the system on labeled examples for that specific task. This matters in areas like assistive robotics and safety monitoring, where AI needs to respond intelligently to behaviors it wasn’t specifically trained on.
This challenge is different from the low-light problem. In low-light pose estimation, the system is trying to recognise a familiar type of movement under unfamiliar environmental conditions. In human-object interaction detection, the action-and-object combination itself may be new. Both are generalisation problems, but they require different solutions.
Challenge 3: The resource gap
Even when researchers know how to make models more robust, applying those improvements isn’t always easy, especially in academic or smaller research settings. Today’s most powerful AI systems depend on massive computational resources in the form of data centers that contain huge numbers of specialised computer chips.
These are often too expensive for university labs or public-sector researchers, and the computing power needed to train leading models has continued to rise. According to the 2026 AI Index Report, the technology industry produced more than 90% of the notable AI models introduced in 2025.
At the same time, a model developed using large computing clusters may ultimately need to operate in a clinic, school, robot or home device, which means running on much smaller hardware. Such systems may also need to respond quickly without continuously sending sensitive data to the cloud. This mismatch creates a widening gap between what’s possible in theory and what’s practical in deployment. Bridging that gap requires not just better models, but more efficient algorithms and open-source tools that broaden access to advanced AI.
Why it matters
These challenges aren’t just academic. They affect how and whether AI tools can be trusted in the real world. Imagine a fall-detection system that fails at night, a workplace safety monitor that misses a crucial action or a robot that misunderstands what a person is doing because it’s never seen that exact interaction before. These aren’t just minor bugs – they’re breakdowns in trust, usability and sometimes even safety.
AI systems are being deployed in homes, hospitals, factories, vehicles and other everyday environments. If they can’t adapt to different environments or recognise new human behaviors, their usefulness becomes limited and their risks amplified. That’s why researchers are increasingly focusing not just on accuracy in ideal conditions, but on robustness, generalisation and real-world readiness.
Looking ahead: Closing the gap
Closing the gap between lab-trained AI models and messy, unpredictable real-world environments won’t happen overnight, but it’s possible. In my research, we’ve explored techniques like using augmented data to simulate challenging conditions and help models adapt. We’ve also worked on enabling AI systems to better generalise to new, unseen situations by using knowledge from foundation models to distinguish unfamiliar interactions from similar ones encountered during training.
Ultimately, I believe that making AI systems more reliable in everyday settings is a challenge worth solving, not just to improve gadgets and apps, but because AI has the potential to support human well-being, whether that means safer streets, smarter healthcare or more secure homes.
Bo Wang, assistant professor of Computer and Information Science, University of Mississippi

A video of Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him criticising Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for allegedly using the 2026 Flydubai incident to build an election narrative, which he compares to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s handling of the 2019 Pulwama attack.
In the video, Lapid can allegedly be heard saying, “Netanyahu is taking a page from Modi’s political playbook. In India, Modi used the 2019 Pulwama attack as an election campaign to frame a political narrative against Pakistan. Now in Israel, Netanyahu is using the Flydubai incident in the same way, turning a security crisis into an election narrative while diverting attention from the devastation in Gaza. Modi had his motherland election; Netanyahu has his fatherland election.” Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Yair Lapid accusing Netanyahu of using the 2026 Flydubai incident for political gains, comparing it to Modi’s use of the 2019 Pulwama attack.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage shows Yair Lapid criticising Benjamin Netanyahu over his handling of the Iran conflict and the US-Iran ceasefire. Lapid does not mention the Flydubai incident, Narendra Modi, or the 2019 Pulwama attack, nor does he accuse Netanyahu of using the incident for electoral gains. AI detection tools also indicated that the audio is likely manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version published on the Al Jazeera English YouTube channel on 09 April 2026, titled “Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid slams Netanyahu for ‘total failure’ in Iran.” In the video, Lapid criticises Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his handling of Iran, accusing him of misleading the public and turning a potential military success into a political disaster. He also says that Iran’s government had not been defeated, the nuclear threat remained, and Israel had no influence over the ceasefire deal. However, Lapid does not mention Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi or the 2019 Pulwama attack anywhere in the original video, indicating that the audio in the viral clip has been added or altered.
We also found a transcript of Yair Lapid’s televised address from 08 April 2026, published by The Times of Israel, while Reuters also published video footage containing excerpts from the speech. Lapid said that although the Israeli military had performed exceptionally well, Netanyahu had turned the military achievement into a “diplomatic disaster” because of poor planning and a lack of diplomatic strategy. He said Israel had no influence over the US-Iran ceasefire agreement and argued that Iran’s nuclear and missile threats had not been eliminated. Lapid also accused Netanyahu of misleading the Israeli public and damaging relations with the United States, arguing that Israel had achieved a military success but suffered a diplomatic setback. Nowhere in the transcript did we find that he criticised Benjamin Netanyahu over the Flydubai incident, accused him of using it to build an election narrative, or compared the incident to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s handling of the 2019 Pulwama attack.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the original footage was paired with fabricated audio to make it appear that Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid was accusing Netanyahu of using the Flydubai incident for political gains and comparing it to Modi’s handling of the Pulwama attack.
However, Yair Lapid accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of “fear-mongering” after warning that the country’s enemies may attack before the October 2026 general election, following the flydubai incident.
To sum up, this viral video of Yair Lapid allegedly saying PM Modi used the Pulwama attack to build an election narrative is AI-manipulated.

EXCLUSIVE: SiriusXM has reframed its statement on the viral Raw Dog Comedy debacle amid ongoing fallout with comics online.
A spokesperson tells Deadline in an exclusive statement, “SiriusXM has proudly supported the comedy community, and we have been listening to comedians speak out this week. Our decision to end Raw Comedy was due to the channel’s underperformance and came prior to Sebastian joining the SiriusXM lineup. While the challenges facing working comedians are bigger than any one person or decision, we remain committed, as we have for more than two decades, to making SiriusXM and Sebastian Maniscalco‘s Comedy Radio a place where comedians at every stage of their careers can be heard.”
What steps SiriusXM will take to address the issue called to their attention by legions of working- and middle-class comics is not yet clear.
Watch on Deadline
Interestingly, while discourse surrounding SiriusXM caught fire across social platforms earlier this week, it concerns a decision announced by the satellite radio provider all the way back in April.
We had the scoop, which was that SiriusXM would be replacing Raw Dog Comedy — a long-running channel on its subscription service — with the 24/7 branded channel Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio.
As subsequently argued by many, including nonprofit Stand Up for Stand Up, this evolution of SiriusXM’s comedy programming had quietly taken away a reliable source of revenue for many of the comics who need it most. Whereas Raw Dog had given airtime, culminating in residuals, to a broad base of stand-ups, what’s happened at the new channel is a concentration of airplay among the industry’s upper echelon of comics — living and dead — which has boxed out many others.
Calling SiriusXM’s move “devastating,” comedian Liz Miele said, “Because of this action, hundreds of comedians will no longer be able to have these royalties. Working class comedians, people that only make money on the road, that have no safety net, that depend on this money to just survive, are going from having that money to nothing.”
Perhaps, she argued, Maniscalco had previously been unaware of the impact of the rebrand on the broader comedy community. “But now you know, and you can help us. You can fix this. We would love to be reincorporated into the channel and start getting the streams and plays that we were getting before you took it over.”
SiriusXM’s statement reflects their perspective that Maniscalco is catching shrapnel in this situation that was not of his own making, and which he does not deserve. Read our original story on the Raw Dog Comedy debacle here; for SiriusXM’s next moves, stay tuned.

Andhra govt says crime rate down by 3.8% this year, Opposition flags women's safety
A run of cases involving deaths, sexual assault and harassment has drawn attention in Andhra Pradesh. The developments have triggered a political dispute as the government points to falling case numbers and new safety measures.
A series of recent cases involving the deaths of women, sexual assault complaints and harassment in Andhra Pradesh has triggered renewed scrutiny of women’s safety and the effectiveness of the police response.
The developments have also sparked a political dispute, with the opposition YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) accusing the TDP-led coalition government of failing to protect women.
The government, however, has maintained that crimes against women have declined and pointed to new policing and technology-based measures aimed at improving women’s safety.
Several cases have been reported from different parts of the state in recent weeks. On October 4, a 22-year-old man died by suicide after the death of 19-year-old Mahalakshmi in Vijayawada’s New Rajarajeshwaripet.
Police said the man attacked the woman with a knife before jumping from a nearby building. Reports based on police information said the two had been facing relationship-related disputes.
In Ongole, police registered a case after two minor girls from a BC Welfare Hostel were taken to the residence of a retired employee. Authorities are investigating the circumstances in which the girls were taken out of the hostel.
The Andhra Pradesh State Commission for Protection of Child Rights has sought a report from district officials. A person has been arrested under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, according to reports.
Other cases include a complaint involving the sexual assault of a 10-year-old girl in Railway Kodur, an assault case involving a woman in Vijayawada’s VAMBAY Colony and a harassment complaint by a woman sub-inspector during a family trip.
Questions have also been raised over an delay in action on a complaint concerning the death of a girl in Anakapalli.
Reports of sexual violence in Hindupur and attacks on women in the constituency of Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha have also added to the concerns.
On September 20, a woman in Mylavaram accused a Jana Sena leader of obscene behaviour, abuse and threats. The complaint remains subject to investigation and legal proceedings.
YSR CONGRESS ATTACKS GOVERNMENT
YSRCP spokesperson Nagamalleswari accused the TDP-led coalition government of failing to provide adequate protection to women and children. She questioned whether the government had taken sufficient steps to ensure justice for victims and sought greater accountability from the police and administration.
She cited police data showing that 16,347 crimes against women and 1,879 POCSO cases were registered in 2025. She also questioned the effectiveness of the government's new women’s safety initiatives compared with the previous Disha system.
The allegations by the opposition are political claims and need to be viewed separately from the crime data released by the police.
GOVERNMENT CITES DECLINE IN CRIME
According to figures presented by Andhra Pradesh DGP Harish Kumar Gupta, crimes against women declined from 16,994 in 2024 to 16,347 in 2025, a fall of around 3.8 per cent. POCSO cases also declined from 2,120 to 1,879 during the same period.
The police also reported 510 convictions in cases involving crimes against women and POCSO offences during 2025.
The government has introduced and expanded several measures aimed at improving women’s safety. The Andhra Pradesh Police’s Women and Child Safety Wing operates the SHAKTHI system, which provides SOS assistance, complaint reporting and travel-tracking services.
Police officials say SOS calls are routed to the nearest police station for a quick response.
In 2025, Home Minister Vangalapudi Anitha announced a new Women and Child Protection Wing and a safety application, saying the government had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards crimes against women.
The government has defended its record by pointing to the decline in registered cases, convictions and new policing initiatives.
However, the recent incidents have renewed questions over prevention, prompt registration of complaints, investigation and continued support for victims and their families.

When The Social Network hit theaters in 2010, it was fair to wonder if the film had come too soon. Facebook had been launched from Mark Zuckerberg’s Harvard dorm room just six years earlier, and nobody really knew how it would reshape digital community in the decade to come.
But, with a breakneck screenplay by Aaron Sorkin, a menacingly propulsive soundtrack by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and a surgical performance from Jesse Eisenberg as Young Zuck, director David Fincher delivered a slick corporate thriller about the major drama to that point: intersecting lawsuits over who owned what percentage of the platform and who could lay claim as a founder. It was an electrifying film that seemed to only lightly fictionalize the newest and perhaps most cutthroat generation of Silicon Valley warlords.
Flash forward 16 years, and Facebook (now Meta) has accumulated more scandals than Hollywood could possibly hope to keep up with. Sorkin tells WIRED that he was approached many times over those years with pitches for a sequel, though he struggled to see an angle of approach. “Before a film can be anything else, before it can be relevant or thought-provoking, it has to be good,” he says. “It has to work as something that you watch while you're eating popcorn.”
Then, Sorkin says, he met Frances Haugen, the former Facebook data engineer who leaked damning internal memos to investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz. Horwitz wrote up what became known as the “Facebook Files” in a far-ranging 2021 series of articles for The Wall Street Journal, exposing much of what the company knew regarding harms to users—everything from hate speech and medical misinformation to body image issues and human trafficking—but had largely brushed aside in pursuit of growth.
Sorkin still wasn’t sure he had a film, but one day he asked Haugen why she finally decided to go to the media. “She just told me in kind of an offhand way, ‘Oh, I had this friend who was radicalized by Facebook after spending too many hours on the platform,’” he recalls. “And I began to get the idea for what is now the opening scene of the movie.”
The cold open of The Social Reckoning, written and directed by Sorkin, depicts an intoxicated woman pulled over on the side of the road in San Mateo, California, with an overheated car. Approached by police officers, she turns combative, pulling out her phone to record a video as she hurls racist abuse at the cops and is at last arrested for threatening to kill one of them. The video turns up on a Facebook page for far-right content, which is where Haugen (Mikey Madison) finds it in 2019, recognizing the woman as an acquaintance from her pilates class who used to hold progressive views. She also learns that this woman is a superuser, intensely active on Facebook for many hours each day.
Haugen first tries to get her colleagues at Facebook to recognize how their own algorithms are pushing many users, including her former friend, into extremist feeds. It’s only when she hits enough walls that she puts her tentative trust in Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a journalist whom Facebook staff have been explicitly warned not to speak to. As they develop the bickering rapport of two focused professionals with clashing ideals—Haugen wants to save the company from itself, while Horwitz suspects it’s too late for that—we see flash-forwards of Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) rehearsing for a congressional hearing on social media misinformation in 2021. In the room are a crisis PR adviser named Raya (Wunmi Mosaku) and Charlie (Bill Burr), a composite ex-employee (as in, not specifically based on any living individual). He’s been brought in as an agitator with the freedom to get under Zuck’s skin and dismantle his practiced talking points.
This plot structure is clunkier than the cross-cutting depositions of The Social Network, which neatly allowed for the characters to recount the early days of Facebook without narrative hand-holding. By comparison, The Social Reckoning is clogged with portentous intertitles (the first sequence is even labeled a “prologue”) and visual cues to remind us where we are in the timeline. From scene to scene, the sharp-edged performances and familiar crackle of Sorkinese dialog (which leaves room for the occasional and delightfully odd non sequitur) make for engaging fare. But the pieces fit together awkwardly—and you do wish Reznor and Ross were around to boost the momentum.
The movie arrives as part of a crowded slate of keenly anticipated tech films. There’s Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s satire about the firing and rehiring of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in 2023; it picked up significant buzz as Amazon MGM dropped it this summer following a $50 billion deal between Amazon and OpenAI. Alex Gibney’s epic documentary Musk covers the exploits of the world’s richest man up through his disastrous reign as a “government efficiency” czar in the White House. And don’t forget You Can See Everything, for which directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gained close access to Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes shortly before she began serving a decade-long prison sentence.
Amid these timely offerings, The Social Reckoning is a just touch out of step. Its climax (spoiler alert) is the January 6 Capitol riot, the horrors of which are blamed in part on Facebook’s failure to either get a handle on election fraud conspiracy theories or remove Donald Trump’s account as he stoked such inflammatory falsehoods. Now, halfway into Trump’s second term, is it all that much of a revelation that he and his movement are emboldened by the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed him in 2024?
Nevertheless, there are big issues at play here. The debate over ethics in tech continually boils over into agonizing questions of how truth is negotiated and who gets the last word on it.
Whether you find Reckoning to be a worthy interrogation of this stuff will probably depend on your appetite for what amounts to a mashup of The Newsroom and The West Wing. There are mic-drop moments that plainly invite the audience to “lib out,” such as when Haugen accuses Horwitz of bias against tech because it’s stealing journalists’ jobs and he fires back that it’s actually because “you are so bad at it.” Or when Zuckerberg taunts his traitorous former friend Charlie for cashing out his Facebook stake for $200 million instead of holding on until it was worth $1.3 billion, and he counters by torching the presumption that he’s “supposed to be embarrassed by that.”
“I love that line, because that is the disease,” Burr tells WIRED. “What you're seeing with these robber baron nerds that are out there right now is the way somebody is addicted to methamphetamine, they are addicted to money. They literally cannot have enough. They are insatiable. They behave like addicts. And an addict will do whatever they have to do, hurt whoever they have to, to get that next fix.”
There is a definite satisfaction to seeing Burr, a caustic stand-up comedian, stick this observation directly into Zuckerberg’s craw. On the other hand, it’s a little naive to imagine that it stings a guy expanding his massive top-secret Hawaii compound to include ancestral burial grounds. In so many ways, Reckoning attempts to shame a ruling class that has proved itself, well, shameless.
At its best, then, the film may serve to underscore Haugen’s bravery in turning whistleblower while capably illustrating the difficulty and dangers of mounting an exposé on a Silicon Valley behemoth. It reminds us that there is always something else these tech firms are concealing. Both Madison and White tell WIRED that Sorkin’s screenplay jolted their understanding of the forces at work in the industry.
“I had an inkling about certain things, but then to be confronted with the real statistics and facts—that really confirmed how I was already feeling about social media as a whole and some of the negative effects it can have on people,” Madison says. White adds that people shouldn’t give companies like Meta the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong. “What you find out in watching this film is, there's a business model, there's a plan, there's engagement,” he says. “They're hyper-aware of exactly what's happening, and they still choose to put their foot on the gas.”
Though as to an actual “reckoning” with this reality, the title may have been an overpromise. The movie’s postscript notes that millions of Americans still get news from Facebook and that in 2025, Meta ended its fact-checking program, opting instead to solicit crowdsourced context notes from users. It’s a downbeat conclusion after Haugen and Horwitz have beaten the odds to drag countless dirty secrets into the light. You wish you could walk away from The Social Reckoning with a sense that this forever changed Facebook, or Zuckerberg, or the internet itself, yet it’s hard to avoid noticing that everyone got away with it.

Former senior Flipkart executives, including Flipkart’s former CEO Mukesh Bansal, former CFO Sanjay Baweja and former chief business officer Ankit Nagori, have reportedly urged Walmart to buyback their vested employee stock options (ESOPs) amid uncertainty over the ecommerce major’s public listing plans. The group is said to have written to Walmart’s board, which includes Flipkart group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy, urging for a complete exit opportunity. “This is not merely a request for goodwill. We contributed our time, effort, expertise and commitment to building the business and creating the value that exists today,” the letter read, as per a report by ET. Demanding a “fair treatment” towards the vested stock options granted to them 10-15 years ago, the ex-Flipkart heads argued that former employees should not be disadvantaged simply because they are no longer on Flipkart’s payroll. The push comes months after Walmart conducted the second tranche of Flipkart's employee stock buyback programme. The July transaction reportedly valued Flipkart at around $38.2 Bn, but eligible employees could liquidate only up to 5% of their vested options. A Walmart spokesperson said that the company would examine the issues raised by the former executives. “We appreciate the perspective of all employees—current and former—and value their feedback. As with anything raised, we take it seriously and look into the matter.” “As we’ve said, an IPO remains an active part of our strategic roadmap, and we will move forward when the timing is right. Transitioning to public markets brings great opportunities, but also real operational responsibility. A thoughtful and disciplined approach will help support a successful transition to public markets,” the statement added. Inc42 has reached out to Flipkart, Walmart, Mukesh Bansal, and Sanjay Baweja for comments on the matter. The emails had not received a response at the time of publishing. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Flipkart Defers IPO Amid Profitability Push At the heart of the matter is Flipkart’s deferred plans as parent Walmart seeks a valuation of $50 Bn for the ecommerce giant. While the company has reverse flipped to India in a bid to list on the domestic bourses, it doesn’t have a concrete timeline for its public market debut. As of now, the company is said to have deferred the IPO till 2028 as it focuses on enhancing its bottom line. Flipkart is targeting breakeven at an EBITDA level by FY27. Flipkart is currently doubling down on its quick commerce vertical, Flipkart Minutes, with projections of it doubling its dark store count to 2,000 by mid-2027. It is also looking to enter new businesses like food delivery and event ticketing in the near future. The company is yet to disclose its financial performance for the fiscal year FY26. For the fiscal year FY25, Flipkart Internet, the group's marketplace arm, reported a 36.7% decline in consolidated net loss to ₹1,494.2 Cr in FY25, while total income increased 14% YoY to ₹20,807.4 Cr.

TP-Link is facing more legal troubles in the US as Florida and three other states filed lawsuits alleging that it lied to consumers about its connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers.
The lawsuits were filed yesterday, about six months after the Federal Communications Commission announced a sweeping ban on consumer-grade routers produced wholly or partly outside of the US. Numerous router makers have obtained exemptions to the ban, but the Trump administration so far has not granted one to TP-Link.
Router makers that received exemptions include Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Amazon and its Eero subsidiary, Calix, Nokia, SpaceX’s Starlink division, and others. For now, TP-Link is unable to sell its latest Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, though models approved before the ban can still be sold.
The state lawsuits claim that TP-Link misled US consumers by telling them its routers are safe. The suits allege that TP-Link committed unfair and deceptive trade acts in violation of the states’ consumer protection laws.
“Chinese state-sponsored hackers exploited TP-Link routers sitting in American living rooms,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said while announcing his lawsuit filed in a Florida county court. Uthmeier said Florida “will not allow families to be misled into handing their personal data to the Chinese Communist Party. We are seeking an injunction, restitution for Florida consumers, and [financial] penalties under Florida law.”
TP-Link criticizes coordinated lawsuits
TP-Link was founded in China but moved its headquarters to California in October 2024 amid investigations into high-profile attacks linked to the Chinese government, including a botnet composed mostly of TP-Link routers. The Florida lawsuit accuses TP-Link of “lying about the safety of its routers and its ties to the CCP,” Uthmeier said.
Uthmeier was one of four Republican state attorneys general to sue TP-Link yesterday. Lawsuits were also filed against TP-Link by Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska.
“The coordinated lawsuits are built on false premises,” said Steve Kovsky, TP-Link’s corporate affairs officer. “They do nothing to advance national security while unfairly penalizing an industry-leading US company.” TP-Link said that for the past few months it has “provided state regulators with clear, verifiable documentation demonstrating two fundamental facts: TP-Link Systems devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam and TP-Link Systems is an independent, US company that is not owned or controlled by any foreign government.”

France halts use of stun grenades in policing of student protests
Protests show no sign of easing, with more than 500 schools closed, and more marches planned for Thursday
The French government said on Wednesday it was pausing the use of stun grenades in its policing of student protests, after a 15-year-old boy’s hand was blown off during a clash with riot police, fuelling protesters’ accusations of police brutality.
Protests showed no sign of easing, with more than 500 schools closed a day after demonstrations swept across the country, and unions representing high-school students, teachers and other workers planning more marches for Thursday.
The wave of protests has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace French President Emmanuel Macron.
At Lycee Lamartine, a high school in central Paris, protesters sang the Marseillaise, chanted slogans and performed Mexican waves as they blockaded the entrance to the school.

Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.
The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.
Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.
Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”
The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.
But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.
Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.
“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.
Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.
Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.
The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.
“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”
Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.
Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.
She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”
Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.
“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

OpenAI Agents Hit Wikimedia OpenAI is under fresh scrutiny over its “rogue” agents. Wikimedia Foundation claims that the AI juggernaut’s agentic system made unauthorised edits on its platforms, crashed its query services and generated millions of automated requests. So, why is the episode raising alarm bells? Rogue AI Vs Wikipedia: The non-profit said that it found unauthorised edits as well as potentially malicious changes to a citation tool’s configuration. OpenAI agents also tried exploiting its Etherpad tool to access other websites and generated millions of API and WDQS queries. This possibly contributed to the Wikipedia outage in May. The foundation found no evidence of data compromise but warned that such scale imposes significant costs on public internet infrastructure. While much of the automotive world sits dumbfounded as China gobbles up all its customers, BMW continues to roll out extremely well-crafted, technologically advanced electric vehicles that impress in both drive quality and price. The latest is the BMW iX4, a coupe-shaped SUV that puts a sportier spin on the automaker’s iX3.
BMW’s iX4 SUV is a 428-mile defensive weapon against China’s EV takeover
The iX4 is a sportier spin on the iX3, with the same powerful Gen6 battery providing class-leading range.
The iX4 is the third vehicle to be released on BMW’s next-generation Neue Klasse platform, following the iX3 and i3 models. The iX4 50 xDrive will come first in March 2027, followed by an even more high-performance M60 xDrive version later in the year. The automaker is positioning this new lineup as its bulwark against the flood of Chinese imports that is currently decimating other European brands. But while the iX4 can certainly compete on range and tech, it’s unclear whether BMW can rival China in terms of sheer affordability.
In that respect, the BMW iX4 50 xDrive starts at $66,200 (excluding fees for destination and handling). And it bears all the hallmarks of BMW’s other Neue Klasse models, such as the “Gen6” high-voltage battery with 112.2kWh of usable energy, an 800-volt architecture for lightning-quick charging top-ups, and up to 428 miles of range based on EPA estimates.
That’s more range than the Tesla Model Y, the best-selling electric vehicle in the world. BMW has been blowing away expectations on range to such a degree that even the experts at InsideEVs are left wondering whether it’s overkill. After all, Tesla and others have done plenty well with EVs in the mid-300s, while Lucid continues to struggle despite exceeding 500 miles in range.
But BMW wants to go the distance, believing that range and efficiency are two of its biggest selling points. The third would be performance, and thanks to a dual-motor setup in both the 50 xDrive and M60 xDrive, the iX4 is sure to delivery plenty of giddy up. The 50 xDrive’s motors put out 463 horsepower and 475lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60mph acceleration of 4.7 seconds. Meanwhile, the M60 xDrive’s motors produce 603hp and 645lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60 time a whole second less than the 50 xDrive.
Like other Neue Klasse vehicles, the electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) in the rear axle serves as the primary drive axle, using electricity instead of permanent magnets to power both its stator outer frame and interior spinning rotor. An inverter acts as the brain of the system, converting direct current from the battery into alternating current for the motor, regulating the electromagnets, and monitoring performance to keep the motor running as efficiently as possible. BMW says this combination helps slash drive-system energy losses by 40 percent and weight by 10 percent.
The Gen6 batteries are built with cylindrical lithium-ion cells measuring 46mm in diameter and 95mm in height that provide a 20 percent increase in energy density compared to the prismatic cells used in BMW’s Gen5 batteries. BMW has eliminated the traditional modules in favor of a “pack-to-open-body” construction where the battery housing serves as the vehicle’s underbody, lowering weight and increasing torsional rigidity.
Like Hyundai and Kia, BMW is building its Neue Klasse EVs to take fast charging to the next level. With its 800V architecture, the iX4 can accept up to 400kWs of DC fast charging, replenishing up to 184 miles of range in 10 minutes, and 10–80 percent charge in just 21 minutes. With a NACS charging port, the iX4 will be compatible with over 80,000 Tesla Supercharger connectors around the world.
The Panoramic iDrive infotainment system is BMW’s redesigned digital dashboard that replaces traditional gauge clusters with a heads-up-style projection along the full width of the lower windshield. The 17.9-inch central touchscreen presents as a free-cut display where you can drag and drop up to six widgets like media, weather, or navigation from the screen directly onto the windshield display.
And like the i3 and iX3, the iX4 can do all sorts of extra stuff, including bidirectional charging with vehicle-to-load and vehicle-to-home capabilities, an intelligent charging flap that opens when a driver approaches a known charging point, and Plug & Charge for automatic charging at 10 different charging providers.
If you look at the whole package, there’s a lot to like. Sure, the Model Y beats the iX4 in a few categories, most importantly price. It’s a bit quicker off the line, and of course, the Model Y comes with the option for Full Self-Driving (Supervised). BMW has something it calls “Symbiotic Drive,” which it describes as a Level 2 system designed for “fluid, intuitive interaction.” In other words, drivers can adjust the steering or even brake without canceling the automated functions. The iX4 also allows for hands-free driving on the highway — but no point-to-point assisted driving. Not until 2027 at the earliest.
Where BMW still bests Tesla is variety. You can get the iX4 50 xDrive, or if you want something sportier, try the M60 xDrive. If you’re rather have a sedan, there’s the i3. Or if you want something a bit more affordable, there’s the iX3. And don’t forget the flagship 7 series. Yep, those are getting Neue Klasse makeovers as well.
Tesla has the Model 3 and Model Y — and that’s about it. (Yes, there’s the Cybertruck, but clearly most people aren’t interested in that. And there’s the Cybercab, but it won’t be on sale anytime soon.) BMW knows its customers want options. And it’s doing it’s best to deliver.

The FCC proposes new mid-band spectrum auction and unlocking 800MHz for drones
The agency is doubling down on direct-to-device service.
The US Federal Communications Commission laid out a trio of proposals for several rule changes around wireless connectivity. The plans will be put to a vote later this month and largely center on direct-to-device communications.
First, the agency suggested overhauling its rules for direct-to-device, or D2D, service. The stated goal is to "promote more flexible terrestrial, satellite, and hybrid business arrangements." Related, the second proposal is to auction 25 megahertz of mid-band spectrum. Bids would be targeting use cases such as "flexible-use terrestrial networks, innovative direct-to-device (D2D) operations, or a hybrid of both" according to the FCC. This could prove enticing to companies like Amazon, which are hoping to join the growing field of satellite-based cellular service.
One such company is SpaceX, which already has spectrum licenses it bought from EchoStar. Yesterday the FCC granted approval to SpaceX for a system of 15,000 satellites to operate at 330km. This push into D2D systems from SpaceX is a separate affair than the company's attempts to launch a network of orbital data centers aimed to provide compute power for artificial intelligence activity and would add to its existing network of more than 11,000 Starlink satellites. Suffice to say, SpaceX has a whole lot of gear overhead.
The final FCC proposal recommends allowing drones to operate on the 800MHz cellular band. Those devices are currently prohibited from using that frequency, and if passed, the change would open up about 50 megahertz for UAVs to use. Over the past year, the agency has been placing more restrictions on the drones that it deemed to be security risks, whether for containing foreign-made parts or for being equipped with tech such as LiDAR.

Puri Jagannath airport gets final environmental clearance despite wildlife concerns
The proposed Shree Jagannath International Airport in Odisha’s Puri has received final environmental clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The proposed Shree Jagannath International Airport in Odisha’s Puri has received final environmental clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, clearing a major hurdle for the greenfield project despite wildlife experts raising concerns over its potential impact on migratory birds and endangered marine species.
The airport, proposed in the Sipasarubali area of Puri district and just about 5 km from the Jagannath temple, will come up on 471.348 hectares, including 27.887 hectares of forest land.
The airport is planned to handle 4.6 million passengers annually in Phase-I, with an international facility proposed in the first phase itself, subject to regulatory approvals. Its capacity is envisaged to rise to 10.18 million passengers per annum in Phase-II and 16.69 million passengers per annum in Phase-III.
Puri collector Dibya Jyoti Parida said the project had received both environmental clearance and Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) clearance from the ministry.
“Forest-related issues were also cleared. We are now awaiting the final approval from the ministry to proceed with the project,” Parida said.
Officials, aware of the development, said the state government is now awaiting a formal no-objection certificate from the ministry and will approach the Airports Authority of India (AAI) for approval to prepare the detailed project report (DPR).
The construction process will be taken up in coordination with the AAI and the state Transport department, Parida said.
Forest clearance and conditions
The ministry had earlier granted Stage-I, or in-principle, approval under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980, for diversion of 27.887 hectares of forest land in the Puri Wildlife Division for the airport. The approval, based on the recommendations of the ministry’s Advisory Committee, came with 33 conditions, including compensatory afforestation over 29.939 hectares of non-forest land.
The committee, at its meeting on February 27, had directed the state government to ensure implementation of mitigation measures and recommendations emerging from impact assessment studies and a site-specific wildlife management plan prepared on the recommendations of the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and Zoological Survey of India.
WII flags bird strike, wildlife risks
The project, however, has faced strong environmental concerns. The WII had recommended that the airport proposal be rejected, citing its proximity to the existing Bhubaneswar airport, the Balukhanda-Konark Wildlife Sanctuary and the Chilika Ramsar site.
According to the WII assessment, as the project boundary is about 16 km from Chilika Lake, a wetland of international importance, the airport could pose a “catastrophic” risk to migratory bird populations and affect critical habitats of endangered marine species, including Olive Ridley turtles.
It also flagged the site’s location along migratory bird corridors forming part of the Central Asian Flyway, saying the proximity could increase the risk of bird strikes, posing a threat both to aviation safety and wildlife.
The WII cited international incidents to underline the danger. At Muan International Airport in South Korea, a bird strike involving migratory Baikal teals in December 2024 killed 179 people. At Bahir Dar International Airport in Ethiopia, a bird strike near Lake Tana in 1988 claimed 35 lives.
Despite the concerns, the project is being pushed as a major infrastructure and tourism initiative for Puri, as the current international airport in Bhubaneswar has reached its maximum potential and can’t be expanded horizontally any further due to human habitations around it.

When the Vinoo Mankad Trophy gets underway on Thursday, young cricketers from Arunachal Pradesh will miss out on the national U-19 tournament.
The side is scheduled to face Sikkim in the Plate Group, at the KIIT Cricket Stadium in Bhubaneswar, but Sportstar understands that the Arunachal Pradesh Association (ACA) has not fielded a team this season due to an ongoing legal case.
Confirming the development, Devajit Saikia, the BCCI secretary, told Sportstar: “We have seen that Arunachal Pradesh is not fielding teams in some of the age-group tournaments. From what we have gathered, there is a court case going on in the Gauhati High Court-Itanagar Bench. There is also an interim stay on the functioning of the Arunachal Cricket Association,” Saikia said.
According to Arunachal News Live, six district associations in the State had alleged violations of rules and procedures in the conduct of the Arunachal Cricket Association (ACA) State executive elections and demanded a re-election.
The associations which disputed the election of president Nabam Vivek and other post holders are Lower Siang District Cricket Association, Upper Subansiri District Cricket Association, Kamle District Cricket Association, Tawang District Cricket Association, West Siang District Cricket Association, Papum Pare District Cricket Association.
The matter was heard in the first week of September. Till date, the judgment has not come and the interim order is in operation.
“Because of the internal bickerings between the two factions, there is litigation and a stay order regarding the functioning of the association. As a result, nobody could take up the matter of team selection or preparation, and ultimately the Arunachal team will not be playing in the age-group tournament,” Saikia said.

This will lead to Arunachal forfeiting the match. As per BCCI’s playing conditions relating to the ‘BCCI Match Referee awarding a match’, section 16.2.1.2 states that, “A match shall be lost by a side which in the opinion of the BCCI Match Referee refuses to play and the BCCI Match Referee shall award the match to the other side.”
The situation could also have a bearing on Arunachal Pradesh’s participation in the Ranji Trophy, which begins on October 11. Arunachal features in the Plate Group, and is supposed to begin its campaign against Nagaland at Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad.
“I have an apprehension about what will happen to the Arunachal Pradesh team when the Ranji Trophy begins on October 11. I cannot say at this moment what will happen in the first match and whether they will be able to field a team or not,” Saikia said.
In Ranji Trophy, there are past instances of teams forfeiting their matches. Services forfeited its 2009-10 Ranji Trophy Plate Division match against Jammu & Kashmir in Srinagar, as it refused to travel to Srinagar, citing security concerns. The BCCI treated it as a forfeit and subsequently banned Services from the remainder of that Ranji season.
The BCCI has, in the past, appointed committees to oversee cricketing operations in state units such as Bihar, Rajasthan and Jammu and Kashmir following court directions. However, in the case of Arunachal, things are different.
“As far as the BCCI is concerned, it cannot step into the matter right now because the matter is sub judice and, till now, the court has not appointed any administrator. The BCCI on its own will not step into the matter when the litigation is going on in the court, and until the matter is resolved,” Saikia said.
This publication spoke to several cricketers from the State, who were clearly shattered with the way things have panned out. Speaking on the condition of anonymity, a senior player from the State said, “If we don’t get to play this season, we will have to seriously weigh our options and decide whether we would like to continue with the sport.”
In 2018, Arunachal Pradesh, along with the other states of Northeast, were drafted into the BCCI-affiliated tournaments after the then Committee of Administrators, appointed by the Supreme Court, granted them full membership. However, since its entry into mainstream cricket, Arunachal Pradesh has found itself marred in several controversies, including charges of corruption against office-bearers.

More than 30 years into his career, Questlove is still open to change.
The Roots frontman and multi-hyphenate has performed in Jimmy Fallon’s in-house band for over a decade, was a producer on the “Hamilton” cast album, is an adjunct professor at NYU, hosts a podcast and has written eight books.
Since 2020, Questlove has also directed four documentaries. It was that endeavor that he was initially most opposed to: “I had to do a lot of work to realize that — I know it’s cliché — I gotta be the change I want to be.”
Questlove sat down with Variety‘s Jem Aswad to discuss embracing vulnerability and being a changemaker at the Variety Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage presented by OUTFRONT.
Questlove said he would have called Prince his North Star when he first entered the industry. Now, with the “residue” of his Earth, Wind & Fire documentary still lingering, he said he feels like a new artist. “I’m still learning what the Questlove brand is,” he said. “I joke that this is Questlove 3.0 happening right now.”
“Earth, Wind & Fire (To Be Celestial vs That’s the Weight of the World)” was released in June. Directed and produced by Questlove, the documentary explores the band’s career and that of its founder, Maurice White. While creating the documentary, he read many of the books White read during the band’s genesis, which inspired his current approach to creativity.
Questlove recalled the “too cool for school” attitude he saw in artists like Miles Davis and his own mindset on his records as protecting vulnerability. “We see it in our politics. We see it in our creativity,” he said. “We’re going to implode as a world if we don’t learn what emotions are and how we can use our vulnerability.”
Questlove’s first documentary project, “Summer of Soul (…or, When the Revolution Could Not Be Televised),” about the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival, came out in 2021. “You can’t discount the timing of everything,” he said of the film’s arrival after the initial lockdown and protests following the murder of George Floyd. He said people saw the film because they were curious, but “they didn’t realize how important it was to celebrate joy.”
His next project, “Sly Lives! (aka The Burden of Black Genius),” focused more on the tendency he noticed in Black creatives to self-sabotage after becoming successful. Then came the Earth, Wind & Fire documentary, which he made because he “wanted to make a film that lets us focus on our dreams.”
Still, Questlove didn’t think he was the right person for the job of documentarian prior to “Summer of Soul.” “I didn’t know I was a storyteller,” he said. “I’m out there like, ‘Well, search for a real storyteller,’ and they’re like, ‘Dude, you’re that storyteller.’ Once I realized it, it became a passion.” He described himself as someone who will use history to attract audiences, but will put things in his films to make the audience reckon with their present.
While he has ventured into filmmaking, Questlove has not left music behind. The Roots Picnic held its 18th iteration this May, headlined by Jay-Z. The festival has grown, but “we’re not just rubber-stamping,” he said. “We are curating the festival. We’re playing with some of the acts, and people really feel like a community.”
On “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon,” The Roots serve as — among other things — the live walk-up music for guests. Some celebrities send requests for their entrance song, but Questlove said, “the magic of the show is what I choose your walk-on song.”
The best thing about “The Tonight Show,” Questlove said, is that it allows the band members to be present with their families. “The Beatles broke up after seven years, and we’re going on year 35 and we’re still like the best of friends,” he said. “We’re still as silly as we were in high school, and still fun. If you’re not friends with your partners, then all this is for naught.”

5 things civil rights data says about public schools
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
The number of kids in preschool rose in the 2023-24 school year, while those in K-12 public schools declined. The population of students with disabilities grew. Black students were more likely to be suspended than students of other races. And the teacher workforce was far less diverse than the student population.
All of this information comes from the latest Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC): a federal survey that paints one of the most comprehensive pictures of how American students are being treated at school. The federal government has been gathering this kind of information for over 50 years, partly to help the U.S. Education Department hold schools accountable for protecting student civil rights.
The Trump administration published the latest CRDC from the 2023-24 school year six months later than promised. When it finally did share the information on Aug. 31, collected from over 97,000 public schools, it was without a usual "First Look Report" that makes the information easier to understand for the public. Now, that too, is available.
The findings are about 49.7 million public school students and include data on enrollment, harassment and the treatment of students with disabilities, among other things. But one group was left out: nonbinary students. While data on nonbinary students was collected under the Biden administration, the Trump administration chose to withhold it from the public release.
Maithreyi Gopalan of the University of Oregon, who helps lead the research and policy group AdvancED Equity, and Dan Losen of the National Center for Youth Law, both independently analyzed the data and shared some of what they learned with NPR.
Here are five things they found striking:
1. Public school enrollment
Some 1.5 million children were enrolled in public preschool programs — a 12% jump from the 2021-22 school year, but still slightly lower than 2019. "It's part recovery, part expansion," says Gopalan. By recovery, she means the number of preschoolers started rising again from a pandemic low. By expansion, Gopalan is referring to the fact that some states are investing more in early childhood education, which may account for some of the increases.
According to the National Institute for Early Education Research, state-funded pre-K enrollment rose nearly 15% between 2021-22 and 2023-24. For example, in 2023-24, California was in its second year of expanding its universal transitional kindergarten (TK) program for 4-year-olds, and the state enrolled nearly 36,000 more children in preschool or TK than the year before. Colorado and New Mexico are among other states that are rapidly expanding preschool access.
At the same time, K-12 enrollment fell almost 1% compared with the 2021-22 school year. The decrease is consistent with other data and could have to do with declining birthrates and an increase in private school and homeschooled students in some states, Gopalan says.
2. School Discipline
The number of students who were suspended increased across the board: 2.5 million students were punished with one or more out-of-school suspensions while 2.3 million students faced in-school suspensions in 2023-24. That's up by about 100,000 students in each category compared with the last report from 2021-22. Notably, nearly 7 out of 10 public schools reported an increase in students seeking mental health services since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to other federal data.
While the increase in suspensions may seem modest, Losen says it shows that the pattern of keeping children out of school as punishment is still widespread in America's public schools. His research shows that most districts suspend students for what he calls minor offenses rather than unsafe behavior.
"It could be truancy, it could be repeated tardiness, dress code violations." Those missed days of school mean missed days of learning: Losen's research shows that about a decade ago, students were losing out on 11 million days of school because of suspensions. According to the latest CRDC, he says they missed over 14 million days in the 2023-24 school year.
"That lost instruction time matters more than people realize," he says. "Even one out-of-school suspension greatly increases the risk of dropping out of a school or winding up in the juvenile justice system."
Loading...
He adds that suspensions are often an ineffective way to change behavior and that there are more constructive ways to help students, including with emotional support and better training for teachers.
Another persistent pattern with school discipline is who faces it: Losen says the latest data show that Black students lost over four times as many days of school compared to white peers because of out-of-school suspension.
3. Students with disabilities
The CRDC reinforces what other national data shows: The population of students with disabilities is on the rise, and boys make up a much bigger share than girls — nearly two-thirds — of these students. While the previous CRDC showed 17% of students had disabilities, the newest data show they made up 19% of all students enrolled in public schools. And they were suspended out of school at disproportionately high rates.
Losen says the lost days of school for these students don't just mean they're missing learning, it also means they may be losing out on key services they get during school, such as mental health counseling or physical therapy.
Disabled students are also among the least likely groups to be enrolled in Advanced Placement (AP) classes in high school. Losen says that's a longstanding pattern, in part, because of assumptions that they can't achieve at high levels. AP classes might not be the right fit for some students with intellectual disabilities, he says, but many students have disabilities that have little to do with their academic potential.
And Gopalan says these classes don't just represent how much rigor students are exposed to. "These are all gateways to college, other opportunities beyond high school. And we see gaps in opportunity and access for students with disabilities."
4. Teachers and other staff
For the first time since the 1970s, the latest CRDC gathered information about teachers' race, ethnicity and sex. It found that the workforce is 75% white, 9% Black and 11% Latino — a drastically different makeup than the students they serve.

Gopalan says the data is valuable partly because teacher diversity can play a role in student success. For example, she says some research shows that "Black students have better achievement, better school discipline outcomes, and a whole host of other outcomes when they're taught by Black teachers." And studies show that having more Black or Latino teachers can help all students.
This collection also captures the qualifications of teachers. "Research shows that access to certified and experienced teachers and to counselors has a positive effect on who finishes high school, who graduates, and who goes on to colleges," Gopalan says. Yet, more than 720,000 students go to schools where fewer than half of teachers met state certification requirements, and Black and Latino students make up 73% of those students.
5. Nonbinary student data hidden
Under President Joe Biden, the CRDC required schools to report the experiences of nonbinary students for the first time. The information was collected for the 2023-24 school year, but the Trump administration chose not to release it, citing an executive order that called for the federal government to "recognize two sexes, male and female."
"There is no Civil Rights Data Collection where they intentionally collected data and then just suppressed it," says Losen, who has been analyzing the CRDC for more than 25 years. He says students who are nonbinary are more likely to face difficulties like bullying at school. "Whatever kinds of injustices they're experiencing, we would start to see that it was beginning to be reflected in those data, and now we can't see it." According to one UCLA analysis, about 3% of children ages 13 to 17 identify as transgender nationwide, which includes nonbinary youth.
In an emailed statement, the Education Department did not answer NPR's questions about its decision to withhold data on nonbinary students, instead highlighting the Trump administration's priority to collect data about sexual offenses on school campuses.
Data for the next CRDC is being collected for the 2025-26 school year, according to the Department. While much of the survey will remain the same, all questions about nonbinary students have been removed from the list. Questions related to whether students are harassed or bullied on the basis of gender identity will also be removed.

A British father asks a Cyprus judge to avoid prison after son's fatal hotel fall
The lawyer for a British man who pleaded guilty to a charge of negligence in the fatal fall of his 3-year-old son from a hotel window in Cyprus has appealed to a judge to avoid a prison sentence
PAPHOS, Cyprus -- The lawyer for a British man who pleaded guilty to a charge of negligence in the fatal fall of his 3-year-old son from a hotel window in Cyprus appealed to a Cypriot judge on Tuesday to avoid a prison sentence, saying his loss was punishment enough.
According to evidence heard in court, the 38-year-old defendant, his son and father-in-law got ready for dinner after a day at the pool and were making their way to the elevator from their fourth-floor room at the King Evelthon hotel on July 12. The father lifted the child to check out the hotel's waterpark visible from a window when the boy somehow slipped and tumbled 12 meters (about 40 feet), falling to his death.
His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told the Paphos District Court that his client's guilty plea acknowledges a momentary lapse of judgment but that he wasn't “willfully negligent.”
“That fraction of a second will haunt him for the rest of his life,” Alexandrou told judge Froso Christodoulidou during mitigation proceedings. “This is punishment he and his family will carry with them for the rest of their lives.”
Alexandrou said the defendant — who prosecutors and the defense haven’t named throughout the proceedings — didn’t recall the circumstances of the fall because it happened so quickly. But he and his father-in-law had told investigators that they thought the glass window pane was shut.
The defendant, sitting in the dock, was visibly distraught and constantly wiped tears from his eyes as he heard the translator next to him recount the details. His parents were also sitting in the rear of the courtroom, his mother's eyes red from weeping.
Addressing the judge, Alexandrou said he wasn't arguing that the defendant be absolved of responsibility but that the court must consider “what kind of mistake was made at that point in time.”
“Justice can be served without imposing the utmost severity in sentencing,” the lawyer said.
Prosecutor Chryso Perganti said that the boy was pronounced dead in hospital a couple of hours after his fall, suffering multiple skull and bone fractures and damage to his vital organs.
He also said a blood sample taken from the defendant roughly six hours after the boy's fall showed that he had consumed alcohol but was under the legal limit. However, experts estimated that this blood alcohol level at the time of the fall may have been more than twice the legal limit.
Alexandrou countered that the defendant's alcohol consumption had no bearing on the case because there's nothing to suggest that he was impaired at the time of the incident.
The lawyer told the judge that his client, an auditor at a major U.K. firm, risks losing his job because of the disciplinary hearing and the prison sentence. He also said even if the sentence is suspended, the man could lose his license to practice.
The charge carries a maximum of four years’ imprisonment and a minimum of a fine. Imprisonment can be suspended if the sentence is three years’ imprisonment or less.
Judge Christodoulidou said she would rule on the matter on Oct. 16.
Cyprus, a former British colony, is very popular with tourists from the U.K., who make up a significant portion of the roughly 4 million holidaymakers the island nation received in recent years.
