OpenAI just posted hundreds more results on major math problems
The new results are likely to expand AI controversy roiling the mathematics community.
OpenAI has posted hundreds of solutions and progress toward 372 major math problems in a release of 722 manuscripts on GitHub, the company announced. The breakthroughs from an unreleased ChatGPT pioneer model, confirmed by a OpenAI's new advisory group, are likely to expand the Navier-Stokes AI controversy roiling the mathematical community.
The results were expected, as OpenAI said last month that its models had resolved "more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics." As part of the release, OpenAI included the model's reasoning, compute estimates and information about the number of problems attempted. The company said the "average result" required around three hours of ChatGPT Pro use.
OpenAI said it followed guidelines for release of the papers as recommended by its independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI). Those included a prompt release of results through traditional academic channels, plus details like the name of the model used, prompts, and compute costs.
"For this release, we're publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations," the company wrote. "We're continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee's guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding."
OpenAI did ignore some of board's suggestions, though. The company didn't release specific compute times for problems or which prompts it used.
Some of the key results claimed by OpenAI are a solution to the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, along with improvements to key computer algorithms and progress toward the hyper-challenging Riemann hypothesis. Nearly every paper was produced in a response to a single prompt given to a single AI agent, OpenAI told Scientific American.
The results still need to be assessed by mathematicians before their impact can be understood. And following the Navier-Stokes imbroglio (read more about that here) there is still a lot of skepticism among scientists. "Until and unless they release the model and people can replicate their results, I think you should treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified," MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland told SciAm.

Do England already have their Kane replacement - or is he yet to emerge?
- Published
Where would England be without Harry Kane?
With every record he breaks and landmark he passes, the question becomes increasingly difficult to tackle. But, now aged 33, there is a growing need for an answer.
The Bayern Munich striker became his nation's joint-highest appearance-maker on Tuesday at Wembley, netting twice in the 3-0 win over Czechia, taking his tally to 91 goals in 125 caps.
He is arguably in the form of his life. He won a league and cup double with Bayern last term - scoring 61 goals in 51 games for the German giants in 2025-26 - and he's among the favourites for the Ballon d'Or.
However, when the next European Championship kicks off in the summer of 2028, Kane will be 35. Alternatives and eventual replacements will surely be on the mind of whoever is at the helm then.
Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel said: "You will not get another Harry Kane, first of all. We look for different options and solutions."
So what are England's options in a world without him? Is the answer already in front of us - or could it be someone yet to even emerge?
- Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record 
  - Published1 day ago
- England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender 
  - Published1 day ago
'I like him as a nine' - new role for Bellingham?
Tuchel seems to think England may have an option within their ranks already in the guise of fellow superstar Jude Bellingham.
He shrugged off question marks over his place in the team ahead of the World Cup to quickly become a rival to Kane as England's most influential player.
"I like him as a nine," Tuchel admitted ahead of England's 7-0 win over Croatia. "He is a natural goalscorer and he has the hunger to be on the scoreboard.
"He wants to be there and have the decisive action, so it makes not a huge difference if he plays as a nine or a 10.
The German has certainly helped Bellingham add a productive edge to his game.
Since the start of the 2026 World Cup, the Real Madrid star has netted 10 times in 12 matches for England, having scored six times in the 48 games beforehand.
BBC Radio 5 Live's senior football reporter Ian Dennis said: "The person who is going to replace Kane has already emerged – and that's Jude Bellingham.
"We have seen it at times, when they play that false nine, Bellingham can go into that advanced role. He will also eclipse Kane in terms of appearances. This is a player who will continue to go from strength to strength."
At Real Madrid, Bellingham played frequently as a false nine in his first season for the club, with Vinicius Jr. and Rodrygo offering penetration from the wide positions.
It was Bellingham's most productive season for Real Madrid, with the numbers indicating just how much of an all-round package he's developed into now.
In a similar style, so much of Kane's good work for England comes from dropping deep, operating as a playmaker and then surging into the box to finish chances.
If England want another player who can straddle the No. 9 and No. 10 positions simultaneously, then Bellingham could be their best fit.
And, with the likes of Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze, there are no shortage of options to fill the Bellingham role.
However former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on 5 Live: "He is not a nine, Bellingham plays off others.
"I do think if England are going to play this system – and remember Kane has a long time left – I don't see Bellingham as the out and out number nine."
- Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest' 
  - Published4 days ago
What about natural number nines?
In terms of natural centre-forward replacements for Kane, England do not have much depth.
Dominic Calvert-Lewin has made a case to be Kane's back-up. He has 17 goals in 40 Premier League appearances since moving to Leeds United last summer.
However, there is a sense that Calvert-Lewin is not a dependable finisher - he underperformed by 2.13 in terms of xG in the Premier League last season - while at 29 he is not a long-term solution to Kane.
Away from the Leeds striker, there are not many centre-forwards making a case.
The only other English strikers to score in the Premier League so far this season are Nottingham Forest's Liam Delap, rebuilding his career after a difficult spell at Chelsea, and Ipswich Town's Chuba Akpom, who both have one goal each.
Across the 2026-27 season, English left-backs, with six, have more goals than English centre-forwards, with five.
Danny Welbeck was pushing for a recall last season with 13 Premier League goals but at the age of 35, his time is likely to have passed and he is certainly no long-term solution.
Ivan Toney and Ollie Watkins, previously considered by Tuchel, are both playing their football in the Saudi Pro League and were both left out of the most recent squad. Both are also already into their thirties.
Do England even need a striker?
If England do have an issue at centre-forward due to a Kane injury or suspension - or his eventual retirement - they could always opt to play without one.
Tuchel has used the tactic before, with Kai Havertz often deployed at the point of the attack during his time as Chelsea boss. Havertz scored 10 goals in the 33 league games in which he was used as a centre-forward by Tuchel.
A more fluid system has also been used to great effect by world and European champions Spain, who have deployed converted wingers Mikel Oyarzabal and Ferran Torres as strikers.
Anthony Gordon, who scored three times during the international break, could fit that particular bill. The winger was used as a striker by Newcastle United late last season and had success in the Champions League, netting 10 times in 12 appearances overall.
Who could be the next striker to break through?
There are some intriguing centre-forward options coming through.
Aston Villa's 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo scored five goals in pre-season for Villa, including one in the UEFA Super Cup against European champions Paris Saint-Germain, bullying the elite centre-back duo of Marquinhos and Willian Pacho throughout.
Madjo has been sidelined for seven weeks since that game because of injury, but he is close to making a first-team return after appearing in a friendly against Sevilla during the international break.
In the Championship, 21-year-old Will Lankshear - a Tottenham academy graduate like Kane - has hit the ground running for Middlesbrough with eight goals in 11 appearances for his new club.
Man City's Divin Mubama, on loan at Southampton, has scored five goals in 10 European under-21 Championship qualifiers, while the likes of Bristol City's Dom Ballard and Millwall's Josh Coburn are seen as young strikers with huge potential.
And Kane could yet give them time to develop having been inspired by the longevity of the newly retired Lionel Messi.
"As you see on the other end with Leo there, he's still performing at the highest level," Kane said after England's semi-final loss to Argentina in the summer. "So I never want to put a limit on these things."
England supporters will hope so. So will Tuchel. That way, the Kane conundrum is likely to be passed on to one of his successors.
"There will be someone else, but it will not be Harry or a copy of Harry," Tuchel added. "We will find a solution when it comes to it but maybe not me. It might be another 10 years."

) India is among the top countries with 90% of the world's chewing tobacco-related health burden, and South Asia is the "epicentre" of chewing tobacco, according to new research published in The Lancet Global Health journal.
Researchers estimated that chewing tobacco contributed to 251,000 deaths globally in 2023 -- there were 241 million chewing tobacco users globally, with use peaking among individuals 60 to 64 years old, they said.
The analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) and covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, distinguishes the burden of chewing tobacco from that of other forms of smokeless tobacco, the team said.
"Chewing tobacco is not a uniform public health problem, and our findings show that a relatively small number of countries bear an overwhelming share of its health burden," lead author Gabriela Gil, research scientist at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington, US, said.
"Understanding how patterns of use differ within these populations is critical to designing more effective prevention and tobacco control strategies," Gil said.
The researchers said despite decades of progress in tobacco control, the global prevalence of chewing tobacco use has remained relatively unchanged. Stroke and lip and oral cavity cancer were found to comprise much of the health loss attributable to chewing tobacco use globally.
South Asia had the highest concentration of chewing tobacco use, with 14.6% of people aged 15 years and above chewing tobacco products in 2023.
The region accounted for 2,10,000 chewing tobacco-related deaths -- about 84% of the global total, the study estimated.
However, more than 90% of chewing tobacco-related deaths and disability burden among men was found to occur in 10 countries, including India, Bangladesh, China, Pakistan and the US.
Among women, more than 90% of the burden was concentrated in countries, including India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Myanmar and China.
The researchers said the figures reflect total deaths and disability, meaning countries with larger populations may account for a greater share of the burden even if their rates are not the highest.
Patterns of chewing tobacco use also varied substantially by age and sex.
"These findings show why chewing tobacco control cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach," senior author Emmanuela Gakidou, professor in the department of health metrics sciences at IHME, said.
"Prevention and cessation strategies need to reflect how patterns of use differ by country, age, and sex, as well as the cultural and social factors that shape tobacco use in each setting," Gakidou said. PTI KRS

Anyone with ovaries who lives long enough will experience menopause. While menopause is a natural transition in midlife, it can strongly affect a person’s quality of life and their current and future risk of heart disease, osteoporosis and other issues. So you might think that whether someone is experiencing or has gone through menopause would be noted in their medical records.
But when we and our colleagues examined the electronic medical records of almost 240,000 women, only 12% included mention of menopause, even though more than half the women reported separately that they were experiencing this transition. Our findings, published in the journal Menopause, reveal a major gap in how clinicians capture basic information about women’s health.
The menopausal women we examined are from a broader group of 400,000 who participated in the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide study run by the National Institutes of Health to compile a wide range of health data from at least 1 million Americans. We looked at how information about menopause was included in electronic health records and how this information differed by demographics, such as age, education, race and income.
Because study participants filled out health surveys upon enrolling, we could track discrepancies between their own reports of menopause and what was in their medical records. Age at menopause and symptoms, such as hot flashes or sleep disturbances, were also largely missing from the medical records and survey.
Missing links
Many aspects of menopause, and the diversity in women’s experiences with it, remain poorly understood.
For example, when menopause begins, as well as how disruptive its symptoms are, can vary greatly. Some women experience extreme hot flashes, sleep disruptions and brain fog, while others do not. One woman may go through natural menopause at age 45, and another at 54. Both ages would be considered normal, but that timing can affect current and future health in distinct ways.
Electronic medical records offer an unmatched opportunity to investigate these knowledge gaps, enabling researchers to study the experience of hundreds of thousands or even millions of people using routinely collected data.
Such large-scale studies may shed light on how menopause symptoms change over time and who is more likely to experience them; how markers of heart disease, bone health or mental health track with menopause; how social determinants of health, such as ethnicity and access to healthcare, affect someone’s lived experience of menopause; and countless other unanswered questions.
Closing the data gap
Our study is not the first to point out how inconsistently menopause status and symptoms are recorded in healthcare settings and electronic health records. But it systematically highlights the enormity of the gap, showing that menopause is often not even recorded at all.
It’s not clear why menopause is so rarely documented in electronic health records. It may be because menopause is not a disease, so it does not generally occur to clinicians to note it as a diagnostic code. It may feel obvious or irrelevant to diagnose or measure. It’s possible that patients themselves often don’t bring it up unless their symptoms are severe. Healthcare providers routinely ask middle-aged patients about their reproductive health – for example, when they had their last menstrual period – but this information rarely ends up getting documented in the electronic health record.
As we see it, not capturing this information is a colossal missed opportunity to drive vital research and improve personalized healthcare. Our team is developing a short, simple questionnaire about menopause status and symptoms for patients to fill out as they check in for medical appointments. These responses could then be added to their medical records for use by both their healthcare team and researchers. We are also developing a computer-based approach to infer menopause-related information from other data in a woman’s health record or genetics.
Finally, we are exploring the All of Us dataset to identify systematic differences – for example, in patients’ cultural background or income level, specific health system practices, urban versus rural settings – that might be linked with whether menopause data gets recorded in medical records. These associations can point to targeted ways to encourage its collection.
It’s impossible to research, and treat, what’s not measured. Capturing the menopause transition is an essential step to improving healthcare for women in midlife.
Audrey Hendricks, University of Colorado Anschutz and Nanette Santoro, University of Colorado Anschutz

Detergent, chemical found in milk as Maharashtra FDA cracks adulteration network
The Maharashtra FDA and Pune Rural Police say they have uncovered an organised milk adulteration network in Pune district after raids and laboratory tests. The probe has traced alleged links from adulterating substances to dairies, collection centres and processors as the crackdown widens.
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cracked an organised milk adulteration network in Pune district, uncovering the use of detergent and Nonylphenol Ethoxylate in milk samples.
The investigation, launched as part of a special campaign against milk and milk-product adulteration, began in the Manchar area of Pune district following confidential information about the supply and use of substances to prepare synthetic or adulterated milk.
On July 4, a joint team of the FDA and Pune Rural Police's Local Crime Branch raided M/s Navkar Distributors in Bhoramala, Avasari Khurd, in Ambegaon taluka. Officials found various types of whey powder, whey permeate powder, detergent, emulsifier and other substances suspected to be used for adulterating milk.
Samples and stocks bearing names including Sonai, Mlekpol, Prabhat Dairy, Milky Mist, Paras and Govardhan were collected and seized. Detergent, emulsifier and whey powder suspected to be adulterants were also seized. A case, Crime No. 215/2026, was subsequently registered at Manchar Police Station.
During questioning, the main accused allegedly revealed the method used for adulteration. According to the FDA, skimmed milk powder was used to increase solids-not-fat (SNF), whey powder to increase protein-related components, edible oil to raise fat content, and emulsifiers and detergent to facilitate mixing of different components.
The probe was then expanded to suppliers and stockists of these substances, as well as milk collection and chilling centres and other establishments in the supply chain.
A major finding came from the analysis of an emulsifier sample collected during the investigation. The FDA laboratory detected Nonylphenol Ethoxylate in the sample.
The probe also found the chemical in milk samples. On July 6, officials inspected M/s Akash Dairy Farm in Manchar, Ambegaon, where milk from M/s Pirsai Milk and Milk Product and other dairies was allegedly being packed and sold.
Six milk samples were collected and sent for analysis. According to the FDA laboratory report dated September 28, all six samples tested positive for detergent. A supplementary report also detected Alphox-200 Ethoxylate, identified as Nonylphenol Ethoxylate, in all six samples.
The samples were also found to have fat and SNF levels below the prescribed standards, the FDA said.
The investigation has also been extended to the milk processing chain. According to the FDA, the adulterated milk was prima facie linked to M/s Indapur Dairy and Milk Products Ltd, also known as Sonai Dairy, at Gokhali in Indapur, with the supply chain from suppliers to milk collection and processing centres being traced.
The FDA has registered two more cases in Malshiras as part of the wider crackdown. A total of 16,730 litres of milk, valued at around Rs 6.69 lakh, was destroyed during the action.
The department said the investigation is continuing to identify all persons and establishments involved in the network, from suppliers of adulterating substances to milk collection, chilling and processing centres.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

Pennsylvania’s explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it’s the largest on record since 1991.
Pennsylvania’s health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April, when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.
Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths—a newborn, a 6-week-old, an 18-year-old, a 20-year-old, and a 40-year-old. All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, measles outbreaks and cases have come roaring back in the past few years. A large outbreak in Texas that spanned January–August 2025 ended with 762 cases, while an outbreak in South Carolina ended in April with 997 cases, the previous record holder. Pennsylvania exceeds that handily with its 1,066 outbreak-linked cases as of today. With 34 new infections reported since Monday, the outbreak does not appear to be close to ending.
Measles emergency
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. Elimination is earned and maintained with vaccination rates that prevent continuous transmission of the virus during a 12-month period. In November, experts at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)—which acts as a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data on whether the US has lost its measles elimination status. Experts widely expect the US has lost the status. Canada lost its elimination status in 2025.

Artificial, the new comedy-drama about OpenAI and the artificial intelligence arms race, is a movie of weird walks.
As OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, Russian actor Yuri Borisov clomps around, like a geeky Frankensteinian monster. As the controversial OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield bounces and skips boyishly—a gait that Altman himself recently commended for its accuracy. And as Elon Musk, Ike Barinholtz puts on a loping swagger, commanding rooms of computer nerds like some sort of alpha gorilla (a semblance matched by his long, pouting faces, which call to mind those old Bored Ape NFTs).
During the movie’s post-premiere Q&A earlier this week at the New York Film Festival, Barinholtz wryly described his character as “a person who walks normally.” Such are the awkward saunters of the march of history in the making.
Artificial, directed by Luca Guadagnino, waltzed into NYFF with some controversy clinging to it. The film was originally set to be released by AmazonMGM, which conspicuously dropped it this summer after Amazon struck a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. (Indie house Neon swooped in to pick it up.) NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim referenced “the circumstances” around the film in his onstage introduction.
That OpenAI may have brooked issues with Artificial makes sense. The film is almost completely unflattering, depicting Altman and other OpenAI stakeholders—as well as all the major drivers of the AI boom—as vain, reckless, and insufferably boring. Where 2010’s The Social Network succeeded in making Silicon Valley computer savants look like robust titans of industry and architects of the future, Artificial works to opposing ends. It depicts its tech titans as self-regarding dweebs.
Comparisons to David Fincher’s Facebook drama are inevitable. There’s the subject matter, of course. And the fact that both films feature Garfield in a lead role. (It should be said that Artificial is really more of a biopic of Sutskever, here depicted as both the prime mover of the current AI wave and its nagging moral conscience, than it is of Altman.) But Guadagnino and writer-producer Simon Rich’s approach to the material feels diametrically opposed to Fincher’s. The Social Network was a steely, polished, wordy drama. Artificial is pitched as a black comedy that verges on the surreal.
Guadagnino, best known in Hollywood for the coming-of-age drama Call Me by Your Name and the three-way tennis romance Challengers, has mastered a strain of tense eroticism. There are shades of that in Artificial, in Altman’s seductive wooing of Sutskever’s character. But the film is, for the most part, literally and figuratively sexless.
The images are plain, and even a little ugly. You can almost feel Guadagnino’s more rococo style begging to break out. A slo-mo sequence of a room of gawky programmers dousing each other in bottles of Jarritos, celebrating their AI’s latest self-learning benchmark, is stickily unsexy. A climactic scene of Altman and his OpenAI lackeys confronting Sutskever on a sloping San Francisco street recalls the green-screen backdrops of Tommy Wiseau’s cult classic The Room. After the screening, Guadagnino claimed the story captured a different strain of desire—what he described as “the desire to prevail.”
It’s a need many viewers might share, as leaders in the AI industry (including Altman) appear united in tamping down the technology’s acceleration. Artificial intelligence, we are told, is developing so rapidly, and is becoming so sophisticated, that it risks compromising life on Earth as we know it. In a recent interview with WIRED, former Anthropic AI employee Jacob Coxon alleged that his former colleagues have described the next few years as the potential “endgame” for humanity itself. Another Anthropic researcher claimed that there’s a chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. (The odds were set below 10 percent, which still seems extremely high.)
Artificial stages these tensions as a kind of a high moral drama. Borisov’s well-meaning researcher—depicted as being temperamentally incapable of lying—pleads for safeguards, slow-downs, and AI’s “alignment” with humanity’s broader interests. Meanwhile, the case for exponential technological and capital growth is argued by, well, basically everyone else.
Even the idea of safety itself as saleable. In one scene, concerns about OpenAI’s capacity for serious harm is framed as being beneficial only to the company’s bottom line. Sounding alarm bells signals transparency and due diligence. And the harmful capacity itself is seen as proof positive of the technology’s advancement. It’s win-win. And it’s also no-win.
Artificial makes a persuasive, and frustrating, point about the ongoing AI contest. Pick a metaphor: The train has already left the station, the horses have fled the barn, the toothpaste is out of the tube. The technology already exists. And so, as with nukes in the last century, it becomes not a question of the power itself but who is allowed to harness it, and how. (In his post-Anthropic exit interview, Coxon directly compared the company to the Manhattan Project.)
Questions of ethics become academic, or just annoying, when everyone involved is playing by a different rulebook. If it’s not OpenAI that controls computing’s future, it will be Anthropic, or Google, or Elon Musk. Or, worst of all—at least according to the Trump administration—China. (An early scene in Artificial sees Sutskever and his mentor, Nobel laureate computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, played by Mark Rylance, rebuff the advances of a Chinese investor eager to use their neural network technology for drones and face-recognition systems.)
It may be hard for the average moviegoer, who may only engage with AI for email rewriting or calendar organization, to gauge just how seriously to take Artificial’s alarmist warnings. Not least of all because basically every character in the film is depicted as at least completely self-serving, if not sociopathic. And of course, one may naturally wince a little bit at a star-studded Hollywood movie raising these alarms, with a lavish premiere at a Rolex-sponsored film festival and a glitzy afterparty attended by stars, famous comedians, and notable filmmakers (including octogenarian Taxi Driver screenwriter Paul Schrader, who recently publicly confessed to being dumped by an “AI girlfriend”).
As a message movie, Artificial seems likely only to confirm the worst misgivings of AI doomers, while riling its diehard boosters. It is, however, genuinely funny in places, regarding the bulk of our future’s self-appointed engineers with withering contempt, from their dorky parties to their weird walks.
It was a stance embraced by Barinholtz, who offered the premiere-night audience his own half-hearted, sarcastic reassurance: “The future is bright! We’re all gonna be fine!” Cue a round of very nervous laughter.

Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately acknowledged that the Iran war and rising fuel prices are creating difficulties for his campaign, telling donors and lobbyists that several factors affecting the race were beyond his control, according to Axios.
Paxton, Texas attorney general and a close ally of President Donald Trump, as per the report, made the remarks during a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, DC, last month.
Axios said it has obtained an audio recording of the meeting from an attendee who opposed Paxton and was granted anonymity because the event was private.
Asked what issues were weighing on his campaign, Paxton said the problem was not tariffs but the war and rising gasoline and diesel prices, according to the recording obtained by the news outlet.
He specifically pointed to diesel prices of more than $6 a gallon, saying higher fuel costs were being felt by consumers and were contributing to increased food prices and other expenses.
Paxton described affordability as the biggest problem facing his campaign and linked it to difficulties with his polling numbers.
When an attendee noted that Paxton could not stop the war, the Republican candidate agreed and said he had no control over gas prices.
He also acknowledged that several factors affecting a federal Senate race were outside his control.
“I don’t make the decisions,” Paxton said, according to the media outlet, adding that he did not know what was behind some of the decisions.
Paxton pointed to his proposed tax-cut plan as a way to address affordability concerns.
The plan includes new deductions related to housing and healthcare, as well as an expansion of the child tax credit, according to Axios.
“I’m just trying to figure out ways I can help people,” Paxton said, adding that his role would be to propose legislation.
The Paxton campaign rejected the significance of the comments, telling Axios that the attorney general was simply acknowledging the high cost of gasoline and diesel and the pressure those prices were putting on Texans.
The campaign said Trump was working to bring prices down and argued that Paxton would go to Washington to support those efforts while seeking to put more money into families’ pockets.
Trump is scheduled to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday.
Paxton is running against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico after defeating Republican Senator John Cornyn in the May primary runoff.
A Talarico victory would mark the first time a Democrat has been elected to the US Senate from Texas since the 1980s.
Paxton has been among Trump's most loyal political allies. Trump backed Paxton during the Republican primary despite appeals from Senate Republicans to support Cornyn.

Japanese city accused of inflating census as country's population shrinks
- Published
Japanese authorities are investigating officials of a city in the central region over claims they inflated population numbers in the most recent census.
Police raided the city hall of Toyama on Saturday after the central government filed a criminal complaint accusing officials of falsely adding more than 2,000 people.
The census is used to calculate funding from the central government. According to a city estimate, Toyama may have received 60 million yen ($378,000; £285,000) more than it should have.
Japan is grappling with declining population that is also rapidly aging.
Last year, Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating. About three in 10 residents are aged 65 or older.
According to Japan's internal affairs ministry, Toyama's actual population last year was 399,197, down from the allegedly inflated figure of 402,133 released in May.
Preliminary investigations suggest that officials involved had falsely added more than 2,000 residents by altering the sizes of households census takers had initially marked as empty.
Toyama's Mayor Hirohisa Fujii said the citys government would cooperate with the investigation, but denied that there was any instruction from senior officials to inflate census numbers.
"I will take due responsibility at the appropriate time," he said at a press conference last Friday, the Japan Times reported.
Under Japanese law, people found guilty of falsifying statistics can be fined or jailed for up to six months.
Officials at Japan's Statistics Bureau expressed outrage when news of the suspected violation first broke last month.
"It is extremely regrettable that such inappropriate handling occurred in the country's most basic and important statistical survey," Akihiro Tamura, director of the bureau's census division, had said.
Japan conducts its national census every five years.
The latest numbers show the country's population, including foreign residents, at nearly 123 million as of 1 October 2025, down 2.5%, or around 3.17 million, from 2020.

Frontier AI research startup FYDY (Fuzzy Dynamics), which is operating in stealth mode, is in advanced talks to raise $12 Mn (about ₹115 Cr) in its maiden funding round, sources told Inc42. Lightspeed Venture Partners and General Catalyst are co-leading the round, the sources said. While questions sent to FYDY didn’t elicit any response, Lightspeed Venture Partners and General Catalyst did not respond. As per FYDY’s LinkedIn page, the startup was incorporated in 2025. It has five cofounders – Alapan Chaudhuri, Shivansh Subramanian, Anvay Karmore, Tanishq Chaudhary, and Zeeshan Ahmed. FYDY says its founding team includes ICPC World Finalists and Physics & Astronomy Olympiad alumni. The San Francisco-headquartered startup’s employees are spread across India and the US. It is currently hiring researchers and engineers, among other roles. FYDY describes itself as a frontier AI research business operating in stealth. It is developing “cognitive machines” that learn continuously from experience, with the long-term goal of building safe artificial superintelligence capable of understanding and acting autonomously in the real world. FYDY has also launched OpenScientist, an AI research studio currently in private beta. According to its website, the startup initially built the platform for its own research and is rolling it out to a small group of labs and researchers. The platform is designed to help users search research papers and databases, explore mathematical problems, run experiments, and analyse data. “We are working with leading researchers across reinforcement learning, world models, robotics and neuroscience. These are the fields we believe converge into machine cognition,” it says on its website. The funding talks come as Lightspeed and General Catalyst continue to back AI startups across scientific research and enterprise applications. In August, AI-powered materials discovery startup Discovered Materials announced a $9 Mn seed round led by Lightspeed India Partners. The startup is developing AI agents to automate semiconductor materials research, including simulation, synthesis, and experimental validation. Meanwhile, Sol Foundry emerged from stealth last month with $4 Mn from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners, DeVC, Peercheque, and Kunal Shah. The startup is building an AI assistant that acts on commitments made over email, preparing research, documents, and other tasks for users to approve. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, AI startups raised $438 Mn across 35 deals during the quarter, making AI the most funded sector. Funding rose 265% YoY, although capital remained largely concentrated in startups building AI applications.

It seems that every other week, we're getting a new cast announcement for the "Harry Potter" TV series that's hitting HBO — most recently, Kit Harington was announced as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two.
But we're getting ahead of ourselves.
Season one of the show, which is set to drop on December 25, will cover the events of JK Rowling's first wizarding book, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," which was first published in 1997. If you live outside the US, you'll know it as "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone," which HBO is going with this time around.
Since HBO's CEO Casey Bloys promised that each season will "dive deep into each of the iconic books," Potterheads expect the TV series to include details that had to be cut from the films for time constraints.
Here are the 10 biggest things we want to see included in season one of "Harry Potter."
The first chapter from Vernon's POV
The first chapter of "Harry Potter" begins not from Harry's perspective, but from his obnoxious Uncle Vernon's. The first chapter follows a typical day in the life of Vernon — except this day isn't typical at all, as it's the day that Lord Voldemort was defeated by his baby nephew, Harry Potter, though he doesn't know it yet.
This first chapter sets the tone for the book series, as it explains how the wizarding world (sort of) blends in with the Muggle world, establishes how bigoted the Dursleys are toward their magical relatives, and shows just how famous Harry is in the wizarding world.
In comparison, the movie begins with Professor Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall rolling up to the Dursleys' house and dropping Harry off.
Speaking of that scene …
More of Harry's life pre-Hogwarts
A not-insignificant chunk of the "Sorcerer's Stone" book is spent explaining what Harry's day-to-day life in the Muggle world is like, including the unexplainable things that happen to Harry, like his hair growing out after a particularly bad haircut or how he somehow jumps up onto the ceiling of his school to avoid bullies.
Also, hilariously, when Harry starts receiving letters addressed to the Cupboard Under the Stairs, the Dursleys, fearing that someone is aware of their abuse, let Harry move into the second bedroom, which had once been occupied by Dudley's toys.
There's also supposed to be a very awkward month between Hagrid's first meeting with Harry and taking him to Diagon Alley, and then the Dursleys dropping him off at King's Cross, which would add some comedy to the proceedings.
A little Sirius Black foreshadowing
In the film (and the book), Harry gets dropped off by Hagrid, the kind half-giant groundskeeper at Hogwarts, who scoops him up from his parents' house and brings him to the Dursleys via a giant, flying motorcycle.
In the movie, Dumbledore asks if there's been any trouble, and Hagrid just replies that Harry fell asleep over Bristol.
However, in the book, Hagrid mentions that he borrowed the bike from "young Sirius Black." This is a small detail, but one that will pay off in two seasons from now, since, of course, Sirius is Harry's godfather, which we don't learn until "Prisoner of Azkaban."
Seeding Sirius' name early on in the TV show is a fun Easter egg for devotees and a little thing to chew on for newbies.
Harry and Draco's first meeting
In the movie, Harry meets Draco for the first time at Hogwarts, right before the sorting ceremony, and he coolly tells Draco he can tell who the "wrong sort" of people are for himself, after Draco tries to befriend the famous Harry Potter.
In the book, this takes place in Diagon Alley, when the two are shopping for robes. They have a brief conversation, during which neither introduces themselves, but Draco insults Hagrid.
They meet once more on the Hogwarts Express, which is when Draco learns who the boy he spoke to at Madam Malkin's was — and they have the same "wrong sort of people" conversation.
Harry's first meeting with Draco is important for a few reasons.
One: It makes the reader and Harry nervous that everyone at Hogwarts is a major snob, so it's a huge relief when Harry meets Ron.
Two: It's effective exposition, showing us that there are hierarchies within the wizarding world based on blood status.
Three: It helps Harry and the reader understand just how much Harry doesn't know about this world he's entering — crucially, this is when he learns about Quidditch.
More of the friendships between Harry and his classmates
Since the movies are pressed for time with all the plot they have to get through, the friendships Harry forms outside Ron and Hermione take a back seat.
But in the books, Harry is relatively popular — at least, in the first book. He's good friends with the other Gryffindor boys, Seamus Finnegan and Dean Thomas, and is protective of Neville Longbottom. He also has strong bonds with the Gryffindor Quidditch team.
We hope that the TV show is able to expand upon the other students at Hogwarts outside the core trio.
Peeves
This might be a little bit of a cheat, since Peeves has already been cast (Peter Serafinowicz will play him in the series), but the omission of Peeves from the entire film series, not just the first movie, is probably one of "Potter" fans' most disliked choices.
This devious poltergeist takes pride in messing with students, professors, and ghosts alike, but when it comes time to protect the residents of Hogwarts from truly evil forces, Peeves is up to the task.
Also, as the series gets darker, it's always nice to have some comic relief from Peeves.
All the Norbert drama
Hagrid acquiring a dragon egg, raising Norbert, and then having to give him away, is a memorable, but truncated plot in the film adaptation, and we don't get to see what happens to the dragon — Hagrid tells the gang that Dumbledore arranged for him to be sent to a dragon colony in Romania.
In the book, it's a way bigger deal. First, it's very illegal for Hagrid to have this egg in the first place, so the stakes are high. Harry, Ron, and Hermione come up with a plan to smuggle Norbert out of the castle at midnight via the Astronomy Tower, where Charlie will pick him up, using the Invisibility Cloak; however, Ron misses all the fun when Norbert bites him and his hand gets infected.
It's one of the more tense chapters in the book, especially when they're busted by Draco, McGonagall, and Filch, the grimy old caretaker. It leads to Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Neville, who snuck out to warn them, losing 50 points apiece for Gryffindor, leading the rest of the house to ostracize them.
Other centaurs, besides Firenze
Harry meets Firenze in the Forbidden Forest while he's completing detention for the Norbert debacle. He rescues him from what we learn later is Professor Quirrell and Lord Voldemort, while they're drinking unicorn blood.
In the movie, Harry only meets Firenze, who leaves Harry with a warning that evil things lurk in the forest.
In the book, Firenze lets Harry ride him, which enrages another centaur, Bane. Yet another centaur, Ronan, has to calm him down.
The centaurs have a small but key role in the story, and also show that the wizarding world doesn't have the strongest record with non-humans, which becomes a bigger deal in "Order of the Phoenix."
It's also interesting to learn about a community living in the Forbidden Forest, expanding the universe.
More Potters in the Mirror of Erised
This is a small but bittersweet detail that's left out of the movie adaptation. In both versions of the story, Harry discovers the Mirror of Erised (yes, desire spelled backward) by mistake while he's running away from Filch.
In the movie, Harry looks into it and sees his parents standing proudly behind him. It's heartbreaking, but the book version is even sadder.
In the book, Harry doesn't just see his parents — he sees his entire extended family going back generations, most of whom he's unfamiliar with, as his Aunt Petunia is ashamed of her sister and brother-in-law and kept Harry from learning about his family.
We don't really learn much about the Potters (or the Evanses) in the books or the films, but the TV series is the perfect time to expand what little we know about them.
The potions challenge to get to the Philosopher's Stone
At the film's climax, Harry, Ron, and Hermione decide to take matters into their own hands to protect the Sorcerer's (or Philosopher's) Stone. To do so, they need to pass a set of challenges, each designed by a different professor.
In the film, we see the trio go up against Hagrid's (his three-headed dog, Fluffy), Professor Sprout's (the Devil's Snare plant), Professor Flitwick's (the room filled with flying keys), Professor McGonagall's (Wizard Chess), and, finally, Dumbledore's (the Mirror of Erised).
In the book, there are two more challenges, though one is more significant than the other.
First, the lesser one: Professor Quirrell's, which Harry and Hermione encounter after Wizard Chess. This one's easy — Quirrell put a troll in the dungeon, and he already incapacitated it, so they don't have to do anything, though it does give us a hint about who's really behind the plot to steal the stone.
The other one is Professor Snape's, who has devised a logic puzzle with a set of potions: One will send you through, one will let you go back, two are wine, and three are poison.
Hermione figures it out and sends Harry through, while she goes back to help Ron.
It's a shame this got cut, since both Harry and Ron got their time to shine in the movie with a challenge each, whereas this one is Hermione's specialty. Instead, her moment in the film is with the Devil's Snare, but in the book, that's more of a team effort.
So, we hope to see Hermione get her big moment. She's the brightest witch of her age, after all.

Trump tells Texas crowd that wife Melania calls him ‘sir’
Bizarre rant kicks off rally for embattled GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton

President Donald Trump on Wednesday told attendees at a rally in Texas that his wife of 21 years, Melania Trump, addresses him the same way as one of his employees rather than using his name or any other term of endearment.
The president was speaking in support of Texas Attorney General and GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton when he began an extended rant alleging that Paxton’s opponent, Democratic state representative James Talarico, is a vegan, which Talarico denies.
But he quickly went off on a tangent about the pronunciation of “vegan” and recalled being corrected on it by his wife.
“You know, my wife told me ‘sir, you have to do me a favor — it’s not vay-gan, it’s vee-gan,” he said.
Talarico, the 37-year-old seminarian who is currently leading Paxton in most recent polls of the Texas Senate race, has repeatedly denied subscribing to a vegan or vegetarian diet — a lifestyle choice that would be politically perilous in a cattle-raising state such as Texas.
But Paxton’s campaign — and Trump — have repeatedly claimed the Democrat abstains from animal products.
The president continued repeating the scurrilous claim about Talarico’s diet, telling the partisan crowd that his claims to a carnivorous lifestyle are fabricated.
“Now he says he loves meat, but he's a vegan — see, Melania? I got that right,” he said.
“He's a vegan. He wants to eat a piece of lettuce, a little piece of lettuce, please.”
Trump then suggested that a recent absence from the campaign trail on Talarico’s part is because of gastrointestinal illness brought on by eating meat for political purposes.
“You know where he is? He's sick because he's been forced to eat meat for political reasons, and he's throwing up all over the place. He's sick,” he said.
He continued with the bizarre story, accusing Talarico of having “forced himself to go to barbecues” and “stuff some little ribs down his throat.”
“But he'd eat, and then what would happen? He'd go to the back of the tent, and he'd throw up all over the place because he doesn't want meat,” Trump claimed.
The GOP’s meat-based attack on the Texas Democrat stems from comments he’d made to the Texas Humane Legislation Network in which he said reducing meat consumption was "existential" for combating climate change.
At no point did Talarico claim to abstain from meat himself, but that hasn’t stopped Republicans from alleging without evidence that he does not partake.
For his part, Talarico has said he has "been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton's first indictment,” a reference to the Republican’s long-running legal troubles.
Trump’s appearance in San Antonio on Wednesday was his fourth trip to the Lone Star State in the last six weeks and comes as Talarico has built a lead over Paxton that, if it holds, could make him the first Democrat to win a statewide election there since Ann Richards won the governorship 36 years ago, in 1990.
A recent Sienna College poll showed Talarico with a 51-45 percent lead over Paxton, while a separate Fox News poll also showed the Democrat leading Paxton by a margin of 51 percent to 49 percent.
The last Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas was Lloyd Bentsen, who won re-election to a fourth term in 1988 even as he lost at the top of the ticket as then-Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis’ running-mate in that year’s presidential race.
Bentsen would resign four years later to become Treasury Secretary in the Clinton administration. His appointed Democratic replacement, Robert Krueger, served in the Senate for three months before losing a special election to Republican Kay Bailey Hutchison.

Watch: Why is the UK reviewing its Chagos Islands deal?
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said, after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".
The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.
The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Caroline Hawley looks at why the government's agreement with Mauritius has stalled.

As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.
The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.
“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”
Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.
It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.
“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”
With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Serum Institute of India’s recombinant Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac has received World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification.
The vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years. Inclusion on the WHO list of prequalified vaccines allows Cervavac to be procured by United Nations agencies, Serum Institute said.
The vaccine was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. It is the 32nd WHO prequalification for products/biologicals received by Serum Institute, the vaccine maker said.
“WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this indigenously developed vaccine reach this achievement,” CEO Adar Poonawalla said.
Approved for use in India by DCGI
Cervavac has been approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). The vaccine is administered for the prevention of diseases caused by the four HPV types — prevention of anal cancer in boys and young men, and cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women. It is also indicated in preventing genital warts, as applicable to the indicated population.
The vaccine is administered intramuscularly and available in 1-dose vials of 0.5 ml and 2-dose vials of 1.0 ml presentations.

Canada yanks sponsorship of disinformation conference discussing U.S. as a threat
Global Affairs says it took issue with the framing of some of panels
The federal government has withdrawn sponsorship of a European disinformation conference that includes panels discussing the U.S. government as a foreign interference risk.
Samantha Lafleur, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada (GAC), said the government took issue with the framing of some panels at the event organized by EU DisinfoLab, a non-profit based in Brussels.
The conference features panels about the U.S. as a source of "foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI)," a phenomenon where foreign governments or actors on their behalf manipulate information to confuse, divide or mislead the public and erode confidence in institutions.
GAC — Ottawa's diplomatic arm — Lithuania's Foreign Ministry and the European External Action Service were initially listed as supporters of the annual conference largely attended by researchers and civil society organizations.
The government of Canada logo was covered up on signs spotted around the anti-disinformation conference. (Submitted)
As the gathering got underway in Vilnius, Lithuania, on Wednesday, their names were covered up on signs spotted around the conference, according to photos shared with CBC News. As of writing, the French government remains a sponsor.
In a statement to CBC News, GAC did not deny that it had concerns with describing the U.S. as a foreign interference threat.
"Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference," wrote Lafleur.
She did not respond to questions about particular changes GAC took issue with or whether the U.S. raised concerns.
According to the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, the description of Wednesday's panel discussing how to push back on the U.S. as a foreign interference threat appears to have been unchanged since Sept. 9.
GAC no longer chairing Arctic panel
A GAC official also pulled out of chairing a session on disinformation in the Arctic scheduled for Thursday, said presenter Ben Shultz with the American Sunlight Project.
The panel proposes to talk about Greenland and "growing evidence that the United States has, in specific Arctic contexts, operated as a FIMI actor."
Shultz shared the initial plan for the panel from months ago, which includes talking about the U.S. as a foreign interference actor.
He called three governments withdrawing a "shock" and questioned whether they were pressured.
"Thankfully every speaker has still shown up, which is awesome, and I think a testament to the resolve of the research community. But it's definitely put a bit of a damper on the atmosphere," he said in an interview.
