OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.
Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generate parts of the wording of the email, including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.
OpenAI was contacted for comment.
An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.
The company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.
OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.
Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.
During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.
“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.
Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”
Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.
The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.
“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”
The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.
“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.
“Best, OpenAI Security Team.”
Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.
“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.
“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”
Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.
The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.
“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.
“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”

Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic. SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem.
Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.

The government on Wednesday (October 8, 2026) reconstituted the Press Council of India (PCI) with the addition of 13 members, mostly editors and working journalists.
The PCI is headed by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai (retd) and it has 14 members, including five MPs, six representatives from newspaper owners and three experts from the Bar Council of India (BCI), University Grants Commission (UGC) and the Sahitya Akademi.
Now, the government has nominated six editors and seven working journalists, other than editors, as members of the PCI.
"In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (a) of sub-section (3) and sub-section (5) of section 5 read with sub-section (1) of section 6 of the Press Council Act, 1978 (37 of 1978), the Central Government hereby nominates the following members to the Press Council of India," a notification issued by the Information and Broadcasting Ministry said.
Those who were nominated in the Working Journalists (Editors Category) are — Pradeep Kumar Jain, Sayed Raza Husain Rizvi, Ankur Dua, Aparna Shukla, Raj Parwana/ Narender Singh and Vinod Bajpai.
Those who were nominated in the Working Journalists (Other Than Editors) are — Vinod Kohli, Geetartha Pathak, Prajnananda Chaudhuri, Kingshuk Pramanik, C K Nayak, Prasanna Kumar Mohanty and Bijoy Kakchingtabam.
The PCI, a statutory autonomous body, has been set up under the Press Council Act, 1978, mainly to preserve the freedom of the Press and improve the standards of newspapers and news agencies in the country.

Two Indian cartoonists, Satish Acharya and Manjul, recently revealed that their Instagram accounts and posts were withheld in India, following orders from the government. While the former’s account was restored on October 6, the latter’s post remains unavailable in India.
On September 23, The Indian Express reported that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning electoral-roll management and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), including changes to Form 6, voter deletions and restorations, the centralisation of electoral-roll data, and appeals against decisions in West Bengal.
The investigation, based on internal notes and correspondence reviewed by the newspaper, showed that the two commissioners repeatedly said certain decisions had been taken without their knowledge or approval by chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with Sandhu at one point describing an SIR-related change as “unauthorised and illegal.” Both Acharya and Manjul had posted cartoons satirising this case.

On September 23, Acharya posted an illustration on Kumar and the SIR controversy. Five days later, on September 28, his account was restricted in India.
However, his profile was still available on Facebook and X, and the said toon was still visible on both platforms.
After his account was banned, on September 28, Acharya posted screenshots of notifications received by Meta, which said that several of his earlier satirical posts were also being banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
On the same day, he posted the screenshot of his account getting restricted in India, contrasting it with a screenshot of Modi’s comment that “cartoons have healing power and cartoonists are closer to God”.
Speaking to Alt News, Acharya said he found out about his account being restricted while checking news reports on the increasing banning of accounts critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. “I thought of checking my own Instagram account status and found that a list of posts were restricted in India, some of them were posted in 2023-24. By the end of day, I found that my entire profile has been restricted in India,” he said.
“For the last one decade, I have regularly faced restrictions on my cartoons on different social media platforms. (Their) aim was to restrict the reach…mostly during elections or major protests like CAA protests & farmers’ protests. This is the first time that my entire profile was restricted in India. It’s quite shameful that they (the government) are scared that the narratives created by the regime over the last two decades will be demolished by cartoons, journalists, and comedians,” he added.
He said that his reach has been affected after the ban, adding that he written to Meta’s grievance cell.

A report by The Indian Express, published on August 18, revealed that between March and July, the government issued a blocking order for online content every 68 seconds on average, which amounted to 1,275 such cases daily and around 2 lakh cases over a period of five months.
According to that report, this government takedowns surged specifically after the Cockroach Janta Party-led students’ protest against the NEET exam irregularities in June and July. Although the government took down social media posts from Facebook, Instagram and YouTube as well, Instagram faced maximum content restrictions given that its user demographic is mostly the Gen-Z. According to the report, out of the total blocking orders, 1,00,000 such orders were for Instagram only while Facebook and YouTube accounted for 80,000 and 15,000 takedown orders, respectively.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Alt News had earlier reported that in February, the government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. The amendment reduced the time available to social media platforms to remove or disable access to unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a valid court order or a “reasoned intimation” from the appropriate government or its authorised agency. This change was notified through a press brief on July 22.
Although the order focused predominantly on countering harms caused by AI generated content and information, critics believe that the amendments have served as a tool to curb anti-establishment content. In our reportage, we found that most of the blocking orders were issued through the Union Home Ministry’s Sahyog portal, a platform created to send such notices, under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000. These orders were issued by various central and state government agencies. Meta has also integrated its Application Programming Interface (API) with the Sahyog portal, enabling content flagged through government directions to be automatically removed from its platforms without being reviewed by a human executive.

The incident took place in the afternoon when the front portion of the four-storey building came crashing down, according to a DFS officer. The DFS received a call regarding the collapse at 3.30 PM. Fire tenders have reached the spot. "Search and rescue operation is ongoing," the DFS officer told PTI. In the latest development, five to six people have been rushed to a nearby hospital as a major rescue operation gets underway. Heavy machinery, including JCB excavators, was spotted at the accident site. Speaking to PTI, Shahdara DCP Rajendra Prasad Meena said, “So far, around five to six people have been taken to the hospital. The rescue operation is still underway. How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
- Published
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.
"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

A video purportedly showing a resourceful monkey rescuing a dog from floodwaters circulated online in late September and early October 2026. 
The 10-second clip allegedly shows a rainy village scene featuring a monkey wading in water and pulling a dog to the top of a log.
For example, an X post (archived) featured the video with a Thai-language text caption translating to English as, "If we're gonna make it, we've gotta make it together, right?" That clip, shared Sept. 27, made the rounds at the same time Thai authorities were reporting about fatalities from flooding following an unusually heavy rainfall. (The same user posted longer, authentic-appearing videos allegedly showing snakes, dogs, puppies and a cow during flooding.)
That X post received millions of views, as did an Instagram post (archived) displaying the clip with the onscreen caption, "Viral: Monkey Grabs A Dog And Climbs Onto A Floating Log Amid Raging Floodwaters." Other users widely shared the video on Facebook (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived). Some specifically claimed a person recorded the video in Thailand.
Some commenters praised the monkey for its alleged act of kindness, while others said they believed someone created the clip using artificial intelligence.
In sum, the video was fake and bore signs indicating it was AI-generated, among those its precise 10-second duration, an inauthentic-sounding audio track and unnatural-looking video artifacts. 
Moreover, reverse image search results matching single frames from the video indicated the oldest post (archived) hosting it resided on the Thai-language Facebook page เรื่องร้อนสตอรี่, a title that means Hot Story in English. That post and others on the page were labeled "AI content."
We emailed the Facebook page's owner to ask whether they created the video with AI or shared it from someone else's post and will update this article if we receive further details.
Examining the video
The video exhibits natural-seeming camera movements and zooms, and realistic visuals of rain falling onto the water in a flooded village. At the beginning, the outline of the clip's frame faintly indicates the camera's point of view may be from behind a window frame, a car window or similar setup, providing the impression of realism.
The signs of fakery far outweigh any indicators of realism, however. For example, we downloaded the video and used Adobe Premiere video-editing software to determine the clip's exact duration. The clip runs at 24 frames per second and lasts exactly 10 seconds and zero addtional frames in length — a common AI-generated video duration. We didn't find a longer version of the clip that would support the alternative explanation that it might have been an authentic video trimmed down to a precise 10 seconds.
The audio track features the sound of falling rain, followed by unrealistic sounds of the dog plopping down on the log and making whining noises that don't appear to match the visuals. Also, at the moment of the plop, the dog's front right paw lands on a pile of debris that doesn't appear to move. (Bear in mind that anyone can add inauthentic audio to a video with authentic visuals, so fake audio alone does not automatically mean the whole video is fake.)
Perhaps one of the key indicators of AI generation or other visual fakery is visible in the animals' movements just before the monkey releases the dog. From the 5-second mark to the 6-second mark, the monkey appears to pick up the dog for the last time to fully situate it on the log. An unnatural video artifact appears at that moment — at about the 00:05:13 mark — when the dog's front right leg raises up and off of the log. For a single frame, the leg appears as a thinner, sharper representation of itself as the vertical black shape in the middle of the yellow circle in the montage below. The vertical black shape doesn't appear in the preceding or subsequent frames:
(Ches Vichet via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
On the subject of odd visuals, several blue objects appear to show up only after the camera zooms in to show the closer view of the two animals. For example, one small light-blue item resembling a hair tie appears to either surface or otherwise inexplicably appear on the left side of the debris pile just after the 7-second mark.
(Ches Vichet via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
AI detection tools and fake animal rescue videos
Scanning the video with AI detection tools produced inconsistent results. The tools we used included Hive's AI-generated & deepfake content detection, Nvidia's synthetic video detector, Pangram's AI image detector (screenshots only), Tencent's Zhuque AI image and video detector and ZeroGPT's AI video detector.
Snopes doesn't rely solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability. Instead, we consider the tools' results as individual data points among many when judging the authenticity of images, text and videos.
During our research process, we made note of numerous other videos allegedly showing animals rescuing other animals (or people) from water. Those clips generally exhibited more-obvious visual indicators of AI, such as inconsistent blurring and smoothness, that the monkey-saving-dog video didn't.
Also, we considered the possibility that the "rescue" may have been staged like other examples of fake animal rescue videos hosted online. Kerry Burton-Galley, a spokesperson for the Lady Freethinker organization, which states as its purpose to "end cruelty for all beings," told us by email that most staged animal rescue content involves humans seeming to rescue animals, adding "but it's certainly not unheard of for videos to feature two or more animals, including one animal apparently coming to another's aid." She continued:
AI-generated animal content is becoming increasingly troubling and will likely pose an even greater challenge as the technology advances. While no real animal is directly harmed in creating a fully AI-generated video, realistic fake rescue content can make it increasingly difficult for people to distinguish genuine rescues from fabricated ones. That can erode public trust and potentially affect donations and support for legitimate rescue organizations doing lifesaving work.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Life is remarkably selective. Life relies on many molecules with what is termed “handedness”—they’re chemically identical but are mirror images of each other. Most chemical reactions will make a 50-50 mix of the left- and right-handed forms of a chemical, but life uses only one of them. In fact, because of the differences between left- and right-handed chemicals, most of the key enzymes used by organisms will fail to work if they’re presented with chemicals that have the wrong handedness.
That poses a bit of a challenge for origin-of-life research, as we’re forced to explain how a world that may have started with an even mix of left- and right-handed chemicals produced organisms that only used one of them.
Today’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to two individuals, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who discovered chemical reactions could be biased, producing large excesses of one of the two forms of a chemical.
Chirality and life
The technical term for molecular handedness is “chirality,” and scientists replace left and right with dextro (D) and levo (L). But the ideas are largely the same. Your hands have all the same components—fingers and thumbs—organized in the same way. Yet if you point your thumb upward, the fingers curl in opposite directions, making one the mirror image of the other. Depending on the arrangements of the chemical bonds, many molecules can form similar mirror-image forms, with all the same parts oriented slightly differently in space.
(For the geekier among the readership: carbon atoms have four potential sites that can form bonds, spread evenly across the surface of the atom’s sphere. If each of those sites is linked to a different chemical, then swapping the chemicals located in any two of them can potentially change the way it’s arranged in 3D space.)
Amino acids come in both D and L forms, but all of life relies on just one of those.
Amino acids come in both D and L forms, but all of life relies on just one of those.
Credit:
Nobel Prize Foundation
This can really matter when it comes to enzymes, which typically latch onto chemicals using binding sites that are sculpted by evolution to fit only that chemical and its close relatives. Try to feed the enzyme the mirror-image version of that same chemical, and it will often fail to fit the binding site. Since life uses nothing but the D form of sugars, all of its enzymes are optimized to latch onto those, and many cannot interact at all with the L form.
There are two ways this could have happened. The first life may not have been as picky about the reactions it catalyzed and only evolved chirality preferences slowly. Or life could have evolved in an environment where one chiral form dominated. Or there was some combination of the two. But either of the latter two cases simply pushes the question back a bit: How could chemistry create an environment where one chiral form dominates?
From theory to practice
Over the years, there have been a number of ideas about how this might occur. Several of those trace back to a physicist, Frederick Charles Frank, who addressed this issue in a data-free, theory-focused paper. (It’s clear from the Nobel Prize Committee’s writing that, were Frank still alive, he might have shared in this award.) One option is that a catalyst with only a slight preference for forming a D or L molecule could, over time, produce a large excess of that form. Another is that a chiral reaction product could itself serve as a catalyst for forming more of the same form. Or the chiral reaction product could inhibit the formation of its mirrored form.
Many chemical reactions reach an equilibrium, finding a point where forward and reverse reactions occur at similar rates. If the reverse reaction is indifferent to chirality, but the forward one is influenced by one of the factors above, then time would allow this to create a large excess of one chiral form.
All of these were hypotheticals, however, until the researchers being honored got to work. Henri Kagan of the University of Paris-Sud also approached his work very theoretically, describing the factors that would be needed to drive reactions that favored a single chirality. But in several cases, he was able to go out and find actual chemical reactions that demonstrated his ideas mattered in the real world.
Kagan worked with a catalyst that was itself chiral. He found that, in a mix of L and D versions of his catalyst, one of the forms was much more active than the other. While the forms might be present at the same level, most of the actual catalysis was performed by just one of them. And, if it was used to catalyze a reaction that produced a chiral product, this difference could lead to much higher levels of a single chirality.
By the mid-1960s, Kagan had found three different reactions that could produce an excess of a single chiral form. Other researchers who followed up on his ideas showed that chiral catalysts could also be selectively activated or inhibited by the addition of non-chiral chemicals, allowing a finer degree of control that found its way into the production of pharmaceuticals.
Self catalysis
About a decade later, Tokyo University’s Kenzo Soai was working on reactions where one of the products of the reaction acted as a catalyst to boost the same reaction. Eventually, he found one that selected for chirality; one form of the reaction product would catalyze the formation of more molecules of the same chirality. He started the reaction with a slight excess of one form of catalyst and found that, after a single round of reactions, the excess in the catalyst had risen to 55 percent. Using that as a catalyst for a new round of reactions would enhance the excess further; after several rounds, 90 percent of the products were a single chirality.
Eventually, Soai found conditions where one product would not only catalyze the formation of more of the same form, but inhibit the formation of the opposite chirality. This allowed him to start with a tiny excess of a single chiral form (0.00005 percent more) and, after a few rounds of reactions, bring the excess to over 99 percent.
Others later found conditions where a similar reaction that reached an equilibrium of forward and back reactions would gradually lead to a single chiral form dominating.
There are three different aspects of this work that are worth celebrating. One is that it’s simply great science; people reasoned through the ways that an excess of one chiral form could emerge, and then others found ways to demonstrate that the behavior took place in the real world. A second is that it has immense practical applications. Many of our drugs work because they interact with proteins, where chirality often matters. And there are many examples of drugs where the wrong chiral form can be inactive or positively harmful. So finding new ways to catalyze the production of specific chiral forms has a lot of utility.
But the final thing comes back to the origin of life. None of these reactions were demonstrated with anything closely related to a biomolecule, so it’s not obvious that this particular work is directly relevant to the origin of life. But it does show that small excesses of some chiral forms—smaller than the 90 percent seen in this work, but still significant—may be common in the natural world.
The current thinking is that those small differences weren’t decisive, but did help push the emergence of life along a pathway that ultimately led to the exclusive chemistry we see now.

Trump’s plan to buy votes, briefly explained
Can Trump bribe his way out of a midterm disaster?
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to bribe his way out of a midterm disaster.
What’s happening? Over the weekend, Trump announced a plan to send $90 payments to more than 20 million Americans 65 years and older, drawing from a pool of money called the Medicare Improvement Fund.
Trump, in a post, described the payments as part of a strategy to “substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors” — but the money, a single nonrecurring payment set to go out this month, was reportedly already earmarked for other programs before Trump decided to redirect it.
Why now? Trump, facing a potentially catastrophic midterms for his party, has been looking for any way to turn out (Republican) voters — up to and including offering them cash, either implicitly or explicitly, in return for their support.
In the implicit category: these $90 payments and a smaller number of $500 Affordable Care Act refunds (fewer than 1 million) that began going out last week.
Much more explicitly, however, he’s also promising Americans $5,000 if they reelect Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has directly linked Medicare payments with the promised checks: “Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People,” he wrote in a post, “they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S. Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!”
Will it work? It’s hard to say for sure, but it feels unlikely: The Medicare payments are relatively small, while the ACA payments are going out to relatively few voters. Polling suggests that voters are not fans of the promised $5,000 checks, and even fewer believe that they’re going to happen (they’re almost certainly correct).
What else should I know? Direct payments to Americans — real or promised — are not the only way Trump is trying to sway the midterms in his favor. He’s also continuing to spend taxpayer dollars on a propagandistic ad campaign, which he personally directed.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
- Published
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.
The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.
But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.
Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.
Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.
However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.
In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.
"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.
"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.
"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."
The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.
Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

You couldn’t imagine a more ideal setting for “The Debut” than Alice Tully Hall on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, where it had its New York premiere Wednesday evening as part of the New York Film Festival.
The third feature film from writer-director Jesse Eisenberg, and follow-up to his Oscar-winning “A Real Pain,” is set in 1990 and follows Mona Friedman (Julianne Moore), a timid, browbeaten housewife in Central Jersey who disrupts her mind-numbing routine by auditioning for the role of the janitor in a community theater production of the musical “Nosy Neighbors.” There, she finds community among her castmates (Halle Bailey and Colton Ryan among them) and clashes with her imperious director (the inimitable Paul Giamatti), as she falls deeper and deeper into character. Eisenberg’s film garnered considerable laughs — and applause — from the theater-going crowd at its starry NYFF screening that saw Eisenberg, the cast, producer Emma Stone and even Claire Danes in attendance.
Eisenberg was born in Queens and grew up in East Brunswick, New Jersey, and said during a post-screening Q&A that he modeled Mona’s journey after “the community that I found” doing local theater, where “the shows were always secondary to the backstage family.”
Popular on Variety
“I’ve done community theater where the talent is just as good as Broadway talent, but they don’t feel this personal ambition to be center stage,” he explained, making it “so much sweeter than what we do.”
But Eisenberg confessed that the “tonally odd” film is, first and foremost, a monument to Moore, who also starred in Eisenberg’s directorial debut. He wrote the role specifically for her and sang the Oscar-winning actress’s praises to the New York crowd.
“If you didn’t know that beforehand, I imagine you can tell that now,” he offered. “Has there ever been a more perfect performance?”
Moore, who is getting plenty of Oscar buzz for her no-holds-barred performance, said she wanted to do another musical after “Dear Evan Hansen,” an experience she “loved” because it was “scary and fun.” She also was attracted to the script and the idea of inhabiting Eisenberg.
“I am in effect his avatar, and the fact that he put his experience in a middle-aged woman’s body is extraordinary,” Moore attested.
She continued: “This is a person who doesn’t feel like they fit into their life and is on the brink of change… What does it mean to step into something just because you have this desire? And where do you go from there?”
Moore said that Eisenberg’s script made Mona relatable to everyone since it “actualized this very human feeling of wanting something and not knowing what it is.”

Under regulatory scrutiny in India, social media giant Meta claims to have taken action against 5.3 Mn pieces of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in the first half (H1) of 2026. The social media giant also noted that more than 98% of this content was identified and addressed proactively before being reported. This comes as Meta has come under fire over its lax policies around taking down child sexual abuse content. Globally, the social media company said that it took down 33.2 Mn pieces of such content during the same timeframe, with a proactive detection rate exceeding 97%. Meanwhile, Meta also said that it has rolled out new AI-powered systems and upgraded its ad review frameworks across Facebook and Instagram in India to detect and take down CSAM. The social media juggernaut also said that it has introduced LLM-driven systems to identify “signposting” within ads to counter predators who advertise illicit material in ways that can evade automated detection. For context, signposting acts as a roadmap to guide and enable users to anticipate what happens next. Meta’s new “signpost” safeguards evaluate where an advertisement leads rather than solely analysing its visible content. Furthermore, the social media company has also deployed AI-driven sweeps to uncover missed CSAM material. It has also integrated “red-teaming” AI agents to probe its own defenses and strengthen detection mechanisms against banned users creating new accounts. It is pertinent to note that red teaming AI agents intentionally probe autonomous AI systems or chatbots to find security flaws and safety gaps before malicious actors do. Meta’s clampdown on CSAM comes as the IT ministry (MeitY) recently pulled up the social media giant over alleged circulation and promotion of CSAM. A BBC investigation earlier this year alleged that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale. The controversy resulted in Meta ultimately agreeing to report child safety matters directly to Indian authorities. It also faced summons from MeitY and an inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) over the matter. Previous reports also suggested that Meta could also lose its “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. This would force the company to face greater legal liability in cases of CSAM or other illegal content being posted on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

India will have its task cut out when it takes to the field against Russia in what will be the Blue Tigresses’ first-ever international appearance in the city of Kolkata.
India, ranked 69th in the world, faces 27th-ranked Russia at the Kishore Bharati Krirangan on October 8, before the teams meet again on October 11. The fixtures mark India’s return to international action following its sixth SAFF Women’s Championship title in June.
The squad carries a different look from the one that faced Russia at the Pink Ladies Cup last year. Head coach Crispin Chettri said its average age is 23, with the youngest players aged 19, and several have progressed from the Under-20 setup.

Quick Answer
Turn rough screen recordings into polished demos with tools that auto-zoom on clicks, follow and smooth the cursor, add clean framing, and highlight key actions. Options include Screen Studio, FocuSee, Screen Awesome, and ScreenCursor.
When you record a two-minute walkthrough of your app, for instance, a setting buried five menus deep, or a spreadsheet trick you are proud of, there is something that can leave you frustrated. You press play, and the cursor is dancing all around without highlighting what you actually wanted to show. Either the text is too small to read on a phone or the whole thing looks like security-camera footage of your desktop. The old-school way is to use a video editor, add zooms by hand, pan the camera to follow your cursor, and nudge keyframes for an hour. Thankfully, there is a newer batch of screen recorders that automatically do that part for you.
In this guide, we have covered four of them. They not only differ in price, platform, and functionality, but each one also has one detail that surprised me.
|  | Screen Studio | FocuSee | Screen Awesome | ScreenCursor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Works on | Mac only | Windows and Mac | Chrome (also Edge, Brave and similar) | Chrome (Mac, Windows, Linux) | 
| Price | $9/mo billed yearly, or $29/mo | Free trial, paid plans | Free | $49 one-time (early pricing) | 
| Best for | Maximum polish on a Mac | All-in-one AI extras | Privacy and zero cost | Pay-once simplicity | 
Table of Contents
Why do raw screen recordings look so rough?
When you use any standard screen recorder, like the one built into your OS, it captures pixels and nothing else. It has no idea what mattered. It doesn’t know if you clicked a tiny button that you want the viewers to look at. The result? You get a full-screen recording of everything, including your cursor wandering here and there. Viewers watch these videos on laptops and phones, and since the important part is not zoomed in or clearly shown, they will miss it. A better screen recording would be one where:
- Zoom is on the action so people can actually read what you click.
- A camera that follows your cursor instead of leaving viewers guessing.
- A cursor that glides rather than jitters.
- A clean frame, such as a gradient background and rounded corners.
With all of the above, your screen recording not only looks professional but also provides clear instructions for viewers.
Screen recorders with auto cursor follow and zoom
Here are some of the best screen recorders that you can use for automatic cursor follow and zoom.
Screen Studio: The one the others get compared to
If you are on Mac, then Screen Studio is one of the best options for screen recording with automatic cursor follow and zoom. When you’re recording using Screen Studio, it looks at what you did, like where you clicked, and zooms in on the moments that matter. Every zoom is balanced and animated automatically; you don’t have to worry about handling them. The best part is that you can choose between two styles: Classic zoom is the one you usually see in polished product videos. Then there is Loupe zoom, which is a magnifier-style alternative. If you want to zoom somewhere the app did not automatically add one, you can drop it onto the timeline and point it where you like. Notably, the cursor gets the same treatment. Shaky movement is smoothed out into a steady glide, and clicks get a soft ripple. Fast movements pick up motion blur so they look filmed rather than captured. You also have the option to change the cursor’s size and style later. Some of the notable features of Screen Studio are:
- Edit by transcript: Delete a sentence from the transcript, and it disappears from the video. Filler words and long pauses can be cleared in one pass.
- One recording, many shapes: Record once, then switch the aspect ratio between wide (16:9), square (1:1), and vertical (9:16). Zooms can be re-aimed, layouts rearranged, and captions moved to stay readable. You can also choose the “Reel mode” that shows where Instagram’s or TikTok’s interface would cover your video, so you’re in the grey area where your inputs get hidden.
- Hide the private stuff: If the recording shows an API key or email address, you can mask it after the recording is complete, and the mask blends into the interface around it.
- iPhone and iPad framing: Plug your iPhone or iPad into a USB cable, pick the device, and record. Screen Studio wraps the footage in a matching device frame.
FocuSee: The Windows-friendly all-rounder
FocuSee comes from the house of iMobie and is a screen recording tool that works on both Windows and Mac. This already makes it the practical choice for many people working on either OS. FocuSee’s auto zoom follows your clicks and even your typing. This tool adds a spotlight to highlight areas worth noticing, making it much easier for anyone following your instructions. You can also choose a “3D Motion” mode that adds tilt and perspective that follows your cursor, for a more cinematic look. The cursor can fade out when you are not actively using it or don’t need it and reappears when you do. Similar to other screen recording tools, you can swap the cursor style and click animations. There are a bunch of features that deserve to be highlighted.
- A built-in teleprompter: You can show your script on screen while recording with the option to adjust the font size, speed, and position. If you tend to forget the script midway, this alone might sell you.
- An annotation suite: You can add text, shapes, arrows, callouts, spotlights, and blur effects. Moreover, you can stack several layers to walk viewers through a tricky step, or blur out something sensitive.
- An AI avatar: This one is for those who are camera-shy or do not want their face in the video. FocuSee can create a digital presenter, or in simple words, an AI avatar. It is a niche feature, but a handy one for company tutorials.
- Smart cleanup: You can remove filler words and silence with just one click, and also enhance voice and reduce noise with just a button.
- Background fixes for your webcam: It can blur or replace a messy room behind you after recording without needing a green screen.
- Add Subtitles: FocuSee supports speech recognition in over 50 languages, with accuracy above 98%. You can add your own subtitles and make it easier for the follower to go through the steps.
Screen Awesome: Free, and it can’t upload your recordings
Screen Awesome is a different kind of tool. It’s actually a free Chrome extension built by a developer named Nitinbhai Viras. On one hand, most apps say “we respect your privacy” and simply ask you to take their word; Screen Awesome does things a bit differently. Screen Awesome points you at Chrome’s own permission screen and requests no access to any website. It is not allowed to contact any server. That means it cannot upload your recordings, even if it wanted to. The best part is that you can verify this yourself in about 30 seconds. Head over to chrome://extensions, find Screen Awesome, click Details, and look at the Site access line. According to the developer, it reads none. On the extension’s settings page, there is a button that jumps you straight there. On top of this security, you get this tool for absolutely free. Here are some features that set Screen Awesome apart:
- Auto-zoom to clicks: While recording a browser tab, Screen Awesome notes where you click. A virtual camera follows each click and pans between them. You have the option to preview it, turn it off, or export the file. This works for tab recording.
- Serious annotation tools: Arrows, pen, highlighter, shapes, text, speech bubbles, step counters, emoji stamps, and a blur that destroys the pixels rather than just smudging them. You can edit all of these marks.
- Product-shot framing: You can place a recording on a backdrop with rounded corners, a soft shadow, and an optional browser window around it, and also change its aspect ratio to 16:9, etc.
- Formats: You can export your recording in MP4, WebM, or an animated GIF.
- Webcam and voice: Screen Awesome lets you mix in your microphone and the tab’s audio, and even add a movable webcam bubble while recording if you want to show your face.
ScreenCursor: Pay once, and record in Chrome
ScreenCursor is another screen recording tool that works as a Chrome extension. However, its approach is the opposite of Screen Awesome’s. Notably, it does one thing and tries to do it well, which is turning clicks into camera moves with as little fuss as possible. When you hit the record button, ScreenCursor waits three seconds before it starts. That gap is deliberate, and it exists because Chrome shows its own “sharing your screen” bar while recording, and unfortunately it cannot be switched off. With this delay, you get the time to collapse the bar before the screen recording starts. Every click, drag, and keystroke gets zoomed in. Each zoom happens a beat before the action; this way, viewers are already looking at the right spot, then the camera holds steady and follows your cursor. ScreenCursor gives you the option to manually retime a zoom, push its depth in or out, switch the motion between snappy and gentle, or delete the zoom you don’t want. Here are some of the highlights of ScreenCursor:
- Zoom focus point: Right-click any zoom, drag a box over the part you want people to see, and the zoom shows exactly that. You can use this on recordings of desktop apps, since ScreenCursor can record your whole screen.

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal
- Published
According to the man who helped catch them, it was blind luck.
Sandpapergate, the scandal that engulfed Australia eight years ago, was blatant cheating played out in real time on live television to a global audience.
As the Aussies prepare for their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering controversy in Cape Town, the director of the TV coverage that day admits serendipity took down Steve Smith and co.
"The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke," Alvin Naicker, in charge of SuperSport's live broadcast from Newlands, tells BBC Sport.
Not just one fluke, but a series of them.
That the "leadership group" of the Australian team hatched their plan during the lunch break on that Saturday afternoon in March 2018; that an alert camera operator lingered on Cameron Bancroft when others would have turned their attention elsewhere; that the big-screen controller showed in the ground what was also being broadcast to millions around the world.
In understanding how Bancroft was rumbled, a little knowledge of how live cricket is shown on TV is helpful.
"Coverage of rugby and football is very coordinated. It's camera one and two, then when the ball is dead you tell the story with close-up shots," explains Naicker, a highly respected and popular figure in the TV industry with more than 30 years' experience.
"Because cricket has so much dead time, there is a lot more storytelling. There are between 80 and 100 people coming together and putting the story together in a matter of seconds, coordinated by the director."
Captain Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Bancroft later explained they cooked up the ball-tampering plot during lunch on the third day of the third Test.
Reverse-swing had been a key factor in the first two Tests of a bad-tempered series: Warner clashed with Quinton de Kock in the first Test in Durban, then Smith was involved in an altercation with Kagiso Rabada in the second.
Australia were exposed before the afternoon session was done, thanks to Naicker and his team. At the time, SuperSport were not on the lookout for cheating, despite the shenanigans of the first two Tests.
"No one mentioned anything to me," says Naicker. "The first Test in Durban spiralled out of control in terms of behaviour, then in Port Elizabeth for the second Test, there were still some fireworks going on. We still didn't understand."
Reports written live by ESPNCricinfo suggest the ball began reversing in the first hour after lunch, 35 overs into the South Africa second innings. In the 43rd over, Bancroft was caught in the act.
"The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft and he was shining the ball," says Naicker. "First it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm.
"When he threw the ball on, he put his hand in his pocket. The cameraman - and these are big, big lens cameras - he zoomed into his pocket. The slow-mo operator looked at it, spooled it back and forth, then zoomed in and could see the yellow spot."

  - Published19 hours ago
Bancroft's work on the ball was not shown live, but as a replay later in the over. Inside Newlands, the operator of the big screen – working independently from Naicker – showed the same footage.
"They take a feed from broadcast but they also have to insert their own graphics and commercialisation," says Naicker.
"Between deliveries they tend to stay with live play, then at the end of the over they go to their commercials or whatever in the stadium. It was quite fortunate that when we showed it, it was in between deliveries, not at the end of the over."
Bancroft would later admit he "panicked" when he saw himself on the big screen. Comically, he hid the sandpaper inside his trousers. SuperSport caught that, too.
"When Bancroft looked up at the screen and saw it, he removed it and put it in his jocks," says Naicker. "The cameraman recorded it. It still wasn't live, we played a replay."
Bancroft, with Smith by his side, was challenged by on-field umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong.
The opener turned out his pockets, revealing only a black bag for his sunglasses. The ball was not changed and Australia were not given a run penalty. Play continued, yet SuperSport were on to what had happened.
"Australia coach Darren Lehmann was on the walkie-talkie to 12th man Peter Handscomb, who went on to the field, then the umpires get involved," says Naicker.
"An entire team of cameramen played their part. There was one following the ball, one on Handscomb, one on Lehmann, one on Warner. They all told a story that I happened to put together with this great team of replay operators."
As for Naicker, there was no hesitation in airing what his team had captured, even with the realisation of the magnitude of what was unfolding.
"A lot of people who watch cricket on SuperSport will know we are quite brave in terms of being quite creative and editorially sound," he says.
"It was a natural instinct. It wasn't something I previewed with 10 other people to say 'What do you think, should we show it?' I just went for it."
The footage was pored over by Naicker's team of commentators, while his phone was "WhatsApping off the hook" with messages from around the world, asking him to show it again and again. Replays drew the attention of the third umpire, Englishman Ian Gould.
"He's got comms with me while I'm directing," says Naicker. "There was a moment when he asked me 'I think that's enough now, do you mind not showing it?'
"My response to him was 'I'm quite comfortable in what I'm doing in my job and I think you should do yours'."
When the day's play finally ended, Naicker and his team went to a bar and heard Bancroft and Smith confess in their news conference. Both men and Warner were sent home from the tour and handed lengthy bans. When he returned to Australia, Smith broke down in a tearful address to the press in Sydney.
"It became disheartening for us," says Naicker. "It started becoming emotional to see how they were feeling.
"The most difficult thing for me was to see Steve Smith shedding tears. That was not nice and never the intention. You have to have some emotion for those guys."
1 of 3
There was still a fourth and final Test to complete. Feelings were raw, and SuperSport's access to interviews from Australia was heavily restricted.
Naicker and his team faced allegations of bias, that they were somehow part of an orchestrated plot to take down the Australians. Now, with the Aussies back in town, Naicker maintains he would have pounced on the same "fluke" had it been South Africa caught cheating.
He also highlights the power of television. Bancroft and Australia were exposed mere moments after their act of cheating. TV viewers knew before the on-field match officials.
Naicker points to a conversation he had with Stuart Broad, who also faced tampering accusations for treading on the ball on a tour of South Africa in 2010 and is now building a post-playing career as a pundit.
"When you played the Broad footage in ultra-motion, it looked worse than it was," says Naicker. "He said he never realised how much control and power the TV crew has until he worked in the commentary box.
"I said that's what you have to remind your team-mates. You can't hide any more in international cricket. There are too many cameras and technology around."

Surface Laptop Ultra hands-on: A beautiful beast powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark
Yes, it's just a premium laptop. But it sure looks pretty.
When we first caught a glimpse of the Surface Laptop Ultra back in June, I was struck by how normal it seemed. Even though Microsoft claimed it was the most powerful Surface Laptop ever, it really looked like a straightforward MacBook Pro clone, even more so than the Surface Laptop (or the Laptop Studio, which nobody talks about anymore). There aren't any weird hinges or flashy Surface features — just pure premium laptop by the looks of it.
After spending a bit of time with it today, I can confirm that remains the case. At the same time, it feels better than any other Windows laptop I've held before. And given its $2,599 starting price, it damn well better be.
There's nothing ostentatious about the Surface Laptop Ultra, but for the AI developers who want a powerful and portable system that can hold up to 128GB of RAM, it could be their dream machine. Even before I got my hands on it, the Laptop Ultra exuded a sense of quality. Its aluminum case glowed amid the studio lights, its screen was surprisingly bright and its overall aesthetic was clean. Think of it like a sturdy and minimalist Volvo, compared to a flashy BMW or Audi.
Beyond just looking great, its keyboard has just the right amount of tactile feedback, something I've always appreciated about Microsoft's keyboards. It's massive haptic touchpad feels smooth and responsive. It's a heavy machine, coming in under 4.5 pounds, but that's par for the course with 16-inch workhorses. It's still lighter than Apple's 16-inch MacBook Pro, and it feels just as sturdy.
I've yet to see the Surface Laptop Ultra in action doing tons of AI work, but researchers I talked to at Microsoft's launch event seem particularly excited about it. Aidan Pinero, an AI researcher and Master's student at UCSC Silicon Valley, said he was excited to finally have a Windows system that could run large AI models. He's been jealous of his friends running MacBook Pros with 128GB of RAM, and he's looking forward to having the same amount of flexibility with Windows thanks to NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform.
NVIDIA's graphical prowess also helps the Surface Laptop Ultra to be a capable gaming system. It ran Gears of War: E-Day smoothly at slightly more than 1080p, and crucially, it did so while it was both connected to power and purely on battery. Microsoft representatives say that's one of the major benefits of RTX Spark: Since it's based on an Arm CPU, it's easier to guarantee a certain level of performance on battery.
The Surface Laptop Ultra has all of the ports you'd want on a premium laptop, including multiple USB-C connections, HDMI and a full-sized SD card slot. But the most interesting port was its slightly offset USB-C connection, which is meant specifically for Microsoft's custom magnetic USB-C cable. It replaces the proprietary Surface Connector, but essentially works the same way: The cable automatically latches onto the USB-C port when it's nearby.
That could hopefully save your laptop if you trip on the cable while it's plugged in. And since the actual charging connection is still just USB-C, you can juice up the Surface Laptop Ultra with any standard USB-C charging cable on that port. The magnetic cable won't work with any other USB-C laptops, a Microsoft rep points out, but you could flip it around on the Surface Laptop's power adapter to get a standard USB-C cable.
If it's not obvious from the Surface Laptop Ultra's $2,599 price and AI focus, this isn't really a system meant for average computer users. And the same could be said of all of the upcoming RTX Spark machines. Microsoft highlighted hybrid intelligence — i.e. using both local and cloud-based AI tools — at its San Francisco event today, something only AI developers will really care about.
While Microsoft and NVIDIA's CEO's patted each other on the back for reinventing PCs, it really seems like they're responding to the sea change that started six years ago with Apple Silicon. RTX Spark is built on Arm processors, relies on fast unified memory and also bundles powerful NPU and GPU hardware, all like Apple's latest processors.
But so far, the benefits around RTX Spark and the Surface Laptop Ultra are really meant for developers and power users, whereas Apple Silicon delivered immediate benefits for everyone buying a new Mac. Perhaps that's something we'll see trickle down from high-end RTX Spark systems, but who knows how long that will take.

Elon Musk blames Starlink hurdles in India on ‘monopolistic chokeholds’
Musk said Starlink is being blocked by “certain oligarchs” in India seeking to maintain a “monopolistic chokehold” on people.
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk on Wednesday alleged that Starlink was being “blocked by certain oligarchs” in India to protect their “monopolistic chokehold” over the country, as the satellite internet company continues to await final clearances to begin commercial services.
Responding to a post arguing that India needs Starlink to bridge connectivity gaps in underserved areas, Musk said: “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!”
A mail to the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) did not elicit a response till the time of going to press.
Also Read | Starlink built India setup to meet security norms, says SpaceX executive; awaits nod
Starlink, owned by Musk’s SpaceX, provides broadband internet using a constellation of low-Earth orbit satellites, allowing connectivity in areas where mobile networks can be difficult to reach. Starlink has received a government licence to provide satellite communication services in India, along with Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications. However, the companies still require spectrum allocation and security clearances before commercial services can begin. Starlink is also awaiting other regulatory approvals, including foreign investment-related clearances.
Starlink has partnered with Bharti Airtel in India. In March 2025, Airtel announced an agreement with SpaceX to explore bringing Starlink services to its customers, including the possibility of selling Starlink equipment through Airtel stores and offering the service to business customers. The two companies also agreed to explore using Starlink to connect communities, schools and health centres in rural areas, and using Airtel’s ground network infrastructure to support Starlink’s operations.

Musk’s post came on the same day that Lauren Dreyer, vice-president of Starlink Business Operations at SpaceX, said at the India Mobile Congress in New Delhi that the company had built its India operations around the country’s security requirements.
“We’ve built our Starlink operations specifically for India in recognition of Indian security requirements and other regulations, establishing controls at every layer for India and keeping India user data within India,” she said. Dreyer said Starlink had already established 20 gateway sites comprising hundreds of antennas and was ready to begin operations.
“We are ready to serve in India, once India is ready,” she said, adding that Starlink had been working with Indian regulators, operators and industry for the past five years. She also said the company could help address the “last mile” connectivity challenge, with people able to “connect within minutes, and not years”.
